Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 1–2 (part 1 of 2):

Page 147

Surat Ta-Ha

It is also called Surat al-Kalim, as al-Sakhawi mentioned in Jamal al-Qurra'. It is Meccan, as Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with them both. Some scholars excepted from it the verse of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And be patient over what they say﴾, and so on.

Al-Jalal al-Suyuti said: "It should be excepted that another verse, for al-Bazzar and Abu Ya'la narrated from Abu Rafi' who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) hosted a guest and sent me to a Jewish man to say: 'Lend me flour until the new moon of Rajab.' He said: 'No, unless you give a pledge.' So I came to the Prophet, peace be upon him, and informed him. He said: 'Indeed, by Allah, I am trustworthy in the heavens and trustworthy on the earth. If he had lent it to me or sold it to me, I would have paid it back. Go and take my armour to him as a pledge.' But I had not left his presence when this verse was revealed: ﴿Do not extend your eyes toward what We have given to pairs of them﴾, and so on." End of quotation.

Perhaps what was narrated from the two rabbis (Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr) regarding the exception of what has been mentioned is based on the majority of it. Its verses, as al-Dani said, are one hundred and forty according to the Syrian count, one hundred and thirty-five according to the Kufan count, four according to the Hijazi count, and two according to the Basran count. The order of its placement, as mentioned by al-Jalal, is that when Allah the Glorified mentioned in Surat Maryam several stories of the prophets, peace be upon them, some of them extensive, such as the story of Zakariyya, Yahya and 'Isa, peace be upon them, some of them between brief and extensive, such as the story of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and some of them concise and summarized, such as the story of Musa, peace be upon him, and He alluded to the rest of the prophets, peace be upon them, in general terms, He, may His majesty be exalted, mentioned in this surah the detailed account of the story of Musa, peace be upon him, which He had summarized there. He covered it to the utmost extent of comprehensiveness and expanded it in the most eloquent expansion. Then He, mighty is His affair, alluded to the detailed account of the story of Adam, peace be upon him, of which only the mention of his name had occurred in Maryam. Then He, majestic is His majesty, included in Surat al-Anbiya' the remainder of the stories of those whose stories were not mentioned in Maryam, such as Nuh, Lut, Dawud, Sulayman, Ayyub, al-Yasa', Dhu'l-Kifl and Dhu'l-Nun, peace be upon them. In it were also alluded to, in brief, the stories of those whose stories were mentioned only by allusion, such as Musa, Harun and Isma'il. It was mentioned right after Maryam so that the two surahs would be like counterparts, and the story of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was expanded in full in what pertains to him with his people, and his situation with his father was not mentioned except by allusion, just as in Surat Maryam his situation with his people was mentioned by allusion and with his father in detail. To what has been mentioned is added the commonality of this surah and Surat Maryam in beginning with the disjointed letters. It has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Jabir ibn Zayd, may Allah be pleased with them both, that Ta-Ha was revealed after Surat Maryam. The connection between the beginning of this one and the end of that one is that He, glorified is He, mentioned there the facilitation of the Qur'an in the tongue of the Messenger, peace be upon him, justified by giving good news to the God-fearing and warning to the obstinate; and here He mentioned what contains a kind of emphasis on that. And narrations came indicating its excellence further.

Al-Darimi, Ibn Khuzayma in al-Tawhid, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab and others narrated from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with them, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah, blessed and exalted, recited Ta-Ha and Ya-Sin two thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth. When the angels heard the Qur'an, they said: 'Blessed is the nation upon which this is sent down, blessed are the bodies that carry this, and blessed are the tongues that speak this.'" Al-Daylami narrated from Anas, traced to the Prophet, something similar.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Umama, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Every Qur'an is lifted from the people of Paradise, so they recite nothing from it except Surat Ta-Ha and Ya-Sin, for they recite these two in Paradise," along with other narrations.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Ta-Ha﴾. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Hafs and Ya'qub emphasized it (pronounced with heavy ta and ha) according to the original, and this is one of the two narrations from Qalun and Warsh; the other narration is that both emphasized the ta and inclined the ha, and this is what is narrated from Abu 'Amr. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr inclined both letters. Perhaps the inclination of the ta, despite it being among the letters of elevation (isti'la'), and elevation prevents inclination, since it descends for the purpose of harmony. These are among the disjointed letters with which the noble surahs open, according to one of the two narrations from Mujahid. Indeed, it was said that this is the case according to the majority of the precise scholars. Al-Suddi said: the meaning is "O so-and-so." It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, in the narration of a group from him, and from al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, 'Ata', 'Ikrima, and it is the other narration from Mujahid, that the meaning is "O man." They differed: it was said that it is so in Nabataean, it was said in Abyssinian, it was said in Hebrew, and it was said in Syriac.

It was said: in the dialect of 'Akal, and it was said: in the dialect of 'Akk. This was narrated from al-Kalbi, who said: "If I said to 'Akk, 'O man,' he would not answer until you say: 'Ta-ha.'" Al-Tabari cited in this regard the verse of Mutammim ibn Nuwayra:

I called "Ta-ha" in the battle, but he did not answer, so I feared for him that he might be a fugitive.

And the verse of another:

Indeed foolishness, "Ta-ha," is among your dispositions;
may Allah not bless the wretched people.

Ibn al-Anbari said: The language of Quraysh agreed with that language in this, because Allah did not address His Prophet (ﷺ) in any tongue other than the tongue of Quraysh. It is not hidden that the question of whether something other than the dialect of Quraysh from the dialects of the Arabs occurs in the Qur'an is a matter of disagreement, and the discussion on it has been expounded in al-Itqan, and the correct view is that it occurs. Al-Zamakhshari guessed about 'Akk, saying: "Perhaps 'Akk modified 'ya hadha,' as though in their dialect they converted the ya into ta, so they said 'ya-ta' and abbreviated this and confined themselves to ha." Abu Hayyan criticized him, saying: there is no occurrence in the language of the Arabs of converting ya, which is for calling, into ta, and likewise the omission of the demonstrative in the vocative while retaining the particle of alerting; no grammarian has said that. It was mentioned regarding the last verse that if it is sound, then "ta-ha" in it is an oath by the disjointed letters, or the name of the surah, on the basis that it is Islamic poetry, like his saying ﴿Ha-Mim, they will not be helped﴾.

It was objected that this is a remote possibility, and it is so in the example as well. Al-Nasa'i narrated it traced to the Prophet, and the wording of the report is: "When the enemy meets you, let your slogan be Ha-Mim, they will not be helped." There is no indication in its context of that. It is possible that "la yunsaruna" is a new sentence, and the slogan is merely the pronouncement of Ha-Mim alone, as if it were said: what happens if our slogan is that? It is said: they will not be helped. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it is an oath which Allah swore by, and it is one of His names, glorified is He. And from Abu Ja'far that it is one of the names of the Prophet (ﷺ).

A group, among them Abu Hanifa, al-Hasan, 'Ikrima and Warsh, read ﴿Ta-He﴾ with a fatha on the ta and a sukun on the ha, like "bal." It was said: its meaning is also "O man." It was said: it is a command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to tread the earth with his two feet, for he, peace be upon him, when he prayed would stand on one foot. This is as narrated from al-Rabi' ibn Anas: "When he prayed he stood on one leg, so Allah the Exalted revealed Ta-Ha," and so on. Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face: when the revelation came to the Prophet (ﷺ), ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾, ﴿Stand [in prayer] the night, except a little﴾, he stood the whole night until his feet swelled, so he began to raise one foot and place the other, so Jibril, peace be upon him, descended to him and said, "Ta-Ha," and the verse.

The original is "ta' " (ṭa'), so the hamza was changed to ha, as they said in "iyyaka," "araqta," "naka hayyaka," "haraqtu," and "lahanaka." Or the hamza in its past and present verb forms was changed to alif, as in the verse of al-Farazdaq:

The camels departed with Maslama in the evening; so graze, O Fazara, may the pasture not be pleasant for you.

And as they said of sa'ala: sala. In the imperative it was deleted because it is final-weak, and the ha of pause (ha' al-sakt) was added to it, and it is necessarily so in such a case, in both writing and pausing. It sometimes makes continuation take the place of pause, so it remains in pronunciation. Some allowed that the original of "Ta-ha" in the famous recitation is "tahha," with "ta" being an imperative addressed to him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to tread the earth with his two feet, and "ha" is a feminine pronoun in the position of the object, referring to the earth even though no prior mention of it has occurred. It was objected that if it were so, the two alifs would not have been dropped from it, and the orthography of the Mushaf, though it is not regular, has as its basis conformity with analogy, so one does not depart from it without a compelling reason. This alif is not in a noun, nor in the middle as in "al-harth" and the like, so as to be deleted, especially since its deletion would cause confusion, so it is not permitted, as detailed in the chapter on orthography in al-Tashil.

This was also objected against interpreting it as "ya rajul" and the like. It was said: the explanation of this according to this original is clear, and from it another explanation of the reading of Abu Hanifa and those with him may be known: that one may say he suffices from "ta'" with a moving ta' and from "ha" the pronoun with ha, then referred to both by their names, so "ha" is not a pronoun but is like the qaf in the verse:

I said to her, "Stop," and she said, "Qaf."

It was also objected that according to this it should not be that the form of the named is written, but the form of the name. It was answered that the writing of names with the forms of what they denote is a matter specific to the letters of spelling. It was objected that what has been mentioned does not cut off the source of the objection, for if it were so the two letters would be separated in writing, written thus: ta ha. If it is said that the orthography of the Mushaf is not regular, it is said against it what has been said, and the truth is that the claim that the orthography of the Mushaf is not regular is very strong, and what is said against it is not relied upon. What is authentically transmitted from the early generations is accepted, and the lack of conformity with analogy does not discredit it, even if conformity is the basis.

It has been narrated from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and al-Rabi' ibn Anas, that they both explained "Ta-Ha" as "Tread the earth with your two feet, O Muhammad." I have not found any criticism in the narration. And Allah knows best.

Regarding its grammatical analysis, there is disagreement according to the disagreement over its meaning. According to what is transmitted from the majority, that its meaning is a group of letters of the alphabet recited in the manner of enumeration, with which the surah opens, it has no place in grammatical analysis. Likewise what follows it, the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿We did not send down to you the Qur'an that you be distressed﴾, for it is a resumptive statement brought to console him, peace be upon him, for the hardship he suffered from the polytheists, for distress is common in that meaning. From it is the proverb "More wretched than a colt's trainer," and the saying of the poet:

The one of intellect is distressed in his delight by his intellect, and the one of ignorance in distress enjoys.

That is: We did not send it down to you that you should exhaust yourself by exaggerating in enduring hardships in dealing with the stubborn and disputing with the tyrants, and excessive regret over their disbelief in it, and grief over their not believing in it, as in His saying, mighty is His affair: ﴿So perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over their footsteps﴾, and so on. Rather, it is so that you may convey and remind, and you have done so; so there is no blame on you if they do not believe after that. Or it is to turn him, peace be upon him, away from the excess in striving in worship in which he was, as you have heard in what Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face. That is: We did not send it down to you so that you would exhaust yourself by ruining your soul and burdening it with arduous exercises and crushing hardships, and you were sent only with the tolerant, easy monotheism. Muqatil said: "Abu Jahl, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and al-Mut'im said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when they saw the abundance of his worship: 'You are indeed wretched by abandoning our religion, and the Qur'an was sent down to you to make you wretched by it.' So Allah the Exalted refuted them by saying: We did not send it down to you for what they said."

The word "shaqa'" in their speech may be understood in its literal meaning, which is the opposite of happiness, and its use in the speech of Allah the Exalted is by way of mushakala (matching). Or it may be that what is meant by it is the Qur'an, by interpreting it as what is challenged by it, of the kind of these letters.

It was permitted that its place be in the nominative case as the subject of a nominal sentence, and the sentence after it is its predicate, and the apparent, namely "the Qur'an," has been placed in the position of

Page 150

the connecting pronoun for a subtle point: that the Qur'an is a mercy in which one finds rest, so how could it descend for wretchedness? It was said: the predicate is omitted. It was also said: it is a predicate of an omitted subject. On both views the sentence is resumptive (mustaʼnafah). It was permitted that its position be accusative by implying "recite" (utlu). It was also said: it is a divine oath from which the particle of oath was omitted, so it took the accusative through a hidden verb, like the saying of the poet: "Indeed, upon Allah it is binding that you swear allegiance." It was permitted that its position be genitive by estimating the particle of oath, like the saying: "from a direction where Kulayb's fingers pointed with palms (a sign)." The sentence after it, on the estimate that an oath is intended, is the answer to the oath.

These possibilities were permitted on the assumption that the intended meaning is the surah. The question of connecting the sentence, on the assumption that it is initial and declarative, if the Qur'an is specific to this surah by way of its definiteness being a specific, present reference, is evident. And if it is general, then the connection is through its inclusiveness of the subject, as is said in such a case as: "Zayd is an excellent man."

Some scholars prohibited the intention of the surah absolutely, since the mushafs agree on mentioning a surah in the heading as "Surat Ta-Ha," and then the construction would be like "the human of Zayd," and they have ruled it ugly. But there is a discussion here that is hardly hidden even to the beasts of the herd. Some scholars held that it is intended on the estimate that the predicate is the sentence after "He said" (qala): because the negation that the descent of the Qur'an is for wretchedness requires that wretchedness occur as a consequence of its descent, definitely, either in reality, as when wretchedness means toil, or according to the claim of the disbelievers, as when it means the opposite of happiness. There is no doubt that this is conceivable only in the descent of what was sent down previously. As for the descent of the noble surah, it is not something by which the prior wretchedness could be consequent, so that it would take up the negation of it. As for the connection through the Qur'an being identical with the surah, it is clear; and as for the connection through inclusion, its outcome would be to say: "This surah—We did not send down the Qur'an which includes it, that you might be wretched." It is not hidden that making it the predicate of something, while the descent of it has no bearing at all on prior wretchedness, is not fitting to the dignity of revelation. End of quotation. Yet it is not without merit.

According to what was narrated from Abu Ja'far, that it is one of the names of the Prophet (ﷺ), it would be a vocative, and its rule is well known, and the sentence is the answer to the vocative. Its position, according to what Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from al-Hibr, that it is an oath which Allah swore by, and it is one of His names—His names are blessed—is accusative or genitive, as you have heard just now.

According to what was narrated from the Commander of the Faithful, may Allah honor his face, and al-Rabi', it would be a verbal sentence, and you have already had the detail of that. The sentence after it is resumptive, either grammatically resumptive or explanatory, as if it were said: "Why do we tread on it?" So it was said: "We did not send down the Qur'an upon you that you might be wretched." Talha recited "ma nazzala ʿalayka al-Qur'an" with the verb doubled and in the passive, attributing it to the Qur'an.

It was objected that what has been mentioned does not cut off the source of the objection, for if it were so the two letters would be separated in writing, written thus: ta ha. If it is said that the orthography of the Mushaf is not regular, it is said against it what has been said, and the truth is that the claim that the orthography of the Mushaf is not regular is very strong, and what is said against it is not relied upon. What is authentically transmitted from the early generations is accepted, and the lack of conformity with analogy does not discredit it, even if conformity is the basis.

It has been narrated from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and al-Rabi' ibn Anas, that they both explained "Ta-Ha" as "Tread the earth with your two feet, O Muhammad." I have not found any criticism in the narration. And Allah knows best.

Regarding its grammatical analysis, there is disagreement according to the disagreement over its meaning. According to what is transmitted from the majority, that its meaning is a group of letters of the alphabet recited in the manner of enumeration, with which the surah opens, it has no place in grammatical analysis. Likewise what follows it, the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿We did not send down to you the Qur'an that you be distressed﴾, for it is a resumptive statement brought to console him, peace be upon him, for the hardship he suffered from the polytheists, for distress is common in that meaning. From it is the proverb "More wretched than a colt's trainer," and the saying of the poet:

The one of intellect is distressed in his delight by his intellect, and the one of ignorance in distress enjoys.

That is: We did not send it down to you that you should exhaust yourself by exaggerating in enduring hardships in dealing with the stubborn and disputing with the tyrants, and excessive regret over their disbelief in it, and grief over their not believing in it, as in His saying, mighty is His affair: ﴿So perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over their footsteps﴾, and so on. Rather, it is so that you may convey and remind, and you have done so; so there is no blame on you if they do not believe after that. Or it is to turn him, peace be upon him, away from the excess in striving in worship in which he was, as you have heard in what Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face. That is: We did not send it down to you so that you would exhaust yourself by ruining your soul and burdening it with arduous exercises and crushing hardships, and you were sent only with the tolerant, easy monotheism. Muqatil said: "Abu Jahl, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and al-Mut'im said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when they saw the abundance of his worship: 'You are indeed wretched by abandoning our religion, and the Qur'an was sent down to you to make you wretched by it.' So Allah the Exalted refuted them by saying: We did not send it down to you for what they said."

The word "shaqa'" in their speech may be understood in its literal meaning, which is the opposite of happiness, and its use in the speech of Allah the Exalted is by way of mushakala (matching). Or it may be that what is meant by it is the Qur'an, by interpreting it as what is challenged by it, of the kind of these letters.

It was permitted that its place be in the nominative case as the subject of a nominal sentence, and the sentence after it is its predicate, and the apparent, namely "the Qur'an," has been placed in the position of

Page 150

the connecting pronoun for a subtle point: that the Qur'an is a mercy in which one finds rest, so how could it descend for wretchedness? It was said: the predicate is omitted. It was also said: it is a predicate of an omitted subject. On both views the sentence is resumptive (mustaʼnafah). It was permitted that its position be accusative by implying "recite" (utlu). It was also said: it is a divine oath from which the particle of oath was omitted, so it took the accusative through a hidden verb, like the saying of the poet: "Indeed, upon Allah it is binding that you swear allegiance." It was permitted that its position be genitive by estimating the particle of oath, like the saying: "from a direction where Kulayb's fingers pointed with palms (a sign)." The sentence after it, on the estimate that an oath is intended, is the answer to the oath.

These possibilities were permitted on the assumption that the intended meaning is the surah. The question of connecting the sentence, on the assumption that it is initial and declarative, if the Qur'an is specific to this surah by way of its definiteness being a specific, present reference, is evident. And if it is general, then the connection is through its inclusiveness of the subject, as is said in such a case as: "Zayd is an excellent man."

Some scholars prohibited the intention of the surah absolutely, since the mushafs agree on mentioning a surah in the heading as "Surat Ta-Ha," and then the construction would be like "the human of Zayd," and they have ruled it ugly. But there is a discussion here that is hardly hidden even to the beasts of the herd. Some scholars held that it is intended on the estimate that the predicate is the sentence after "He said" (qala): because the negation that the descent of the Qur'an is for wretchedness requires that wretchedness occur as a consequence of its descent, definitely, either in reality, as when wretchedness means toil, or according to the claim of the disbelievers, as when it means the opposite of happiness. There is no doubt that this is conceivable only in the descent of what was sent down previously. As for the descent of the noble surah, it is not something by which the prior wretchedness could be consequent, so that it would take up the negation of it. As for the connection through the Qur'an being identical with the surah, it is clear; and as for the connection through inclusion, its outcome would be to say: "This surah—We did not send down the Qur'an which includes it, that you might be wretched." It is not hidden that making it the predicate of something, while the descent of it has no bearing at all on prior wretchedness, is not fitting to the dignity of revelation. End of quotation. Yet it is not without merit.

According to what was narrated from Abu Ja'far, that it is one of the names of the Prophet (ﷺ), it would be a vocative, and its rule is well known, and the sentence is the answer to the vocative. Its position, according to what Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from al-Hibr, that it is an oath which Allah swore by, and it is one of His names—His names are blessed—is accusative or genitive, as you have heard just now.

According to what was narrated from the Commander of the Faithful, may Allah honor his face, and al-Rabi', it would be a verbal sentence, and you have already had the detail of that. The sentence after it is resumptive, either grammatically resumptive or explanatory, as if it were said: "Why do we tread on it?" So it was said: "We did not send down the Qur'an upon you that you might be wretched." Talha recited "ma nazzala ʿalayka al-Qur'an" with the verb doubled and in the passive, attributing it to the Qur'an.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 3:

﴿Except as a reminder﴾ is in the accusative as an exceptive of disconnected type (istithna' munqati'), meaning: We did not send it down to distress you, but as a reminder ﴿for him who fears﴾, i.e., for one whose nature is to fear God Exalted and to be affected by warning, due to the tenderness of his heart and the softness of his disposition; or for one whom God Exalted knows will fear when warned. The prepositional phrase (al-jar wa-al-majrur) is connected to "reminder" or to an elided adjective describing it. The one who fears is singled out for mention even though the Qur'an is a reminder for all people, because others are treated as if they did not exist, since he is the one who benefits from it.

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that ﴿reminder﴾ (tadhkirah) be an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) for "We sent down" (anzalna), and it is in the accusative because the conditions are gathered, unlike the first object, since the agent is not unified in it. The well-known view of the majority is that its fulfilment of the conditions is required for the accusative, and therefore it is in the genitive here. It is permissible for the cause to be multiple without a conjunction or apposition when the direction of the action differs, as here, since it is evident that the second is a clear object and the first is a prepositional phrase. Likewise when they are unified and one of the two causes is a cause of the verb while the other is a cause of it after its own causation, as in "I honoured him because he is a stranger, hoping for reward," or when the second cause is a cause of the first cause, as in "God Exalted does not punish the penitent, because of His forgiveness of him for his Islam." So what is said against it, that it is not permissible for the cause to be multiple without following, is not accepted.

In al-Kashf it is said that the meaning on this aspect is: We did not send the Qur'an down upon you so that you bear its hardships and toils, except so that it might be a reminder. Its essence is that it is like "I struck you for discipline only out of compassion," and the meaning returns to: I disciplined you with striking only for compassion. Likewise the meaning here: We did not make you wretched by sending down the Qur'an, except for reminder. Its essence: Be content with what you have borne of the toils of conveying, and do not exhaust your body, for in that is sufficient delivery. End of quotation. It has been objected to the view of making it like "I struck you for discipline only out of compassion" that it requires that there be between the two causes a connection of causation and caused, necessarily, as in the example mentioned; and in your saying, "I did not rebuke him harshly so that he would be hurt, except to deter others," the discipline in the first is caused by compassion, and the hurting in the second is a cause for deterring others. And between wretchedness and reminder there is an evident contrast, and it does not help to mean by it fatigue in general, which is compatible with reminder, because it is evident that there is no connection between them of the causation and caused described; it would be conceivable only if it were said, in place of "except as a reminder," "except to increase your reward," for the reward is in proportion to the toil, as in the hadith. End of quotation.

Perhaps the one who says this denies that the connection described must exist between the two causes, or claims that it is realised between them in the verse, on the basis that the reminder, that is the warning, is a cause of toil, as the commentator's words in the last summary indicate: "Be content with what you have borne of the toils of conveying," and so on. The meaning of the verse on this aspect was obscure to Ibn al-Munir, who said: "In it there is remoteness, because then wretchedness would be the cause of the revelation, even if the lam is not causal; and if it were for becoming (lil-sayrurah), for example, there would be nothing in it of what God Exalted's custom has been with His Prophet (ﷺ) of forbidding him from wretchedness and grief over the disbelievers and tightness of chest because of them. And it seems that the content of the verse contradicts His saying: ﴿So let there be no discomfort in your breast﴾, ﴿Perhaps you would destroy yourself over their traces﴾." End of quotation. And you know, after understanding the intended meaning, that there is no contradiction. Yes, this aspect is remote, and that the verse is like "I struck you for discipline only out of compassion" is something that taste itself bears witness to. It is permissible that it be a state (hal) from the kaf (of "you") or from "the Qur'an," and the exception is then "disengaged" (mufarragh), and the verbal noun is interpreted as an adjective, or it is intended for emphasis.

Al-Hufi permitted that it be a substitute (badal) from "the Qur'an." And al-Zajjaj permitted that it be a substitute from the position of "to be wretched" (li-tashqa), because exception from a non-affirmative sentence permits substitution in it. It has been objected that this is when the exception is connected, that is, when the excepted item is of the same genus as what it is excepted from; and substitution then is partitive substitution (badaliyyah al-b'diyyah) according to the well-known view, and it was said: total substitution from the total. It is not hidden that the realisation of this between reminder and wretchedness does not hold. The claim of substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal) in such a case, to validate substitution here on the basis that reminder includes toil, is something none of the grammarians has said.

Considering it, for this inclusion, to be of the genus of wretchedness, so that it is as if united with it, does not make the exception connected, as has been said; and you have heard its condition. In sum, this aspect is not the sound one, and Abu 'Ali objected to it against al-Zajjaj. He also permitted that it be an object of purpose for "We sent down," with "so that you be wretched" being a stable adverbial phrase in the position of an adjective for "the Qur'an," meaning: We did not send down the Qur'an that is present or sent down for your toil, except as a reminder. In this there is the omission of the complement joined with lam, and the relative pronoun is elided along with part of its clause, which some grammarians have rejected; and that ʼal is the definite article is contrary to what is apparent. It was said: it is in the accusative as a verbal noun for an elided verb, meaning: "But we reminded him with it as a reminder."

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿a revelation﴾ (tanzil). "Thus" means: He sent it down as a revelation. The clause is a new, independent sentence that confirms what precedes it.

It was also said that it relates to what the exceptive clause (al-jumla al-istithna'iyya) conveys, since it implies that one might say: "We sent it down as a reminder." The first view, however, is more suitable to what follows it because of the shift of person (iltifat).

It was also said that it is in the accusative as a praise (al-madh) and specification (al-ikhtisas).

It was said that it is governed by ﴿yakhsha﴾ (fears) as its object. Abu Hayyan judged both of these views unlikely, and he regarded the second as extremely remote, because ﴿yakhsha﴾ is the final word of the verse (ra's ayah), so it is not suitable for ﴿tanzilan﴾ to be its object. It was also objected that linking fear and dread and similar states to the bare fact of revelation is not usual. Yes, such a link has been made with some parts of it that contain warning and the like, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The hypocrites fear that a surah will be sent down against them, informing them of what is in their hearts﴾.

You know that the meaning on this view is: "[It is] only a reminder for one who fears," [meaning] the thing sent down from the All-Mighty, the Subduer. This is something free of any defect, and the matter of its lack of being usual is minor. It was also said that it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿tadhkiratan﴾ (a reminder), on the basis that it is a circumstantial state (hal) of the kaf (the pronoun), or of ﴿al-Qur'an﴾, as was previously reported, and this is a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal). Abu Hayyan criticised it by saying that making the verbal noun a circumstantial state is not a regular practice. Even so, there is a subtle difficulty here that is not hidden. Substitution from it is also not permitted on the assumption that it is an object of purpose (mafʿul lahu) for ﴿anzalna﴾ (We sent down), whether in wording or in meaning, because the substitute is the intended element, so the meaning would become "We sent it down for the sake of revelation." This involves explaining a thing by itself, if ''inzal'' and ''tanzil'' have the same meaning by linguistic convention, or by its type if ''inzal'' is general and ''tanzil'' is specific to the gradual [mode]. Both are impermissible.

Ibn 'Abla read ﴿tanzilu﴾ with a nominative (raf') ending, on the basis that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "It is a revelation" ﴿from the One who created the earth and the heavens above﴾. The phrase ﴿mimman khalaqa﴾ is linked to ﴿tanzil﴾. It was also permitted that it be linked to a hidden verb, which would be an attribute of it, emphasising by the added genitive the inherent grandeur of its indefiniteness. The attribution of the revelation to the relative pronoun is by way of a shift to the third person, after the attribution of the sending down to the plural of majesty (nun al-'azama), in order to show His grandeur, Exalted is His majesty, in terms of His acts and attributes, following the explanation of these in terms of His essence, by way of vagueness and then specification, for the sake of greater confirmation of the statement. The possibility that ''anzalna'' and what follows is a quotation of the words of Jibril and the angels who descended with him, peace be upon them, is extremely remote.

The specification of the creation of the earth and the heavens by mention, although what is meant is their creation together with everything connected to them, as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿To Him belongs what is in the heavens and what is on the earth﴾ and so on, is because they are primary and what is other than them follows them. It was also said that what is meant by the two is what is in the lower direction and what is in the upper direction. The mention of the creation of the earth first was said to be because it precedes the creation of the seven heavens in existence, as is evident from the verse of Ha Mim al-Sajda: ﴿Do you indeed disbelieve in the One who created the earth in two days?﴾ and so on. Likewise the apparent meaning of the verse: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth, then turned to the heaven and made them seven heavens﴾ and so on.

Al-Wahidi reported from Muqatil that the creation of the heavens comes first, and many of the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) preferred this, because the heavens are mentioned before the earth in most of the verses in which both are mentioned, and because wisdom requires the more noble to be created first, and the heaven is more noble than the earth in essence and attributes, together with the apparent meaning of the verse: ﴿Are you more difficult to create, or is the heaven? He built it﴾ and so on. Some verifiers chose that the creation of the heavens means bringing them into being with their matter before the creation of the earth, and the creation of them means making them manifest through their effects after the creation of the earth. By this the verses that seem to conflict can be reconciled. The heavens are mentioned before the earth at times, and the reverse at other times, according to what the context requires. This is closer to verification. On this view, and on what preceded it, the creation of the earth is mentioned first here. It was said that this is because it fits better with the revelation, which is one of the rulings of His mercy, Exalted is He, as is indicated by what follows it and by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Most Merciful. He taught the Qur'an﴾, and as what precedes it alludes to. The favour upon people through the creation of the earth is more evident and complete, and it is closer to the senses. It was also said that it is because it fits better with the opening of the surah, on the basis that ''Ta Ha'' is taken as a verbal sentence, meaning "Step on the earth with your two feet." Or it fits His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an to you so that you would be distressed﴾, on the basis that this is a new sentence, to turn the Prophet (ﷺ) away from what he was doing, lifting one of his feet off the ground during prayer, as reported in the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul).

The description of the heavens as ''al-'ula'' (the high), which is the plural of ''al-'ulya'', like ''al-kubra'' is the feminine of ''al-a'la'', is for the sake of emphasising grandeur, together with what it contains of regard for the rhyme-endings (fawasil). All of this, up to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿To Him belong the most beautiful names﴾, is directed towards magnifying the status of the One who sent it down, Mighty and Majestic, which entails magnifying the place to which it was sent down, and it calls the rebellious, who have turned away from the rank of height and tyranny, to be drawn down and won over to remembrance and faith.

[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 5 (part 1 of 4)]

﴿The Most Merciful﴾ is in the nominative as a laudatory epithet (madh), meaning: He is the Most Merciful.

Ibn 'Atiyyah allowed that it could be a substitute (badal, an apposition that replaces the word it modifies) for the concealed pronoun in (khalaqa, "He created"). Abu Hayyan criticised this, saying: "I think such a thing is not permissible, because a substitute must be able to take the place of the word it replaces, and here it cannot, lest the relative clause be left without a returning pronoun (ca'id)." End of quotation. Some scholars denied that this substitution must always be possible, and then said: "Even if we accept it, it is permissible to put the noun in place of the returning pronoun, as in the verse:

"And you are the one in God's mercy I hope for."

Yes, treating it as a substitute goes against the apparent meaning. It is also permissible that it be the subject of a sentence (mubtada'), with the definite article indicating a previously known reference, and the relative pronoun (al-ladhi) referring back to it, and its predicate being the words of the Exalted: ﴿Established Himself upon the Throne﴾. One may take it that the predicate is implied as "He," and make it a predicate about the subject if we accept the substitution reading. On the first reading, it becomes a second predicate after a first predicate that was implied earlier, according to what is in al-Bahr and elsewhere.

Jana ibn Hubaysh transmitted from some people that they read (al-Rahmani) in the genitive. Al-Zamakhshari explained it as an attributive adjective (sifa) of (man, "whoever"). Abu Hayyan criticised this, saying: "The position of the Kufis is that incomplete nouns, which are not complete without their relative clauses, such as (man) and (ma), cannot be described except by (alladhi) and (allati). So it is permissible to describe these two words [by these relatives], and according to them, this explanation is not permissible. Therefore, the best reading is that (al-Rahman) is a substitute for (man). In the Qur'an it functions like a proper name in its occurrence after governing words." It has also been said that (man) may be an indefinite noun described by an attributive clause, with (khalaqa) as its description, and (al-Rahman) being a description after a description. This is not one of the descriptions of incomplete nouns which are not complete without their relative clauses; the only thing in this matter is that the description by a clause precedes the description by a single word, and this is permissible. Abu Hayyan said: "And that is as you see."

The clause ﴿Established Himself upon the Throne﴾, according to this reading, is a predicate of the implied subject. The prepositional phrase, on all these possibilities, is connected to (istawa, "established Himself"), and was placed before it to suit the rhyme (fawasil) of the verse.

The word (al-'arsh, "the Throne") in the language means the seat of kingship. In religious usage it means a seat with legs, carried by angels, peace be upon them, above the heavens, like a dome. That it has legs is shown by what the two Sahihs (Bukhari and Muslim) transmit from Abu Sa'id, who said: "A man from the Jews came to the Prophet ﷺ, having slapped his face, and said: 'O Muhammad, a man from your companions has slapped my face.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Call him.' He said: 'Why did you slap his face?' The man said: 'O Messenger of God, I passed by the market and he was saying: "By Him who chose Moses above mankind." I said: "O wicked one, and above Muhammad ﷺ?" Anger seized me and I slapped him.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Do not make distinctions among the prophets, for people will swoon [on the Day of Judgment], and I will be the first to revive. Then I will find Moses holding one of the legs of the Throne. I do not know whether he revived before me or was recompensed with the swoon of Mount Sinai.'" That it has bearers from the angels, peace be upon them, is shown by the words of the Exalted: ﴿Those who bear the Throne and those around it glorify their Lord with praise and believe in Him﴾.

And what Abu Dawud transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "God has permitted me to narrate about an angel from the angels of God, the Mighty and Majestic, one of the bearers of the Throne: that the distance between his earlobes and his shoulder is a journey of seven hundred years."

And that it is above the heavens like a dome is shown by what Abu Dawud also transmitted from Jubayr ibn Muhammad ibn Jubayr ibn Mut'im, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: "A Bedouin came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and said: 'O Messenger of God, souls have suffered, wealth has been ruined or destroyed; so ask God for rain for us. We seek your intercession with God, and we seek God's intercession with you.' The Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'Woe to you! Do you know what you are saying?' And the Messenger of God ﷺ glorified God, and he continued glorifying Him until the effect of this was seen on the faces of his companions. Then he said: 'Woe to you! No one can seek God's intercession over any of His creatures. God's affair is greater than that. Woe to you! Do you know what God is? God is above His Throne, and His Throne is above His heavens, like this,' and he gestured with his fingers like a dome, '—and it creaks with Him like the creaking of a new saddle under its rider.'"

From the poetry of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt:

"Glorify God, for He is worthy of glory,
Our Lord who in the heavens has become Great.

With the lofty structure that dazzled people,
And He set above the heaven a throne.

A canopy which the eye's glance cannot reach,
Around it you see angels in forms."

Some of the scholars of kalam (speculative theology) held that it is circular, surrounding the world from all directions, encompassing the world from every side, and that it delimits directions. They sometimes called it the Atlas sphere (al-falak al-atlas) and the ninth sphere (al-falak al-tasi').

Some of the commentators on the creed of al-Tahawi criticised this, saying: "This is not correct, because it is established in the religious law that it has legs carried by the angels, peace be upon them. Also, the two Sahihs transmit from Jabir that he said: 'I heard the Prophet ﷺ say: "The Throne of the Most Merciful shook at the death of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh."'"

According to them, the ninth sphere is always in motion with an uniform movement. Whoever interprets that as meaning that the shaking refers to the rejoicing and happiness of the Throne's bearers must provide proof that the context and wording of the hadith, as transmitted from Abu al-Hasan al-Tabari and others, is far from that possibility. Also, it is found in Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Juwayriyah bint al-Harith, that it has a weight which is the heaviest of weights, while the sphere, according to them, is neither heavy nor light. Furthermore, the Arabs do not understand from (the Throne) a sphere, and the Qur'an was revealed in the language they understand.

The most that the report of Abu Dawud from Jubayr ibn Mut'im indicates is the rounding (taqbib, the domed shape), and this does not imply circularity from all sides as in the sphere, and it needs a separate proof. Furthermore, these people, even until the Trumpet is blown, have no proof that the spheres are limited to nine, nor that the ninth is a starless sphere, and it is other than the Footstool (al-Kursi), according to the correct view. Ibn Jarir said: Abu Dhar, may God be pleased with him, said: "I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: 'The Footstool in relation to the Throne is nothing but like a ring of iron thrown in the middle of a desert of the earth.'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah transmitted in his book on the attributes of the Throne, and al-Hakim in his Mustadrak, and said that it meets the conditions of the two Sheikhs (Bukhari and Muslim), from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Footstool is the place of the feet, and the Throne—no one can measure its size except God, the Exalted." It has been reported as a prophetic report (marfu'), but the correct view is that it is a statement of the scholar Ibn 'Abbas (mawquf). It has also been said: "The Throne is a metaphor for kingship and sovereignty." Someone criticised this, saying: "This is a distortion of the words of God, the Exalted. How would the one who says this respond to His words: ﴿And on that Day eight will bear above them the throne of your Lord﴾? Would he say: 'Eight will bear His kingdom on that Day'? And the words of the Prophet ﷺ: '...then I find Moses holding one of the legs of the Throne'? Would he say: 'Holding one of the legs of the kingdom'? Both statements are not said by anyone who has even the slightest taste (for language)." Likewise, it is said: Would he say about "The Throne of the Most Merciful shook," and so on, "the kingdom of the Most Merciful shook and His sovereignty"? And in what al-Bukhari and others transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, traced back to the Prophet ﷺ: "When God had decreed creation, He wrote in a book which is with Him above the Throne: 'My mercy has overcome My wrath.'" So He, Glorified and Exalted, is with it above the kingdom and sovereignty, and this is like those two statements.

Istiwa' ("establishing oneself") upon something comes with the meaning of rising and ascending over it, and with the meaning of settling, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And it came to rest upon al-Judi﴾, and ﴿that you may sit firmly upon their backs﴾. Since the apparent meaning of this is impossible for Him, the Exalted, it has been said: "Istiwa' here means istila' (taking control), as in the verse:

'Bishr has taken control over Iraq.'"

This was criticised, saying: "Taking control means the attainment of dominance after weakness, and that is impossible with regard to Him, the Exalted. Also, one says 'so-and-so took control over such-and-such' only when there is a rival contesting him, and this too is impossible with regard to Him, the Exalted. Also, that is said only when the thing taken control over existed before, while the Throne came into being through His creation and origination, glorified is He. Also, taking control is one and the same in relation to all creatures, so there is no benefit in specifying the Throne by mention."

Imam al-Razi answered that if taking control is interpreted as power (iqtidar), then all these objections are completely removed. The condition of this answer is not hidden from a fair-minded person. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Since establishing oneself upon the Throne, which is the seat of kingship, is only achieved together with kingship, they made it a metaphor for kingship, saying: 'So-and-so established himself upon the Throne,' meaning he became king, even if he never sat upon the Throne at all. They expressed the attainment of kingship in this way because it is more explicit, more expansive, and more indicative of the image of the matter. Similar to it is your saying: 'So-and-so's hand is outstretched' and 'So-and-so's hand is chained,' meaning that he is generous or stingy. There is no difference between the two expressions except as you have said, so much so that whoever never stretched out his hand with gifts, or had no hand at all, is said to have 'an outstretched hand,' because in their usage it is equivalent to their saying 'generous.' From this is the words of the Exalted: ﴿The Jews say, 'The Hand of God is fettered'﴾, and so on. They meant by it the description of stinginess, and it was answered: 'He, His majesty be exalted, is generous without any imagining of a hand or a chain or an outstretching.'" End of quotation.

Al-Razi criticised him, saying: "If we opened this door, the interpretations of the Batiniyyah (esotericists) would open, for they also say: 'The meaning of the words of God, the Exalted, ﴿Take off your sandals﴾ is total devotion to the service of God without imagining any sandal. And the words of the Exalted: ﴿O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham﴾ means the rescue of Abraham, peace be upon him, from the hand of that tyrant, without there being any fire or address at all.' Likewise is the case in everything that has come in the Book of God, the Exalted. Rather, the rule is that every word that has come in the Qur'an must be understood in its literal sense, unless there is a definitive rational proof that requires turning away from it. How I wish those who know nothing would not dive into it!" End of quotation.

It is not hidden from you that opening the door in this verse does not necessarily lead to the opening of the esoteric interpretations regarding the verses mentioned, since there is no reason for them there. The motive for interpretation given by al-Zamakhshari is strong in his view. Perhaps it is an escape from the necessity of an impossibility while preserving the eloquence (jaza lah) of the meaning, for what he chose is more eloquent than the meaning of taking control, whether it is a literal meaning of istawa, as is the apparent sense of the words of al-Sihah, al-Qamus, and others, or a figurative meaning, as is the apparent sense of their considering it an interpretation.

Al-Razi argued for the invalidity of the apparent meaning with several arguments. The first: He, glorified and exalted, existed when there was no Throne, and when He created creation, He did not need what He had been independent of. The second: What is established upon the Throne must have a part of it on the right side of the Throne different from the part of it on the left side, so He, glorified and exalted, would be composite in Himself, and that is impossible with regard to Him, the Exalted, because it entails being created. The third: What is established upon the Throne is either able to move and transfer, and then it follows that He, glorified and exalted, is a locus of motion and stillness, and this is a statement of createdness; or it is not able to do that, and then He, the Exalted, would be like time, rather in worse condition than it, exalted is God above that with great exaltation. The fourth: If it is said that He, glorified and exalted, is specified by this container which is the Throne, He would need a specifier, and that is a neediness from which God is exalted. If it is said that He, the Mighty and Majestic, is present in every place, it entails what no sane person would say. The fifth: the words of the Exalted ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ are general in negating similarity; so if He were sitting, someone would be similar to Him in sitting, and then the verse would be invalidated. Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 5 (part 3 of 4):

We do not know. Would it not have sufficed them to hear the words of Allah, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾? Then, in discussing His ﷺ saying related by Muslim: "Indeed the hearts of the children of Adam, all of them, are between two of the fingers of the Most Merciful, like one heart, which He turns however He wills," he mentioned after that the choice between tafwid (delegation of the meaning to Allah, tafwid being the practice of leaving the meaning of an ambiguous text to Allah) but on condition of negating the jarihah (bodily limb) without fail, and clarifying what this wording contains of aspects of tanzih (declaring Allah free from imperfection). It is mentioned that this is obligatory upon the scholar when it becomes necessary in refuting an innovator who anthropomorphizes and likens Allah to creation. He also said, concerning what was transmitted from him by his student, the verifier Isma'il ibn Sudakin, in the commentary on al-Tajalliyat: "It is not permissible for the servant to interpret what has come in the reports of revelation (akhbar al-sam') merely because they do not agree with his rational proof, such as the reports of the Descent and others. For if the address departed from what it was laid down for, it would have no benefit. We know that he, upon him be peace, was sent to explain to people what was sent down to them. Then we see that he ﷺ, despite his eloquence, breadth of knowledge and unveiling, did not tell us that 'His mercy descends.' Whoever says 'His mercy descends' has carried the address to rational proofs. The Truth in His essence is unknown, so it is not valid to judge Him by an attribute restricted in meaning. The Arabs understand the attribution of descent absolutely, and do not restrict it with a judgment other than the one given. And when it is established among them that He, glorified and exalted be He, 'there is nothing like unto Him,' the meaning comes to them absolute and transcendent. Perhaps it will be said to you: 'Reason makes this impossible.' So say: 'The matter is this, if it is valid that the Truth is among the objects of the intellects, for then its judgments apply to Him, glorified and exalted be He.'" End of quote.

His student, Shaykh Sadr al-Din al-Qunawi, said in Miftah al-Ghayb, after expounding a discussion on a principle of great importance, the gist of which is that the difference between essences requires a difference in the attribution of qualities to them, the following text: "This is a principle whoever knows it, or whose secret is unveiled to him, knows the secret of the verses and reports that give the impression of tashbih (likening Allah to creation) to people of weak intellects. He comes to know their intended meaning, and is saved from the two pitfalls of ta'wil (interpretation) and tashbih, and witnesses the matter as it was described, together with complete tanzih." End of quote.

The summary of the discussion at this point is that there have come in the Noble Book and in the sound hadiths words that give the impression of tashbih, tajsim (corporealism) and what is not befitting to Allah, the Exalted, the Mighty. The mujassima (corporealists) and mushabbiha (anthropomorphists) clung to what they imagined, so they went astray and led others astray, deviated from the right path and inclined away. A group held that they are destroyed and disbelieving in their Lord. Others held that they are innovators. Some made a distinction and said: they are disbelievers if they say that He, glorified and exalted be He, is a body like other bodies, and innovators if they say: a body, not like bodies. Allah, the Exalted, protected the People of Truth from what they went to, and they relied upon it in their beliefs. A group among them affirmed what came as it came, together with complete tanzih free from tajsim and tashbih. So the reality of istiwa' (settling), for example, attributed to Allah, exalted be His state, does not entail what it entails in the witnessed world. He, majestic and exalted, is settled upon the Throne, while He is free from need of it, and bears it by His power, bears the Throne and its bearers, and there is no contact with it nor a spatial separation between Him, exalted be He, and it. And when it is valid for the theologians to say: He, exalted be He, is neither the essence of the world, nor within it, nor outside of it, although self-evidence almost decides the falsehood of this between one thing and another, it is valid for this group to say that concerning His istiwa', exalted be He, which is established by the Book and the Sunnah.

So Allah, glorified be He, and His attributes lie beyond the realm of the intellect, so His judgment is not accepted except in what is within the realm of thought. For the thinking faculty's task is to manipulate what is in the imagination and memory of the forms of sensed things and particular meanings, and by arranging them according to rule, another knowledge is obtained by the intellect, between it and these things there is a relation. And since there is no relation between the essence of the Truth, majestic and exalted be He, and anything, knowledge of the reality is not deduced from the premises that the intellect arranges. So the palms of inquiry are paralyzed, the necks of reaching for knowledge of the reality are shackled, the feet of striving toward tashbih are fettered, and the eyes of sight and insight are blinded from comprehension and encompassment:

A goal whose target is far beyond the intellect in it,
and short of its reach is a hand that does not perish.

Al-Lalaka'i in Kitab al-Sunnah has transmitted through the route of al-Hasan from his mother, from Umm Salama, that she said: "Istiwa' is not unknown, the modality (kayf) is not conceivable, affirming it is faith, and denying it is disbelief." And through the route of Rabi'ah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, that he was asked: "How did He settle upon the Throne?" He said: "Istiwa' is not unknown, the modality is not conceivable, sending it is from Allah, the Exalted, the delivery is upon His Messenger, and submission is upon us."

When they say the negation of necessary implications (lawazim) entirely, the objections mentioned earlier are repelled from them and they are preserved from all other pitfalls. This group is said to be the Salaf al-Salih (the pious predecessors). It is also said that the Salaf, after negating what is imagined of tashbih, say: "We do not know what that meaning is, and Allah, the Exalted, knows His intended meaning."

It has been objected that the verses and reports containing the like of this are very numerous, and it is extremely far-fetched that Allah, the Exalted, and His Messenger ﷺ would address the servants concerning belief with what they do not know the meaning of. Also, reports have come that indicate the addressee understood the meaning from the like of this. Abu Nu'aym transmitted from al-Tabarani, who said: Ayyash ibn Tamim narrated to us, Yahya ibn Ayyub al-Maqabiri narrated to us, Salm ibn Salim narrated to us, Kharijah ibn Mus'ab narrated to us, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from 'Ata' ibn Yasar, from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'Indeed Allah, the Exalted, laughs at the despair of His servants and their hopelessness, and at the nearness of mercy to them.' So I said: 'May my father and mother be your ransom, O Messenger of Allah, does our Lord laugh?' He said: 'Yes, by Him in whose hand is my soul, indeed He laughs.' I said: 'Then He will not deprive us of good when He laughs.'" For she, may Allah be pleased with her, had she not understood a meaning from His laughing, exalted be He, she would not have said what she said.

It is also established from some of the Salaf that they did give interpretations. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Mujahid said: "Istawa 'ala al-'Arsh (settled upon the Throne): rose above the Throne." And Abu al-'Aliyah said: "Istawa 'ala al-'Arsh: ascended." It has been said that the Salaf are of two categories. One category, after negating tashbih, specified the apparent meaning, free from implications; and another category saw that it is valid to specify that and valid to specify another meaning that is not impossible for Him, exalted be He, as some of the later scholars did. They observed good manners and were cautious regarding the attributes of the Lord, and said: "We do not know what that meaning is," i.e., the meaning intended by Him, mighty and majestic, and Allah, the Exalted, knows His intended meaning.

A group of those who declare Allah free from tashbih and tajsim went to the view that the intended meaning is not the apparent meanings with negation of implications, but rather a specific meaning, which is such-and-such. Often that is a figurative meaning, and it may be the literal meaning of the word. These are a group of the later scholars. It may also happen that they delegate the intended meaning to Him, majestic and exalted be He, as well, and that is when the figurative meanings or the literal meanings that do not give rise to any feared harm are multiple, and there is no indicator with them that prefers one of them. Then they say: "The word may bear such-and-such and such-and-such, and Allah, the Exalted, knows His intended meaning therein."

The school of the Sufis, according to what Shaykh Ibrahim al-Kurani and others mentioned, is to let the ambiguous texts (mutashabihat) pass according to their apparent meanings with negation of implications and tanzih by "there is nothing like unto Him," like the methodology of the first Salaf, and their saying about tajalli (manifestation) in the loci of manifestation is on this pattern. The words of the Greatest Shaykh (Ibn 'Arabi), may his secret be sanctified, on this matter are inconsistent, as is witnessed by what I heard transmitted from him earlier, together with what he mentioned in the second chapter of the second section of al-Futuhat. For he said, in enumerating the tanzih groups: "And a group of the tanzih also, namely the 'Aliyah, and they are our companions. They emptied their hearts of thought and reflection and left them vacant, and said: 'There has arisen in our souls, from the glorification of Allah, the Truth, majestic is His majesty, to such a degree that we cannot reach knowledge of what has come to us from Him through subtle thought and reflection.' So in this creed they resembled the modern people whose beliefs are sound, in that they did not reflect nor interpret, but said: 'We did not understand.' Our companions agreed with their statement. Then they moved beyond the rank of these people, by saying: 'For us is to follow another path in understanding these words, which is by emptying our hearts of discursive reflection, and sitting with the Truth, exalted be He, through remembrance, on the carpet of good manners, watchfulness, presence, and readiness to receive whatever comes from Him, exalted be He, until the Truth, glorified and exalted be He, becomes the one who teaches us through unveiling and realization," when they heard Him, exalted be He, say: ﴿And fear Allah, and Allah teaches you﴾, and ﴿If you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion﴾, ﴿And say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾, ﴿And We taught him knowledge from Us﴾. So when their hearts and aspirations turned toward Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and they took refuge in Him, glorified and exalted be He, and cast away from themselves what others clung to of claims of inquiry and examination and the conclusions of intellects, their intellects were sound and their hearts pure and empty. When they had this readiness, the Truth manifested to them openly and clearly, and that witnessing made them know the meanings of those words all at once. So they knew the tanzih meaning for which they were brought, and it differs according to the differing stations in which they are uttered. This is the state of one group of us, and the state of another group of us as well: they do not have this manifestation, but they have inspiration, revelation, meeting, and writing, and they are protected in what is cast upon them by signs known only to them. So they report what they were addressed with, what they were inspired with, and what was cast upon them or written." End of quote.

Perhaps whoever says the ambiguous texts should be left on their apparent meanings with negation of implications, like the methodology of the first Salaf among the Sufis, belongs to a group that did not attain what those two groups attained. And grace is in the hand of Allah, He gives it to whom He wills.

This remains: is what the Salaf hold called ta'wil or not? The well-known view is that what the mufawwidah among them hold is not called ta'wil. Some called it ta'wil, as the later scholars hold. Al-Laqani said: "The later scholars agree, and they are referred to as the mu'awwilah (interpreters), and the Salaf, who are referred to as the mufawwidah (delegators), agree on His, exalted be He, transcendence above the impossible meaning indicated by the apparent sense, and on interpreting it and removing it from its impossible apparent sense, and on belief in it, that it is from Allah, the Exalted, brought by His Messenger ﷺ. They differed only in specifying a conveyed meaning that is sound, and in not specifying it, based on the premise that the pause (waqf) is at His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And those firmly grounded in knowledge﴾, or at His saying, glorified be He: (except Allah). The ta'wil of the Salaf is called general (ijmali), and the ta'wil of the later scholars is called detailed (tafsili)." End of summary.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 5 (part 4 of 4):

Our shaykh, the scholar ʿAlaʾ al-Din, used to say: "What the *mufawwida* (those who delegate the knowledge of the meaning to God, *tafwid*) hold is one interpretation (*ta'wil*), and what the *mu'awwila* (those who interpret) hold is two interpretations. Perhaps this returns to what you have heard. As for what those hold who affirm the apparent meanings (*zawahir*) while negating the necessary implications (*lawazim*), it has been said that there is also an interpretation in it, because of the negation of the necessary implications. The apparent sense of the words themselves requires those implications, so in it there is the removal of the wording from what its apparent sense requires, and removing the wording from that for a proof, even a weaker one, is an interpretation. What is meant by their being 'those who affirm the apparent meanings' is that they affirm them in general terms."

It has also been said: "There is no interpretation in it, because they consider the wording from the standpoint of its ascription to Him, glorified is His majesty, and from this standpoint it does not require the implications. So there is no removal of the wording from what its apparent sense requires. Do you not see that the People of the Sunna and the Community (*Ahl al-Sunna wa al-Jama'a*) unanimously agreed on the vision of God, exalted is He, in the Hereafter, while negating the implications of vision in the visible world, such as facing, and a specific distance, and other things? Yet none of them said that this is in any way a matter of interpretation."

Some of the virtuous scholars said: "Whoever explains (*tafsir*) has interpreted, and whoever does not explain has not interpreted, because interpretation is explanation. So everyone other than the *mufawwida* is an interpreter." This is what the apparent sense of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And none knows its interpretation except God. And those firmly rooted in knowledge say: We believe in it﴾ requires, on the basis that the pause is at "except God." It is not hidden that the claim that those who affirm the apparent meanings while negating the implications are among the interpreters, and not among those firmly rooted in knowledge, on the basis of that stop, cannot be reconciled with the claim that they are among the early generation (*salaf*), who they are. It may be said that they are included among those firmly rooted, and the interpretation (*ta'wil*) in another sense becomes apparent through investigation and reflection. The discussion of what is meant by the *mutashabihat* (ambiguous verses) has already preceded, and we mentioned what indicates the disagreement about the meaning of interpretation. I lean toward interpretation, and toward not affirming the apparent meanings while negating the implications, in some of what is ascribed to God, exalted is He, such as His saying, glorified is He: ﴿We will attend to you, O two heavy ones﴾ and His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Alas for the servants﴾, as in some readings. Likewise is his saying (ﷺ), if it is sound: "The Black Stone is the right hand of God on His earth; whoever kisses it or shakes its hand, it is as if he shook hands with God, exalted is He, and kissed His right hand."

So make the speech about it take the form of a figure of speech (*tashbih*), because the indicator is clear. I do not say that the Black Stone is among His attributes, as the early generation said regarding the "right hand." I see that whoever affirms the apparent meanings while negating the implications in all cases stands between it and the doctrine of the unity of existence (*wahdat al-wujud*), in the way that the verifying Sufis (*muhaqqiqu al-Sufiyya*) stated it, as the distance between the blackness of the eye and its whiteness.

I also lean toward the view that the Throne is spherical (*taqbib al-'arsh*), because the report about it is sound, and what is closest to rational proof is the view that it is a sphere (*kurriyya*). Whoever holds this answers the earlier reports in a way that is not hidden from the discerning.

The Greatest Shaykh, Muhyi al-Din, may God sanctify his secret, said in the three hundred and seventy-first chapter of the *Futuhat*: "It has four corners and four faces, which are its original legs, and between every two legs there are legs, and their number is known to us, but I will not specify them," up to the end of what he said. His speech implies that its legs are not in the sense that comes to mind. He stated explicitly that he is one of its bearers, and that it was sent down at the best of the legs, which is the treasury of mercy. He mentioned that blindness encompasses it, and that the image of the whole world is a circular, celestial image. He lengthened the discussion in this chapter and brought in marvels of wonder. Yet for most of what he mentioned in it there is no basis that we know from the Book of God, exalted is He, or the Sunna of His Messenger (ﷺ). Some of it is such that we may not say its apparent sense is true. The apparent view is that the Throne is one, though some Sufis said that it is multiple. It is not hidden what there is in ascribing the istiwa' (settling) to Him, exalted is He, under the title of the Most Merciful (*al-Rahmaniyya*), which greatly strengthens hope in Him, mighty and exalted is He. Glory be to Him whose mercy encompasses everything.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 6:

The subject of "istiwa'" (ascending, rising over, settling) is taken to be what is in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, with "to Him" (lahu) being connected to it, according to what is required by what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, that the pause is at ﴿the Throne﴾. The meaning would be: everything was made to be upright (istaqama) for Him, Exalted is He, and it is in accordance with His will, by His, Mighty and Majestic is He, making it so, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven and made them seven heavens﴾. Or: everything became level (istawa) in relation to Him, Exalted is He, so that nothing is nearer to Him, glorified is He, than anything else, as is indicated by (the hadith): "Do not prefer me over Ibn Matta."

This is something that should not be paid any attention at all, and the narration from Ibn 'Abbas is not authentic. Perhaps what moved the one who said it to it is fleeing from attributing istiwa' to Him, majestic is His majesty. Alas, what will he do with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Most Merciful, over the Throne, is established﴾, which by its apparent meaning he thinks contradicts what his intellect requires, such as ﴿The Most Merciful over the Throne is established﴾? Rather, "lahu" is the predicate placed first, and what is ﴿in the heavens﴾ is the postponed subject, i.e., to Him alone, Mighty and Majestic is He, not to another, with no partnership and no independent share, in terms of ownership, disposal, giving life, causing death, bringing into existence and annihilating: all that is in the heavens and the earth, whether by being a part of them or by indwelling in them. ﴿And what is between them﴾ of the existing beings that are constantly in the atmosphere, such as the air and the clouds, and creatures we do not know, which He, glorified is He, knows, or the majority of them, such as the birds that we see. ﴿And what is beneath the soil (al-thara)﴾, i.e., what is beneath the seventh earth, according to what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from Muhammad ibn Ka'b. He also narrated from al-Suddi that it is the rock that is beneath the seventh earth, and it is a green rock. Abu Ya'la narrated: "From Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked, 'What is beneath the earth?' He said: 'Water.' It was said: 'What is beneath the water?' He said: 'Darkness.' It was said: 'What is beneath the darkness?' He said: 'Air.' It was said: 'What is beneath the air?' He said: 'The soil (al-thara).' It was said: 'What is beneath the soil?' He said: 'The knowledge of the created beings ends at the knowledge of the Creator.'"

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him something similar in a long hadith. Others said: al-thara is moist earth, or the dirt which, when moistened, does not become mud, like al-Thurayya (the Pleiades) with its long vowel. It is said that its dual is tharayan and tharawan, and its plural is athra'. It is also said: "thariyat al-ard" (the earth became moist), in the pattern of radiya, yuthri, thara, so it is thariyya, like ghaniyya, and thar'a', when it became moist and soft after drought and dryness; and "athrat" means its moisture increased; and "tharaa al-turba tathriyatan" means he moistened the soil; and "rashsha al-makan" means he sprinkled the place; and "fulanan alzama yadahu al-thara" means he made his hand cling to the soil (i.e., he was reduced to poverty). It has been explained as the general term for dirt, i.e., His is what the dirt covers, and it was mentioned alongside its inclusion under what is in the earth in order to add emphasis. When what is in the earth includes what is upon it, the matter is evident; and what preceded of the indication that what is meant is that everything is His, in ownership and disposal, is the apparent meaning.

It has also been said: the meaning is that He has knowledge of all that, i.e., His knowledge encompasses all of that. The first is the apparent meaning, and upon it the saying of the Exalted will be:

[Page 163 begins within this passage.]

﴿And if you speak aloud with speech﴾ and so on: this is an explanation of the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of all things, following the explanation of the all-encompassing scope of His power over all creatures. According to what al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit) states, the address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and what is meant is his community (ummah), upon him be blessings and peace. It is also permissible that it be general, meaning: and if you raise your voice, O human being, with speech, ﴿then indeed He knows the secret﴾, i.e., what you have confided to others without raising your voice with it, ﴿and [something] more hidden (akhfa)﴾, i.e., something more hidden than that, which is what you have let pass through your mind without ever uttering it at all. This was narrated from al-Hasan and Ikrimah. Or [the meaning is] what you have kept secret within yourself and what you will keep secret within yourself. This was narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. It was also narrated from the two leaders al-Baqir and al-Sadiq that "the secret is what you have concealed within yourself, and the more hidden is what has passed through your mind and then you forgot it."

It has also been said: "akhfa" is a past-tense verb conjoined to "yaʿlamu" (He knows), meaning that He, exalted is He, knows the secrets of His servants and conceals from them what He knows, may He be glorified. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they do not encompass Him in knowledge﴾. Abu al-Shaykh narrated this in al-ʿAẓama from Zayd ibn Aslam, but it is very contrary to the apparent meaning. Therefore, what is relied upon is that it is an elative form (af'al al-tafdil), and the indefiniteness is for intensification in hiddenness. What is most readily understood from "qawl" (speech) includes the remembrance of God, exalted is He, and other than it, and some have adopted this view. A group restricted it to the remembrance of Him, glorified is He, and His supplication, and on this basis the definite article is for reference to a known matter, because the equality of loud and secret speech before Him, glorified is He, which is implied in the discourse, requires that the loudness mentioned is in His address, mighty and majestic is He.

According to both opinions, His saying, exalted is He, "﴿then indeed He﴾" and so on serves in place of the answer to the conditional clause, and the answer is not in reality [the answer], because His knowledge of the secret and the more hidden is established before speaking aloud, after it, and without it.
