According to some, the underlying structure is: "And if you speak aloud, know that God knows it, for indeed He knows the secret and [something] more hidden, let alone that." According to the majority, it is: "And if you speak aloud, know that God, glorified is He, is independent of your loudness, for indeed He..." and so on. This, as has been said, is guidance for the servants to be careful and cautious at the time of speaking aloud, for whoever knows that God, exalted is He, knows his loud speech will not speak evil. Loudness was singled out for this because most dialogues and people's addresses to one another are by it. It has also been said: it is guidance for the servants that raising the voice in the remembrance of God, exalted is He, and His supplication, is not for making Him, glorified is He, hear, but for another purpose: shaping the self with remembrance, fixing it therein, preventing it from occupying itself with other than Him, cutting off whisperings, and other things. It has also been said: loud remembrance and supplication are forbidden, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and in fear, and without loudness of speech﴾. You know that the claim that loud remembrance and supplication are forbidden should not be taken in its absolute sense.

What Imam al-Nawawi explicitly stated in his fatawa is that loud remembrance, wherever there is no legal prohibition, is legislated and recommended. Indeed, it is better than silent [remembrance] according to the school of Imam al-Shafi'i. This is also the apparent position of Imam Ahmad, and one of the two narrations from Imam Malik, as quoted by al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar in Fath al-Bari. It is also the view of Qadi Khan in his fatawa, in the chapter on the rules of recitation, and in his statement in the chapter on washing the dead: "Raising the voice in remembrance is disliked." The apparent meaning is that this applies to one who walks with the funeral procession, as is the position of the Shafi'is, not absolutely, as the wording of al-Bahr al-Ra'iq and others implies. This is also the view of the two Imams regarding the takbir of the Feast of Fitr, as with the Feast of Adha. There is also a narration from Imam Abu Hanifa himself, may God be pleased with him. Indeed, in his Musnad there is what apparently indicates the recommendation of loud remembrance absolutely. Yes, Ibn Nujaym said in al-Bahr, quoting the verifier Ibn al-Humam in Fath al-Qadir, the following text: "Abu Hanifa said: raising the voice in remembrance is an innovation (bid'ah) contrary to the command in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And remember your Lord within yourself﴾, etc. Therefore, one should limit oneself to the source of the Shariʿa. It has been reported regarding it in the Feast of Adha, namely His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And remember God during the appointed days﴾."

Al-Suyuti, in Natijat al-Dhikr, answered the use of the previous verse as evidence in three ways. First, it is Meccan, and when the Prophet ﷺ emigrated, that ruling lapsed. Second, a group of exegetes, among them ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam and Ibn Jarir, understood the verse as referring to remembrance during the recitation of the Qur'an, and that the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, was commanded to remember in this manner, in honor of the Qur'an, that voices should not be raised in its presence. This is strengthened by the verse's connection to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited﴾ and so on. Third, what some Sufis mentioned: the command in the verse is specific to the Prophet ﷺ, the perfect and perfecting one. As for others, upon him be blessings and peace, who are subject to whisperings, they are commanded to speak aloud, because it is more effective in repelling them. There is much to be said about this.

Some verifiers chose that what is meant is less than excessive loudness or loudness beyond the measure of need, so moderate loudness and loudness to the extent of need fall within what is commanded. For more than twenty hadiths are authentic indicating that the Prophet ﷺ frequently spoke aloud in remembrance.

It is authentically reported from Abu al-Zubayr that he heard ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr say: "When the Messenger of God ﷺ finished his prayer with the salam, he would say with his loud voice: 'There is no god but God alone, He has no partner. To Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs praise, and He is over all things capable. There is no power nor might except with God. We worship none but Him. To Him belongs grace, to Him belongs bounty, and to Him belongs good praise. There is no god but God, sincere to Him in religion, even though the disbelievers dislike it.'"

This is to be understood as being due to the need for teaching and the like. What is in the two Sahihs from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ashʿari, who said: "We were with the Prophet ﷺ, and whenever we ascended a valley we would say 'La ilaha illa Allah' and 'Allahu Akbar', and our voices would rise. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'O people, be gentle with yourselves, for you are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent. Indeed He is with you; indeed He is Hearing, Near.'"

This is to be understood as meaning that the prohibition derived by implication from the command "irbaʿu" (be gentle), which means "be easy and do not exhaust yourselves", is intended to forbid exaggeration in raising the voice. By dividing loudness and the varieties of its rulings, the two differing narrations from Imam Abu Hanifa are reconciled. As for what is mentioned in the Waqiʿat regarding Ibn Masʿud, that he saw people chanting "tahlil" with raised voices in the mosque and said: "I see you only as innovators," until he expelled them from the mosque, this is not authentic according to the hadith verifiers among the imams. Even if it were authentic, it is opposed by what proves that Ibn Masʿud himself raised his voice, as related by more than one of the memorizers, or it is to be understood as referring to excessive loudness. The report "the best remembrance is the hidden, and the best sustenance or livelihood is what suffices" is sound.

Imam al-Suyuti attributed it to Imam Ahmad, Ibn Hibban and al-Bayhaqi from Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas. Abu al-Fath, in Silah al-Mu'min, attributed it to Abu ʿAwana in his Musnad, also sound. It is to be understood as applying to one who is in a place where he fears showing off, self-admiration, or the like. It is also authentically established that he, upon him be blessings and peace, spoke aloud in supplication and in admonitions. But more than one of the eminent scholars said: concealing supplication is better.

The limit of loudness, as mentioned by Ibn Hajar al-Haytami in al-Manhaj al-Qawim, is that it is such that it makes others hear, while silence is such that it makes only oneself hear. According to the Hanafis, in one narration: the minimum of loudness is making oneself hear, and the minimum of quietness is articulating the letters. This is the view of al-Karkhi. In the book of Imam Muhammad there is an allusion to it. The most correct view, as in al-Muhit, is the statement of the two shaykhs, al-Hindawani and al-Fadli, and it is what most hold: that the minimum of loudness is making others hear, and the minimum of quietness is making oneself hear.

From here, in Fath al-Qadir, it is said: articulating the letters without sound is an indication of the letters through the muscles of the articulation points, not letters. For letters are a manner of contact with sound. When the sound that is manifested is absent, the letter that is manifested is absent. Where there is no letter, there is no speech in the sense of the speaker, and there is no recitation in the sense of speaking, which is an act of the tongue. Thus there is no quietness when sound is absent, just as there is no loudness. End of the edited quotation.

Shaykh Ibrahim al-Kurani, may God have mercy on him, wrote two excellent treatises on verifying this question. The first he named "Nashr al-Zahr fi al-Dhikr bi al-Jahr" (The Spreading of the Flower in Remembrance Aloud), and the second "Ithaf al-Munib al-Awwah bi Fadl al-Jahr bi Dhikr Allah" (The Gift to the Penitent Sorrowful One concerning the Merit of Loud Remembrance of God). In them he refuted some scholars of the ninth century among the Hanafi scholars, among the notables of the state of Mirza Ulugh Beg ibn Shah Rukh al-Kurkani, who categorically stated that loud remembrance is a forbidden innovation, and he wrote a treatise on that. Perhaps, if God wills, more elaboration for verifying this question will come later. And God is the Granter of success.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 8:

As for His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Allah﴾, it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the sentence is a resumptive (istinaf) clause (istinaf: a new sentence that resumes the discourse), brought to explain that the one described by the attributes of perfection mentioned is that true deity, that is, the One described by the sublime attributes mentioned is Allah, mighty and majestic. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿There is no deity except Him﴾, is a confirmation of the truth and an explicit statement of what the preceding words contain of the exclusivity of divinity (uluhiyyah) to Him, glorified is He. For what is ascribed to Him, mighty is His majesty, of creating all existing things, of the elevation befitting His majesty over all created beings, of the all-merciful nature (rahmaniyyah) and the ownership of the higher and lower realms, and of all-encompassing knowledge, is something that clearly requires this. His saying, blessed is His name, ﴿To Him belong the most beautiful names﴾, is an explanation that what was mentioned of creating and other things are His names and attributes, exalted is He, without any plurality in His essence, exalted is He. The word "name" (ism) is used in the sense of "attribute" (sifah), and from this is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And they have set up partners for Allah. Say: name them﴾. The word "the most beautiful" (al-husna) is the feminine form of "the most beautiful" (al-ahsan), and an adjective of a singular feminine noun is applied to a broken plural (jam' taksir), and what makes this fitting is that it occurs as a closing rhyme (fasilah). It was also said: it implies a reference to the non-plurality in reality, based on the premise that His attributes do not add to His essence and are one with it, and on the superiority of the names of Allah, exalted is He, over all other names, which is most evident. Abu Hayyan permitted that the noble name be the subject (mubtada'), with the sentence ﴿There is no deity except Him﴾ as its predicate, and the sentence ﴿To Him belong the most beautiful names﴾ as a second predicate after a predicate. The apparent tenor of his treatment requires that he preferred this, since it is what comes first to the mind,
Page 165
and it is not hidden from the careful reader that the earlier view is more primary.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 9:

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Has the story of Musa reached you?﴾ is brought (masuq) to establish the matter of tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness), which is where the course of the narrative arrives, and to show that it is a matter that continues among the Prophets, peace be upon them, one from another in succession. It was addressed to Musa, peace be upon him, when it was said to him, ﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me﴾, and with it he, peace be upon him, concluded his speech when he said, ﴿Your deity is only Allah, other than whom there is no deity﴾. It has also been said that it is brought to console the Prophet (ﷺ), like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an upon you that you be distressed﴾ [this is based on what is reported from Muqatil regarding the occasion of revelation]. However, the first (interpretation) is a consolation to him, peace be upon him, by rejecting what his people said, while this is a consolation to him (ﷺ) that his brethren among the Prophets, peace be upon them, were afflicted by their nations with what afflicted them, and the final outcome was in their favour. And He mentioned the beginning of the prophethood of Musa, peace be upon him, as a parallel to what He mentioned concerning the sending down of the Qur'an upon him, peace be upon him.

It has also been said: it is brought to encourage the Prophet (ﷺ) to take Musa, peace be upon him, as an example in bearing the burdens of prophethood and in patience in enduring the hardships of conveying the rulings of the message, after He, glorified is He, addressed him that He had assigned him the arduous task of conveying it. This is based on the view that the meaning of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an upon you that you be distressed﴾ ﴿but as a reminder for one who fears﴾ is: "We sent down the Qur'an upon you so that you might bear the toils of conveying (the message) and the disputes of the obstinate among the enemies of Islam, and their fighting you, and other kinds of hardships and the burdens of prophethood; and We did not send down upon you this exhausting, arduous toil except that it would be a reminder." Thus the waw (and), as many have said, is for conjoining one narrative to another, and no consideration is given in this to the connection between the two in terms of goodness or request; rather, the connection is required in what is to be narrated. Moreover, the conjunction here may be interpreted as a statement (khabar).

It is not hidden that what has preceded applies to all the other aspects and sayings concerning the previous verse and its occasion of revelation, and nothing of that contradicts it. The interrogative (istifham) is for affirmation (taqrir). It has also been said: "hal" here means "qad" (indeed). It has also been said: the interrogative is for denial (inkar), and its meaning is negation, i.e., We did not inform you before this surah of the story of Musa, peace be upon him, and now We are informing you of it. The reliable view is the first. The hadith (ḥadīth, report/narrative) is "news," and it applies to both little and much, and its plural is aḥādīth, by irregular (non-analogical) formation.

Al-Farra' said: "We consider that the singular of aḥādīth is uḥdūthah, then they made it a plural of ḥadīth." Al-Raghib said: "Ḥadīth: every speech that reaches a person by way of hearing or revelation, whether in his waking state or in his sleep; and it may be a verbal noun (maṣdar) meaning speaking." Some have taken it in this sense here, by the indication of (fa-qāla) etc., and His saying, exalted is He, is attached to it.

﴿When he saw﴾ a fire. He did not allow it to be attached (to the verb) if the word is taken as a noun meaning "the story," with the predicate (being the verb in the sense of the event). Since it would then be like a non-derivative noun (jawamid, "fixed nouns"), it would not govern anything. The more evident view is that it is a noun for what was mentioned, because that is what is well known. Moreover, describing the story as "coming" (al-ityan) is better than describing it as "speaking about" or "relating" it. The question of attachment is simple, since the adverbial complement (zarf, a prepositional or adverbial element of time or place) needs only a trace of the verb's sense to attach to it. For this reason al-Sharif (al-Jurjani) reported from some scholars that the words "story" (qissa), "narrative" (hadith), "report" (khabar) and "news" (naba') may govern adverbial complements specifically, even if they are not meant in their verbal-noun sense, because their meaning includes the notions of occurrence and existence.

It is also permitted that it be an adverbial complement to a deleted verb placed later, meaning: "When he saw a fire, such-and-such occurred." It is also permitted that it be an object of a deleted verb placed earlier, meaning: "Remember the time of his seeing a fire." It is related that Musa, peace be upon him, asked Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, for permission to leave Madyan for Egypt to visit his mother and his brother. The period since his offence in Egypt had grown long, and he hoped that the matter had been forgotten. Permission was granted. He, peace be upon him, was a jealous man. He left with his family and did not take along a company, so that his wife would not be seen. She was riding a she-ass, and on her back was a saddlebag (juwaliq) containing the household goods, and he had with him his sheep. He, peace be upon him, took a route off the main road, out of fear of the kings of Syria. When he reached the valley of Tuwa, which lies on the western side of Mount Tur, a son was born to him on a dark, cold, snowy night. It was a Friday night. He had lost the way, his flock had scattered, he had no water, and he struck his flint but it did not yield a spark. While he was in this state, he saw a fire on the left side of the road, on the side of the mountain. ﴿He said to his family: "Wait here"﴾, that is, "Stay where you are." He, peace be upon him, told them this so that they would not follow him in what he had resolved upon, going to the fire, as was customary, and not so that they would move to some other place, since that did not occur to the mind. The address (in "wait") is said to be to the woman, the child and the servant; and it is said to be to the woman alone. The plural is either because of the apparent wording "family" (ahl), or for honour, as in the words of one who said:

"Even if you wish, you may forbid all women except you."

Al-A'mash, Talha, Hamza and Nafi', in one transmission, read "li-ahlihi imkutu" with a damma on the ha' (ahlihimkuthu, "li-ahlihi umkuthu" with the pronoun vowel changed). ﴿Indeed I have perceived﴾ a fire, that is, I have seen it with a clear sight in which there is no doubt. From this comes "the pupil of the eye" (insan al-ayn), and "human" (ins) is the opposite of "jinn." It is said that "iyanas" (perceiving) is specific to seeing something that brings comfort; and it is said that it has the meaning of "finding" (wijdan). Al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:

"She perceived a sound, and the hunting-hounds had frightened her one day, when evening had drawn near."

The clause is an explanation of the command and of what was commanded. Since the perceiving was certain and definite, he confirmed it for them with the word "inna" (indeed), in order to settle their minds, even though there was no hesitation or denial. ﴿Perhaps I will bring you from it﴾, that is, I will come to you from the fire, (with a qabas) with a kindled brand, one set on the top of a stick or the like. So qabas is a verb in the sense of a passive participle, and it is the meaning intended by shihab (torch) and qabas, while in another place jadhwa (ember) is used. Explaining it as "a live coal" is not correct. This prepositional phrase is attached to "I will bring you." As for "from it" (minha), it may be attached to that, or to a deleted element that serves as a circumstantial qualifier of "qabas," according to what Abu al-Baqa' said. ﴿Or I will find at the fire guidance﴾, that is, a guide who will show me the way. This is either a verbal noun used to designate the agent for emphasis, or an idafa has been deleted from it, meaning "one possessing guidance," or it is because when the guide is found, guidance is found. Al-Zajjaj said that the intended meaning is a guide who will show me the water, for he, peace be upon him, had lost his way to the water. Mujahid and Qatada said the intended meaning is a guide who will lead me to the gates of religion, for the thoughts of the righteous are immersed in religious aspirations in most of their conditions, and no distraction turns them from it. But this is far-fetched, since the context of the noble verse is consolation for his family, and moreover the Surah of al-Qasas explicitly states what implies what preceded, where He says: ﴿Perhaps I will bring you from it news or a brand﴾, and so on. The commonly known spelling of this word is with a ya'.

Abu al-Baqa' said: The better course is to write it with an alif and not to incline it (imala), because the alif is a substitute for the tanwin in the established view. Some have inclined it, and there are three possible views on this. The first is that it is like the alif of tanwin in the final letter of the word, so that the pronunciation of both is the same in the restricted (maqsur) form. The second is that it is the radical letter of the word, and nothing was substituted for the tanwin in the accusative case. The third is that it is according to the opinion of those who stop in all three cases without substitution. End of quote. The word "aw" (or) here indicates prevention of the absence of both but not their combination. The preposition "ala" (on) retains its primary meaning of elevation, and "upon the fire" is a well-known metaphor which has become a conventional literal usage for being upon a place close and adjacent to it, as Sibawayh said regarding "marartu bi-Zayd" (I passed by Zayd): it is attachment to a place near to him. Many have said that the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier of "guidance," and it was (originally) in the position of a qualifier of it, but it was placed first. The sense is: "or I will find a guide, or one possessing guidance, overlooking the fire." The intended meaning is one warming himself by it, and the usual practice of one warming himself is to draw near the fire and to overlook it.

Ibn al-Anbari said that "ala" here has the meaning of "ind" (at), or of "ma'a" (with), or of the letter "ba'" (with). There is no need for this, and the apparent word would have been "alayha" (upon it), but the apparent noun was used to make explicit what is in the nature of a cause for finding guidance, since a fire is never without people beside it. The sentence is introduced with the particle of hope (la'alla), because his coming and what is conjoined to it are not certain to happen; rather they are awaited and hoped for. This particle, according to what is in Irshad al-Aql al-Salim, is either a cause of a deleted verb, relied upon through what is indicated by the command to wait and the report of the fire's perceived presence, and to avoid explicit mention of what would alarm them; or it is a circumstantial qualifier of its agent, meaning: "Go to it so that I may come to you," or "in order that I may come to you," or "hoping that I will come to you from it with a brand," and so on. It is said that it is a qualifier of "naran" (a fire). Whenever that is permitted, the clause of hope may be made a relative clause, as in his words:

"Indeed I am one who hopes for a glance before the one that, perhaps, if I go far from her homeland, I may visit her."

So it may be made a qualifier, for the relative clause and the qualifier are close to one another. The problem with this is not hidden.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 11:**

﴿When he came to it﴾, meaning the fire that he had sensed. According to some reports from Ibn Abbas, it was in a green, ripe jujube tree (*unnab*). Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said it was in an acacia tree (*sumrah*). It was also said to be in a boxthorn tree (*awsaj*).

Imam Ahmad reported in *al-Zuhd*, and Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported, on the authority of Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: When Musa (peace be upon him) saw the fire, he set out walking until he stopped near it. Suddenly he saw a great fire blazing from the leaves of a green tree of intense greenness, called *al-Alij*. The fire, as it appeared, did not grow except in size and blaze, and the tree did not grow, despite the intensity of the burning, except in greenness and beauty. He stood looking, not knowing how its matter would end, except that he thought it was a tree that would burn. He threw a torch at it, and it caught fire and was burned. The fire was prevented from consuming it only by the intensity of its greenness, the abundance of its water, the density of its leaves and the greatness of its trunk. So he left its matter at that and stood there, hoping that some piece would fall from it so that he could take a light from it. When this went on for a long time, he reached toward it with a bundle of twigs in his hand, wanting to take a light from its flame. When he did this, it leaned toward him as if it wanted him, so he drew back from it and was afraid. Then he returned and circled around it, and it kept tempting him and he kept being tempted by it. Then the fire was about to go out. His amazement increased at that, and he pondered its matter, and said: "This is a fire that cannot be taken a light from, yet it blazes in the heart of a tree without burning it. Then its extinguishing is proportional to its size, in less than the blink of an eye." When he saw that, he said: "Indeed, this has a matter." Then he left its affair to the view that it was commanded or created, not knowing its matter, nor what it was commanded with, nor who created it, nor why it was created. So he stood bewildered, not knowing whether to return or to remain. While he was in this state, he cast his gaze toward its branch, and behold, there was a greenness more intense than anything, shining into the sky, covering the darkness as he looked at it. Then the greenness kept shining, turning yellow and white until it became a bright light, a pillar between heaven and earth, having something like the rays of the sun, the eyes unable to bear it. Whenever he looked at it, it nearly snatched away his sight. At that point his fear and sorrow intensified, so he placed his hand over his eyes, pressed himself to the ground, and then heard a sound so great that none of the hearers had ever heard the like. When distress reached Musa (peace be upon him) and the terror grew severe, there occurred what Allah the Exalted has related.

It is also reported that whenever he (peace be upon him) drew near to it, it withdrew, and when he turned away, it followed him. So he became certain that this was one of the affairs of Allah the Exalted that break habit, and he stood bewildered. He heard from the sky the glorification of the angels, tranquility (*al-sakinah*) was cast upon him, and what happened, happened.

They (the scholars) said: Fire has four kinds. One kind eats but does not drink, and it is the fire of this world. One kind drinks but does not eat, and it is the fire of the green tree. One kind eats and drinks, and it is the fire of Hell. One kind neither eats nor drinks, and it is the fire of Musa (peace be upon him). They also said: it has four types. One type has light and burning, and it is the fire of this world. One type has neither light nor burning, and it is the fire of trees. One type has burning without light, and it is the fire of Hell. One type has light without burning, and it is the fire of Musa (peace be upon him). Indeed, some of them said: it was not fire at all, but a light from the Light of the Lord, blessed and exalted. This was reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and it was mentioned using the word "fire" in accordance with Musa's (peace be upon him) own supposition. There is no objection in his (peace be upon him) reporting according to his supposition, as some have imagined. Abu Hayyan favoured this view, and al-Mawardi adopted it.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it was the fire itself, and it is one of the veils of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He cited as evidence what was reported from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, on the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "His veil is fire. Were He to uncover it, the glories of His Face would burn away whatever of His creation His sight reached."

This was mentioned by al-Baghawi, and it is mentioned in the *Tafsir al-Khazin* that the hadith was narrated by Muslim. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that when he (peace be upon him) came to it, he was called (*nuditha*) without delay. On this basis, some of the Mu'tazilah rejected the earlier reports indicating an interval of time between the coming and the calling. You know that such an interval does not harm the matter mentioned. They also claimed it is impossible for an extraordinary event to manifest at his coming to the fire before he was made a prophet, unless that were a miracle for another of the prophets (peace be upon them). In our view, this is one of the preliminary signs (*irhas*), which the Mu'tazilah deny. The apparent view is that the substitute for the subject of *nuditha* (was called) is the pronoun referring to Musa (peace be upon him). It was also said that it refers to the verbal noun, i.e., *nuditha al-nida'* (he was called the call). It was also said that it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O Musa﴾, etc. This seems to be based on treating the calling as implying the meaning of speech, and intending this utterance as the sentence. Otherwise, it has been said that a sentence cannot be a subject or substitute for the subject in such a construction except through this kind of interpretation.

In *al-Bahr*: the view of the Kufis is to treat *al-nida'* (the calling) as treated like speech (*al-qawl*), while the view of the Basrans is to supply the verb of speech in such a verse, i.e., *nuditha* (he was called), so that it is said (*fa-qila*):

[page 167]

[Page 168]

**"O Musa! Indeed I am your Lord"** ﴿يا مُوسى﴾ ﴿إنِّي أنا رَبُّكَ﴾. For this reason the hamza of *inna* (إنَّ) is kasra in the recitation of the majority (*al-Jumhur*), while Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a fatha (إنَّ → أنَّ), by supposing a preposition (*harf al-jarr*) before it, meaning *bi-anni* ("that I..."). The prepositional phrase, according to Abu al-Baqa' and others, is connected to *nudiya* ("he was called"). Calling (*al-nida'*) may be connected to a preposition. Abu 'Ali recited:

*"I called by the name of Rabi'a ibn Mukarram; indeed, the one renowned by his name is the trusted one."*

The structure of the sentence according to this derivation is not hidden from anyone of sound taste, and it is only pleasant if the vocative is not a separating element.

It has also been said: it is with a supposed *harf al-ta'lil* (preposition of causation, "because"), connected to the imperative verb that follows it. But this, as you see, is weak. It has been preferred that the speech is with a supposed "knowing," i.e. "know that I..." etc. The repetition of the first-person pronoun is for emphasizing the indication, establishing the knowledge, and removing doubt.

It has been deduced (*istuzhira*) that Musa's knowledge, peace be upon him, that the one who called him was Allah the Exalted, came about by necessity (*bi-l-darura*), through a creation of Allah the Exalted in him. It has been said: through reasoning (*bi-l-istidlal*) from the extraordinary event (*khariq*) he had witnessed before the call. It has also been said: through what came to him of that after the call. For it is narrated that when he was called, "O Musa," he, peace be upon him, said: "Who is speaking?"

He said: "I am your Lord." Then the accursed Iblis whispered to him: "Perhaps you are hearing the speech of a devil." Musa, peace be upon him, said: "I know that it is the speech of Allah the Exalted, because I hear it from all directions, with all the limbs." The extraordinary element in it is two matters: hearing it from all directions, and that this is with all the limbs, both those which are suited to hearing and those which are not. It has been said: the extraordinary element in it is one matter, which is hearing with all the limbs, and this is what is meant by hearing from all directions. Whatever the case, the validity of the argument for the intended conclusion from this is not hidden; however, the soundness of the report is obscure, and I have not found a reliable chain (*sanad*) for it. The presence of Satan and his whispering to Musa, peace be upon him, in that sacred valley and that noble presence, is far-fetched.

The Mu'tazila (*al-Mu'tazila*) required that knowledge be by reasoning from the extraordinary event, and did not permit that it be by necessity. They said: "Because if the necessary knowledge occurred that this call was the speech of Allah the Exalted, then necessary knowledge of the existence of the powerful, knowing Creator would have occurred, since it is impossible for the attribute to be known by necessity while the essence is known by reasoning. And if the existence of the Exalted Creator were known by necessity, Musa, peace be upon him, would have been excluded from being a responsible person (*mukallaf*), because the occurrence of necessary knowledge contradicts responsibility (*taklif*). By consensus he, peace be upon him, was not excluded from responsibility. So we know that Allah the Exalted made him know that by an extraordinary event." The identity of that event is disputed.

Some said: "We have no need to know what that extraordinary event was." Ahmad and others narrated from Wahb that when the terror intensified upon him, he was called from the tree, and it was said, "O Musa!" He answered quickly, not knowing who had called him, and his quick answer was only from comfort with intimacy. He said, "Here I am," several times. "Indeed I hear your voice and I sense your presence, but I do not see your place. Where are you?" He said: "I am above you, with you, before you, behind you, and nearer to you than yourself." When Musa, peace be upon him, heard this, he knew that such a thing is not proper except for his Lord, the Exalted, so he became certain of Him and said:

*"Thus are You, O my God. Is it Your speech I hear, or Your messenger's?"* He said: "Rather, it is I who speak to you."

It is not hidden that this report's explanation according to the doctrine of the *salaf* and the doctrine of the Sufis is clear, and that certainty is not attained merely by hearing what should not be except for Allah the Exalted among attributes, once the door of whispering is opened. Furthermore, this report clearly shows that Musa, peace be upon him, heard the verbal speech (*al-kalam al-lafzi*) from Him, the Exalted, without intermediary. For this reason he, peace be upon him, was singled out with the title "the one who spoke with Allah" (*al-Kalim*). This is the doctrine of a group of Ahl al-Sunna, and that speech is eternal (*qadim*) according to them. They answered the objection that verbal speech implies occurrence (*huduth*), since none of it exists except with the passing of other parts, by saying: this only follows from uttering with an instrument and a bodily organ, which is the tongue. But when it is without these, it exists all at once, as is observed in letters impressed by a seal-stamp without a pen. They are bound to interpret His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then when he came to it, he was called﴾ etc., by saying: the meaning is "when he came to it, he heard the call" or something like that. Otherwise, the coming of the fire is an occurrence, and what is consequent upon an occurrence is an occurrence.

For this reason the people of Transoxiana (*ahl ma wara' al-nahr*) among the Ahl al-Sunna, who hold the eternity of speech, claimed that this speech which Musa, peace be upon him, heard was occurrent, and it was a sound that Allah the Exalted created in the tree. The People of innovation (*Ahl al-Bid'a*) all agreed that verbal speech is occurrent. However, some of them permitted that occurrent things subsist in Him, exalted is His majesty, and some did not permit it, and claimed that what Musa, peace be upon him, heard was created by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in a body among bodies, such as the tree or others.

Al-Ash'ari said: Allah the Exalted made Musa, peace be upon him, hear His soul-speech (*al-kalam al-nafsi*), which is neither a letter nor a sound, and there is no way for the intellect to know it. Some have verified it by saying: he, peace be upon him, received that speech by a spiritual reception, as the angels, peace be upon them, receive His speech, exalted is He, not from a bodily organ. Then the emanation of it onto the soul-faculties by the power of the intellect, and it was imprinted on the common sense (*al-hiss al-mushtarak*) in the forms of particular words, so that because of the strength of his imagining it, it was as if he heard it from outside. This is like the sleeper who sees that he is speaking and being spoken to.

As for the standing of the passing devil in the report you heard, on this view it may be explained that this is possible, and it may be explained by physiognomic perception (*al-tafarrus*), from the fact that his bodily state, peace be upon him, was that of one listening and reflecting upon what he hears. But this, as you see, is weak. You have already been given in the Introductions what may benefit you to review here, so review it and reflect. Know that the affair of Allah, exalted is His affair, is entirely wondrous, and glory be to Allah, the Mighty, the Wise.

﴿So take off your two sandals﴾ *fa-khla' na'laika*: remove them from your feet. *Al-na'l* (the sandal) is well-known, and it is feminine. Its diminutive is *nu'ayla*. It is also said *na'al* with a fatha on the 'ayn. Al-Farra' recited:

*"He has a sandal whose smell does not sicken the dog; and if it is placed among the assemblies, it is smelled."*

The Prophet ﷺ commanded this because they were made of the hide of a dead donkey that had not been tanned, as is narrated from al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, 'Ikrima, Qatada, al-Suddi, Muqatil, al-Dahhak, and al-Kalbi. It is also narrated that they were of donkey hide in a rare hadith.

Al-Tirmidhi, with his chain, narrated from the Prophet ﷺ who said: "Upon Musa, peace be upon him, on the day his Lord spoke to him, was a woolen cloak, a woolen robe, a woolen *kumma* (that is, a small cap), and woolen trousers, and his sandals were of donkey hide." From al-Hasan, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Ibn Jurayj, it is narrated that they were of the hide of a slaughtered cow. But he, peace be upon him, was commanded to remove them so that he would place his feet on the earth, and the blessing of the sacred valley would reach him.

Al-Asamm said: "Because going barefoot (*al-hifwa*) is more conducive to humility and good manners. For this reason the pious predecessors (*al-salaf al-salihun*) used to circumambulate the Ka'ba barefoot." It is not hidden that this is prohibited according to the one who holds that prayer in sandals is superior, as came in some reports. Perhaps al-Asamm did not hear this, or he answers it.

Abu Muslim said: "Because He, the Exalted, secured him from fear and stationed him in a pure place, and he, peace be upon him, only wore them out of caution against impurities and fear of insects." It has also been said: the meaning is "empty your heart of family and wealth." It has been said: "of this world and the Hereafter."

The reasoning for this is that by "sandal" may be meant everything one uses for comfort, and it has come to be applied to the disparaged matters; for this reason, "sandal" is used for a wife as found in the books of lexicography. It is not hidden from you that this is far-fetched, even if it is interpreted in this way; and it is more suitable to the mode of allusive interpretation (*bab al-isharа*).

The *fa'* (in *fa-khla'*) indicates the ordering of the command upon what precedes it, since His lordship over him, the Exalted, is one of the causes and motives of the command. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed you are in the sacred valley﴾ is an explanation of the cause for removing the sandals, which were commanded, and a clarification of the reason for the command's arrival due to the nobility and sanctity of the place. It is narrated that when he, peace be upon him,

[Page 170]

was commanded to remove them, he took them off and threw them behind the valley, *Tuwa* (طُوًى), with a *damma* on the *ta'*, not nunated.

The Kufans and Ibn 'Amir read it with a *damma* and nunation. Al-Hasan, al-A'mash, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu al-Sammal, and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a *kasra* and nunation. Abu Zayd, from Abu 'Amr, read it with a *kasra* without nunation. It is a proper noun for that valley, so it is either a *badal* (substitution) or an *'atf bayan* (explicative apposition). Whoever nunates it interprets it as "the place," and whoever does not nunate it interprets it as "the spot," in which case it is diptote (*mamnu' min al-sarf*) for being a proper noun and feminine. It has been said that *Tuwa* with a *damma* on the *ta'* and without nunation is diptote for being a proper noun and *'adl* (a form of morphological deviation), like *Zufar* and *Qutham*. It has also been said: it is diptote for being a proper noun and foreignness (*'ujma*). Qutrub said: it is said *tuwa min al-layl*, meaning "an hour," i.e., "it was made holy for you for an hour of the night," and that was the hour when he was called. In this case it is the object (*ma'mul*) of *al-muqaddas* ("the holy"). Al-Kirmani in *al-'Aja'ib* said: it has been said it is an arabized word meaning "at night," and he seems to have meant Qutrub's view. It has also been said: it is a man's name in Hebrew, and on this view it is apparently a vocative. Al-Hasan said: *Tiwa* with a *kasra* on the *ta'* and nunation is a verbal noun like *thinan*, both in form and meaning; in his view it is also the object of *al-muqaddas*, i.e., "it was made holy once after another." It is also permitted that it be the object of *nudiya*, i.e., "he was called two calls." Ibn al-Sayyid said: it is what is folded from a snake's skin, and it is said: "he did the thing *tuwan*," i.e., twice; in which case it is placed in the position of the verbal noun. Al-Tabarsi cited for 'Adi ibn Zayd:

*"O blamer, indeed the blame is without its real cause, upon me, twice, from your wandering error."*

Al-Raghib mentioned that when it means "twice," its first letter is opened and also kasra'd. It is not hidden from you that the more evident view is that it is the name of the valley in all the readings.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 13:

﴿And I have chosen you﴾, i.e., I have selected you from among mankind, or from among your people, for prophethood (nubuwwah) and messengership (risalah). Al-Sulami, Ibn Hurmuz and al-A'mash, in one narration, recited (wa-innā) with a kasra on the hamza and a shaddah on the nun, followed by an alif, (ikhtarnāka) with the nun and alif. Likewise Talhah, Ibn Abi Layla, Hamzah, Khalaf and al-A'mash in another narration recited it, except that they put a fatha on the hamza of anna, and this is by way of the implied (i'lam), meaning "and know that We have chosen you." It is, according to what has been said, a conjunction (ataf) upon (ikhla') ("take off"). It is permissible, according to those who read (innī anā rabbuka) with a fatha, for the conjunction to be upon it, whether it is connected to (nūdiya) as has been said, or is an object of an implied (i'lam), as has been chosen.

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be with an implied lam, and that it be connected to what follows it, meaning "because We have chosen you, so listen (fa-istami')." This is as you see. The fa in His words, exalted is He, (fa-istami') indicates the sequencing of the command and what is commanded upon what precedes it, for his selection, peace be upon him, for what has been mentioned is among the necessitating factors of listening and of the command to it. The lam in His words, glorified is He: ﴿to what is revealed﴾ is connected to (istama'a). It was also permitted that it be connected to (ikhtarnāka). Abu Hayyan rejected this, saying that in that case it would be of the type of "al-a'mal" (the cases of two verbs governing one complement), and it would then be necessary, or preferable, to repeat the pronoun with the second, by saying: "fa-istami' lahu lima yuha" (so listen to Him to what is revealed).

It was answered that what is meant is the permissibility of connecting it to either of the two verbs alternatively, not that it is of the type of "al-a'mal." It was objected to this that the words of the Exalted

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 14:**

﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me﴾ is in apposition (badal) to (what is revealed) [﴿مَا يُوحَى﴾]. There is no doubt that His choosing him (peace be upon him) is not for this alone, and the connection with "We have chosen you" (ikhtarnaka) requires it in whatever way it is. It is answered that this is from the category of explicit statement (tansis) on what is most important and the fundamental root. It has also been said: it is a sword-like (sayf khatib) [i.e., a separate, independent sentence] and so it has no connected element, as in ﴿radifa lakum﴾, and (ma) is a relative pronoun.

It is permitted that it be a verbal-noun (masdariyyah) [ma], meaning: "So listen to what is revealed to you," or "to the revelation." In His command to him (peace be upon him) to listen there is an indication of the magnitude of that and that it requires preparation for it. Abu al-Fadl al-Jawhari said: When Musa (peace be upon him) was told "Listen to what is revealed," he stood upon a stone, leaned against a stone, placed his right hand upon his left, let his chin rest upon his chest, and gave his whole attention (asgha bi-shara'shirihi).

Wahb said: The etiquette of listening is the stillness of the limbs, lowering the gaze, attentive hearing, presence of mind, and resolve to act. That is the listening to what Allah, the Exalted, loves. The omission of the agent in (yuha) is because it is known, and its being a fasilah (verse-end) beautifies it, for if it were in the active voice it would not be a fasilah. The fa' in His words, the Exalted, ﴿fa'budni﴾ is for the ordering of the commanded matter upon what precedes it, for the exclusivity of divinity to Him, the Exalted in His majesty, is among the requirements of specifying worship to Him, the Mighty and Majestic. Its meaning is the utmost humility and submission to Him, the Exalted, in all that He obligates. It has been said: the meaning of it here is tawhid, as in His words, glory be to Him, ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾. The first is preferable. ﴿And establish the prayer﴾: prayer is singled out for mention and given a separate command, although it is included in the command to worship, because of its excellence and its superiority over the other acts of worship, by what is connected to it of remembrance of the Worshipped and occupying the heart and tongue with His remembrance. Allah, the Exalted, has named it faith in His words, glory be to Him: ﴿And Allah would not have let your faith be lost﴾.

The scholars differed regarding the disbelief of one who abandons it out of laziness, as is detailed in its proper place. His words, the Exalted, ﴿for My remembrance﴾: the apparent meaning is that it is connected to "establish," i.e., establish the prayer so that you remember Me in it, because it includes the remembrances (adhkar). This is narrated from Mujahid. Close to this is what has been said: that is, so that you may be one who remembers Me, not forgetful, in the manner of the sincere ones who keep the remembrance of their Lord in mind and entrust their resolve and thoughts to it. He distinguished between the two by saying that the meaning of establishment in the first is the balancing of the pillars (ta'dil al-arkan), and in the second it is persistence (idamah). In the first, the prayer is made a place and abode of remembrance and its cause; in the second, the establishment of prayer, i.e., its persistence, is made a cause of the persistence of remembrance, as if it were said: persist in the prayer so that you may seek help through it in absorbing your thought and concern in remembrance, as in His words, the Exalted: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾. It is also permitted that it be connected to "worship Me" or to "establish," on the basis that it belongs to the category of actions (bab al-a'mal), i.e., so that you may be one who remembers Me through worship and establishing the prayer. If remembrance is generalized to include the heart's and the body's, it is permissible to consider the category of actions in the first as well, though this is contrary to the apparent meaning.

It has been said: the meaning is "establish the prayer for My remembrance" specifically, that you do not show off by it nor mix it with the remembrance of other than Me; or for the sincerity of My remembrance and seeking My face, and do not intend by it another aim, as in His words, the Exalted, ﴿So pray to your Lord﴾; or so that I may mention you with praise, i.e., that I may praise you and reward you by it; or for My remembrance of it in the divine books and My command to it; or for the times of My remembrance, which are the appointed times of the prayers. In that case the lam is temporal, meaning "at," like its use in His words, the Exalted, ﴿Would that I had sent forth for my life﴾, and your saying: "That happened on the fifth night after they had passed." Some people understood the remembrance as the remembrance of the prayer after forgetting it, and this was narrated from Abu Ja'far. In that case the lam is either temporal or causal, and the meaning is "establish the prayer at the time of remembering it," or "because of remembering it," and the speech is according to an elided noun, the original being "for the remembrance of My prayer." Or it may be said: the remembrance of the prayer is a cause of the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted, so the effect is used to denote the cause. Or the pronoun of Allah the Exalted has been placed in the position of the pronoun of the prayer, because of its nobility. Or the meaning is for the remembrance that arises from Me, so the remembrance is attributed to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because of this association. What led the one who said this to this interpretation is that it is established in the Sahih, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, that he (ﷺ) slept through the Fajr prayer, and when he made it up he said: "Whoever forgets a prayer, let him perform it when he remembers it, for Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Establish the prayer for My remembrance﴾." That speaker thought that if this interpretation were not adopted, the causal reading would not be valid, and this is some of the mistaken assumption, for the causal reading, as in al-Kashf, is valid, and the remembrance is as explained in the first aspect, and he (peace and blessings be upon him) intended that when one remembers the prayer, one moves from remembering it to remembering that for which it was legislated, which is the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted, and so he takes it to mean establishing it. Some of the researchers said: since the ultimate purpose of the prayer is the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted, which is always a sought-after objective at every time, when the specified time for it is missed, one should hasten to it as much as possible. This is from the indication of the text, not its explicit wording, so that it does not need strained interpretation. Understand this.

The attachment of (dhikr) to the pronoun may be an idafah of the verbal noun to its object, or an idafah of the verbal noun to its subject, according to the difference in interpretation.

Al-Sulami, al-Nakha'i and Abu Raja' read (lil-dhikra) with the definite article and the feminine alif; a group read (lidhikri) with the feminine alif without the definite article; and another group read (lil-dhikri) with the definite article and the masculine form.

And His saying, ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming﴾, is a reason (ta'lil) for the obligation of worship and the establishment of prayer, meaning: it will certainly occur. He expressed it with "coming" (al-ityan) to affirm its occurrence, by presenting it in the form of a certain matter directed toward those addressed. ﴿I almost conceal it﴾ means: I am near to concealing the Hour and not disclosing it, by saying that it is coming. Were it not that informing them of it contains kindness and removes excuses, I would not have done so. Its summary is: "I almost go to the extreme in concealing it, so I do not state it in detail, just as I have not specified it." The approximation (al-muqaraba) here is metaphorical (majaz), as Abu Hayyan explicitly stated. Or it is intended: the concealment of its specific time and not disclosing it. To this view went al-Akhfash, Ibn al-Anbari and Abu Muslim. Also, there is the use of kada in the sense of arada (to intend), as Ibn Jinni mentioned in al-Muhtasib, citing the verse:

"Kadat wa kidtu, and that is the best intention, / Were the past times of the passion's frivolity to return."

It is narrated from Ibn Abbas and Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the meaning is "I almost conceal it from myself." This is supported by the fact that in the codex of Ubayy it reads so, and Ibn Khalawayh narrated from him that with the addition "so how shall I make you know of it?" And in some readings with the addition "so how shall I make it manifest to you?" And in the codex of Abdullah with the addition "so how shall any created being know it?" This is to be understood according to the custom of the Arabs, that when one of them wishes to emphasize the concealment of something, he says: "I almost conceal it from myself." Among that is the verse:

"Days when Hind accompanies me, and I inform her / of news that I almost hid from myself."

Similar to this in exaggeration is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith of the seven whom Allah shades under His shade: "A man who gave charity and concealed it, until his left hand does not know what his right hand spends."

By taking that as a case of exaggeration, the objection is dispelled that concealing it from Himself, Glorified is He, is impossible, so it is not appropriate for kada to be applied to it. There is no need for what is said: "The meaning of 'from myself' is 'of My own accord' and 'from Me'; the indication of this omitted element is its affirmation in the codices, and its being an external indication does no harm, since it is not required that the indication be present in the speech." It is also said: the evidence for it is that "ukhfiha" must have an object, namely that from which it is concealed. It cannot be from the creation, because He, Exalted is He, concealed it from them, as His saying, Glorified is He, indicates: ﴿Indeed, Allah has with Him the knowledge of the Hour﴾. So what was mentioned is determined. In this there is the point that the non-validity of estimating "from the creation" is disputed, since it is permissible that the intention is the concealment of its details and its specification, along with the fact that it is permissible that no object is estimated for it, and the meaning is: "I bring about its concealment, and I do not say: it is coming."

Abu Ali said: The meaning is "I almost manifest it," with the verb "ukhfi" used in the sense of negation (min alfaz al-salb), meaning: "I remove its concealment," that is, its covering. Originally, it is that with which a waterskin or the like is wrapped, such as a cloth and what is similar to it. Among that is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"If you bury the disease, we shall not conceal it, / And if you kindle war, we shall not sit idle."

This is supported by the reading of Abu al-Darda, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Humayd, and it is narrated from Ibn Kathir and Asim: (ukhfiha) with a fatha on the hamza. For "khafahu" in the sense of "azharahu" (he manifested it) is, according to the well-known view, the only usage. Abu Ubayda, as transmitted by Abu al-Khattab, one of the leaders of the language, said: "khafaytu" and "akhfaytu" have one meaning. The object of concealment, according to the aforementioned way of explaining the reading of the majority, and that of manifestation, are not one thing, so that the two readings do not contradict each other.

A group said: the predicate (khabar) of kada is omitted: "I almost come with it," as it is omitted in the saying of Sabi al-Burjumi:

"I resolved and did not act, and I almost did, would that I had left his wives weeping over Uthman."

Meaning: "and I almost acted." The speech is complete, then he resumed with informing that He, Exalted is He, conceals it. Al-Nahhas preferred this view. Another group said: "akad" is superfluous (za'ida), having no bearing on the meaning; rather the intention is informing that the Hour is coming and that Allah, Exalted is He, conceals the time of its coming. This meaning was narrated from Ibn Jubayr. They argued for the superfluity of kada by His saying: ﴿He almost did not see it﴾, and by the saying of Zayd al-Khayl:

"Swift to battle, his weapon ready, / Yet his opponent scarcely breathes."

There is no proof in this, as is not hidden.

﴿So that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives for﴾: the phrase (li-tujza) is related to (atiya), as said by the author of al-Lawami' and others, and what comes between them is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD), not a qualifier, so that there would be no need to make the active participle that is qualified operate, which is impermissible according to the view of the Basrans. Or it is related to (ukhfiha), on the basis that the intended meaning is "I manifest it," not "I conceal it," because there is no sense in your saying, "I conceal it for the sake of recompense." Some permitted that, with the reasoning that obscuring its time makes one wait moment by moment, so one guards against sin and strives in obedience. This was objected to as an evident forced interpretation (takalluf), and moreover it has no validity except by estimating "so that he waits for the recompense" or "so that he fears and dreads." "Ma" is a verbal-source particle (masdariyya), i.e., "for recompense by its striving and its deed, if good, then good, and if evil, then evil." This generality is the apparent meaning. It is also said: "so that it is recompensed by its striving in attaining what has been mentioned of the matters commanded," and the specifying of it in the context of purpose for its coming, though it is for the recompense of every soul according to what proceeds from it, whether it was striving in what has been mentioned or complete abstention from it, or striving in attaining its opposite, is to signal that the primary purpose of its coming is the reward for worship; as for punishment for abandoning it, that is a consequence of the bad choice of the disobedient. And also that what is commanded is in the force of obligation, and the Hour is in such intensity of terror and horror that both require of every soul that it strive to comply with the command and earnestly seek to attain what saves it from the acts of obedience, and guard against committing what destroys it of acts of disobedience. End.

And what is in it is not hidden. It is also said: "ma" is a relative pronoun (mawsula), meaning: "by that in which it strives." In this there is the deletion of the returning pronoun governed by the preposition, together with the absence of its condition. It may be answered that the speaker may not stipulate that condition. It is also said: one estimates it as an accusative object by way of extension (tawassu').

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 16:

﴿So let not one who does not believe in it and follows his desire divert you from it, lest you perish.﴾ This is an address to Musa, peace be upon him. Some have claimed that it is addressed to our Prophet (ﷺ) in wording, while its meaning concerns his community, but this is extremely remote. ﴿From it﴾ means: from the Hour; what is intended is "from mentioning it and being mindful of it." It was also said: "from believing in its coming." The first view was preferred, because it is most fitting to the station of Musa, peace be upon him, even though the prohibition is in the manner of stirring up and inciting. The return of the pronoun in "from it" to the Hour is the apparent meaning, and likewise the return of the pronoun in "in it" in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿who does not believe in it﴾. It was also said: both pronouns refer to the prayer. It was said: the pronoun in "from it" refers to the prayer, and the pronoun in "in it" refers to the Hour. It was said: both pronouns refer to the phrase ﴿There is no god but Me﴾. It was said: the first refers to worship and the second refers to the Hour. It was said: both refer to the qualities mentioned. The placing of the prepositional phrase before the subject is for the reason already mentioned more than once: concern with what is placed first and arousing anticipation for what is delayed, and because a delayed element carries a kind of length which its fronting might disturb the eloquence of the noble composition. And the prohibition, although on its apparent reading it is a prohibition to the disbeliever against diverting Musa, peace be upon him, from the Hour, is in reality a prohibition to him, peace be upon him, against being diverted from it in the most eloquent and emphatic manner. For the prohibition against the causes and beginnings of a thing that lead to it is a prohibition against it by demonstrative method, and a nullification of causation at its root, as in His words: ﴿Let not [their hatred] incite you﴾ and so on. For the disbeliever's diverting him, insofar as it would be a cause of his being diverted, peace be upon him, the prohibition against it is a prohibition against its very origin and its ground, and a complete nullification of it. It is permissible that it be a prohibition against the cause, on the basis that what is meant is his prohibition, peace be upon him,
page 174
from displaying gentleness of demeanour toward the disbelievers, for that is a cause of their diverting him, peace be upon him, just as in the saying: "Let me not see you here," where what is meant is the prohibition of the addressee from being present before him, which would bring about seeing him. So it is as if it were said: be firm of resolve and hard of forehead, so that there appears in you no softness to one who disbelieves in the Hour and denies the Resurrection such that he hopes to divert you from what you are upon. Therein is an exhortation to firmness in religion and to avoiding the softness that gives hope to whoever disbelieves ﴿and follows his desire﴾, that is, what his soul desires of sensual, perishable pleasures, so that it diverts him from faith. ﴿Lest you perish﴾, that is, lest you be destroyed, for neglect of the Hour and of acquiring what saves one from its states necessarily entails destruction.

Al-Allama al-Tibi mentioned that it is possible to understand ﴿one who does not believe﴾ as one who turns away from the worship of God, Exalted is He, who is consumed by the world and immersed in its pleasures and desires, as indicated by "and follows" and so on; and the prohibition of diverting may be understood as a prohibition against gazing at its enjoyments, the splendour of the worldly life, so that it is in the manner of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses] and the great Qur'an﴾, ﴿Do not extend your eyes toward what We have given to pairs of them﴾ and so on. And following desire may be understood as inclination to settle upon the earth, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿But he inclined toward the earth and followed his desire﴾. The meaning is: devote yourself to My worship, and do not turn toward what the disbelievers are engaged in, for it is destructive; what We have bestowed upon you and chosen for you is the highest aim. In this is a great exhortation to occupation with worship and a forceful deterrent from inclining to the world and its delights. It is not free of beauty, although it is contrary to the apparent meaning.

﴿Fa-tarda﴾ may be read as accusative, as an answer to the prohibition, or as nominative, the clause then being the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "so you perish because of that." Yahya read ﴿fa-tirda﴾ with a kasra on the ta'.

This is the start of the narration of the matters entrusted to him (peace be upon him) that concern creation, following the narration of the matters specific to himself that he was commanded to carry out. Here *mā* is interrogative, in the nominative position as the subject (*mubtada'*), and *tilka* is its predicate (*khabar*). Or the reverse, and this is more suitable in meaning and better fits the answer. *Bi-yamīnika* is attached to an implied verb that functions as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from *tilka*, meaning: "What is that which is held or taken in your right hand?" The governing element is the sense of pointing contained in the demonstrative, as in His words, mighty and exalted, in narration: ﴿And this is my husband, an old man﴾ (Q. 11:72). Grammarians call this a *ʿāmil maʿnawī* (a governing element that is meaning-based rather than a verb or particle).

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: *tilka* is a relative pronoun (*ism mawṣūl*), and *bi-yamīnika* is attached to an omitted element that serves as its relative clause, meaning: "What is that which is situated in your right hand?" This is according to the view of the Kufans, who hold that every demonstrative noun may be a relative pronoun. The view of the Basrans is that this is not permitted except with *dhā* under its conditions. The interrogative here is for confirmation (*taqrīr*), and the explanation of its intended meaning will come shortly, God willing, Exalted is He.

[Page 175]

﴿He said, "It is my staff."﴾ He attributed it to himself, peace be upon him, to confirm that it was in his right hand, and as a preface to the actions attributed to him that follow. Its name, according to what is related from Muqatil, was Nab'ah. Peace be upon him had taken it from the house of the staves of the prophets, peace be upon them, which had been with Shu'ayb when he hired him to tend the flock. Adam, peace be upon him, had brought it down from Paradise, and it was said to be of myrtle (ās). Wahb said: it was of 'awsaj (a thorny shrub), and its length was ten cubits, equal to his height, peace be upon him. It was also said: twelve cubits by the cubit of Musa, peace be upon him.

He mentioned the musnad ilayh (the predicate's subject, i.e. "it") though it is the original element, because of his desire, peace be upon him, for intimate converse and his increased delight in it. Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-Jahdari read ﴿عَصِيَّ﴾ (ʿaṣiyya), by changing the alif into a yā' and assimilating it into the yā' of the first person, according to the dialect of Hudhayl, for they change the alif that precedes the yā' of the first person into a yā' for harmony, just as what precedes it is kasra-ed in the sound form. Their poet said:

"They preceded my desire and loved their own desires, so they were cut off, and for every side there is a place of fall."

al-Hasan read ﴿عَصايَ﴾ with a kasra on the bā' (ʿaṣāy)... and this is also narrated from Ubayy ibn Ishaq and Abu 'Amr; this kasra is for the meeting of two unvocalized letters, as in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit). From Ibn Abi Ishaq: ﴿عَصايْ﴾ with the yā' sukūn, as if he regarded the waqf (pause) and disregarded the meeting of the two unvocalized letters. The staff is among the feminine nouns that are known only by transmission (samaʿiyya), and the tā' marbūṭa is not attached to it. The first solecism heard in Iraq, as al-Farra' said, was: "hadhihi ʿaṣātī" (this is my staff, with a tā'). It is pluralized as ʿiṣiyy, with the first letter kasra-ed or damma-ed, and as uʿṣ and aʿṣāʾ.

﴿I lean upon it﴾, that is, I lean heavily on it in walking, in standing at the head of the flock, and the like.

﴿And I beat down with it﴾, that is, I strike with it the leaves of the trees and beat them so that they fall ﴿upon my sheep﴾ so that they may eat them. al-Nakha'i read it as Abu al-Fadl al-Razi mentioned, and Ibn 'Atiyya (read) ﴿أهِشُّ﴾ (ahišš) with a kasra on the hā'; its meaning is the same as that with a damma on the hā', and on both readings the object is omitted, as we have indicated.

Abu al-Fadl said: It may be that this is from hashsha, yahushshu, hashāshatan, when it inclined, that is, I incline it toward my sheep, by what sets it right of driving them and shaking down the leaves for them to eat, and the like. It is said: the leaves, the herbage and the plants "hashsha" when they dry and become soft and finish. On this view there is no omission. al-Hasan and ʿIkrima read ﴿أهُشُّ﴾ with a damma on the hā' and the unpointed sīn, from al-hass, which is driving the sheep. Its transitivity with ʿalā is because it implies the sense of inḥāʾ (driving toward and raising over); it is said: "unaḥḥī ʿalayhi bi-l-ʿaṣā" when one raises the staff over him, feigning a strike, i.e. "I drive them, raising it over them." In the book Kitab al-Sin wa-l-Shin by the author of al-Qamus it is said: "hassa al-shay'" and "hashshahu" when he crushed and broke it, and they have the same meaning. Ibn Khalawayh related from al-Nakha'i that he read ﴿أهُشُّ﴾ from ahashsha (the quadriliteral form).

The author of al-Lawami' mentioned from ʿIkrima and Mujahid ﴿أُهِشُ﴾ with a damma on the hā' and lightening of the shīn with a dot, then said: "I do not know its meaning, except that it may be with the sense of ahušš with doubling, but he fled from it because the shīn in it is spread (tafashshin), so doubling and spreading together were considered heavy, and so it is like the lightening of ẓalta and the like." And this is in the utmost remoteness. A group read ﴿غَنَمِي﴾ with the sukūn on the nūn, and others (read) ﴿عَلى غَنَمِي﴾ on the basis that ʿalā is a preposition with its object, and ﴿غَنَمِي﴾ is the explicit object of the preceding verb. I have not found mention of how this group read that verb; on the reading of the majority it is not evident that it is transitive to the sheep, and likewise on the readings of others except with some forced effort. The ghanam is the sheep (shāh), a feminine noun assigned to the genus, applying to males and females alike, and there is no singular from its own form; its singular is shāh. When you diminutive it you say ghunayma with the tā' marbūṭa, and it is pluralized as aghnām, ghunūm and aghānim. They also say ghunmān in the dual, meaning two pieces.

He, peace be upon him, placed first the statement of the benefit to himself in his saying "I lean upon it," and he followed it with the benefit to his flock in his saying "And I beat down with it upon my sheep." Perhaps that is because he, peace be upon him, was recently engaged in leaning, so it came first to his mind, and the beating down upon his flock came next.

Imam Ahmad related that after his Lord, glorified is He, had called to him and he realized that He, exalted is He, was the one calling, He, glorified is He, said to him: "Come near to Me." So he gathered his hands upon the staff, then leaned heavily until he stood upright. His muscles trembled until they were in disorder, his legs shook, his tongue was cut off, and his heart broke; not one bone of him was left that could bear another, so he was like one dead except that the spirit of life flowed in him. Then he crept, terrified, until he stopped near the tree from which he had been called. The Lord, blessed and exalted, said to him: "What is that in your right hand, O Musa?"

He answered as the Mighty and Majestic related. It was said: perhaps the mention of leaning on it came first because it fits the question "what is that in your right hand," then he, peace be upon him, described its attributes in his saying ﴿And I have in it other uses﴾, that is: other needs, and its singular is ma'raba, with the rā' having three vowels. In the description it was treated as if it were singular, so he did not say "ukhar" (plural), and that is permissible outside the fawasil (verse-endings) and within them, as here, is more permissible and better.

al-Ahwazi related in the book al-Iqna' from al-Zuhri and Shayba that they both read ﴿مَآرِبُ﴾ without a hamza, and perhaps he means without a clear hamza; its substance is that they softened the hamza to an intermediate sound (bayn bayn). Imam Ahmad and others related from Wahb concerning the identification of these uses that it had two prongs and a hook beneath them. When a branch grew long he bent it with the hook, and when he wished to break it he twisted it with the two prongs. When he, peace be upon him, wished, he would lay it upon his shoulder and hang upon it his bow, his quiver, his bag, his garment, and provisions if he had any. When he grazed in the wilderness where there was no shade, he would plant it, then lay across its two prongs the two arms (the upper arm and the lower arm), and throw his cloak above it, and he would shade himself beneath it for as long as he was grazing. When he came to water that was beyond the reach of his rope, he joined it to the staff, and he would fight off wild beasts from his sheep with it.

Some have mentioned that he, peace be upon him, would draw water with it, and it would lengthen with the length of the well, and its two prongs would become a bucket, and they would become two candles at night. When an enemy appeared it would fight on his behalf. When he desired fruit he would plant it, and it would put forth leaves and bear fruit. He would load his provisions and a waterskin upon it, and it would walk alongside him. He would plant it and water would spring forth; when he lifted it, the water would dry up. It would protect him from venomous creatures, and it would converse with him and make him feel at ease. al-Tabarsi related much of what is mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them.

The apparent view is that these things were in it afterwards, and some have strained to claim that they were before that. It is possible, if a report on this is authentic, though I do not think anything authentic on it exists. It seems that the purpose of the Exalted's question to him, peace be upon him, was that he should enumerate the many benefits he had attached to the staff, and count them great and magnify them. Then the Exalted showed him after that the great sign, as if the Exalted, glorified is He, were saying: "Where are you from this supreme benefit and great use, in whose presence every benefit and use you regarded and took pride in is forgotten?" So ma here is for the attribute, or the benefit is estimated after it. Choosing what indicates distance in the demonstrative, ﴿تِلْكَ﴾ (that), is for indicating glorification; likewise in the address there is a hint of it, and the enumeration in the answer is for its sake. "Other uses" completes the magnification by saying they are more than can be counted. Mentioning the staff in the answer serves to attach to it the praising attributes, and in that there is a magnification of its status that is absent if its mention were omitted. With this is answered what is raised as an objection, that on this view it would follow that ﴿It is my staff﴾ is an unnecessary addition, since it has no bearing on the enumeration of benefits.

It is also possible that the intent was for him, peace be upon him, to show its insignificance, so that the Mighty and Majestic might show him the magnitude of what He creates in a dry piece of wood, which indicates His dazzling power, glorified is He, just as is the practice of one who wishes to display something great from a lowly thing: he presents it to those present and says, "What is this?" They say, "It is such-and-such a thing," and they describe it in terms far from what he wishes to display in it, then he displays that. So ma here is for the genus, and ﴿تِلْكَ﴾ is for belittling, and the enumeration in the answer is for its sake. "Other uses" completes that as well, indicating that what is left unsaid is of the same kind as what is said, so it is as if he, peace be upon him, had said: "It is a dry piece of wood that benefits only with the benefits of all other pieces of wood." For this reason he, peace be upon him, mentioned the staff and applied to it what he applied.

It was also said: when he, peace be upon him, saw of the signs of his Lord what he saw, awe and dread overcame him, so He, glorified is He, asked him and spoke with him to remove that awe and dread. So ma is either for the attribute or for the genus, and the repetition of the address is to increase intimacy. Perhaps the choice of what indicates distance in the demonstrative is to place the staff in the position of the distant, because of his, peace be upon him, heedlessness of it through what overcame him of that. The vagueness in his saying ﴿And I have in it other uses﴾ may be a hope that He, glorified is He, would ask him about those uses, so that he would hear the speech of the Mighty and Majestic once more; the conversation would be prolonged and the delight for which he had lengthened at first would increase. How sweet is the conversation of the Beloved! Hence it was said:

"He recounted a discourse that is sweet, would that I had committed sins so that His reproach might be long."

It may also be that the dread returned to him, peace be upon him. Some have claimed that He, exalted is He, asked him, peace be upon him, to confirm that it was a piece of wood, so that when he turned it into a serpent he would not fear it; but that is nothing. On all these views the question is one and the answer is one, as is evident. It was said: ﴿I lean upon it﴾ and so on is an answer to a different question, namely that when he said ﴿It is my staff﴾, He said to him: "What do you do with it?" So he said: ﴿I lean upon it﴾ and so on. It was said: He, exalted is He, asked him about two things concerning the staff: by His saying, glorified is He, ﴿And what is that﴾, and about what he possesses of it by His saying, exalted and majestic is He, "in your right hand." He, peace be upon him, answered the first with "It is my staff," and the second with "I lean upon it" and so on. It is not hidden that neither of these two statements should be leaned upon, especially the last.

This is what has been said. The verse has been cited as evidence for the recommendation of leaning on a staff even if the person is not one whose bow needs a string, and for the recommendation of moderation in pasturing by beating down (hashsh), which is striking the tree so the leaves fall without uprooting it, so that it may regenerate and others may benefit from it.

The Imam (al-Razi) has mentioned in it benefits, some of which we shall mention in the section on the allusive (ishara), for that is more suitable to it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 19–20:

﴿Said﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) answering a question that naturally arises in the mind, as if it were said: "Then what did Allah, Mighty and Majestic, say, so that it was answered?" He said: ﴿Throw it down, O Musa﴾, so that you may see of its affair what you will see. And al-ilqa' (casting, throwing) is to cast on the ground, and from it is the poet's saying:

"So she cast down her staff, and the seeds settled in it, just as the traveler's eye is cooled by returning home."

The repetition of the address is for the sake of further alerting and emphasis concerning the affair of the staff. That the speaker of this is Allah, exalted is He, is the apparent meaning. Some claimed that the speaker could be the angel (malik) by the command of Allah, exalted is He, but he has gone to the utmost extreme of remoteness. ﴿So he threw it down﴾ immediately after he was told, "Throw it down." ﴿Then behold, it was a serpent moving swiftly﴾: it walked and moved quickly.
