The word hayyah (serpent) is a generic noun applied to the small and the large, the female and the male. It had changed, when he (peace be upon him) threw it, into a thu'ban, which is the great one among serpents, as His saying, exalted is He, clarifies: ﴿Then behold, it was a manifest serpent﴾. Its being likened to a jann, which is the small one among them, in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿When he saw it moving as if it were a jann﴾, is in respect of its boldness and speed of movement, not in respect of the smallness of its body, so there is no contradiction. It was also said: when he (peace be upon him) threw it, it changed into a yellow serpent, as thick as the staff, then it swelled and grew thicker, and for this reason it was likened to a jann at one time and called a thu'ban at another; and it was described by the general name for both states. The first view is the most fitting to the context, given the evident requirement of the verse we mentioned and its distance from interpretation.

Imam Ahmad and others have related from Wahb that he (peace be upon him) glanced at it after he had thrown it, and behold, it was the greatest serpent that onlookers had ever seen: it was moving as if seeking something it wished to seize; it passed by a rock like a herd of she-camels, swallowed it, and struck with a fang from its teeth at the root of a great tree, uprooting it. Its two eyes were blazing with fire, its hooked part had become a crest with hair like shooting stars, and its two forks were like a wide well, having molars and fangs that gnashed.

In some reports it is said that between its two jaws there was forty cubits. When Musa (peace be upon him) witnessed this, he turned back fleeing and did not look back, and he went on until he had gone far, and he saw that he had overcome the serpent.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 21:

Then He mentioned His Lord, glorified is He, and he stopped out of shyness before Him, mighty and majestic is He. Then he was called: "O Musa, (to Me) return to where you were." So he returned, and he was in great fear. Then the Glorified and Exalted commanded him to take it, which is what Allah related in His saying, mighty is He, saying: ﴿He said﴾, i.e., Allah, mighty and majestic is He, and the sentence is a resumption (istinaf), as has preceded. ﴿Take it﴾, i.e., the serpent, and it was, as related from Ibn 'Abbas, male. And from Wahb: that He, exalted is He, said to him: "Take it with your right hand." ﴿And do not fear﴾ from it. Perhaps that fear was of what human nature necessitates, for the human being by the disposition of his nature fears upon witnessing the like of that, and this does not contradict the greatness of his rank.

It has been said: he, peace be upon him, feared only because he saw a tremendous matter issuing from Allah, mighty and majestic is He, without intermediary, and did not comprehend the reality of the matter. This is not like the fire of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, because that fire issued at the hand of the enemy of Allah, exalted is He, and its reality was like a fire on a sign (a mark), so Ibrahim, peace be upon him, did not fear from it as Musa, peace be upon him, feared from the serpent. It has also been said: he feared because he knew what had befallen that kind (the serpent kind) from it, since it had a part in the expulsion of his father from the Garden. The prohibition was conjoined to the command to indicate that the absence of what is forbidden is intended for its own sake, not merely to realize what is commanded. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We shall return it﴾, i.e., after taking it, ﴿to its former state﴾, i.e., its condition, ﴿which is the staff﴾. It is a resumption (istinaf) given to explain the compliance with the command and the prohibition, for returning it to what it was is among the requirements of taking it and of not fearing it. As for the claim that in this, together with that, there is a noble promise by showing another miracle at his hand, peace be upon him, and a notification that it is subjugated to him, peace be upon him, so that he would be at peace regarding his matter and no doubt would afflict him that would shake him at the disputation with Pharaoh, it is not free from obscurity. Some have mentioned that the wisdom of its transformation into a serpent, his command to take it, and his prohibition from fear is to comfort him regarding what Allah, glorified is He, knows will befall him from Pharaoh. Perhaps this is the basis of that claim.

It has been said: at this address, peace be upon him, reached such a degree of trust and absence of fear that he would put his hand into its mouth and grasp its jaws. In the narration of Imam Ahmad and others from Wahb: when Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to take it, he lowered the edge of the woolen cloak which was upon him, having loosened it with threads of reeds, over his hand. An angel said to him: "Do you see, O Musa, if Allah, exalted is He, permitted what you fear, would the cloak avail you anything?" He said: "No, but I am weak, and I was created of weakness." So he uncovered his hand, then placed it upon the mouth of the serpent until he heard the sound of the molars and the fangs, then he seized it, and behold, it was his staff which he knew, and behold, his hand was in its place where he used to place it when he leaned between the two prongs.

The first narration is more suited to his lofty station, peace be upon him.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he, peace be upon him, was called the first time: "O Musa, take it," and he did not take it. Then he was called the second time: ﴿Take it and do not fear﴾, and he did not take it. Then he was called the third time: ﴿Indeed, you are among the secure﴾, and he took it. Makki mentioned in his tafsir that it was said to him in the third time: ﴿We shall return it to its former state﴾. It is not hidden that what has been mentioned is far from the station of prophethood, so perhaps the report is not sound.

Al-sira (the state, the manner) is a form (fi'la) from al-sayr (going), said of the condition and state in which a thing is; then it was generalized to the mere condition and state in which a thing is. Among this is its use in the sense of the way and the method, as in their saying: "the sira of the predecessors" (sirat al-salaf), and the saying of the poet:

"So do not be angry at a sira you yourself have followed; the first to be pleased with a sira is the one who follows it."

It has been differed over the parsing of its accusative in the verse. It has been said: it is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, the original being "ila sirataha" or "li-sirataha," and this is common, though they said it is not analogical. This is the apparent view of al-Hufi, that it is a second object of nu'idu-ha, with the preposition elided, like ﴿and Musa chose his people﴾. Ibn Malik went to this and approved it, and Ibn Hisham endorsed it. Al-Zamakhshari allowed that it may be ('ada) transitivized from 'ada, meaning 'ada ilayhi (returned to it), and from it is the saying of Zuhayr:

"So sever her rope, since she has severed it, and your return (to her) is that meeting her is hostility."

It then transitivizes to two objects. The apparent view is that this is other than the first parsing, because of considering transitivization in it, and the preposition is elided from a'ada without regard to its triliteral form, and 'ada transitivizes by itself when transitivization has been confirmed. Al-Tibi related from al-Asma'i that 'ada-ka in the verse is transitive in the sense of sarafaka (turned you away), and likewise al-Fadil al-Yamani related. In al-Mughrib: al-'awd is becoming, first and again, and it transitivizes by itself, and with ila, 'ala, fi, and li.

Page 179

In Mashariq al-Lugha by al-Qadi 'Iyad, the same is stated, and from the hadith is related: "Have you returned a fitna-causer, O Mu'adh?"

Abu al-Baqa said: it is a substitute for the object pronoun, a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal), and he allowed that the accusative may be adverbial (zarfiyya), i.e., "We shall return it in its first way."

Abu Hayyan criticized him, saying: sirataha and tariqataha are a restricted adverb, so the verb does not reach it in the adverbial manner except through the mediation of fi, and elision is not permitted except in necessity or in what the Arabs have made anomalous. The summary is that the condition of adverbial accusative here, which is indefiniteness (ibham), is absent. In the Sharh al-Tashil from the grammarians of the Maghrib, they divided the indefinite into categories, among them what is derived from the verb, like al-madhhab, and the verbal noun placed in the position of the adverb, such as qasdaka, and they did not distinguish between that ending in ta' and other. So the adverbial accusative in what has been mentioned is not anomalous nor necessary. Al-Zamakhshari allowed, and found it good, that "We shall return it" be independent in itself, not connected to sirataha, meaning that it was created first as a staff, then it went away and became a serpent by transformation, so "We shall return it" after the going, as We created it first; and "its former state" is accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of an elided verb, i.e., "it shall go its former course," that is, "We shall return it going in its former course, where you used to lean upon it and beat your flock with it, and you had in it the benefits you know." End.

The apparent view is that he made the sentence, from the elided verb and its agent, a circumstantial clause (hal), and it may be a resumption. You should not be unaware that what he mentioned, though good in meaning, is contrary to what is apparent.

This, and the verse is clear on the permissibility of a thing's transformation from its reality, like the transformation of copper into gold, and this is said by a group. There is no obstacle, in power, to the directing of the creative command to that, and the specification of will for it. It has been said: it is not permitted, because the reversal of realities is impossible and power does not relate to it. The first truth is in the sense that Allah, exalted is He, creates in place of copper, for example, gold, according to the view of some verifiers; or by stripping the parts of copper of the attribute by which it became copper and creating in it the attribute by which it becomes gold.

(According to the view of some theologians, from the homogeneity of substances and their equal receptivity of attributes; the impossible is only its becoming gold while being copper, because it is impossible for a thing to be copper and gold at the same time. The transformation of the staff into a serpent occurred by one of these two considerations, and Allah, exalted is He, knows best which of them it was. What I incline to is the second, for in the creation of a substitute being a transformation there is an obscurity, as is not hidden.)

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Draw your hand to your side﴾. This is a command to him, peace be upon him, after he had taken the serpent and it had turned back into a staff as it was. *Al-dammu* means gathering together. *Al-janah* (wing), as in the *Qamus* (the lexicon *al-Qamus al-Muhit*), means the hand, the upper arm, the armpit, the side, and the essence of a thing. Its plural is *ajniha* and *ajnuh*. In *al-Bahr* (*al-Bahr al-Muhit* of Abu Hayyan), *al-janah* is literally the wing of a bird or of a king, and then it was extended to mean the hand, the upper arm, and the side of a man.

It has also been said that the two flanks of an army are called its two wings, by way of metaphor (*isti'arah*, a figure in which a word is used for something other than its literal meaning on the basis of a resemblance). The wing of a bird is so named because it inclines (*yujnihuhu*) it, that is, tilts it, when flying. The intended meaning is: insert your right hand through the opening of your coat of mail and place it beneath the armpit of your left side, or beneath its upper arm near the armpit, or beneath it at the armpit. There is then no contradiction between this and His saying: ﴿And insert your hand into your bosom﴾ and ﴿It will come out white, without evil﴾.

Some have held that *yakhruj* (it will come out) is in the jussive mood (*majzum*, the mood of a verb after a command or condition) as a response to the command mentioned, on the understanding that *idkhal* (insert) carries the sense of insertion. Abu Hayyan and others said: it is in the jussive mood as the response to an implied command, and the original sense of the speech is: draw your hand in, and it will be drawn in; and bring it out, and it will come out. The first clause's response was omitted, and the second clause's command was omitted, while what indicates each is retained in the other. This is a concision called *al-ihtibak* (a form of ellipsis in which each of two parallel elements omits a part that the other supplies).

The accusative of *bayda'* (white) is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) from the pronoun in *takhruj*. The prepositional phrase *min ghayri su'in* is either attached to a hidden element that serves as a circumstantial phrase from the pronoun in *bayda'*, or it is a qualifier of *bayda'* as al-Hufi stated, or it is attached to it as Abu Hayyan stated, as though it were said: it turned white without evil, or it is attached to *takharruj* (coming out), as more than one scholar has permitted.

*Al-su'* means badness and ugliness in anything. It is used as a euphemism for leprosy (*baras*), just as *al-sau'ah* is used as a euphemism for nakedness (*al-'awrah*), because natures recoil from it and ears reject it. It is the most hateful thing among the Arabs. For this reason they used euphemisms for Judhaymah, the companion of al-Zabba', who was leprous, calling him "the one with the mottled skin" (*al-abrash*) and "the bright one" (*al-wadda*). The purpose of stating the negation of that caution is that if the verse had been limited to His saying ﴿It will come out white﴾, it would have led one to suspect, even if remotely, that this was from leprosy. It is also possible that the caution is against the suspicion of a defect in its coming out from its original form, so that the meaning is: it will come out white without defect or ugliness in that coming out, or against the suspicion of any defect at all.

It is related that it came out white, with a radiance like the radiance of the sun that dazzles the sight, and he, peace be upon him, was of dark complexion.

﴿Another sign﴾, that is, another miracle besides the staff. Its accusative is circumstantial (*hal*) from the pronoun in *takhruj*. The correct view is that it is permissible for a circumstantial phrase to be multiple for a single subject. It may also be from the pronoun in *bayda'*, or from the pronoun in the prepositional phrase, as has been said, or it may be in apposition (*badaliyyah*) to *bayda'*, which returns to being circumstantial from the pronoun in *takhruj*. It is also permissible that it be accusative by a hidden verb, meaning: take a sign, the verb being omitted because the context indicates it.

The apparent sense of al-Zamakhshari's speech is that it is permissible to take *dunaka* (take it, or here is it) as an operating element (*'amil*), and this is based on what appears to be the view of Sibawayh, namely the permissibility of a verbal noun (*ism al-fi'l*) operating when it is omitted. Abu Hayyan rejected this, because it is a substitute for the verb, and a substitute and what it substitutes for are not omitted together. This was objected to on the basis of the vocative particle *ya*, which is omitted although it substitutes for *ad'u* (I call). It has been said that it is a second object of a hidden verb together with its first object, meaning: We made it, or We gave you, another sign. This speaker made His saying, exalted is He:

﴿لِنُرِيَكَ مِن آياتِنا الكُبْرى﴾ متعلِّقًا بذلك المحذوفِ. ومَن قدَّرَ *khudh* (خُذْ) ونحوَه جوَّزَ تعلُّقَه به، وجوَّزَ al-Hufi (الحُوفِيُّ) تعلُّقَه بـ*idmum* (اضْمُمْ)، وتعلُّقَه بـ*takhruj* (تَخْرُجْ)، وأبو al-Baqa' (أبُو البَقاءِ) تعلُّقَه بما دلَّ عليه (*ayah*) (آيَةً)، أي دلَّلْنا بها لِنُرِيَكَ. ومنعَ تعلُّقَه بها لأنها قد وُصِفَتْ.

وبعضُهم علَّقَه بـ*alqi* (ألْقِ)، واختارَ بعضُ المُحقِّقين أنه متعلِّقٌ بمُضْمَرٍ يَنْساقُ إليه النظمُ الكريمُ، كأنه قيل: فعلْنا ما فعلْنا لِنُرِيَكَ بعضَ آياتِنا الكُبْرى، على أنَّ (الكُبْرى) صفةٌ لـ(آياتِنا)، على حدِّ ﴿مَآرِبُ أُخْرى﴾ (*ma'arib ukhra*)، أي على نحو قوله تعالى ﴿مَآرِبُ أُخْرى﴾، و(مِن آياتِنا) في موضع المفعول الثاني، و*min* (مِن) فيه للتبعيض. أو: لِنُرِيَكَ بذلك الكُبْرى مِن آياتِنا، على أنَّ (الكُبْرى) هو المفعولُ الثاني لـ(نُرِيَكَ)، و(مِن آياتِنا) متعلِّقٌ بمحذوفٍ حالٍ منه، و*min* فيه للابتداء أو للتبعيض. وتقديمُ الحالِ مع أنَّ صاحبَه معرفةٌ لِرِعايةِ *al-fawasil* (الفَواصِلِ)، أي رعايةِ انتهاءاتِ الآيات المُسجَّعة. وجوَّزَ كلا الإعرابَيْنِ (*i'rab*)، أي التحليلَ النحويَّ، في ﴿مِن آياتِنا الكُبْرى﴾ al-Hufi (الحُوفِيُّ) وابنُ عطيةَ وأبو البقاءِ وغيرُهم.

واختارَ في *al-Bahr* (البَحْرِ) الإعرابَ الأولَ ورجَّحَه بأنَّ فيه دلالةً على أنَّ آياتِه تعالى كلَّها كُبْرى، بخلافِ الإعرابِ الثاني، وبأنه على الثاني لا تكونُ (الكُبْرى) صفةَ العصا واليدِ معًا، وإلا لَقِيلَ: *al-kubrayayn* (الكُبْرَيَيْنِ)، أي بصيغة المثنى. ولا يمكنُ أن يُخَصَّ أحدُهما، لأنَّ في كلٍّ منهما معنى التفضيلِ. ويَبْعُدُ ما قاله al-Hasan (الحَسَنُ)، ورُوِيَ عن ابنِ عباسٍ رضي الله تعالى عنهما، من أنَّ اليدَ أعظمُ في الإعجازِ من العصا، لأنه ليس في اليدِ إلا تغييرُ اللونِ، وأما العصا ففيها تغييرُ اللونِ، وخلقُ الزيادةِ في الجسمِ، وخلقُ الحياةِ والقدرةِ والأعضاءِ المختلفةِ، مع عَوْدِها عصًا بعد ذلك، فكانت أعظمَ في الإعجازِ من اليدِ. وجُوِّزَ أن تكونَ (الكُبْرى) صفةً لهما، ولاتحادِ المقصودِ جُعِلَتا آيةً واحدةً وأُفْرِدَتِ الصفةُ لذلك. وأن تكونَ صفةً لليدِ والعصا غنيةٌ عن الوصفِ بها لظهورِ كونِها كُبْرى.

وأنتَ تعلمُ أنَّ هذا كلَّه خلافُ الظاهرِ. وكذا ما قيل: مِن أنَّ (مِن) على الإعرابِ الثاني للبيانِ، بأن يكونَ المرادُ: لِنُرِيَكَ الآياتِ الكُبْرى مِن آياتِنا، لِيَصِحَّ الحملُ الذي يقتضيه البيانُ، ولا يترجَّحُ بذلك الإعرابُ الثاني على الأولِ، ولا يُساويهِ أصلًا. ولا يخفى عليك أنَّ كلَّ احتمالٍ من احتمالاتِ متعلِّقِ اللامِ، خلا من الدلالةِ على وصفِ آيةِ

العصا بالكِبَرِ، لا ينبغي أن يُعوَّلَ عليه، ويُعْتَذَرَ بأنَّ عدمَ الوصفِ للظهورِ مع ظهورِ الاحتمالِ الذي لا يحتاجُ معه إلى الاعتذارِ عن ذلك المقالِ. فتأمَّلْ، واللهُ تعالى العاصمُ من الزَّلَلِ.

﴿Go to Pharaoh﴾: this is a transition (takhallus) to the main purpose, after the preliminary matters that preceded it. It is separated from the preceding commands to signal that it is the principal one. That is, go to him with the great signs that you have seen from Us, call him to worship Me, and warn him of My vengeance.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, he has transgressed﴾, is a causal explanation (ta'lil) of the command, or of the obligation of what is commanded. That is, he exceeded the limit in arrogance, rebellion and tyranny, to the point that he dared to claim the great thing, which is the claim of lordship (rububiyyah).

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Allah, exalted is He, said to Musa, peace be upon him: "Come near." He kept bringing him nearer until He supported his back against the trunk of a tree. He settled, the trembling left him, he gathered his hand into the staff, and he lowered his head and neck. Then, after informing him of His blessing upon him, He said to him: "Go forth with My message, for you are before My eyes and within My hearing. Indeed, with you are My hands and My help. I have clothed you with a shield of My authority, by which you will complete your strength in My affair. You are a great soldier of My soldiers. I have sent you to a weak creature of My creation who has been insolent toward My blessing, felt secure from My plan, and been deceived by the world, until he denied My right, rejected My lordship, worshipped others besides Me, and claimed that he does not know Me. By My might, I swear that were it not for the excuse and the proof that I have placed between Me and My creation, I would strike him with the strike of a tyrant, at whose anger the heavens, the earth, the mountains and the seas would be angered. If I commanded the sky, it would pelt him; if I commanded the earth, it would swallow him; if I commanded the seas, they would drown him; if I commanded the mountains, they would destroy him. But he is insignificant to Me, he has fallen from My sight, My forbearance has encompassed him, I am self-sufficient through what I have, and it is right for Me that I am the Self-Sufficient, and there is no self-sufficiency other than Mine. So convey My message to him, call him to My worship, to My oneness, and to sincerity toward My name. Remind him of My days, warn him of My vengeance and My might, and inform him that nothing can stand against My anger. Speak to him in between that with gentle words, perhaps he will remember or fear. Inform him that I am quicker to pardon and forgive than I am to anger and punish. Do not let what I have clothed him with of worldly garments alarm you, for his forelock is in My hand; he does not blink, nor speak, nor breathe except by My permission. Say to him: 'Answer your Lord, for He is vast in forgiveness.' Indeed, He has granted you respite for four hundred years, during all of which you have been waging war against Him, imitating and impersonating Him, and turning His servants away from His path, while He sends rain upon you from the sky and makes the earth grow for you. You have not fallen ill, you have not grown old, you have not become poor, and you have not been defeated. Had He willed to make that for you by your own means, He would have done so, but He is patient and possessed of great forbearance." In a lengthy speech.

In some narrations, when Allah, exalted is He, commanded him, peace be upon him, to go to Pharaoh, he remained silent for seven days. It was also said that it was more. Then an angel came to him and said: "Carry out what your Lord has commanded you." However, there is some doubt in the heart about the soundness of this report.

[Tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis)] "He said" is an explanatory resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani), as if it had been asked: "What did Musa, peace be upon him, say when he was told what he was told?" The answer is that he said: "My Lord, expand for me my breast; and ease for me my affair." The apparent view is that this is connected to the words of Allah the Exalted, "Go to Pharaoh," and so on. Musa, peace be upon him, understood from the command to go to him, and from the reason given for it, that he was charged with a great task and a momentous matter, which required him to bear what only one with a steady heart and a broad breast can bear. So he asked his Lord, exalted is He, to expand his breast and make him forbearing and tolerant, able to face whatever might come upon him on the path of conveying the message and calling to the bitter truth, of hardships that would drive away the patience of the patient, with graceful patience and firm steadfastness. He also asked that his affair, which is the greatest and most important of matters and the most difficult and frightening of trials, be made easy for him, through the facilitation of means and the removal of obstacles. Thus, what is meant by expanding the breast is making it such that it does not become weary or anxious at what human nature would ordinarily make one weary and anxious about, from hardships. In seeking this there is also a manifestation of complete need for Him, mighty and majestic, and a total turning away from self-regard:

"It is fitting to show composure before enemies, but only weakness is ugly before loved ones."

Al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) mentioned that the root meaning of sharh (expansion) is spreading out and the like, and that expanding the breast is spreading it with divine light, tranquility from Allah the Exalted, and a spirit from Him, mighty and majestic. They have other expressions on this, some of which will come, if Allah the Exalted wills, in the section on allusion (ishara). Some have said: this request is connected to what Allah the Exalted addressed him with, from His words, glorified is He, "Indeed, I am your Lord, so take off your sandals," up to this station. Thus, Musa, peace be upon him, asked for the expansion of the breast so that he could comprehend the subtleties of knowledge and the secrets of revelation, perform the rites of service and worship in the most complete manner, and not grow weary of the hardships of conveying the message. It has also been said: when he, peace be upon him, was appointed to that great station and addressed with what he was addressed with in that situation, he needed arduous duties: receiving revelation, persevering in serving the Creator, glorified and exalted is He, and reforming the lower world. It was as if he were charged with managing the two worlds, and attending to one of them would prevent him from occupying himself with the other. So he asked for the expansion of the breast so that there would be poured upon him from strength what would be sufficient to manage both worlds. It may also be said: the command to go to Pharaoh contained an allusion to the station of prophethood, which entails duties fitting to it, some of which relate to the Truth and some of which are entrusted to creation. Musa, peace be upon him, sensed all of that, so he spread the palm of humble supplication to seek what would help him fulfill this in the most perfect way. Therefore the generalization of the expansion of the breast is not restricted to its connection with the beginning of the speech, as is not hidden. Furthermore, the "breast" (sadr) among the scholars of the outward forms (ulama' al-rusum, i.e., the jurists and exoteric scholars) is taken to mean the heart, because it is the perceiver or that by which perception occurs, and the link is evident.

The scholars of the hearts (ulama' al-qulub, i.e., the Sufis) have discourse on this which will come, if Allah the Exalted wills, in the section on allusion, along with some of what the Imam (al-Razi) expanded upon in his commentary on this verse. Regarding the mention of the word "for me" (li) when the sentence would be complete without it: it is an emphasis on the request for expansion and facilitation, by first leaving the expanded and the facilitated vague and then explaining them afterward. For when he said "expand for me," he knew that there was something expanded that belonged to him, even if he had stopped there. When it is said "my breast" it conveys explanation and detail; but if it were said "expand" and that alone were used, it would not. The same applies to "ease for me." It has also been said: "for me" is mentioned to increase the connection, as in the words of Allah the Exalted, "The reckoning of the people has drawn near for them" (21:1). This was countered by saying that there is no contradiction, and it is this that conveys this meaning. In al-Intisaf (by Ibn al-Munayyir) it is stated that the benefit of mentioning it is to indicate that the benefit of the expansion of the breast returns to him, for He, exalted is He, is not concerned with its existence or its non-existence. Apply the same to "ease for me my affair."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 27:

﴿And loosen the knot from my tongue﴾ It is related that there was in his tongue, peace be upon him, a speech impediment (ratta) from an ember which he had put into his mouth in his childhood.

This was because Pharaoh once carried him, and he took hold of a lock of his beard, because of the jewels that were in it. It was also said: he slapped him. And it was said: he struck him a blow on the head with a staff that was in his hand, so he became angry (tatayyara), and he called for the executioner. Then Asiya daughter of Muzahim, his wife, who loved Musa, peace be upon him, said: "He is only a child who does not distinguish between the ruby and the ember." So they were brought, and he intended to stretch his hand out to the ruby, but Jibril, peace be upon him, turned his hand toward the ember. He took it and placed it in his mouth, and his tongue was burned. In this is a proof against the corruption of the view of those who say that fire burns by its nature, without any role for the permission of God Most High in that, for if the matter were as they claim, it would have burned his hand. As for the wisdom behind God Most High's permitting it to burn his tongue rather than his hand, it is mentioned that his hand had become an instrument for what outwardly was a humiliation of Pharaoh. Perhaps its whitening (tabyid) was also for this reason, and that his tongue was an instrument for the opposite of that, based on what is related: that he, peace be upon him, supplicated with what small children use to supplicate to their fathers. It was also said: his hand, peace be upon him, was also burned, and Pharaoh strove to treat it, but it did not heal.

Perhaps that was so that he, peace be upon him, would not bring it into one story together with Pharaoh, so that the bond of eating together (hurmat al-mu'akala) would be lost between them. When he called him, he said: "To which Lord do you call me?" He said: "To the One who healed my hand, which you were unable to do." According to this, the apparent course would have been for him, peace be upon him, to throw the fire from his hand and not bring it to his mouth. Perhaps he did not feel the pain until after it reached his mouth, or he felt it, but he did not distinguish between throwing it on the ground and throwing it into his mouth, and all of that was by God Most High's decree, that God might accomplish a matter that was already decreed. It was also said: the knot in his tongue, peace be upon him, was innate (khilqa). And it was said: it occurred after the intimate conversation (munajat), and this is far-fetched.

Scholars differed about whether it was removed completely. Whoever held that it was removed, such as al-Hasan, relied on the words of God Most High: ﴿You have been given your request, O Musa﴾. Whoever did not hold that, such as al-Jubba'i, argued with the words of God Most High ﴿He is more eloquent than me﴾ and His saying, glorified is He, ﴿and he can hardly express himself clearly﴾.

And by what is related: that there was in the tongue of al-Husayn, may God be pleased with him, a speech impediment and a stammering, and the Prophet ﷺ said about him: "Indeed he inherited it from his uncle Musa, peace be upon him."

He answered the first by saying that he, peace be upon him, did not ask for the complete loosening of the knot of his tongue, but a knot that prevents comprehension. For this reason he made it indefinite and described it with His words ﴿from my tongue﴾, and he did not make it an idafa, although that is more concise; and that is not suitable for being a description except with the assumption of an omitted noun. He made (min) partitive, meaning a knot existing from among the knots of my tongue, for the knot belongs to the tongue, not from it.

Al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 28:

Its ﴿that they may understand my speech﴾ is taken as the answer to the request and the purpose of the supplication. Thus, by untying the knot in general, the granting of his request (peace be upon him) is realized. This has been objected to on the grounds that His saying ﴿he is more eloquent than I﴾, which he (peace be upon him) said before asking for the knot to be untied, is evidence that the speech impediment did not remain. This is because it indicates that Musa (peace be upon him) was eloquent, the only point being that his brother's eloquence was greater. A residual speech impediment contradicts the linguistic eloquence (fasaha, "clarity and fluency of speech") intended here, as shown by His saying ﴿tongue﴾. What supports this incompatibility is what Ibn Hilal said in Kitab al-Sina'atayn (The Book of the Two Crafts): "Eloquence is the completeness of the instrument of expression (bayan). For this reason, God, exalted is He, is not called eloquent (fasih), though His speech may be called eloquent. For this reason, one who lisps (al-alsagh) or stammers (al-tamtam) is not called eloquent, because his instrument is deficient in producing letters." It is also objected that His saying ﴿and he cannot express himself clearly﴾ means he does not produce an argument or proof. The accursed one (Pharaoh) said this as a deception, to turn people's faces away from him (peace be upon him). Yet if the meaning were the negation of expression and conveying speech, due to the tongue being tied, it would indicate that the knot had not been removed at all, and no one has held that. It is also objected that we do not accept the soundness of the report, and that the indefinite form of (ʿuqdatan, "a knot") may be because it is small in itself.

As for one who permits its (the prepositional phrase's) attachment to (uhlul, "untie"), as al-Hufi held and Abu Hayyan favoured, the reasoning is that when the thing untied is attached to something and joined to it, then just as untying relates to it, so too does it relate to that thing, in respect of removing it from it or its beginning to occur from it. And on the assumption that it (min) attaches to a deleted element that functions as an adjective of ʿuqdatan, we do not accept the necessity of positing a deleted noun (mudaf) and making min partitive (tab'idiyya). There is no obstacle to its being in the sense of fi (in), without any deletion, meaning "a knot in my tongue." It has also been said that there is no obstacle to making it initial (ibtida'iyya) without any deletion, and what corruption is there in our saying: "a knot arising from my tongue"?

The conclusion is that what has been cited as evidence for the persistence of some knot in his tongue (peace be upon him), and that it was not removed entirely, is not conclusive. However, some have said: the apparent meanings require it, and they suffice in such matters, and the heaviness of what is in the tongue does not lessen a person's worth.

It has been mentioned that in the tongue of the awaited Mahdi, may Allah be pleased with him, there is a hesitation (hubsa), and sometimes speech becomes difficult for him until he strikes with his right hand, so take his left foot. You have heard what has been reported of his merit.

Some have said: the eloquence of the essence does not compete with the i'rab (grammatical inflection) of words. And he recited the saying of the poet:

The secret of eloquence lies hidden in the essence,
for the properties of spirits, not for tongues.

And the saying of another:

A tongue eloquent and correct in its speech,
how I wish it would be safe on the Day of Gathering!

And what benefits i'rab if there is no piety?
And a non-Arabic tongue does no harm to one who is pious.

Page 184

Yes, what impairs the matter of conveying the message is a lisp (ratta), which would prevent the revelation from being understood with it, and would repel the listener from hearing it. This is among what the prophets (peace be upon them) are too exalted for. They are all eloquent in speech: nothing said by them escapes the listener, and no one is repelled from hearing it, though they differ in their levels of that eloquence. It seems that he (peace be upon him) did not seek the highest levels of eloquence and fluency of tongue, according to al-Jubba'i and those who agreed with him, because he did not see great merit in that. The most that has been said about it is that it is an ornament of the adornments of this world and a splendour of its splendours. The great merit lies in eloquence of expression (fasahat al-bayan) in the well-known sense among the people of rhetoric (ma'ani) and expression (bayan). What has come of reports indicating its blame is not absolute, as has been explained in the commentaries on the hadiths.

Furthermore, the well-known interpretation of lisan (tongue) is the organ itself, and some have interpreted it as the speech faculty residing in the organ. Fiqh (understanding) means knowledge of a thing and comprehension of it, as in the Qamus and elsewhere. Al-Raghib said: it is arriving at a hidden knowledge through a visible knowledge, so it is more specific than knowledge ('ilm).

The apparent meaning here is understanding (fahm), that is: "Untie a knot from my tongue so that they may understand my speech."

**Qur'an 20:29–30**

﴿And appoint for me a minister from my family,﴾ ﴿Aaron, my brother﴾. That is, a helper in bearing the burdens of what I have been charged with. The derivation of *wazīr* is from *wizr* (with a kasra and then a sukun), meaning a heavy load. It is then an adjective from that root, and its sense is *ṣāḥib wizr*, that is, one who carries a heavy load. The one who takes charge of a kingdom's affairs was named thus because he bears the burden and weight of its matters for the ruler. Alternatively, it is a refuge in which one seeks protection through his opinion. On this view, the derivation is from *wazar* (with two fatḥas), whose original meaning is a mountain in which one takes shelter, and then it was used in the general sense of a refuge, as in the verse:

*The worst of beasts of prey is what lies beyond it, a refuge,*
*and the worst of people is what lies beyond them, a refuge.*

*How many a company were safe, and no beast harmed them,*
*and you see no human whom no human has harmed.*

The minister of a king was named thus because the king seeks protection in his opinion and turns to him in his affairs. Thus *wazīr* is *faʿīl* in the sense of *mafʿūl*, by elision and transitivity, meaning one who is relied upon. Or it is for relation (*nisba*). It has also been said that its original form is *azīr*, from *azr* meaning strength, so that *faʿīl* is in the sense of *mufāʿil*, like *ʿashīr* and *jalīs*. Its hamza was changed to a waw, as it was changed in *muwāzir*, and in it the waw was changed to a yāʾ because of the preceding ḍamma. *Wazīr* has the same meaning, so it was made analogous to it. Analogy of one like to its like is frequent in their speech. However, *muʾāzir* is attested without substitution, and *azīr* is not attested without it. Moreover, with the clear derivation that has preceded, there is no need for this derivation and the claim of metathesis.

Its accusative case is because it is the second object of *ijʿal* (appoint). It was placed before the first object, which is the words of Exalted God, *Hārūn* (Aaron), to show concern for the matter of the ministry, since it is what is sought. *Lī* (for me) is a complement of *ijʿal*, or it is attached to an elided element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) modifying *wazīran*, and originally it is a qualifier of it. *Min ahlī* (from my family) is either a qualifier of *wazīran* or a complement of *ijʿal*. It has also been said that its two objects are *lī wazīran* (for me a minister), and *min ahlī* (from my family), according to the two aspects that have passed. *Hārūn* is an apposition (*ʿaṭf bayān*) to *wazīr*, based on the view of al-Zamakhsharī and al-Radī that agreement in definiteness and indefiniteness is not a condition. It has also been said that it is a substitute (*badal*) for *wazīran*. It has been objected that in that case it would be the intended referent in the relation, while his ministry is the primary intended matter here.

It has been permitted that it is in the accusative by a verb understood in answer to the question "who?", i.e., "appoint Hārūn." It has also been said that its two objects are *wazīran min ahlī*, and *lī* is an explanatory element, as in *saqyan lahu* (watering for him).

It was objected that the condition for the two objects in the chapter of the abrogating (*nawāsikh*) particles is that a nominal sentence can be formed from them. If you began with *wazīran* and gave *min ahlī* as its predicate, it would not be valid, since there is no justification for beginning with an indefinite noun. It was answered that the speaker's meaning is that *min ahlī* is the first object, interpreted as "some of my family," as if it were said: "appoint some of my family a minister," and it was placed first for emphasis. The sense of the meaning requires this, though its remoteness is not hidden. For this reason it has been said that the best view is that the sentence is a supplication (*duʿāʾ*), and an indefinite noun may be used as a subject in it, as the grammarians have stated explicitly. So it is the same after the entry of the abrogating particle. This is as you see. It has also been said that what justifies beginning with an indefinite noun here is that the definite noun *Hārūn*, coordinated with it as an apposition, comes after it. This is strange. It was also permitted for *Hārūn*, on this view as well, to be an object of an elided verb, or to be a substitute. You have heard what is in it.

The apparent view is that *lī* may also here be a complement of *ijʿal*, just as it may be an explanatory element on some of the preceding aspects. I have not seen the reason why this possibility was not mentioned there, nor the reason why the possibility of its being a complement of *ijʿal* was not mentioned here. What is understood from the words of some is the permissibility of each of the two possibilities here and there. Likewise it is also permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause modifying *wazīran*, and perhaps that facilitates the matter of formation according to what has been said, though in it there is what there is.

*Akhī* (my brother), on the aspects mentioned, is an apposition to *wazīr*. There is no harm in its being multiple for one thing, or for Hārūn. It is not required that the second be more famous, as has been imagined, since clarification is achieved from the whole, as was verified in *al-Muṭawwal* and its glosses. There is no need to claim that what is attached to a pronoun is more definite than a proper noun, because there is disagreement about it. Likewise there is no need for what is in *al-Kashf* that *akhī* in this context is more famous than his proper name, because Mūsā (peace be upon him) is the well-known proper name, and the addressed one described by intimate converse and honour, and the one made known is in reality the definite; moreover, the clarification is not with respect to Him, Exalted is He, since nothing is hidden from Him. Rather, Mūsā (peace be upon him) brought it in the manner of what preceded in his words, *"it is my staff"*, etc. It has also been permitted that *akhī* is a subject whose predicate is ...

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verses 31–32:

﴿Strengthen my back through him﴾ ﴿and make him a partner in my task﴾. Abu Hayyan criticised this, saying that it is contrary to the apparent meaning, so one should not turn to it without need. Discussion of expressing a request through a nominal (inshai'i) sentence is well known. The sentence, on this view, is resumptive (isti'nafiyyah). Al-azr (الأزر) means strength, and al-Raghib restricted it to intense strength. Al-Khalil and Abu 'Ubayda said that it means the back (الظهر), and this is also narrated from Ibn 'Atiyyah. The intended meaning is: I make my strength firm through him, and I make him my partner in the matter of the message, so that we may cooperate in discharging it as it should be discharged.

The separation of the first supplication from the preceding one is due to the complete connection between them: tightening the back (شد الأزر) is an expression for appointing him as a minister (وزيرا). As for making him a partner in the matter, since it is among the rulings of the ministry, the conjunctive particle (العاطف) was placed between them, so it is said. However, in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud the reading is ﴿واشْدُدْ﴾ with the conjunction, coordinated with the preceding supplication, and from Ubayy (it is read) ﴿أشْرِكْهُ في أمْرِي واشْدُدْ بِهِ أزْرِي﴾. So reflect.

Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and al-Hasan and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿أشْدِدْ﴾ with a fatha on the hamza, and ﴿وأُشْرِكْهُ﴾ with a damma, taking them as two jussive imperfect verbs in answer to the supplication, namely his saying ﴿اجْعَلْ﴾ (make). The author of al-Lawami' said: from al-Hasan that he read ﴿أُشَدِّدُ بِهِ﴾, the imperfect of shaddada, for intensification and repetition. On the earlier reading, the intended meaning of "the matter" (al-amr) is not the message (al-risalah), because that is not in the hand of Musa, peace be upon him; rather it is the matter of guidance and calling to the truth. Harun, as al-Hakim reported from Wahb, was taller than Musa, peace be upon them both, fuller in flesh, fairer in complexion, larger in bones, and older; it is said he was four years older, and it is said three years. He died three years before him as well. Peace be upon him was deliberate and of great forbearance.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 33–34:

﴿That we may glorify You much﴾ ﴿and remember You much﴾. This is a purpose (ghayah) for the last three supplications, for the act of each of these two, glorification (tasbih) and remembrance (dhikr), while it increases the other and multiplies it by being joined to it, also increases it in itself, by strengthening and supporting it. The intended meaning of tasbih and dhikr is not what is done by the heart or in private solitude, such that their state would not vary between when they are plural and when they are singular. Rather, it is what is done of them in the midst of conveying the message and calling the rebellious, obstinate tyrants to the truth. There is no doubt that there is a difference between the two states, plurality and singularity, for each of them issues, through the support of the other, in the manifestation of the truth what would hardly issue from its like when alone. ("Much," kathiran, in both places is an adjective of a omitted verbal noun (masdar) or an omitted time (zaman), meaning: we exalt You above what is not fitting for You of attributes and actions, among which is what the insolent Pharaoh claims and his rebellious faction accepts from him, of association in divinity, and we describe You with what is fitting for You of attributes of perfection and qualities of beauty and majesty, an abundant exaltation and an abundant description; or an abundant time, among which is the time of Pharaoh's call and the occasion of disputation with him. Thus it is in Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim.)

Abu Hayyan permitted that it be in the accusative as a circumstantial (hal), meaning: we glorify You with glorification in a state of its abundance, and the same is said of the last one. But this is not so. The priority of tasbih over dhikr is from the rule of priority of takhliyah (clearing away) over tahliyah (adorning). It was also said: because tasbih is exalting (tanzih) from what is unfitting, and its locus is the heart, while dhikr is praise with what is fitting, and its locus is the tongue, and the heart takes precedence over the tongue. It was also said: the meaning is "that we may pray to You much, and praise You and extol You much for the blessings You have bestowed upon us and the favours You have bestowed upon us by bearing Your message." It is not hidden that the context does not support this.

It was also said: the meaning is "that we may pray to You much, and praise You and extol You much for the blessings You have bestowed upon us and the favours You have bestowed upon us by bearing Your message." It is not hidden that the context does not support this.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 35:

﴿Indeed You are ever, of us, Seeing﴾, knowing our circumstances, and that what You have asked of me, by which You would set us right and benefit us in fulfilling what You charged me with, namely establishing the rites of the message, and that Harun is an excellent helper in carrying out what You commanded. The preposition "bi" (with/of) is connected to "basiran" (seeing) and placed before it for the sake of observing the rhyme (fawasil), and the sentence stands in the position of a causal clause (ta'lil) for the first causative element, after considering its causation by the first cause. 

Abd ibn Humayd related from al-A'mash that he pronounced the kaf of the pronoun (in "innaka," "bika," "lika") with sukun in the three places. It has also been reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) made a supplication similar to this one, except that he appointed Ali, may Allah honour his face, in the station of Harun, peace be upon him. Ibn Mardawayh, al-Khatib and Ibn Asakir reported, "from Asma' bint Umays, who said: 'I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) facing Thabir, and he was saying: "Shine forth, Thabir! Shine forth, Thabir! O Allah, I ask You, as Your servant and brother Musa asked You, to expand my chest for me, to ease my affair for me, to loosen a knot from my tongue so that my speech may be understood, and to make for me a minister from my family, Ali, my brother; strengthen my back through him and make him a partner in my affair, so that we may glorify You much and remember You much. Indeed You are ever, of us, Seeing."'"

It is not hidden that the command here must be understood as the command of guidance and calling to the truth, and it is not permissible to understand it as prophethood. Nor is it valid to derive from this the caliphate of Ali, may Allah honour his face, after the Prophet (ﷺ) without interval. Similar to this, in what has been mentioned, is what is authentically reported from his saying, upon him be blessings and peace, to him when he appointed him as deputy over his family during the expedition of Tabuk: "Are you not pleased that you stand to me in the same position as Harun stood to Musa, except that there is no prophet after me." As explained in al-Tuhfa al-Ithna 'Ashariyya. Indeed, in that there is an indication of the great excellence of Ali, may Allah honour his face, which is not hidden. It is also fitting that his request (ﷺ) for the loosening of the knot be interpreted as meaning the continuation of that, since he, upon him be blessings and peace, was the most eloquent of people in speech.

He said: "You have indeed been given your request, O Musa." That is, you have been given what you asked for. So *fa'l* here means *maf'ul*, as in *al-khubz* (bread) and *al-ukl* (food) meaning *al-makhbuz* (what is baked) and *al-ma'kul* (what is eaten). Giving (*al-iti'a*) is an expression for the certain attachment of God's will to the occurrence and realization of those requests for him, peace be upon him. God's decree of them is binding, so all of them are realized for him, peace be upon him, even though the actual occurrence of some of them is set in order afterward, such as the facilitating of the matter and the strengthening of his support. In this sense it was said: ﴿We will strengthen your arm through your brother﴾. The apparent meaning of some reports indicates that Harun, peace be upon him, was made a partner in prophethood, that is, that his being made a prophet like Musa, peace be upon him, took place at that moment, even though he, peace be upon him, was not with his brother at that time. Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas that he said, regarding God's words ﴿and make him a partner in my task﴾: "Make Harun a prophet at that hour, when Musa, peace be upon them both, was made a prophet." Calling him, peace be upon him, is an honor to him by direct address, following an honor.

Page 187

﴿And We had certainly bestowed favour upon you﴾ is a resumptive clause (istinaf, a new sentence that begins without grammatical connection to what precedes it), brought to confirm what came before it and to further reassure the soul of Musa (peace be upon him) that his request will be accepted. The explanation is that God, the Exalted, when He bestowed upon him those perfect blessings without any prior supplication or request from him, then it is more fitting and more appropriate that He bless him with the like of them when he is seeking them and calling upon Him. The opening with the oath is for the utmost concern with this matter, meaning: "By God, We had certainly bestowed favour upon you ﴿another time﴾," that is, at a time other than this time. The word "ukhra" (another) here is a feminine form of "akhar" (other), in the sense of "different." "Marratan" (a time) is an adverb of time, and what is meant by it is the extended period in which what will be mentioned later occurred, if God the Exalted wills, of the great and numerous favours. Essentially, "marra" is a noun for a single passing, then it was applied to every single act, whether transitive or intransitive. Then it became common for every single individual among the things that have individuals which recur, so it became a specific term for that, until it was made a measure for what is similar in meaning among all other things. Thus it is said: this is the pattern of "marra" (the form فَعْلَة), and close to it are "karra" (a turn or occurrence), "tara" (an occurrence), and "daf'a" (a push or instance).

Abu Hayyan said: What is meant by it is other than this favour, and "ukhra" is not the feminine of "akhir" with a kasra on the kha, so as to be the counterpart of "the first." Some of them have imagined that, saying: He, glory be to Him, named it "another" while it is the first, because it is "another" in mention.

[Page 188]

It is a time clause (*zarf*) governing *mannana* ("We bestowed favour"), whether it is a substitute for *marrah* ("a time") or not. It was also said to be a causal clause, but that is contrary to the apparent meaning. According to the majority, the "revelation" (*iyha'*) here means inspiration (*ilham*), as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord revealed to the bee﴾. This has been criticised on the grounds that it is far-fetched, because He, exalted is He, said in Surat al-Qasas: ﴿We shall return him to you and make him one of the messengers﴾, and such a thing is not known through inspiration. This criticism is not valid, because she may have witnessed from him, peace be upon him, what indicated his prophethood and that God, exalted is He, would not abandon him. The inspiration of pure souls (*al-anfus al-qudsiyyah*) of this kind is not far-fetched, for it is a type of unveiling (*kashf*). Do you not see the words of 'Abd al-Muttalib, when he named our Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, Muhammad? He was asked: "Why did you name your son Muhammad when there is none of that among the names of your forefathers?" He said: "He will be praised." In another narration: "I hoped that he would be praised in the heavens and on the earth." Yet that this is included in what is inspired is not necessary.

Abu Hayyan inclined to the view that an angel was sent to her, not in the capacity of prophethood, just as one was sent to Maryam. This is based on the premise that an angel is sent to those other than prophets, peace be upon them, and this is the correct view. However, it has been said against this that, in that case, the definition of a prophet as "one to whom revelation has been made in the capacity of prophethood" would be invalidated, which is a circular definition. It is answered that this does not necessarily follow. If it were said: "one to whom revelation of legal rulings has been made but who was not commanded to convey them," no problem would arise.

Al-Jubba'i said that it was by showing (*al-ira'ah*) in a dream. It was also said that it was through the tongue of a prophet of her time, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when I revealed to the disciples﴾. This has been criticised as contrary to the apparent meaning, for it is not reported that there was a prophet in Egypt in the time of Pharaoh before Musa, peace be upon him.

It is answered that this does not depend on the prophet being in Egypt. Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, was a prophet in the time of Pharaoh in Madyan, so it is possible that he informed her of this. Moreover, the multitude of prophets among the Children of Israel, peace be upon them, is something widely known and spread. The truth is that denying that this is contrary to the apparent meaning is obstinacy.

The name of his mother, peace be upon him, has been disputed. The well-known view is that it was Yuhanadh. In al-Itqan it is said that she was Mihyanah bint Yasahr ibn Lawi. It was also said: Barkha, and it was said: Bazakht. As for what is famous about her having the property of opening locks by means of him after a specific discipline, we have found no trace of it, and it is perhaps a fable.

By "what is revealed" is meant what God, exalted is He, relates later about the command to cast him into the chest. The casting into the sea was first left vague, to make it awesome and to magnify his status, and then it was explained so that it would be more reassuring to the soul. It was also said: its meaning is "what ought to be revealed and not neglected," because of the greatness of his status and the intense concern for him, just as one says: "This is something that should be written down." It was also said: "It is not known except through revelation." The first view is most fitting for each of the earlier meanings intended by revelation, except that it has been said against it that if what was intended were magnification and awe, it would have been said: "When We revealed to your mother what We revealed," just as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾, and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then there covered them from the sea what covered them﴾. If this holds, then what was said about its meaning second is better. So reflect.

The commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 39:

"An" in His words ﴿Cast him into the chest﴾ is either an explanatory "an" (mufassira), since revelation is a form of speech, or a verbal "an" (masdariyya) from which the preposition "bi" has been omitted, meaning "bi-an iqdifihi" (by casting him). Ibn 'Atiyya said: "an" and what follows it are in the sense of a verbal noun, and are a substitute (badal) for "ma". The discussion of joining the verbal "an" to an imperative verb has already been covered. The meaning of "qadhf" (casting) here is "placing" (al-wad'). As for His words ﴿cast him into the sea﴾, the meaning there is "throwing" (al-ilqa') and "dropping" (al-tarh). It is also permissible that the meaning in both places is "placing." "Al-yamm" is the sea. It is not broken into plural forms nor made into a sound plural. In the Qur'an it is the name for fresh water. It was said to be the name specifically for the Nile, but this is not correct. This distinction is the meaning of His words ﴿So when you fear for him, then cast him into the sea﴾, not casting without a chest. ﴿Then let the sea bring him to the shore﴾: "bi-al-sahil" means "to its shore," which is the side free of water. It is derived from "sahl al-hadid," meaning filing and peeling iron. It is an active participle in the sense of a passive participle, because the water files it, meaning it peels it. Or it is for attribution, meaning "one having a filing," where the matter returns to something filed. It was said that it is on its literal meaning, in the sense that it files the water, meaning it divides and wastes it. It was said that it is from "sahil," which is braying, because a sound is heard from it. The meaning of "shore" here is what is opposite the middle, which is the part of the sea adjacent to the shore, where its water flows into the river of Pharaoh (Fir'awn).

It was said: the meaning of "shore" is the side and the edge in general, and the meaning of the imperative is the declarative, chosen for emphasis. Among this is his saying ﷺ: "Stand up, and I will pray for you." Placing this in the form of a command gives a good answer afterward. Many others said: since the sea's casting him onto the shore was a matter that must occur, because the divine will is attached to it, the sea was treated as though it were a discerning being obedient to a command to do so. The answer was expressed in the form of a command. So in "al-yamm" there is an implicit metaphor (isti'ara bil-kinaya), and attributing a command to it is imaginative (takhyil). It was said: in His words ﴿then let him cast him﴾ there is an explicit subsequent metaphor (isti'ara tasrihiyya tab'iyya). All the pronouns refer to Musa (peace be upon him), since he is the one spoken of, the one cast into the sea, and the one thrown onto the shore. Although the chest is the primary object, since what is intended in essence is what is in it, the chest was treated as subordinate to him in this. It was also said: the first pronoun refers to Musa (peace be upon him), and the last two pronouns refer to the chest. Whenever a pronoun is suitable to refer to the nearer or the farther antecedent, referring to the nearer is preferred, as the grammarians stated explicitly. On this basis Ibn Hazm's claim is refuted, in his argument that the pronoun in His words ﴿for it is an abomination﴾ refers to meat (lahm), because that is what is spoken of, and not to pork (khinzir). Therefore, according to him, its fat, cartilage, bone and skin are permissible. The truth is that non-separation in what we are dealing with is preferable, and what the grammarians stated is not absolute, as is not hidden. ﴿He shall be taken by an enemy of Mine and an enemy of his﴾ is the answer to the command to cast. Repeating "enemy" is for emphasis, in that it indicates that his enmity is many, not one. It was said: the first refers to the actual and the second to the expected, and it is not repetition for emphasis at all, because that would be a branch of the permissibility of saying "an enemy of mine and of his," which is not allowed except according to those who permit combining the literal and the metaphorical. It was answered that this is permissible and does not involve the combination mentioned. Pharaoh at the time of the taking was characterized by enmity toward God, the Exalted, and toward him in reality. As for his characterization by enmity toward God, the Exalted, this is evident. As for his characterization by enmity toward Musa, it is because he hated every newborn in that year. If we say that he was not characterized by enmity toward Musa (peace be upon him) at that time, it is still permissible to say this, and the generality of the metaphor is considered, which is what frees it from combining the literal and the metaphorical in what is claimed in it.

[p. 189]

Al-Khafaji said: there is no need for combination, because "enemy" ('aduww) is an attributive adjective (sifa mushabbaha) indicating stability (thubut) that encompasses both the actual and the expected. It is not hidden that this is a statement that stability in the attributive adjective means permanence. He himself said, in commenting on His words ﴿and do not walk on the earth exultantly﴾, that the meaning of its indication of stability is that it does not indicate renewal and occurrence, not that it indicates permanence as the grammarians mentioned. So what is said, that "exultant" (maraḥan) is an attributive adjective indicating stability, and that its negation does not entail negation of its root, is a sophistry arising from not understanding the meaning of stability in it, end of quote. Moreover, his statement here, setting aside its conflict with what he said before, is not free of some problem.

From what he mentioned earlier about the meaning of stability, it is known that the use of this verse to argue that Pharaoh's faith was not accepted and that he died a disbeliever, as is the truth, is not correct, and there are many valid proofs for it. Apparently He concealed this enemy from her and did not inform her of his name, for otherwise she would not have said to his sister ("follow him") (qussiyhi).

﴿And I placed upon you love from Me﴾: the word "min" is connected to an omitted element that occurred as an attribute of a noun, confirming what the indefiniteness of it contains of intrinsic grandeur with relational grandeur. That is, a great love proceeding from Me, which I have planted in hearts, so that everyone who saw you loved you such that they could not bear to be apart from you. Muqatil said: there was a charm in his eyes; no one saw him without loving him. Ibn 'Atiyya said: a sheen of beauty was placed upon him, such that whoever saw him could hardly bear to be apart from him. It is narrated that when what was revealed to his mother was revealed to her, she placed him in a chest of wood. It was said: of papyrus, made by a believer of Pharaoh's family, and she sealed its gaps, lined it with a mat, and it was also said with cotton that had been carded. She sealed its mouth, plastered it, coated it with pitch, and cast it into the sea. Then Pharaoh was in a place overlooking the Nile, with his wife with him, when he saw the chest near the shore. He commanded that it be opened, and there was a child who was the most beautiful of people in face. He and his wife loved him intensely.

It was said: the chest came by water to the landing place where Pharaoh's wife's maidservants drew water. They took the chest and brought it to her, thinking there was money in it. When she opened it she saw him (peace be upon him), loved him, informed Pharaoh, and asked him to adopt him as a son. She said: "A delight of the eye for me and for you; do not kill him." He said to her: "He will be yours, but as for me, I have no need of him." From here the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said, as narrated by al-Nasa'i and a group from Ibn 'Abbas: "By Him in whose name one swears, if Pharaoh had acknowledged that he be a delight of the eye for him, as his wife said, God would have guided him by it, as He guided his wife by it, but God, Mighty and Majestic, deprived him of that." It was said: Pharaoh was sitting at the edge of a pool of his in a garden with his wife, and he saw the chest, which the water had pushed into the pool from a river branching off from the sea. He commanded that it be taken out, and it was taken out. When it was opened there was a child most beautiful of people in face. He loved him so much that he could hardly bear to be apart from him. It is narrated that there were four hundred boys and girls in his presence when he saw the chest. When he gestured for it to be taken, he promised manumission to whoever would be first to do so. They all raced, and only one of them succeeded in taking it, and he freed them all. In this there is something that encourages the negligent among the believers to hope for God's mercy, for He, glorified is He, is the Most Merciful of the merciful and the most Generous of the generous. It was said: the phrase "min" is connected to "alqaytu" (I cast), so the love cast according to the taste (dhawq) is God's love for him, meaning "I loved you," and whoever God loves, hearts will inevitably love. Al-Qadi objected to this, that in childhood a person is not described as being loved by God, since that love returns to conferring reward, which applies only to the morally responsible. It was answered that God's love according to those who interpret it means willing good and benefit, which is more general than whether it is a reward for an act or not. The rejection is more evident according to those who do not interpret it. Some permitted that the second meaning be intended on the first view of the connection, and the first meaning on the second view, and claimed that the reason for the specification is not apparent, which is not hidden

[p. 190]

to one of straight mind and sound taste.

His words ﴿and that you be reared under My eye﴾ are connected to "alqaytu" on the basis that it is conjoined to a hidden cause, meaning "so that you would be shown affection and so that you would be reared." Or it is connected to a hidden verb later, meaning "and so that you would be reared, etc., I did that," that is, the casting of love upon you. Someone claimed that it is connected to "alqaytu" on the basis that the waw is inserted, which is nothing. "Under My eye" means "in My sight," connected to an omitted element that occurred as a circumstantial clause from the concealed pronoun in "tuṣna'a" (be reared). This is an illustrative metaphor (isti'ara tamthiliyya) for protection and preservation, since what is preserved is placed in sight. "Ṣun'" means kindness. Al-Nahhas said: one says "I reared the horse" if I was kind to it.

The meaning is: so that He would bestow upon you favor and kindness, and you would be nurtured with tenderness and compassion, while I am watching over you and observing you, as a man watches a thing with his eye when he cares for it. This is taken as an illustration, which avoids what al-Wahidi said, that interpreting "under My eye" as mentioned before is correct, but there would be no specification of Musa (peace be upon him) in that, since all things are in God's sight, the Exalted. Moreover, it may be said that this specification is for honor, like the specification of Jesus (peace be upon him) as God's word, and the Ka'ba as God's house, even though all things exist by "Be," and all houses are the house of God, glorified is He. Qatada said: the meaning is "that you be nourished by My love and My will." This is the choice of Abu 'Ubayda and Ibn al-Anbari, and al-Wahidi claimed it was the correct view. Al-Hasan and Abu Nuhayk read "wa-litaṣna'a" (with a fatha on the ta'), and Tha'lab said: the meaning is "so that your movement and conduct would be under My eye, lest you disobey My command."

Abu Ja'far, in one narration, read "wa-litusna'" with a kasra on the lam and jussing of the verb by it, since it is the lam of command, and commanding the addressee with lam is anomalous. But since the verb here is in the passive voice, and its original form was attributed to the third-person absent, and there is no issue with commanding by lam, it was retained after being transferred to the passive for brevity. The apparent reading is that it is coordinated with His words ﴿and I placed upon you love from Me﴾, except that this involves conjoining an imperative to a declarative, on which there is a well-known discussion. But it was said here that the matter is made easier because the imperative has the meaning of a declarative.

The author of al-Lawami' said: the conjunction is with His words ﴿then let him cast him﴾, so there is no conjunction of an imperative with a declarative in it.

Shayba and Abu Ja'far in another narration read it the same way, except that he made the lam quiescent, and it is also the lam of command. The rest of the discussion is similar to what has passed.

It is possible that it is the lam of purpose (lam kay), made quiescent for lightness, and the fatha of the 'ayn was not shown because of assimilation. Al-Khafaji said: this is very good.

[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 40:]

﴿When your sister was walking﴾ is an adverbial clause (*zarf*, a temporal complement) governed by ﴿you were made﴾, as al-Hufi and others said. The intended meaning is the time in which the sister's walking occurred, together with what followed from it: her speaking and returning to his mother, and his mother's nurturing him with tenderness. This is the fulfilment of the Exalted's words ﴿and so that you might be reared under My eye﴾, since no compassion is greater than a mother's compassion and her care for him in accordance with the Exalted's protection.

It is also permitted that it be an adverbial clause governed by ﴿We cast﴾, and that it be a substitute (*badal*) for ﴿when We revealed﴾, on the basis that the intended meaning is an extended period of time. Thus the two adverbial clauses coincide, and the substitution is valid, and it is not of the kind of substitution of one of two different things (*ibdal ahad al-mutaghayirayn*), which does not occur in eloquent speech.

Sahib al-Kashf preferred this view and said: "It is more suited to the context of favour, because it enumerates the blessing in a more eloquent manner, and because specifying the casting or the nurturing to the time of the sister's walking is a departure from the apparent sense. Before that, he (peace be upon him) was beloved and protected. Then, the better of the two views is to make it an adverbial clause of ﴿you were made﴾. As for the accusative by implying ''remember'' (*nasb bi-idmar udhkur*), it is weak." (End of quotation.) You know that the apparent sense is that it is an adverbial clause of ﴿you were made﴾, and the restriction by ﴿under My eye﴾ removes the nurturing before this from the eye, in other than the mother's lap.

Abu Hayyan objected to the substitution view, saying that each of the two adverbial clauses is restricted and not extended, since it is specified by what is attached to it; and that this is unlike a year in its extension. There is room for reflection on this. The name of his sister (peace be upon him) was Maryam, and it was said Kulthum. The use of the present tense is to narrate a past situation. The same applies to the Exalted's words ﴿Shall I direct you to one who will take charge of him?﴾, meaning, will take him into his own care and raise him.

﴿So We returned you to your mother﴾. The ''fa'' is eloquent (*fa fasihah*), meaning: they said, ''Show us where he is,'' and she came with your mother, and so We returned you to her ﴿that her eye might be cooled﴾ by your meeting. It was read ﴿that she might be cooled (taqirr)﴾ with a kasra on the qaf. Jannah ibn Hubaysh read ﴿that she might be cooled (tuqarr)﴾ in the passive. ﴿And that she might not grieve﴾ means that grief should not come upon her by your separation after that. Otherwise, the removal of grief precedes the joy expressed by ''the cooling of the eye,'' for clearing away (*takhliyah*) precedes adornment (*tahliyah*).

It was said: the concealed pronoun in ''she might not grieve'' refers to Musa (peace be upon him), meaning: ''and you should not grieve, by the loss of her compassion.'' Although the noble text does not refuse this, the grief of the infant is not apparent. What is in Surah al-Qasas requires the first view, and the Qur'an explains part of itself by another part.

A group narrated from a long report from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that when Asiyah took Musa (peace be upon him) out of the chest and asked Pharaoh to give him to her, and he gave him to her, she sent to those around her from every woman who had milk, to choose a wet-nurse for him. But he would not accept the breast of any of them, until she became worried that he would refuse milk and die, and this grieved her. So she ordered that he be taken out to the market, the gathering place of people, hoping to find a wet-nurse for him whose breast he would take. But he did not do so. His mother became distracted and said to his sister: ''Follow his trail and search for him; do you hear any mention of him? Is he alive, or have the beasts eaten him?'' She forgot what Allah the Exalted had promised her. Then his sister saw him from afar, and said out of joy: ''I will direct you to a household who will take him for you, and they will be sincere toward him.'' They took hold of her and said: ''How do you know their sincerity toward him? Do they know him?'' They doubted this. She said: ''Their sincerity toward him and their compassion for him is from their desire for the king's approval and to draw near to him.'' So they left her and asked her to guide them. She went to his mother and informed her of the news. She came, and when she placed him in her lap he turned to her breast and suckled it until his sides were full of satisfaction. The good news went to Pharaoh's wife, saying to her: ''We have found a wet-nurse for your son.'' She sent for her, and she was brought with him. When she saw what he was doing with her, she said to her: ''Stay with me and nurse this son of mine, for I have never loved anything as I love him.'' She said: ''I cannot leave my house and my child, lest it be lost. If your soul consents to giving him to me, I will take him to my house, and he will be with me, and I will not spare him any good, that I will do. Otherwise, I will not leave my house and my child.'' Then the mother of Musa recalled what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had promised her, and so she refused Pharaoh's wife in this matter, certain that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, would fulfil His promise. She returned with her son to her house the same day, and Allah made him grow well and preserved him for what He had decreed concerning him. When he grew up, Pharaoh's wife said to his mother: ''Show me my son.'' So she promised her a day on which she would visit her with him. Pharaoh's wife said to her treasurers and stewards: ''None of you should remain but that he meets my son with a gift and honour; I wish to see that in him. I will send a trustworthy person who will record what each of you does.'' Gifts, presents and honour kept coming to him from the time he left his mother's house until he entered upon her. When he entered, she honoured him, gave him presents, and rejoiced in him, and she also gave presents to his mother for the goodness of her care of him. Then she took him to Pharaoh so that he might give him presents and honour him. This was the cause of what had preceded, from the pulling of his beard.

From this report it is known that the intended meaning of ''when your sister was walking'' is: walking along the road in search of you and to confirm your affair, and saying to those who had you in their hands, seeking a wet-nurse to suckle you: ''Shall I direct you...?'' etc.

In another narration, when he was taken from the chest, the news spread that the people of Pharaoh had found a boy from the Nile who would not suckle the breast of any woman, and they were compelled to search among the women. His sister went out to learn his news, and came to them disguised, and said what she said, and they said what they said. The meaning according to this view is: ''when your sister was walking to the house of Pharaoh, and said to Pharaoh and Asiyah, or to Asiyah, ''Shall I direct you...?'' etc.

[Page 192]

﴿And you killed a soul﴾: it was the soul of a Copt, whose name was Qanun, against whom the Israelite sought help. The Israelite's name was Musa ibn Zafar, and he is the Samiri. The age of Musa (peace be upon him) when he killed, according to what is in the sea, was twelve years. In a report from the rabbi Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that when he (peace be upon him) killed the Copt, he was among the men, and his killing of him was by a blow, as indicated by the Exalted's words ﴿Musa struck him and finished him off﴾. The intended meaning was: ''and you killed a soul, and so a grief afflicted you'' ﴿and We delivered you from grief﴾, which is the grief arising from the killing. It came to him from two directions: fear of the punishment of Allah the Exalted, because the killing did not occur by His command, glory be to Him; and fear of retaliation by Pharaoh. Allah the Exalted delivered him from this by forgiveness when he said ﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me﴾, and by emigrating to Madyan. It was said: it is the grief of the chest. It was said: the grief of the sea. Both views are nothing. Grief (*ghamm*) in origin is the covering of a thing, from which comes ''cloud'' (*ghamam*), for its covering the light of the sun. It is said of that which distresses the heart by reason of fear or the loss of an aim. It is distinguished from worry (*hamm*) by the fact that grief is about a past matter and worry about a future matter.
