The apparent statement of many is that there is no distinction, and that grief includes whatever is of a past matter and whatever is of a future matter.

﴿And We tried you with a trial﴾: that is, We tested you with a test. ''Trials'' (*futunan*) is a verbal noun of the form *fu'ul* from a transitive verb, like ''perdition'' (*thubur*), ''thankfulness'' (*shukur*) and ''disbelief'' (*kufur*). Most often in this pattern it is the verbal noun of an intransitive verb. Alternatively, ''trials'' is from ''testing,'' taking it as the plural of *fitan*, like *dhunun*, the plural of *dhann*; or the plural of *fitnah*, disregarding the ta' because it is treated as separate, as they said of *hujuz*, the plural of *hujzah*, and *budur*, the plural of *budrah*. The placing of trial within the sequence of favours: it was said that the meaning is that We tested you and examined you by placing you in tribulations and delivering you from them. It was said that the meaning is: We placed you in ordeal, which is what is hard for a person. The placing of this in that sequence is by the consideration that it entails reward, so it is of the kind of blessings. But this is nothing. It was said that ''We tried you'' means ''We purified you,'' from the saying ''I tested the gold with fire'' when you purify it of its impurity by it. Its beauty is not hidden. The meaning, whether ''trials'' is taken as a verbal noun or as a plural, is: We purified you again and again. This is evident if the sense is plurality. As for taking the sense as a verbal noun, the context requires this. This is a summary of what he (peace be upon him) suffered on his journey of emigration from his homeland, leaving behind his family, walking on foot, and lacking provisions.

A group narrated that Sa'id ibn Jubayr asked Ibn Abbas about the trials, and he said to him: ''Continue the day, O son of Jubayr, for it has a long report.'' When morning came, he came to him, and Ibn Abbas began to mention it, and he mentioned the story of Pharaoh and his killing of the sons of the Children of Israel; then the story of the casting of Musa (peace and blessings be upon him) into the river, and the picking up by the people of Pharaoh, and his refusal to suckle from outsiders, and his return to his mother; then the story of his seizing Pharaoh's beard, and Pharaoh's anger at that, and his intention to kill him, and the placing of the ember and the jewel before him, and his taking the ember; then the story of his killing of the Copt; then his flight to Madyan, and his becoming a hired man for Shu'ayb (peace be upon him); then his return to Egypt, and his losing his way on the dark night, and the scattering of his sheep in it. Each time he completed one of these, may Allah be pleased with him, he would say: ''These are among the trials, O son of Jubayr.'' But it was said: what the noble text requires is that his hiring himself out and what came after it should not be counted among those trials, because the intended meaning of them is what happened before his arrival at Madyan, by the consequence of the ''fa'' in the Exalted's words ﴿Then you remained years among the people of Madyan﴾. There is no doubt that the hiring mentioned and what came after it occurred after their arrival. Mention of his staying among them, rather than his arrival among them, indicates all the varieties of trials that he endured (peace be upon him) during the period of his stay. It is said that this period was ten years. Wahb said it was twenty-eight years: he remained ten of them tending the sheep of Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) as dowry for his daughter, and eighteen with his wife, and children were born to him in them. This is most suited to his being commissioned at the age of forty, if we say that his age when he left for Madyan was twelve years. Madyan is the town of Shu'ayb (peace be upon him), eight stages from Egypt.

﴿Then you came﴾: that is, to the place where I called you. The word ''then'' (*thumma*) implies that his arrival (peace be upon him) came after the many afflictions of losing the way and the scattering of the sheep on the dark wintry night and other things. ﴿At an appointed time﴾: that is, measure (*qadar*), and what is meant by it is the decreed, that is, you came at the time that I had decreed and appointed for speaking to you and making you a prophet, without advance or delay. It was said that it means a quantity (*miqdar*): that is, you came at a measure of time in which revelation is given to the prophets (peace be upon them), namely at the age of forty years. This was considered weak, because what is known in this sense is ''qadr'' with a sukun, not with a vowel. It was said that the meaning is ''according to a promise We made you,'' and this was narrated from Mujahid, and it requires that the promise was made earlier through the tongue of some prophets (peace be upon them), and this is as you see. The Exalted's words ﴿O Musa﴾ are an honouring of him (peace be upon him) and an alert to the ending of the narration, which is a detailing of the other occasion that occurred before the occasion narrated first.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 41:

His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿And I have chosen you for Myself﴾ is a reminder of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and I have chosen you﴾, and a preparation for sending him, peace be upon him, to Pharaoh, supported by his brother, as he had asked after the reminder of the previous favours, as a confirmation of his, peace be upon him, certainty of the occurrence of their like in what is to come. Al-Imam (al-Razi) placed this within the series of the favours recounted. The placement of the vocative (the call "O Musa") after the preceding verses supports what has been mentioned. Al-stina'a (iṣṭināʿ, "making someone one's own") is an iftiʿal form derived from ṣunʿ (ṣunʿ, "making, craftsmanship"), in the sense of ṣanīʿa (ṣanīʿah, "a favour, a kindness"), which is beneficence. So the meaning of iṣṭanaʿahu is: he made him the object of His favour and beneficence. Al-Qaffal said: it is said "fulan iṣṭanaʿa fulanan" when he has been good to him to the point that he is attributed to him, so one says: "this is the creation (ṣanīʿ) of so-and-so and his product." The meaning of ﴿for Myself﴾ is what has been related from Ibn ʿAbbas: for My revelation and My message. It was also said: for My love. He expressed it by "self" because it is the most specific thing to Him. Al-Zajjaj said: the intended meaning is, I chose you to establish My proof, and I made you between Me and My creation, until you became, in conveying from Me, in the position in which I would be if I addressed them and manifested Myself to them. Several of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) said: this is an illustration of what He, mighty and majestic, has bestowed upon one whom He made a prophet, noble, a speaker (with God), bestowing upon him excellent blessings, by the king's bringing near the one he sees as worthy of being brought near, so he takes him for beneficence and special favour and makes him one of the elite of his own self and his intimate companions. The beauty of this metaphor is not hidden, and it is more fitting to His speech. His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿for Myself﴾ is clear in its meaning. The summary of the meaning: I made you one of My elect and I chose you for My message and My speech. And in the shift away from the plural of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓama) occurring in His saying, glorified is He, ﴿and We tested you﴾ and its two preceding parallels, there is a preparation for the singular "self," which is fitting to the context, for it is more effective in realizing the meaning of making one's own (iṣṭināʿ) and selecting (istikhlāṣ).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 42:

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Go, you and your brother, with My signs﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to explain what is intended by "isti'naf" [the act of making/choosing Musa as a prophet]. ﴿And your brother﴾ is the subject (fa'il) of a verb that is implied, meaning: "and let your brother go, as you requested." It was also said that it is conjoined (ma'tuf) to the hidden pronoun (damir mustatir) that is emphasized by the explicit pronoun, and many a thing is valid as a follower (taba'an) but not valid independently.

The "signs" (ayat) are the miracles (mu'jizat), and what is meant by them is the matter of the hand, the staff, and the untying of the knot. From Ibn 'Abbas: the nine signs. It was also said: only the first two. The use of the plural for two is common. This is supported by the fact that when Pharaoh said to him, peace be upon him, "Bring a sign," he threw down the staff and drew out the hand, and said: ﴿These are two proofs﴾.

Some said: although they are two, in each of them there are various signs, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Clear signs: the standing place of Ibrahim﴾. The turning of the staff into a living creature is a sign. Its being a great serpent whose size cannot be measured is another sign. The swiftness of its movement despite its great bulk is another sign. Its being, despite that, subjected to him, peace be upon him, such that his hand is in its mouth and it does not harm him, is another sign. Then its returning to a staff as it was is another sign. Likewise the white hand: its whiteness in itself is a sign, its radiance is a sign, and then its return to its original state is another sign.

It was also said: what is meant by them is what he, peace be upon him, was given of miracle and revelation. What the heart inclines to is that they are the staff and the hand, for what you have heard from the supporter, along with what has preceded, that He, exalted is He, after commanding him to cast down the staff and take it up after it became a snake, said, glorified is He: ﴿And draw your hand to your side; it will come out white without harm, another sign﴾, then He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Go to Pharaoh; indeed he has transgressed﴾, without specifying other than those two signs, and without any mention of the untying of the knot being a sign or anything else.

Furthermore, the ba' (in "bi-ayati") is for accompaniment (lil-musahabah), not for transitivity (lil-ta'diyah), since what is meant is their going to Pharaoh while connected to the signs, holding fast to them in enforcing the rulings of the message and completing the call, not merely taking them there and delivering them to him. This is evident that the signs were realized at that time, and most of the nine had not yet been realized.

﴿And do not slacken﴾ from al-wany, meaning weakness (futur). It is an intransitive verb, and when made transitive it takes fi or 'an. Some of the Baghdadis claimed that it is a defective verb (fi'l naqis) among the sisters of zala (to continue) and with its meaning, and Ibn Malik chose this. In al-Sihah: "Fulan yiny yaf'alu kadha," meaning he does not cease doing such-and-such. It seems this meaning is derived from the negation of weakness. Ibn Thabit recited "wa la tini" with a kasra on the ta' following the vowel of the nun. In the codex of 'Abd Allah: "la tahina." Its essence is also: do not weaken ﴿in My remembrance﴾ with what befits Me of exalted attributes and beautiful acts, when conveying My message and calling to My worship. It was said: the meaning is: do not slacken in conveying My message, for remembrance is used figuratively for all acts of worship, and it is among the most noble and greatest of them.

This was related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. It was also said: "do not forget Me wherever you turn, and seek help and support through it, and know that no matter of affairs is accomplished or made possible except through My remembrance."

The plural was used for Harun together with Musa, peace be upon him, in the form of the prohibition addressed to a present person, based on the view that he was absent at that time, by way of prevailing (taghlib), and there is no distance in this, as is not hidden. Likewise his inclusion in the form of the command addressed to a present person, based on that as well, in

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 43:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Go, both of you, to Pharaoh; indeed, he has transgressed.﴾ It is related that Harun (Aaron), while he was in Egypt, was revealed to, to go out to meet Musa (Moses), upon them both be peace. It was also said: he was inspired with this. And it was said: he heard of Musa's approach, so he went out to meet him. It is possible that he went to Mount Tur (Sinai) and they met there, and both were addressed together. It is also possible that this command came after Musa, upon him be peace, came down from Tur toward Egypt and met Harun, upon him be peace, who was approaching him from Egypt. Some scholars distinguished between this and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Go, you and your brother﴾, on the ground that there it did not specify to whom they were to go, whereas here it did. Others said that here they were commanded to go to Pharaoh, whereas the command there was to go to the people of the call in general. Others said that Harun was not addressed there but was addressed here. Others said that the command there was for each of them to go separately, explicitly or by implication, whereas the command here is for them to go together, explicitly. The force of some of these distinctions is not hidden from one who considers them. The difference is clear between this command and the command in His saying, exalted is He, first addressed to Musa, upon him be peace: ﴿Go to Pharaoh; indeed, he has transgressed.﴾

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 44:

﴿Speak to him with gentle speech.﴾ Abu Mu'adh recited (*layinan*) with a light pronunciation. The *fa'* (so) indicates that what follows is arranged upon his transgression, for softening speech is among the things that break the obstinacy of the stubborn and soften the harshness of the tyrants. It is known from this that the command to speak gently is not for the sake of *tarbiyah* (nurturing/education), as has been said. The meaning, as Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: "Do not be harsh with him in your speech, and be gentle with him in the invitation." This is realized through various expressions, among them what will come soon, if Allah wills, namely ﴿Indeed, we are two messengers of your Lord﴾ and so on, and among them what is in *al-Nazi'at*, namely ﴿Would you like to purify yourself?﴾ ﴿And I would guide you to your Lord, so you would fear Him.﴾ This is extremely evident. And [it is found] in gentleness in the invitation, for it is in the form of presentation and consultation. It was also said: "Address him with a kunyah (teknonym)." This was cited as evidence for the permissibility of addressing a disbeliever by his kunyah. This is narrated from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, also, and from Sufyan al-Thawri. He had four kunyahs: Abu al-Walid, Abu Mus'ab, Abu al-Abbas and Abu Murrah. It was also said: "[The meaning is] that He prolonged his youth such that he would not age after it, and [granted him] a kingdom that would not be taken from him except by death, and that the pleasure of food, drink and marriage would remain for him until the time of his death." It is narrated from al-Hasan: "Speak to him: Indeed, you have a Lord, and indeed you have a return, and indeed before you are a Paradise and a Fire. So believe in Allah, and He will admit you to Paradise and protect you from the punishment of the Fire." It was also said: "He, glorified be He, commanded them both to present the promise before the threat, without specifying a particular statement," as has been said:

*He led with the promise before the threat, so that he might restrain the tribes whose ignorant ones...*

And it is narrated from Ikrimah that the gentle speech is "There is no god but Allah," and its gentleness is its lightness upon the tongue. This is the most remote of the sayings, and the closest is the first. Al-Fadl ibn Isa al-Raqashi, whenever he recited this verse, would say: "O One who shows affection to one who opposes Him, how then toward one who allies with Him and calls out to Him?" It was recited in the presence of Yahya ibn Mu'adh, and he wept and said: "My God, this is Your gentleness toward one who says, 'I am the god'; so how is Your gentleness toward one who says, 'You are Allah'?" In it is evidence for the recommendation of gentle speech toward the wrongdoer when admonishing him. ﴿Perhaps he will remember﴾ and reflect, and so he will concede fairness from himself and submit to the truth, and that will lead him to faith. ﴿Or he will fear﴾ that the matter is as you describe, and so his denial will draw him into destruction, and that also calls him to faith, except that the first is for the firmly grounded, and therefore it is put first. It was also said: "He will remember his state when the Nile was withheld, so he went to its bank and went far off, and fell down prostrate before Allah, the Exalted, hoping that He would not disgrace him. Then he mounted, and the Nile began to follow the hoofprint of his horse." From this one derives the greatness of Allah's forbearance and generosity. Or [it means] "he will fear and beware of the seizure of Allah, the Exalted, and His punishment, glorified be He." What is relied upon is what has preceded.

*La'alla* here is for hope (*tarajji*), and it refers to the addressees. The clause is in the position of an accusative, a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun *huma* in (*qawlan*). That is: "Speak to him a gentle speech, hoping that he will remember or fear." The word *aw* (or) is for preventing the absence of both.

The summary of the statement: Undertake the matter as one who hopes and expects that his work will bear fruit and his effort will not be in vain, so he strives willingly and exerts himself to the utmost of his capacity. It was also said: it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun *huma* in (*idhhaba*, go), but the first is better. It was also said: *la'alla* here is interrogative, meaning "will he remember or fear?" Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated this from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. It was said: "This is the gentle speech," and he presented it in the manner of your saying: "Say to Zayd: will he stand?"

Al-Farra' said: *hiya* here has the meaning of *kay* (in order that), the causal (*ta'lili*) sense, which is one of its meanings, as a group went to, among them al-Akhfash and al-Kisa'i. Al-Baghawi cited from al-Waqidi that everything in the Qur'an with *la'alla* is for causation, except the saying of the Exalted: ﴿That perhaps you may abide forever﴾, where it is for comparison (*tashbih*), as in Sahih al-Bukhari. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through al-Suddi from Abu Malik, who said: "*La'alla* in the Qur'an means *kay* in more than one verse, and in ﴿That perhaps you may abide forever﴾ the meaning is 'as if you would abide forever'." He also narrated from Qatadah that he said: "It was recited thus." It is not hidden that its being for comparison is strange, which the grammarians did not mention, and taking it as interrogative here is remote. The causal sense comes to many minds before the sense of hope. But the correct view, as in al-Bahr, is that it is for hope, which is its well-known meaning. It was also said: the hope is a metaphor for the general sense of demand, and this refers back to Him, Mighty and Majestic. What is not valid from Him, glorified be He, is hope in its literal sense. The verifiers hold the first view. The benefit of sending the two of them, peace be upon them, to him, despite knowing that he would not believe, is to establish the proof and cut off excuses.

The Imam claimed that the secret of sending them to him is not known, despite His knowledge, exalted be He, that faith would not come from him. None knows it except Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and in such a station there is no way except submission and abandoning objection.

Some of those who follow [the tradition] used this verse as evidence for the one who holds that Pharaoh will be saved. He said: "*La'alla* from Allah, the Exalted, is necessarily realized. So the verse indicates that one of the two matters, remembrance or fear, has occurred, and this is the basis of salvation." What would show the corruption of this argument has already been mentioned to you. There is no need for us to [accept] what has been said, that he did remember and fear, but since that did not benefit him, and that was at the time of drowning. Rather, it is not valid to take remembrance and fear here as including the remembrance and fear which the speaker claimed Pharaoh attained. So reflect.

[Page 197]

**﴿They both said﴾**: This is an explanatory resumptive clause (*istinaf bayani*, a clause answering an implied question). It is as if it were asked: "What did they both say when they were commanded to do what they were commanded?" So it was said: "They both said," and so on. The saying is attributed to both of them, although the speaker was Musa (peace be upon him), according to the view that Harun (peace be upon him) was absent, by way of *taghlib* (giving precedence to one party in a combined reference), as has passed.

It is possible that Harun (peace be upon him) said this after he had met Musa (peace be upon him), and so the words of Harun are related together with the words of Musa when the verse was revealed. This is like the saying of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾, for this address has been related to us in the plural form, although each of those addressed was addressed only individually. It was also allowed that the two were gathered together at Mount Tur and said together: ﴿Our Lord, we fear that he will hasten against us﴾, that is, that he will hurry to punish us and not wait until the completion of the call and the showing of the miracle. It comes from *faruta*, meaning to go ahead. From it comes *al-farit*, one who goes ahead to the watering place and the stopping place, and *faras farit*, a horse that outruns the other horses. On this reading the subject of *yafruta* is Pharaoh.

Abu al-Baqa' said: It is possible that the intended meaning is "that some saying will come from him against us," so he omitted the saying, as you say *faruta minni qawlun* ("a saying went ahead from me"). This is contrary to the apparent meaning.

Yahya, Abu Nawfal, and Ibn Muhaysin, in one transmission, read *yufrata* with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *fatha* on the *ra'*, from *afrattuhu*, meaning that you carried him to haste. That is, "we fear that some bearer will carry him, out of arrogance or out of fear for his kingdom or other things, to hasten the punishment." A group and al-Za'farani from Ibn Muhaysin read *yufrita* with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *kasra* on the *ra'*, from *al-ifrat* in harm, meaning excessive injury.

This view raised a difficulty together with the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿We will strengthen your arm with your brother, and We will give you both authority, so they will not reach you﴾. This is mentioned before their saying here, as indicated by *sanashuddu* ("We will strengthen"), and it shows that they were protected from his punishment and harm, so how could they fear that? It was answered: It is not necessary that the meaning be "they will not reach you with punishment," since it may mean "they will not reach you to oblige you with the proof." Moreover, the earlier sequence is not known, and even if it were mentioned earlier in the narration, the conjunction *wa* does not indicate order. The explanation mentioned is transmitted from many of the early generations, including Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid, and it is what the apparent meaning requires.

The Imam claimed that they were secure from anything that would cut them off from conveying the message, by rational proof, but they asked, by what was mentioned, for something that would increase the firmness of their hearts, by adding textual proof to rational proof. This is similar to what happened to Ibrahim (peace be upon him) in his saying: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead﴾. It is not hidden that the claim that they knew the rational proof implies that what would cut them off from conveying the message did not occur, which makes the request pointless.

A difficulty was also raised about Musa (peace be upon him) feeling fear, since that prevents the expansion of his breast, which is established by the saying of Allah, the Exalted, after his request: ﴿You have been given your request, O Musa﴾. The Imam answered that expanding the breast means his strength in preserving those commands and prohibitions and guarding those laws in a manner in which error and distortion cannot reach them. That is something other than the removal of fear. You know that many commentators held that expanding the breast here means its widening, which is the absence of distress and inner anxiety at the hardships that come in the path of conveying the message, and receiving them with beautiful patience and good steadfastness.

This was answered by saying that there is no contradiction between fearing something, being patient with it, and not being distressed by it when it occurs. Do you not see that many of the perfected people fear calamity and ask Allah, the Exalted, for protection from it, and when it befalls them, they meet it with a wide breast, are patient with it, and do not become distressed by it? It was also said that they (peace be upon them both) feared punishment only because it would cut off the conveying that was hoped to bring guidance. So their fear, in reality, was only from the interruption and the non-completion of the conveying. Musa (peace be upon him) did not ask for the expansion of the breast in order to bear that.

It was objected that Musa (peace be upon him) had already asked and been given the ease of his affair through the facilitation of means and the removal of obstacles, so how could he fear that conveying would be cut off by punishment? It was answered that this is an explicit request for the removal of a specific obstacle after the request for the removal of a general obstacle, and a request for explicit mention of its removal for greater concern with that matter.

It was said that in the verse there is *taghlib* by him over his brother Harun, placing himself second, and there had been nothing before that indicating Harun's security from it, so consider this carefully. A difficulty was also raised about their not going and their pretext of fear, given the repetition of the command, since it indicates disobedience, and disobedience is not permissible for the prophets (peace be upon them), according to the correct view. The Imam answered that the implication is granted only if the command indicates immediacy (*al-fawr*), and it does not, so it is not. Then he said: This is one of the strongest proofs that a command does not require immediacy, when you combine with it what indicates that disobedience is not permissible for the prophets (peace be upon them).

The *aw* in the saying of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿or that he will transgress﴾ is for preventing a third state (*li-man' al-khulluw*), and the intended meaning is "or that he will increase in transgression until he says about your affair what is not fitting, because of the completeness of his boldness, harshness, and freedom from good manners." In it is a seeking of His mercy, the Exalted, and the appearance of the word *an* (that), although the meaning is sound without it, to show the complete care for the matter and to indicate that fear is established from each of the two conjoined items.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 46:

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive sentence (istinaf), as has passed. Perhaps the attribution of the verb to the third-person pronoun, as has been said, is to indicate a shift of the discourse from one line to another, since what precedes it, the verbs in the first-person form, is a narration about Musa, peace be upon him, unlike what will come, God willing. ﴿Do not fear; indeed you are the superior﴾ also precedes in the form of a narration about the Messenger of God ﷺ, as if it were said: "What did their Lord say to them when they humbly besought Him, glorified is He?" So it was said: He said, that is, to them, ﴿Do not fear﴾ of what you have mentioned. God the Exalted's statement ﴿Indeed I am with you﴾ is a reason for the requirement of the prohibition and an added consolation to them. By His being with them, glorified is He, is meant complete protection and support, as one says, "God the Exalted is with you," as a supplication. He confirmed this by His statement, exalted is He, ﴿I hear and I see﴾, and it is with the object omitted, that is, what passes between you and Him of speech and action. So I will do in every case what befits it of repelling evil and bringing good.

Al-Qaffal said: It is possible that this is in response to the previous statement, and the two of them meant that we fear he will exceed the bounds against us by not listening to us, or that he will transgress by killing us. So He, glorified is He, answered them with His statement: ﴿Indeed I am with you, I hear﴾, that is, your speech, so I will make him [Pharaoh] subservient to listening (وأرى) to his actions, so I will not leave him to do to you what you dislike. He also left the object implied, but it is, as you see. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that nothing be supposed, and it is as if it were said: I am the Guardian of you both and the Helper, Hearing, Seeing. And if the Guardian and the Helper are like that, the protection is complete. This indicates that there is no consideration of the object, and the transitive verb has been made to function as intransitive, because what is intended is the completion of what protection and support depend on by themselves. It is not of the kind of the saying of al-Mutanabbi:

"The grief of his envious rivals and the rage of his enemies that a seer sees and a hearer hears"

according to what al-Tibi claimed. He argued from the verse that hearing and sight are attributes additional to knowledge, on the basis that His statement, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed I am with you﴾, indicates knowledge; and if ﴿I hear and I see﴾ indicated it, repetition would follow, and that is contrary to the original principle.

[Page 198]

﴿So go to him﴾: a command to go to him, which means arriving at him after they were commanded to set out toward him. Hence there is no repetition. It is coordinated with ﴿Do not fear﴾, with regard to the fact that the latter is the reason given for it by what follows. ﴿And say: "We are two messengers of your Lord"﴾: they were commanded to say this from the outset, to establish the truth, so that the tyrant would know their status and build his reply upon it. In the mention of the title of Lordship together with its attribution to his (Pharaoh's) pronoun there is a gentleness that is not hidden, even though the accursed one saw in it a belittling of himself, since he claims lordship for himself, and he did not count this among harsh speech. Likewise is the saying of the Exalted, ﴿So send with us the Children of Israel﴾ to the end of the verse, contrary to the view of the Imam. The fa' in (fa-arsil, "so send") indicates that what follows is consequent upon what precedes, for their being the two messengers of His Lord, may He be exalted, is what necessitates sending the Children of Israel with them. By "sending" is meant releasing them from captivity and removing them from under his oppressive hand, not obliging them to go with them to Syria, as His saying, glorified is He, ﴿and do not torment them﴾ indicates, meaning: by leaving them in the torment they were in. For they were under the rule of the Copts, who used them in hard labour such as digging, building and carrying stones, and they would kill their sons in one year and leave them in the next, and use their women for service.

Perhaps they began with asking for the sending of the Children of Israel rather than calling the tyrant and his people to faith, for the sake of gradualness in the call, since releasing the captives does not require changing belief. It was also said: because freeing the believers from the disbelievers is more important than calling them to faith. This, even after accepting it, is based on the premise that the Children of Israel were believers in Moses, peace be upon him, inwardly, or were believers in other prophets, peace be upon them, and this requires evidence. It was also said: he began with asking for their release because of what it contains of removing the obstacle to calling them and their following, and this is more important than calling the Copts.

It was objected that the context here is about calling Pharaoh and repelling his tyranny, so it is the more important, not calling the Children of Israel. It was also said: the first thing they asked of him was faith, as the verse of al-Nazi'at indicates, except that it is not explicitly stated here, being sufficed by what is there, just as it is not explicitly stated there, being sufficed by what is here. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, we have come to you with a sign from your Lord﴾ is an explanatory resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani), and in it is a confirmation of what the preceding speech contained of the claim to messengerhood and a reason for the obligation of sending. For their coming with a sign from Him, exalted is He, is what establishes their messengerhood, confirms it, and makes obedience to their command obligatory. The explicit mention of the name of the Lord in place of the pronoun, together with its attribution to the pronoun of the addressee, is for emphasis on what has been mentioned of confirmation and reasoning. Qad is used for certainty and emphasis as well, and it was forced to indicate expectation (tawaqquʿ). The singular "sign" is used despite there being several, because the purpose is to establish the claim by its proof, not to state the multiplicity of the argument. It is as if it were said: "We have come to you with what establishes our claim." It was also said: the sign here means the hand. It was also said: the staff. And the two statements are as you see.

﴿And peace be upon the one who follows the guidance﴾: that is, safety from punishment in both abodes for whoever follows that by affirming the signs of God, exalted is He, which guide to the truth. So "peace" (al-salam) is a verbal noun meaning safety, like al-ridaʿ and al-ridaʿah. "ʿAlā" here carries the meaning of "lām," as the reverse has been reported in His saying, ﴿for them is the curse (al-lanʿah)﴾. Prepositions frequently interchange, and the harmony of wording (mushakalah) has made this good here, since ʿalā has been used in His saying, exalted is He,

**[Page 199]**

﴿Indeed, it has been revealed to us﴾ from our Lord ﴿that the punishment﴾, both worldly and otherworldly, ﴿is for those who deny﴾ His signs, ﴿Exalted and Majestic, and turn away﴾, meaning: turn away from accepting them. Al-Zamakhshari said: "That is, the peace (salam) of the angels who are the guardians of Paradise is upon the rightly guided, and the rebuke of the guardians of the Fire and the punishment is upon the deniers." The verification of this, as it has been said, is that he made peace the greeting of the guardians of Paradise to the rightly guided, which includes the promise of Paradise for them. It also contains an allusion to others, through the rebuke of the guardians of the Fire, which includes the threat of its punishment for them, because the context calls for encouragement toward what has a good outcome, namely affirming the Messengers, peace be upon them, and deterrence from opposing them. So if salam were taken to mean safety (salamah), it would not convey that this applies in the outcome.

As for what has been said, that there is no indication in the wording of this specification, that is not accepted. And the claim that it is not a greeting, since it was not at the beginning of the meeting, is refuted by the fact that it was not the greeting of the two brothers, peace be upon them, but the greeting of the angels, peace be upon them. You know that this interpretation is wholly contrary to the apparent meaning, and denying that is obstinacy.

In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit by Abu Hayyan), it says: "This is a strange interpretation. If by the punishment is meant the punishment in both abodes, and by peace is meant safety from that punishment, then encouragement toward affirmation and deterrence from its opposite are achieved in the most complete way." Abu Hayyan also said: "The apparent meaning is that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and peace﴾ etc., is a separate statement. ﴿And peace﴾ here means a greeting, and this came in accordance with the custom of greeting at the end of speech, except that they, peace be upon them, disassociated themselves through it from Pharaoh and singled out the followers of guidance with it, encouraging him to join their ranks." He also used it as evidence for prohibiting greeting the disbelievers, and that when one needs to address them in speech or writing, this formula is used.

In the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) it is reported that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) wrote to Heraclius: "From Muhammad, Messenger of God, to Heraclius, great one of the Romans: Peace be upon him who follows guidance." Abd al-Razzaq also narrated it in al-Musannaf, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, from Qatadah, who said: "The greeting to the People of the Book when you enter their houses is that you say: Peace be upon him who follows guidance." It is not hidden that the aforementioned inference is not far-fetched, had their speech, peace be upon them, ended with this greeting. But it did not end with it; rather, after it they said: ﴿Indeed, it has been revealed to us﴾ etc. And this sentence, according to all the interpretations, appears to be a resumptive clause giving the reason. It may be used as evidence for the validity of the view that implied meaning (mafhum) is valid, so reflect on this. The apparent view is that both sentences are part of the speech that was taught to them.

Some have claimed that the taught speech ended at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We have come to you with a sign from your Lord﴾, and that what follows is the words of the two of them, peace be upon them, brought for promise and threat. The Murji'ah (a theological sect holding that faith is not affected by deeds) used His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Indeed, it has been revealed to us﴾ etc., as evidence that non-disbelievers are not punished at all. It is answered that this holds only if the definite article in "the punishment" is for the generic or comprehensive sense. But if it is for a specific known punishment, that is, the punishment arising from intense anger or the lasting punishment, for example, then it does not hold. Likewise, if the generic or comprehensive sense is meant as a rhetorical hyperbole, and the extreme punishment that is followed by endless safety is regarded as no punishment, it does not follow that the believer who fell short in deeds is never punished at all.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 49:**

﴿He said﴾, that is, Pharaoh, after they had come to him and conveyed to him what they had been commanded. He omitted mention of this for brevity, and to indicate that when they were commanded to do so, they hastened to comply without delay, and that this was so evident that there was no need to state it explicitly. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that when they were commanded to go to him and say what was mentioned to him, they came together to his gate and waited for a time without being admitted. Then he admitted them after a severe screening, and they entered, and what Allah the Exalted has related took place.

Ahmad and others related from Wahb ibn Munabbih that when Allah the Exalted commanded Musa, peace be upon him, with what he was commanded, he set out toward Pharaoh in a city around which lions had been placed in a thicket that he had planted, and the lions were there with their keepers; if you set them loose on anyone, they would devour him. The city had four gates, and the thicket surrounded it. Musa, peace be upon him, approached by the main road that Pharaoh could see. When the lions saw him, they
[p. 200]
roared like foxes, and the keepers were astonished and feared Pharaoh. He continued until he reached the gate and struck it with his staff. He was wearing a woollen cloak and trousers. When the doorkeeper saw him, he was amazed at his audacity, so he left him and did not admit him. He said: "Do you know whose gate you are striking? You are only striking the gate of your master." He said: "You, and I, and Pharaoh are all servants of my Lord, and I am His helper." The doorkeeper informed the one next to him among the doorkeepers, until the matter reached the lowest of them. Beyond him were seventy chamberlains, each of whom had under his command as many soldiers as Allah willed, until the report reached Pharaoh. He said: "Bring him in to me." When he came to him, Pharaoh said to him: "Do I know you?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Did we not raise you among us as a child?" Musa, peace be upon him, gave the answer he had given before. Pharaoh said: "Seize him." Musa, peace be upon him, hastened and threw down his staff, and behold, it was a clear serpent. It charged at the people, and they fled from it, and twenty-five thousand of them died; some of them killed others. Pharaoh stood up in retreat until he entered the house, and said: "O Musa, set between us and you a term that we may consider." Musa said: "I have not been commanded to that. I was only commanded to confront you, and if you do not come out to me, I will enter upon you."

Then Allah the Exalted revealed to him: "Set between you and him a term, and say to him: 'You set it.'" Pharaoh said: "Make it forty days." He did so. Pharaoh would not go to the privy except once every forty days, so that day recurred forty times. Musa, peace be upon him, left the city, and when he passed the lions, they bowed to him with their tails, and walked with him, escorting him, without provoking him or anyone of the Children of Israel.

It is apparent that Harun was with him at the time of the coming, and perhaps he was not mentioned in this report because Musa, peace be upon him, sufficed. It has also been said that when the two of them presented to Pharaoh what they presented, he consulted Asiyah, who said: "It is not fitting for anyone to reject what they call to." Then he consulted Haman, who never decided a matter without his opinion, and he said to him: "I used to believe that you were a man of intellect; you would be a possessor and become a possessed, and a lord and become a subject." So he refused to accept what Musa, peace be upon him, had proposed. The apparent sense of this is that the consultation came before the discussion, though it is possible that it came after it. In such accounts, the better course is to rely on what is in the Revealed Text (the Qur'an) and not to turn to anything else, unless its authenticity is reliable, or unless the Revealed Text contains nothing that conflicts with it, like the preceding report. For Pharaoh's making the term conflicts with what will come, if Allah wills, in the words of Musa, peace be upon him, when Pharaoh asked him to set an appointment: ﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾. The apparent sense is that the incident was not repeated. The sentence is an explanatory resumption, as if it were said: "What did he say when they came to him and said to him what they said?" It is answered: ﴿He said: "Who is your Lord, O Musa?"﴾ He did not attribute the Lord to himself, not even by way of relating what is in the words of the Exalted: ﴿We are the messengers of your Lord﴾, and His words, glory be to Him: ﴿We have come to you with a sign from your Lord﴾, owing to the extreme of his arrogance and the utmost of his tyranny. Rather, he attributed it to the two of them, since the sender must necessarily be lord of the messenger. It has also been said that this is because they had already declared His lordship over all, by saying: ﴿We are the messengers of the Lord of the worlds﴾, as occurred in surah al-Shu'ara'. The restriction here to mention of His lordship over Pharaoh suffices for the purpose intended. The particle "fa" (so) indicates that the question follows from what preceded, namely that they were the messengers of their Lord. That is: "If you are the messengers of your Lord who sent you, then tell me who is your Lord who sent you." The address is specified to Musa, peace be upon him, though the address is directed to both of them, because it was apparent to him that he was the principal in the mission, and Harun was his minister. It is possible that this is an insinuation that he himself is Musa's lord, as he said: ﴿Did we not raise you among us as a child?﴾ It has been said that this is more fitting to his deception of a foolish people. It has also been said that he knew that Musa, peace be upon him, had a speech impediment (ratta, a lisp or difficulty in pronunciation), so he wanted to silence him. This is based on the view of many exegetes that some impediment remained in the tongue of Musa, peace be upon him, to some degree, and the discussion of this has already preceded.

[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 50]

﴿He said﴾: that is, Musa (peace be upon him), who took the lead in answering because he was singled out for the question. ﴿Our Lord﴾ is a mubtada' (subject).

[Page 201]

The words of the Exalted, ﴿who gave everything its creation﴾, are its khabar (predicate). It has also been said that it is the khabar of an omitted mubtada', meaning: "He is our Lord," and the relative clause is its description. The apparent meaning is that by the first-person pronoun he (peace be upon him) meant himself and his brother (peace be upon them both).

Some of the verifying scholars (al-muhaqqiqun) said: he meant all created beings, as a confirmation of the truth and a refutation of the accursed one (Pharaoh). This is shown by what is contained in the relative clause. ﴿Everything﴾ is the first object of a'ta (gave), and ﴿its creation﴾ is the second object. It is a masdar (verbal noun) in the sense of the passive participle (ism al-maf'ul). The pronoun in the genitive refers to "thing." The generality derived from "kull" (every) is to be considered after it has been referred back to "thing," so that the well-known objection raised against this kind of construction is avoided. The apparent meaning is generality of individuals: He gave every one of things the matter it sought through the tongue of its readiness (isti'dad), such as its form, shape, benefit, harm, and other things. Or [it means] the matter appropriate to what has been attached to it of properties and benefits, corresponding to it. Just as He gave the eye the shape that corresponds to seeing, the ear the form that suits hearing, and likewise the nose, the hand, the foot, and the tongue: each one of them corresponds to the benefit attached to it, without being alien to it. It has also been said that khalq (creation) remains in its verbal-noun sense, meaning existence (al-ijad). That is, He gave every thing the existence for which it was prepared, or the existence appropriate to it, in the sense that He, the Exalted, brought every thing into existence according to its readiness, or in the manner appropriate to it. And this, as you see, is [weak].

Some scholars took the generality to be generality of kinds (al-anwa') rather than generality of individuals. It has been said that this is so that a contradiction would not follow. The objection is answered by saying that some individuals did not reach completion because of an accident that befell them. The truth is that God, the Exalted, takes wisdom into account in what He creates and commands, out of grace and mercy, not as an obligation. This is among the matters on which the People of the Sunnah and the Community (Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah) agreed, as transmitted by the author of al-Mawaqif and 'Uyun al-Jawahir. Thus every thing is perfect in its rank and good in its own essence. Indeed, He, the Exalted, said: ﴿the Mighty, the Merciful, who made everything He created good﴾. Making the generality here a generality of kinds is something hardly anyone would hold.

He, glorified be He, also said: ﴿You see no disproportion in the creation of the All-Merciful﴾. That is, from the standpoint of its being attributed to the All-Merciful, and of His creating it in accordance with wisdom, by the requirement of generosity and mercy. Disproportion among things arises only when some of them are compared with others. So turning away from the apparent meaning of generality of individuals to generality of kinds, for the reason mentioned, arises from little verification.

It has also been said that the reason for departing [from the apparent meaning] is that a'ta (gave) is literally in the past tense. If "everything" were taken as generality of individuals, it would follow that all of them had already come into existence and been given [their creation], whereas many of them, indeed most of them, have not yet come into existence nor been given [anything] yet. By contrast, if it is taken as generality of kinds, there is no such problem, since all kinds have already come into being, and no new kind will appear after that, although that would be possible. There is clear discussion of this, so let it be understood.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, and al-Suddi that the meaning is: He gave every male animal its counterpart in creation and form, a female. They appear to have treated "kull" as meaning a multitude, since otherwise universal generality is invalid, as is not hidden. In my view this meaning is among the branches of the earlier meaning that we mentioned. Perhaps the intent of the one who said it was an illustration; otherwise it is very far-fetched, and hardly anyone to whom it is attributed would say it.

It has also been said: ﴿its creation﴾ is the first object, and the masdar is also in the sense of the passive participle; the pronoun in the genitive refers to the relative pronoun, and ﴿everything﴾ is the second object. The meaning is: He, glorified be He, gave His creatures everything they need and by which they gain benefit. He placed the second object first to give it importance, because the intended purpose is to bestow favor through it. This view is attributed to al-Jubba'i (a Mu'tazili theologian). The first view is more apparent in wording and meaning.

'Abd Allah, some of the Companions of the Messenger of God (may God's blessings and peace be upon him), Abu Nahik, Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-A'mash, al-Hasan, Nusayr from al-Kisa'i, and Ibn Nuh from Qutaybah and Salam read ﴿khalaqahu﴾ (He created it) in the active past tense form. [The clause is then a description of the genitive-attached noun or of the noun modified], by way of an irregularity, and the second object is omitted for brevity, being indicated by the context. The meaning is: He gave every thing that He, the Exalted, created what would set it right or what it needs. al-Zamakhshari (the Mu'tazili exegete) took this to be from the class of "a'ta and mana'a" (gives and withholds), meaning: every thing that He, glorified be He, created, He did not leave devoid of His gift and bounty. He preferred this in al-Kashshaf, on the ground that it is more eloquent and more evident. It has also been said that the first is better in grammatical construction and more suited to the context. In my view, however, the first is more in keeping with the first meaning for the first reading. There is some hesitation about what he said in al-Kashshaf.

﴿Then He guided﴾: that is, He directed and showed, glorified be He, by this, to His existence. Whoever considers these created things and the subtle wisdom they contain knows that they have a Maker who necessarily exists, of great giving and generosity. The sum of the verse is: "Our Lord is He who created everything according to its readiness, or in the manner appropriate to it, and made it a sign pointing to Him, majestic is His majesty." This making, though it is posterior in essence to the creation and there is no interval of time between them at all, has nonetheless been introduced with the particle thumma (then) to indicate a separation in rank, as its aspect is not hidden from the reflective one. In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim (Abu al-Su'ud's exegesis), [it says]: "﴿Then He guided﴾ to the way of benefiting from and gaining advantage from what He gave, and taught it how to reach its survival and its perfection, either by choice, as in animals, or by nature, as in inanimate things and the natural powers, both vegetative and animal."

Since creation, which is the composition of parts and the arrangement of bodies, precedes guidance, which is an expression for the bringing into being of the moving and perceiving powers in those bodies, he placed the particle of separation between them. [End of quotation.] You should know that creation in linguistic usage is more general than what he mentioned; the moving and perceiving powers fall under the generality of ﴿everything﴾, whether it is generality of individuals or generality of kinds; and some kind of metaphor must be assumed in "guided" according to that interpretation. It has also been said, according to the interpretation narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and those with him: "Then He guided it to coming together with its mate and to mating." It has been said otherwise as well. God, the Exalted, has a fine reply here; how concise it is, how comprehensive, and how clear, for one who applies his mind and looks with the eye of fairness and is seeking the truth. From here it has been said: It would have been apparent for him (peace be upon him) to say, "Our Lord is the Lord of the worlds," but he took the path of guidance and the wise manner, and pointed to the origination of all existent things, their total need of Him, glorified be He, the diversity of their ranks, and that He, the Exalted, is the Powerful, the Wise, the Rich, the Bountiful, in absolute terms.

The verse has been used as evidence that Pharaoh was knowledgeable of God, the Exalted, but was obstinate, because the relative clause must be known [to the listener], and whenever this clause was known to him, he knew Him, glorified be He. This is the view of some about him, may the curse of God be upon him. They also argued for this with the words of the Exalted: ﴿You know that none sent these down but the Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾; and His words: ﴿They denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance﴾; and His words in Surah al-Qasas: ﴿They thought they would not be returned to Us﴾, for that contains only the denial of the return, not of the origin; and His words in al-Shu'ara': ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ up to His words, glorified be He: ﴿Indeed your messenger who was sent to you is surely mad﴾. He meant by this: "I ask him for the explanation of the quiddity (mahiyyah), and he explains existence." This indicates that he acknowledged the basic fact of existence, and that his rule did not extend beyond the Copts and did not reach Syria. Do you not see that when Musa (peace be upon him) fled to Madyan, Shu'ayb said to him: ﴿Fear not; you have escaped from the wrongdoing people﴾? How then would he believe that He is the God of the world? And [how could he be] rational, since he was accountable, and every rational person knows necessarily that he came into being after non-existence; and whoever is such needs a governor, so he would be a believer in a governor. And [it is also argued] that he asked here "by whom" seeking the mode (kayfiyyah), and in al-Shu'ara' "what" seeking the quiddity.

The apparent view is that the question "by whom" came first. It is as though Musa (peace be upon him), when he had established the proof for existence, left the dispute with him on this point, knowing its clarity, and turned to a more difficult matter, because the knowledge of His quiddity, the Exalted, is not attainable by human beings.

[Page 203]

There is much debate about these proofs, and not all is clear. Some people have said that he was ignorant of God, the Exalted, given the agreement that a rational person cannot believe of himself that he is the creator of the heavens and the earth and what is between them. They differed about the mode of his ignorance. It is possible that he was a dahri (materialist who denies a Creator altogether), and perhaps he used to say that a possible thing needs no effective cause for its existence, and that the existence of the world is by chance, as is reported from Democritus and his followers. It is also possible that he was a philosopher who believed in an efficient cause that necessitates [its effect]. It is possible that he was a worshipper of the stars, possible that he was a worshipper of idols, and possible that he was of the incarnationist Hulul sect (the view that God dwells in created bodies).

As for his claim to lordship for himself, it means that whoever is under his hand must obey him, submit to him, and not be occupied with obeying another. Scholars argued from the fact that Musa (peace be upon him) started a debate and asked for proof, rather than engaging in folly and shouting, although [Pharaoh] was a tyrant of great brutality, that shouting and folly with one who calls to the truth is extremely ugly. Thus it is not fitting for one who claims Islam and knowledge to accept for himself what Pharaoh himself would not accept. From the fact that Musa (peace be upon him) busied himself with establishing evidence for the sought matter, [it is also inferred] the corruption of blind imitation (taqlid) in such matters, and the corruption of the saying of one who claims that knowledge of God, the Exalted, is derived from the word of the Messenger. And from the recounting of Pharaoh's words and Musa's reply (peace be upon him), [it is inferred] that it is permissible to report the words of one who is in error together with the reply, so that doubt does not remain; and that the one who is in the right must listen to the objection of the one in error, so that he may be able to occupy himself with resolving it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 51:

﴿He said: "What then is the state of the former generations?"﴾ When the accursed one (al-La'in) witnessed the luminous proof that he (peace be upon him) had arranged in the course of his reply, in a splendid form, he feared that the truth of his (peace be upon him) statements and the clear falsehood of his own fabrications would become manifest to the people. So he wanted to divert him (peace be upon him) from his methods toward matters that do not concern him, namely stories that have no real connection to the message, while giving the impression that they are connected to it, and to occupy him from what he was engaged in. Perhaps some kind of heedlessness would appear in him, and he would then climb up by that means to claim, before his people, some kind of knowledge. So he said, ﴿What then is the state of﴾ etc.

The word al-bal (بال) originally means thought (al-fikr). It is said: "such-and-such came to my mind (khatara bi-bali)," and then it was applied to the condition that one takes care of, and this is the meaning intended here. It is not dualized or pluralized, except anomalously in their saying bi-alat (بآلات). It seems that the fa' (ف) is for making what follows a consequence of the claim to prophethood, i.e., "If you are a messenger, then inform me of the condition of the past generations and the earlier nations, and what detailed events befell them."

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 52:**

﴿He said﴾ Musa, peace be upon him, ﴿Its knowledge is with my Lord﴾. That is: this is among the unseen matters that none knows except Allah, the Exalted. I am only a servant who knows of them nothing except what He has taught me of matters related to the prophetic mission, and knowledge of the conditions of past generations and what befell them in detail, which has no connection to the station of prophethood, as you suppose.

It has been said: he asked him about that only to test whether he was a prophet or was among the storytellers (qussas) who studied the stories of earlier nations. Al-Naqqash said: when the accursed one heard the admonition of the believer of Pharaoh's family, ﴿O my people, indeed I fear for you a day like the day of the factions﴾ (40:30), and so on, he asked about that. So Musa, peace be upon him, referred its knowledge to Allah, the Exalted, because the Torah had not yet been revealed to him, since its revelation came after the destruction of Pharaoh.

Some have said: the question is built upon his, peace be upon him, saying ﴿And peace be upon him who follows guidance﴾ (20:47), etc. That is: what is the state of the past generations after their death, in terms of happiness and misery? The intent is to explain that in detail, as if it were said: if the matter is as you have mentioned, then explain to us the state of those who passed away, in terms of happiness and misery. Therefore he, peace be upon him, referred the knowledge to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Thus the objection is dismissed that if what was asked about were the happiness and misery mentioned, it would have been answered by explaining that whoever among them followed guidance was safe, and whoever turned away was punished, as indicated by His saying, ﴿And peace be upon him﴾ etc.

It has also been said: it is connected to His saying, ﴿Indeed it has been revealed to us﴾ (20:48), etc. That is: if the matter is so, what is the case of the earlier generations, that they denied and yet were not punished? It has also been said: it is connected to that, and the question is about the Resurrection (ba'th), and the pronoun in ﴿its knowledge﴾ refers to the Hour. Both opinions are as you see, and returning the pronoun to the Hour is more calamitous than the matter of the connection (wa-amarr).

It has been said: it is connected to Musa's answer, as an objection to what it implies of Allah's knowledge of the details of things and their particulars, which entails the comprehensiveness of His power, the Exalted, over all things. As if it were said: if Allah's knowledge is as you indicated, then what do you say about the past generations, given their multitude, the length of their period, and the distance of their regions? How does His knowledge encompass them, their parts, and their conditions? So he answered that His knowledge encompasses all of that, up to the end of what Allah the Exalted related. The singling out of the earlier generations by mention, on this view, though generalization is more appropriate, is said to be because Pharaoh knew some of them, and by that he could recognize the truth of Musa, peace be upon him, if he explained their conditions. It has also been said: it is to silence Musa, peace be upon him, and humble him before his people in the quickest time, since he supposed that if he generalized, perhaps Musa, peace be upon him, would occupy himself with detailing Allah's knowledge of the observable, apparent existents, and the period would be prolonged and what he intended would not be accomplished. In any case, what was said falls away: that this opinion rejects the singling out of the earlier generations from among all beings, for if he had taken them in their entirety, it would have been more evident and more powerful in accomplishing what he intended. Yes, the remoteness of this opinion is not something to be denied.

It has been said: it is an objection to him by another way, as if it were said: if what you mentioned as proof for establishing the Origin is so clear, then what of the earlier generations, that they forgot Him, the Glorified, and did not believe in Him, the Exalted? If the proof were clear, it would have been obligatory for them not to be heedless of it. Its implication, as the Imam said, is the opposition of proof to imitation (taqlid). Close to this is what is said: that it is connected to His saying ﴿Then He guided﴾ (20:50), according to the first interpretation, as if it were said: if the matter is so, what of the earlier generations, that they did not reason from that and so did not believe? The summary of the answer on both views is that this is among the secrets of divine decree (qadar), and its knowledge is with my Lord, may His majesty be exalted. ﴿In a Book﴾: the apparent view is that it is a second predicate (khabar thani) of ''ilmuha'' (its knowledge), and the first predicate is ﴿with my Lord﴾.

It is permitted that the two be one predicate, like "this is sweet sour" (hadha hulwun hamid), and that the predicate be ﴿with my Lord﴾, while ﴿in a Book﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial (hal) from the concealed pronoun in the adverbial complement (zarf), or it is a complement (ma'mul) of it. It is also permitted that the predicate be ﴿in a Book﴾, and ''with my Lord'' be in the position of a circumstantial from the concealed pronoun within it, the governing element being the adverbial complement, which governs in a delayed position according to the opinion of al-Akhfash. It has been said: it is a circumstantial from the genitive noun (mudaf ilayh) in ''ilmuha'', and it has been said: it is an adverbial complement of the second adverbial complement, and it has been said: it is an adverbial complement of the knowledge. Abu al-Baqa' mentioned all of these, then said: it is not permissible for ﴿in a Book﴾ to be connected to ''ilmuha'' while ﴿with my Lord﴾ is the predicate, because the verbal noun (masdar) does not govern what comes after its predicate.

You know that the first of these possibilities is the most probable. It seems that by the Book, peace be upon him, he meant the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), that is: its knowledge is recorded in the Preserved Tablet with its details. This is a figurative usage (majaz), since what is literally recorded is only the inscriptions indicating the words that contain the explanation of their conditions, which are known to Him, the Exalted. It is also permitted that the intended meaning of the Book is the register (daftar), as is well known in the language, and this would be an image (tamthil) of its firm establishment and settlement in the knowledge of Him, the Mighty and Majestic, by what the knower has entrusted to memory and recorded with his scribes on a scroll. Perhaps this is the better one. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿My Lord neither errs nor forgets﴾ hints at it, for the absence of error and forgetfulness is more fitting to the perfection of knowledge. Apparently, on both views, it repels the suspicion of need, because recording in a book is done by one who does so out of fear of forgetting, and Allah the Exalted is exempt from that. Recording in the Preserved Tablet is for wisdoms and benefits, some of which those who know are aware of. It has been said: on the first view, this clause is a completion to repel what might be suspected, that recording in the Tablet is due to need, out of the possibility of error or forgetfulness, from which Allah, glorified be He, is exalted. On the second view, it is a concluding phrase (tadhyil) to emphasize the preceding clause, and the meaning is: my Lord does not err initially, in that nothing among things enters outside the scope of His vast knowledge, so His knowledge, glorified be He, would not be comprehensive of things; nor does anything escape Him subsequently, by leaving the circle of His knowledge, the Majestic, after having entered it. Rather He, the Mighty and Majestic, encompasses everything in knowledge, eternally and everlastingly. The explanation of the two clauses in this manner is what al-Qaffal went to, and some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) agreed with him, and its excellence is not hidden.

Ibn al-Mundhir and a group related from Mujahid that the two verbs have one meaning, but that is not right. The two verbs: it is said that they are treated as intransitive (munazzalan manzila al-lazim), and it is said that they remain transitive, with an omitted object, meaning: he does not err any of the things nor forget it. It is said: [the object is] some of the conditions of the earlier generations. From al-Hasan: he does not err at the time of resurrection, nor forget it. It seems he made the question about the resurrection, and singled out the object for its sake, and you know its state. From Ibn Abbas: the meaning is: He does not leave whoever disbelieved in Him until He takes vengeance upon him, nor leave whoever affirmed His oneness until He rewards him. It seems that Allah, may He be pleased with him, made the question about their conditions from the aspect of happiness and misery, and the answer about that in a general way. So reflect, and do not be heedless.

Some have claimed that the clause is in the position of an attribute (sifah) of ''kitab'' (Book), and the returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: my Lord does not err it, nor forget it. It has been said: the returning pronoun is a concealed pronoun in the verb, and ''Rabbi'' (my Lord) is put in the accusative as object, meaning: my Lord does not err the Book, that is, lose it. In ﴿yansa﴾ (forgets) there is also a pronoun returning to it, meaning: nor does He forget the Book anything, that is, He does not leave it, in the manner of ﴿It leaves out no small thing nor great, but enumerates it﴾ (18:49).

The greatest wonder is the deviation from the apparent meaning to opinions like these. And the mention of "my Lord" in a place where a pronoun would be expected is to delight in mentioning Him, the Exalted, and for increased affirmation and to indicate the causal basis of the ruling, for lordship (ruburriyyah) necessarily entails the absence of error and forgetfulness.

Al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Jahdari, Hammad ibn Salamah, Ibn Muhaysin, and Isa al-Thaqafi read ﴿lā yuḍillu﴾ (does not err) with a damma on the yā' (from aḍalla), and it is said they have the same meaning: aḍlaltu al-shay' and ḍalaltuhu. In al-Sihah, from Ibn al-Sikkit: it is said, "aḍlaltu ba'iri" (I lost my camel) when it has gone away from you, and "ḍalaltu al-masjid wa al-zad" (I lost the mosque and the provision) when you do not know their location; and likewise every fixed thing that cannot be found. A similar statement is related from al-Farra' and Ibn Isa. Abu al-Baqa', in explaining this reading, mentioned two aspects: he made "rabbi" accusative as object, and the meaning is: no one causes my Lord to err from His knowledge; and he made it the subject, and the meaning is: my Lord does not find the Book lost, that is, perished. Al-Sulami read ﴿lā yuḍallu rubbī wa lā yunsā﴾ with both verbs in the passive voice (passive form, not naming the agent).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 20, Verse 53:**

﴿Who made the earth for you a cradle﴾ etc. It is possible that this is the beginning of a speech from Him, Exalted and Majestic, and that Musa's speech, peace be upon him, was complete at His words: ﴿and He does not err, nor forget﴾. In that case the relative clause is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the sentence, as some have said, is a resumptive explanatory clause (*isti'naf bayani*), as if Glorified is He, when He related Musa's speech up to his words, ﴿My Lord does not err, nor forget﴾, was asked what Musa meant by "my Lord," and so He, Glorified is He, said: He is the One ﴿who made﴾ etc. The Imam chose this and even said: it is necessary to affirm it definitively. It is also possible that it is part of Musa's speech, peace be upon him, on the basis that he heard it from Allah, Exalted and Majestic, and incorporated it word for word into his speech; this is why he said "for you" (*lakum*) and not "for us." This is of the kind of *iqtibas* (weaving Qur'anic wording into one's own speech). In that case the relative clause is either in the nominative position, as a qualifier of "my Lord," or the predicate of an omitted subject as in the previous possibility, or in the accusative position as a praise (*madh*). Al-Zamakhshari chose this. On both possibilities, there is without doubt an *iltifat* (shift of grammatical person) in His words: ﴿so We brought forth﴾; or it is on the basis that Musa, peace be upon him, said that from himself, without having heard it from Allah, Exalted and Majestic. He said: "so He brought forth with it," with the verb *akhraja* attributed to the third-person pronoun, but when Allah related it, He attributed it to the first-person pronoun, because the one relating is the one being related about, so the referent of the two pronouns is one. The apparent sense of Ibn al-Munir's words points to choosing this, where he said after explaining it: "This is a good and subtle view, and it is the closest of the views to *iltifat*."

Some have denied that there is *iltifat* in it, or [said] that he, peace be upon him, said it from himself in this wording, unaltered in the relating. His words "We brought forth" are like the speech of a king's close attendants: "We commanded," "We built," "We did," when they mean only the king. Or it is attributed to a plural pronoun, meaning: "We, the community of servants, brought forth by that water, by tilling, pairs of various plants," as has been said. In this view, and in what precedes it, there is no *iltifat* in "We brought forth." It is also possible that this is Musa's speech up to His words, Exalted is He, ﴿water﴾, and what follows is the speech of Allah, Exalted and Majestic, whom He, Glorified is He, joined to Musa's speech at the time of relating it to our Prophet (ﷺ). In my view, the first possibility is the best, indeed it almost is the only one; then the second, then the third; and all the other possibilities are of no account. The reason for this is hardly hidden. Something similar to this verse will come, if Allah, Exalted is He, wills, in *al-Zukhruf*.

*Al-mahd* (cradle) is originally a verbal noun, then it became a generic noun for what is prepared for a child. Its accusative status is as a second object of *ja'ala* if it means "made" (*sayyara*), or as a circumstantial (*hal*) if it means "created" (*khalaqa*). The meaning is: He made it for you like a cradle. It is also permissible for it to remain a verbal noun without being transferred, for the reason mentioned. The meaning would then be: He made it a possessor of a cradle, or prepared, or the very essence of a cradle, for emphasis. It has also been permitted that it is accusative by a verb implied from its own root, i.e. *mahadaha mahdan*, meaning he spread it out and made it level, and the clause is then a circumstantial clause of the subject or the object.

Kathir read *mihadan* (with *kasra*), and this, as al-Mufaddal said, is like *al-mahd* in being a verbal noun and in being transferred. Abu 'Ubayd said: *al-mihad* is a noun and *al-mahd* is a verbal noun. Some said it is the plural of *mahd*, like *ka'b* and *ki'ab*, though the familiar plural is *muhud*. The meaning on the plural reading is: He made every place of it a cradle for each one of you.

﴿And He made for you paths therein﴾, i.e. He provided you with roads, and placed them between the mountains and the valleys, which you travel from region to region, so that you may fulfill your needs from them and benefit from their advantages and conveniences. To indicate that the benefit is specifically for humans, He repeated "for you," having mentioned it first to explain that the primary intended beneficiary of that is the human being.

﴿And He sent down from the sky﴾, from its direction or from itself, according to what is in some reports, ﴿water﴾, which is rain, ﴿so We brought forth thereby﴾, i.e. with that water and by means of it, since Allah, Exalted is He, deposited in it what He deposited, as the Maturidiyya and others among the righteous predecessors have held. However, it has no effect except by the permission of Allah, Exalted is He, like all other causes; so this does not contradict His, Exalted and Majestic, being the true agent. Glorified is He did this despite His complete power to create whatever He wills without any intermediary, just as He created some things in this manner, out of regard for wisdom.

It has also been said: "by it" means "with it" (*'indahu*), and the Ash'ariyya went to this view. So water, in their view, is like fire in that it has no inherent power to, for example, quench thirst, and fire is like water in that it has no inherent power to burn. The difference between them is that Allah, Exalted is He, has the custom of creating satisfaction upon drinking water and burning upon contact with fire, and not the reverse. They claimed that whoever says that any of the causes has an inherent power of influence deposited in it by Allah, Exalted is He, is nearer to disbelief than to faith. By my life, this is an extreme leap of judgment.

The apparent expression would have been "so He brought forth," but He shifted to the first-person to draw attention to what is evident in it of the indication of complete power and wisdom, through the fact that a great matter is attributed only to the Great; and to announce that it cannot be accomplished except by a powerful, obeyed, greatly exalted One, to whose command diverse things submit and to whose will they yield. For this kind of expression is used by kings and great men whose commands are carried out. This past tense, which indicates certainty, and the *fa'* (which indicates swiftness), strengthen this, for it denotes immediate sequence, as some verifying scholars have stated. He explained the sending down and the bringing forth as expressions for the will to send down and to bring forth, justified by the impossibility of the act being carried out by Him, exalted is His state.

This was objected to with a point of dispute; and it does not harm this that it is an customary sequence, nor that it has not been made to indicate causation, since that is already understood from the *ba'* (of "with it").

Al-Khafaji said: You may say that the *fa'* indicates the causation of the will by the sending down, and the *ba'* indicates the causation of the plant by the water, so there is no repetition, as in His words: ﴿so that We may give life thereby﴾. Perhaps this is closer. End of quote.

You know that the sequential sense is more apparent and more eloquent. This pattern of *iltifat* for the aforementioned purpose also occurs in His words: ﴿Do you not see that Allah sends down water from the sky, and We bring forth thereby fruits of varying colours?﴾ and His words: ﴿Is He not best who created the heavens and the earth and sent down for you water from the sky, and We caused to grow thereby gardens of delight?﴾ and His words, Glorified is He: ﴿And it is He who sends down water from the sky, and We bring forth thereby the vegetation of every thing﴾; ﴿pairs﴾, i.e. kinds, which were named so because they come in pairs and some of them are joined to others.

﴿of vegetation﴾ is an explanation and a qualifier of "pairs." Likewise His words, Exalted is He: ﴿diverse﴾, i.e. dispersed, the plural of *shatit*, like *marid* and *mardá*, and its *alif* is for the feminine. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a qualifier of "vegetation," since it is originally a verbal noun in which the singular and plural are alike.
