He means: they are diverse in benefit, taste, colour, scent and form; some are suitable for people and some for beasts.

They said: Among the blessings of Him, Mighty and Exalted, is that the provision of His servants comes about only through the work of livestock; and Allah, Exalted is He, has made their fodder from what exceeds their need, and they cannot eat it.

[Page 206]

And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Eat and graze your livestock﴾ is an object (*maʿmūl*) of a deleted verb of saying (*qawl*), which functions as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) of the pronoun in ﴿So We brought forth﴾. That is, We brought forth the kinds of plants, saying ﴿Eat﴾ and so on, meaning: preparing them for your benefit, both directly and indirectly, having given permission for that. It is also permissible for the saying to be a circumstantial state of the object, meaning: We brought forth various pairs, with this being said of them. The first is more suitable and preferable.

*Raʿā* (to graze), as al-Zajjaj said, is used both intransitively and transitively. It is said: "The animal grazed (*raʿat*) grazing (*raʿyan*)," and "its owner pastured it (*raʿāhā*) with care (*riʿāyatan*)" when he let it out to pasture, sent it forth, and gave it rest.

﴿Surely in that﴾ refers to what has been mentioned of His affairs, exalted is He, and His acts. The distance implied by "that" serves to indicate the exaltedness of His rank and the remoteness of His station in perfection. It has been said that it is because the thing referred to has not been mentioned explicitly by name. The indefiniteness in His saying, glorified is He, ﴿signs﴾ (*li-āyāt*) is for magnification, both in quantity and in quality, meaning: numerous, glorious signs, clear in their indication of God's affairs, exalted is He, in His essence and attributes. ﴿For people of intellect﴾ (*li-ulī al-nuhā*): the plural of *nuhya* with a *ḍamma* on the *nūn*. Reason (*ʿaql*) is called *nuhā* because it restrains (*nahy*) its possessor from following falsehood and committing ugliness, just as it is called *ʿaql* and *ḥijr* because it binds and restrains its possessor from that.

*Nuhā* may also come in the singular with the meaning of reason, as in the *Qāmūs*, and this is the apparent meaning of what has been narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas here, for he said: "That is, for those possessing reason." In another narration from him, he said: "For those possessing piety." This is perhaps an explanation by way of a necessary consequence.

Abu ʿAlī permitted that it be a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), like *al-hudā* (guidance), while most scholars hold it to be a plural, meaning: for those with restraining minds that prevent them from falsehoods. The specification of these being signs for them is because the aspects of their indication of God's affairs, exalted is He, are known only to the intelligent. For this reason their benefit is in truth ascribed back to them, so He, glorified is He, said ﴿Eat and graze﴾ rather than "Eat, you and the livestock."

[Page 208]

﴿from it﴾: i.e., from the earth.

﴿We created you﴾: i.e., within the creation of your father Adam, peace be upon him, from it. Every individual of mankind has a share in his creation, peace be upon him, since his original nature was not confined to himself, peace be upon him, but was a pattern that comprised the nature of all the individuals of the species, in a comprehensive inclusion that entailed the effects of that nature passing over all of them. Thus his creation, peace be upon him, from it was a creation of all of them from it. It was also said:

[Page 209]

The meaning is: We created your bodies from the drop (nutfah) produced from foods, which are produced from the earth, through intermediaries.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ata al-Khurasani, who said: "The angel goes and takes some dust from the place where the person will be buried, and scatters it over the drop, and so he is created from the dust and the drop."

﴿And in it We shall return you﴾: by death and the separation of the parts. This, and what follows it, is based on the majority, on the basis that some people's bodies do not decay, such as the prophets, peace be upon them. The choice of the word fi (in) over ila (to) indicates lasting settlement within it.

﴿And from it We shall bring you forth once again﴾: by reassembling your scattered parts, which are mixed with the dust, into their former form, and returning the spirits from their abode to them. That this bringing forth is "once again" is in view of the fact that our creation from the earth is a bringing forth of us from it, even if it is not in the manner of the second time. Or, "taratan" (once) originally denotes a single turn (of a wheel), which is a motion, and then it was applied to each single one of the successive acts, as was explained regarding "marrah" (once). How subtle is the mention of His words, Exalted is He, ﴿From it We created you﴾, etc., after the mention of plants and their bringing forth from the earth. Every bringing forth includes subtle bodies from the dense earth, and the emergence of the dead is most like the emergence of plants.

* * *

(From the Sufi allusions in the verses) ﴿Ta Ha﴾: O one purified by Us, guiding to Us; or O circumambulator of the Ka'bah of Unity within the sanctuary of Selfhood, and guide of the pure souls to the lofty stations. It was also said: since the letter ta, by the abjad reckoning, is nine, and when the numbers it contains are added together (I mean one, two, three, and so on up to nine), they reach forty-five, an allusion to Adam, because the numerical values of his letters are the same. And since ha, by the abjad reckoning, is five, and the numbers it contains reach fifteen, an allusion to Hawwa' without the hamza. The allusion by the two together is that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is the father and mother of creation. It is as if it were said: O one from whom creation came into being. The gnostic Ibn al-Farid, may Allah sanctify his secret, alluded to this in his saying, in the voice of the Muhammadan Reality:

"Though I am the son of Adam in form,
I have in me a meaning that bears witness to my fatherhood."

And Shaykh Abd al-Ghani al-Nabulusi, may Allah have mercy on him, said concerning this:

"Ta Ha the Prophet, all creation came into being from his light,
Even if the quail were left (…)"

(It was also said: in reckoning, Ta Ha is fourteen, which is an allusion to the rank of fullness (al-badriyya), as if it were said: O full moon of the heaven of the world of possibility.) ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an upon you for you to be distressed﴾ ﴿but as a reminder to him who fears﴾. That is: only to remind him who fears of the days of union that were before the attachment of spirits to bodies, and to inform them that something similar will come to them, so that their souls may be content and their spirits at rest; or to remind them of those days so that they may long for them, let their tears flow over them, and strive to attain what will be a cause of their return. Exalted is Allah, how well has the one who said:

"May Allah water days and nights of ours
that passed, and tears flowed from remembering them.
Would that those days might one day return,
and would that I might return to the land of the Beloved."

[Page 209]

It was also said: those who fear are the scholars, according to His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾. And since knowledge is a place where pride and vanity and the like may arise, it is fitting that its possessor should mention the greatness of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, so that this would be a wall for him, preventing anything of what was mentioned from reaching him. ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾. The Throne is a great body that Allah, Exalted is He, created, as is said, of luminous light, and made it the place of the light of the simple intellect, which is the dawning place of the lights of eternity, and honored it by attributing to it the establishment that cannot be comprehended. It was also said: it was created from four lights of different colors, which are the lights of: Glory be to Allah, Praise be to Allah, There is no god but Allah, and Allah is the Greatest. For this reason it is called al-Atlas (the Empty one). This is the view adopted by the recently emerged group in our time called the Kashfiyya (Unveilers).

Some Sufis mentioned that the Throne is an allusion to the heart of the believer, to which the relation of the well-known Throne is like the relation of a mustard seed to the wilderness, or rather like the relation of a drop to the encompassing ocean. It is the locus of the Truth's gaze, the platform of His manifestation, the descent-place of His command, and the abode of His descent. In the Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din of the Proof of Islam al-Ghazali, it is related that Allah, Exalted is He, said: "My heavens and My earth do not contain Me, but the heart of My servant, the believer, soft and gentle, contains Me." That is, the tranquil, at rest. In al-Risydah of Sadr al-Din al-Qunawi, may Allah sanctify his secret, the wording is: "My earth does not contain Me, nor My heavens, but the heart of My servant, the believer, pious, pure and gentle contains Me." This heart is not an expression for the pine-cone-shaped lump (the physical heart), for in the view of every intelligent person it is too insignificant in form to be the locus of His secret, Exalted is He, let alone to contain Him, Glory be to Him, or to be the object of His highest gaze and His station, Mighty is His affair. Although it is called a heart, that naming is only by way of metaphor, naming the attribute and the bearer by the name of the qualified and the carried. Rather, the human heart is an expression for the comprehensive reality that unites the divine attributes and affairs and the cosmic, spiritual and natural properties and states, and that reality arises from the midpoint of the social configuration between the divine and cosmic attributes and realities, and what these two principles contain of moral qualities and necessary attributes, and what is produced between them after discipline and purification. The pine-cone-shaped heart is the abode of the descent of the outward form from among what we have mentioned, which is the form of the heart's reality. The meaning of the heart's "containing" Him, Exalted is He, according to the path of the intermediate and near way, is that it is a comprehensive manifestation of the Names and Attributes in a manner that does not contradict the transcendence of the Truth, Glory be to Him, from indwelling, union, division, the existence of the Eternal in the temporal, and the like of the matters impossible for Him, Exalted is His affair. However, it should be known that this report, although it is widespread among the Sufis, may their secrets be sanctified, has been criticized by the hadith scholars. Al-Iraqi said: "I have not found any basis for it."

Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya said: "It is mentioned in the Isra'iliyyat, and it has no known chain of narration from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace." It seems that by what is in the Isra'iliyyat he referred to what Imam Ahmad narrated in al-Zuhd from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: "Allah, Exalted is He, opened the heavens for Ezekiel until he looked at the Throne, and Ezekiel said: 'Glory be to You, how great You are, O Lord!' Then Allah, Exalted is He, said: 'The heavens and the earth were too weak to contain Me, but the heart of My servant, the believer, soft and gentle, contains Me.'"

Yes, there is something that bears witness to it. Al-Allamah al-Shams Ibn al-Qayyim said in Shifa' al-'Alil, and its text is: "In the Musnad and elsewhere, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: 'The hearts are the vessels of Allah, Exalted is He, on His earth, and the dearest of them to Him are the hardest, the most delicate and the purest.'" End of quotation.

Al-Tabarani narrated from the hadith of Abu Anbasa al-Khawlani, raised to the Prophet: "Allah, Exalted is He, has vessels from the earth, and the vessels of your Lord are the hearts of His righteous servants, and the dearest of them to Him are the softest and most delicate." This hadith, although its chain contains Baqiyya ibn al-Walid, who was a mudallis (one who conceals defects in transmission), nevertheless he explicitly stated the transmission in it.

[Page 210]

From the combination of the two hadiths it is known that the heart that is most beloved to Allah, Exalted is He, has four attributes: softness, which is for receiving the Truth; hardness, which is for preserving it; so what is meant by it is the attribute of combining softness, purity and delicacy, and these are for seeing Him. His establishment, Exalted is He, upon the Throne with the attribute of "the Most Merciful" rather than "the Most Compassionate" is to indicate that everyone has a share of His vast mercy, Exalted is He.

﴿And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and what is more hidden﴾. It was said: the secret is a matter hidden in the heart like the hiddenness of fire in green wood, until desire stirs it. The angel does not perceive it, nor does Satan, nor does the soul sense it, nor does the intellect feel it; otherwise what is in the inner part of that would be hidden.

According to some Sufis, the secret is a subtle point between the heart and the spirit, and it is the mine of spiritual secrets. The hidden (al-khafi) is a subtle point between the spirit and the Divine Presence, and it is the descent-place of the divine lights. The details of this are in their proper place. Some people have used this verse as evidence that dhikr (remembrance of Allah) aloud is not prescribed. The truth is that it is prescribed under its conditions. They differed over whether it is better than silent dhikr or silent dhikr is better than it. The truth regarding what no text has enjoined to be done aloud, and what no text has enjoined to be done quietly, is that which is better differs according to individuals, circumstances and times: so loud dhikr is sometimes better than silent, and silent is sometimes better than loud.

﴿And has there come to you the story of Moses?﴾ ﴿When he saw a fire﴾. Shaykh Ibrahim al-Kurani, may Allah have mercy on him, said in Tanbih al-'Uqul: "That fire was the locus of Allah's manifestation, Mighty and Majestic, and His self-manifestation, Glory be to Him, within it, out of regard for wisdom, since it was what Moses, peace be upon him, sought. He argued for this from a hadith that he narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, which we will mention, God willing, at His words, Exalted is He, ﴿When he came to it, he was called: Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it﴾, the verse."

﴿So take off your sandals﴾: leave aside turning toward this world and the Hereafter, and journey with your heart wholly absorbed in knowledge of Allah, Exalted is He, and do not turn toward anything other than Him, Glory be to Him. ﴿For you are in the sacred valley, Tuwa﴾: it is the valley of the holiness of the majesty of Allah, Exalted is He, and the transcendence of His might, Mighty and Majestic.

It was also said: the two sandals are an allusion to the two premises from which the proof is composed, since by them the intellect reaches the goal, just as a person walks to his destination by means of sandals he wears. It is as if it were said: do not turn toward the two premises; leave off inference, for you are in the valley of the knowledge of Allah, Exalted is He, filled with the traces of His divinity, Glory be to Him.

﴿So worship Me﴾: He placed this command first to indicate the great nobility of servanthood. And He followed it with His words, Glory be to Him: ﴿and establish prayer for My remembrance﴾, because prayer is among the signs of servanthood and the ladders to the holy Presence.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 55 (part 2 of 3):

﴿What is that in your right hand, O Moses?﴾ This is an act of intimacy (*inias*) from Him, exalted is He, toward him, peace be upon him. Moses, peace be upon him, was overwhelmed when He, glorified is He, spoke with him about matters related to divinity, so He asked him about something in his hand, about which he would hardly err, so that he would speak and answer, and his bewilderment would pass away. It has been said: Likewise the believer is treated after his death, for when he dies he arrives at the presence of the Lord of Majesty, and what overcomes him overcomes him, so He asks him about the faith that was in his hand in the world, and he would hardly err about it. When he mentions it, what had overcome him leaves him.

It has also been said: When Allah, exalted is He, made him know the perfection of divinity, He wished to make him know the deficiency of humanness, so He asked him about the benefits of the staff, and he mentioned some of them. Then Allah, exalted is He, informed him that in it there is what is greater in benefit than what he mentioned, as a reminder that the intellects are incapable of knowing the attributes of a thing that is present. So, were it not for divine grace (*tawfiq*), how could he reach knowledge of the most majestic and greatest of things?

﴿So he threw it, and behold, it was a snake, moving swiftly.﴾ In this there is an indication of the manifestation of the effect of majesty (*jalal*), and for this reason Moses, peace be upon him, feared. So He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Take it and do not fear.﴾ This fear was from the perfection of knowledge, because he did not feel safe from the plotting (*makr*) of Allah, exalted is He, even though the intimacy had already preceded from Him, glorified is He. In some reports: (O Moses, do not feel safe from My plotting until you have crossed the Sirat.)

It has been said: His fear was of losing the countable benefits, and for this reason He gave the reason for the prohibition with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We shall return it to its former state.﴾ [Page 211] But this is ignorance of the station of Moses, peace be upon him.

Likewise is what has been said: that when he saw the terrifying matter he fled, since he had not reached the station of ﴿So flee to Allah﴾, and had he reached it he would not have fled. And what has also been said: Perhaps when he attained the station of speaking with Allah, pride remained in his heart, so Allah, exalted is He, showed him that he was still far in possible deficiency and had not left the world of humanness, and that victory and steadfastness are from Allah alone, exalted is He.

﴿And draw your hand to your side; it will come out white without harm.﴾ He, glorified is He, wished to show him a sign within himself after He had shown him, peace be upon him, a sign in the horizons, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿We shall show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves.﴾ This is from the utmost of His care, majestic is His majesty.

They have mentioned in this story some subtleties and allusions, among them: When He, glorified is He, pointed to the staff and the right hand with His saying, exalted is He, ﴿What is that in your right hand?﴾, there arose in each of them a dazzling proof and an overpowering miracle. So one of them, which is inanimate, became living, and the other, which is dense, became luminous and subtle. Then He, exalted is He, looks upon the heart of the servant three hundred and sixty times each day, so what is strange if his heart, hard and dark, becomes living and illuminated?

Among them: The staff became prepared for life through the blessing of the right hand of Moses, peace be upon him, and became a living snake. So how should the heart of the believer, which lies between two of the fingers of the Most Merciful, not become prepared for life and become living?

Among them: The staff, by a single gesture, came to the point of swallowing the magic of the magicians. So the heart of the believer is more deserving of becoming, by the increase of the Lord's gaze every day several times, such that it swallows the magic of the commanding self (*nafs ammara*).

Among them: His saying, exalted is He, at the beginning, ﴿Take off your sandals,﴾ is an allusion to emptying (*takhliya*) and purifying the tablet of the heart from other-than-Allah, and what follows it are allusions to adorning (*tahliya*) and attaining what should be attained.

Glorified is He indicated the knowledge of the origin (*'ilm al-mabda'*) with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I am Allah﴾; and the knowledge of the intermediate (*'ilm al-wasat*) with His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿So worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance﴾, and in it is an indication of bodily and spiritual deeds; and the knowledge of the return (*'ilm al-ma'ad*) with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming.﴾

Among them: He, exalted is He, began the address with His saying, Mighty is He, speaking: ﴿And I have chosen you﴾, which is the utmost of gentleness, and concluded the speech with His saying, majestic and exalted is He: ﴿So do not let one who does not believe in it turn you away from it, lest you perish﴾ — up to — ﴿perish﴾, which is a form of subjugation, as a reminder that His mercy preceded His wrath, and that the servant must necessarily travel on the two feet of hope and fear.

Among them: Moses, peace be upon him, had something on his foot, which is the sandal, and something in his hand, which is the staff. The foot is the instrument of flight and the hand is the instrument of seeking. So He commanded the abandonment of what was on both, as a reminder that the traveler, as long as he is in the station of seeking and fleeing, is occupied with himself and seeking his own share, and so he does not attain the complete immersion in the sea of gnosis (*'irfan*).

In it is also: Moses, peace be upon him, despite the greatness of his rank and the loftiness of his status, could not reach the presence of Majesty until he removed the sandal and threw down the staff. So how can you, with a thousand burdens of sins, reach His threshold and presence, majestic is His majesty?

These verses have raised a difficulty, in that they indicate that Allah, exalted is He, addressed Moses, peace be upon him, without an intermediary, whereas He addressed our Prophet (ﷺ) through an intermediary, Jibril, peace be upon him. This would entail the superiority of the Interlocutor (Kalim) over the Beloved (Habib), upon both of them be blessings and peace.

The answer is that He, exalted is His station, addressed our Prophet (ﷺ) also without an intermediary on the night of the Mi'raj. The most that can be said is that He, exalted is He, addressed Moses, peace be upon him, without an intermediary at the beginning of his prophethood, and addressed His Beloved, upon him be blessings and peace, at the beginning of his prophethood through an intermediary. Yet this alone does not establish a superiority. Moreover, His address to His most noble Beloved (ﷺ) without an intermediary occurred with the unveiling of the veil and his seeing Him, upon him be blessings and peace, in a manner not granted to Moses, peace be upon him. By this, what is supposed regarding the delay of the direct address from the beginning of the prophethood is remedied.

Consider the difference between His saying, exalted is He, about our Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿His sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾ and His saying about Moses, peace be upon him: ﴿He said, it is my staff﴾, etc. You will see the difference clearly between the Beloved and the Interlocutor, although each has the rank of honour, may Allah, exalted is He, bless him and grant him peace.

Some have mentioned that the verses also indicate a difference between them, upon both of them be blessings and peace, from another aspect, and that is [Page 212] that Moses, peace be upon him, used to lean on the staff, whereas the Prophet (ﷺ) used to rely upon the grace and mercy of Allah, exalted is He, saying with his community: ﴿Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.﴾ Therefore, concerning him it was revealed: ﴿Allah is sufficient for you and for those of the believers who follow you﴾, in the sense of: and sufficient is He for whoever follows you.

Also, he, peace be upon him, began with the concerns of his own self in his saying: ﴿I lean upon it﴾, then the concerns of his flock in his saying: ﴿and I beat down leaves with it for my sheep﴾; whereas the Prophet, may Allah, exalted is He, bless him and grant him peace, did not occupy himself except with the reform of the affairs of his community: "O Allah, guide my people, for they do not know." Therefore, Moses, peace be upon him, will say on the Day of Resurrection: "Myself, myself," whereas the Prophet, may Allah, exalted is He, bless him and grant him peace, says: ("My community, my community"). End of quotation, and it is taken from the words of the Imam; indeed there is no difference except very slightly.

By my life, it is not befitting to follow him in such speech, as will not be hidden from those of understanding. I have only quoted it to draw attention to not being deceived by it. We seek refuge in Allah, exalted is He, from failure.

﴿My Lord, expand for me my breast﴾: He, peace be upon him, did not mention by what his breast would be expanded, and there are possibilities regarding this.

Some people said: He, exalted is He, mentioned ten things and described them as light:

The first is His own essence, glorified is His majesty: ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth.﴾ The second is the Messenger, may Allah, exalted is He, bless him and grant him peace: ﴿There has come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book.﴾ The third is the Book: ﴿And they followed the light that was sent down with him.﴾ The fourth is faith: ﴿They wish to extinguish the light of Allah.﴾ The fifth is the justice of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And the earth shone with the light of its Lord.﴾ The sixth is the moon: ﴿And He placed the moon therein as a light.﴾ The seventh is the day: ﴿And He made the darkness and the light.﴾

The eighth is the clear signs: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which is guidance and light.﴾ The ninth is the prophets, peace be upon them: ﴿Light upon light.﴾ The tenth is knowledge: ﴿The likeness of His light is like a niche in which is a lamp.﴾

So Moses, peace be upon him, first said: ﴿My Lord, expand for me my breast﴾ by knowing the lights of the majesty of Your greatness; second: ﴿My Lord, expand for me my breast﴾ by adopting the characteristics of Your messengers and prophets; third: ﴿My Lord, expand for me my breast﴾ by following Your revelation and carrying out Your command and prohibition; fourth: ﴿My Lord, expand for me my breast﴾ by the light of faith and certainty in Your divinity; fifth: ﴿My Lord, expand for me my breast﴾ by becoming acquainted with the secrets of Your justice in Your decree and judgment.

Sixth: ﴿My Lord, expand for me my breast﴾ by moving from the light of Your sun and moon to the lights of the majesty of Your might, as Ibrahim, peace be upon him, did; seventh: ﴿My Lord, expand for me my breast﴾ from contemplating Your day and night to contemplating the day of Your bounty and the night of Your subjugation; eighth: ﴿My Lord, expand for me my breast﴾ by becoming acquainted with the collections of Your signs and the knots of Your clear proofs in Your earth and Your heavens; ninth: ﴿My Lord, expand for me my breast﴾ that I may be a true successor to the earlier prophets and resemble them in submission to the judgment of the Lord of the worlds; tenth: ﴿My Lord, expand for me my breast﴾ by making the lamp of faith like the niche in which is the lamp. End of quotation.

It is not hidden how much of what has been mentioned is mutually implicating and dependent on one another. He also said: The expansion of the breast is an expression for kindling the light in the heart until it becomes like a lamp. It is not hidden that the one who kindles a lamp needs seven things: a flint, a stone, a striker, sulphur, a lamp-holder, a wick, and oil. So the flint is the flint of the striver: ﴿And those who strive in Us﴾; the stone is the stone of supplication: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾; the striker is restraining desire and forbidding the self from desire; the sulphur is repentance: ﴿And turn penitently to your Lord﴾; the lamp-holder is patience: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾; the wick is gratitude: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾; and the oil is contentment: ﴿And be patient for the decree of your Lord﴾, that is, be content with His decree.

Then, when these tools are sound, do not rely upon them; rather, you should seek the goal from the presence of your Lord, majestic and exalted is He, saying: ﴿My Lord, expand for me my breast.﴾ Then you will hear: ﴿You have been granted your request, O Moses.﴾

Furthermore, this spiritual light is superior to the bodily sun for several reasons:

The first: the sun is veiled by clouds, whereas the sun of gnosis is not veiled by the seven heavens: ﴿To Him ascends the good word.﴾

The second: the sun sets at night, whereas the sun of gnosis does not set at night: ﴿Indeed, the rising at night is more potent in impression and more upright in speech﴾, and those who seek forgiveness in the pre-dawn hours: ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night.﴾

[Page 213] The night is a veil for lovers,
O, would that its hours might last.

The third: the sun passes away: ﴿When the sun is wound up﴾, whereas gnosis does not pass away. Its root is firm and its branch is in the sky: ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful.﴾

The fourth: when the moon confronts the sun, the sun is eclipsed; whereas the sun of gnosis, which is (there is no god but Allah), when it is not joined with the moon of prophethood, which is (I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, may Allah, exalted is He, bless him and grant him peace), the light has not reached the world of the limbs.

The fifth: the sun blackens the face, whereas gnosis whitens faces: ﴿On the day when some faces will be white.﴾

The sixth: the sun scorches, whereas gnosis ascends.

The seventh: the sun burns, while knowledge prevents burning. (Jiz ya mu'minu fa-qad atfa'a nuruka lahabi: "Pass over, O believer, for your light has extinguished my flame.") The eighth: the sun's benefit is in this world, while knowledge's benefit is in both abodes. ﴿So We shall surely grant him a good life, and We shall surely reward them with the best of what they used to do.﴾ The ninth: the sun is heavenly in form and earthly in meaning, while divine realities are the reverse. The tenth: the sun falls upon both friend and enemy, while knowledge is attained only by the friend of God (wali). The eleventh: the sun makes known the conditions of creation, while knowledge brings the heart to the Creator.

Since the expansion of the breast, which is the first of the stations of the spiritual realities, is more noble than the highest of the stations of the corporeal realities, Moses, peace be upon him, began by requesting it, saying: ﴿My Lord, expand my breast for me.﴾ The sign of the expansion of the breast and the entry of the divine light into it is withdrawal from the abode of delusion and desire for the abode of eternity. They likened the breast to a fortress: the first (the expansion) is like its moat, and the second (the breast itself) is like its wall. When the moat is great and the wall is sound, the army of Satan is unable to enter through desire, pride, self-admiration, miserliness, bad opinion of God Most High, and all the other blameworthy qualities. When they are not like this, the army enters, and then the kingdom becomes confined to the palace of the heart and the matter becomes constricted for it.

They distinguished between the breast (sadr), the heart (qalb), the inner heart (fu'ad), and the core of the intellect (lubb): the breast is the seat of Islam ﴿Is one whose breast God has expanded for Islam…﴾; the heart is the seat of faith ﴿God has endeared faith to you and made it beautiful in your hearts﴾ and ﴿those in whose hearts He has inscribed faith﴾; the inner heart is the seat of witnessing ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾; and the core is the station of tawhid (oneness of God), (﴿Only those of understanding are reminded﴾), meaning those who have emerged from the husk of metaphorical existence and remained with the core of true existence. Moses, peace be upon him, requested the expansion of the breast rather than the heart because the expansion of the breast necessarily entails the expansion of the heart, but not vice versa. Also, the expansion of the breast is like a prelude to the expansion of the heart, and a free person is sufficed by a hint. So when the Master, glory be to Him, knows that the seeker desires the prelude, it does not befit His generosity to withhold the result from him. Also, he, peace be upon him, observed courtesy in the request, so he limited himself to asking for the lesser, and therefore He gave him what he sought, and it was said: ﴿You have been granted your request, O Moses.﴾ And when he ventured to ask for the vision, it was said to him: ﴿You will not see Me.﴾

The difference between the words of Moses, peace be upon him, to his Lord, Mighty and Majestic ﴿My Lord, expand my breast for me﴾, and the words of the Lord to His beloved (ﷺ) ﴿Did We not expand your breast for you?﴾ is not hidden. From it is known that the interlocutor Moses, peace be upon him, is a seeker, while the Beloved (ﷺ) is one who is sought, and the difference is as clear as the morning.

The difference becomes even more evident: it is reported that Moses, peace be upon him, in the divine presence requested for himself, whereas our Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, when it was said to him there, "Peace be upon you, O Prophet," said: "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of God." The Imam has extended the discussion of this verse with matters of this kind; refer to him if you wish. ﴿And loosen the knot from my tongue﴾, ﴿that they may understand my speech.﴾ It is as if he, peace be upon him, requested the ability to express the divine realities in clear language, for the matter is difficult, and there is hardly any expression that makes it easy, so that the listener is safe from stumbling. For this reason you see many people going astray through the expressions of some of the great Sufis (mystics) concerning the explanation of divine secrets.

It was said: he, peace be upon him, requested the loosening of the knot of shyness, for he was shy to address the enemy of God in the same tongue with which he had addressed the Truth, exalted and sublime. Perhaps he intended by the speech mentioned, the speech through which guidance is given to the servants, for the aspiration of the knowers does not seek speech and conversation with people concerning that which yields no guidance for them. Yes, speech as such is a great virtue and a mighty gift, and for this reason He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿The Most Merciful, taught the Qur'an, created man, taught him eloquence﴾, without any conjunction.

It is related from Ali, may God honor his face: "What is man, were it not for the tongue, but a formed image or a neglected beast?"

He, may God be pleased with him, also said: "A man is hidden beneath the folds of his tongue, not beneath his cloak."

He, may God be pleased with him, also said: "A man is by his two smallest parts: his heart and his tongue." Zuhayr said:

"The tongue of a youth is half, and half is his heart;
nothing remains but the form of flesh and blood."

Some people praised silence because it is safer:

"A youth dies from a slip of his tongue,
and a man does not die from a slip of his foot."

In Nawabigh al-Kalim (a book of proverbs): "Guard your mouth, lest your nape be struck." The fair position is that silence in itself is not a virtue, because it is a privative matter, and speech in itself is a virtue, but it may become a vice due to accidental causes. The truth is what he (ﷺ) indicated by his saying: "May God have mercy upon a person who speaks good and profits, or remains silent and is safe."

It has been mentioned, regarding why Moses, peace be upon him, did not request complete eloquence, that it is the portion of the Beloved, may prayers and peace be upon him, for he (ﷺ) was the most eloquent of all who spoke the Arabic letter ḍād, so it was not for him to ask for what was his. ﴿And appoint for me a minister from my family﴾, ﴿Aaron, my brother﴾, ﴿Strengthen my back through him﴾, ﴿and make him a partner in my affair.﴾ In this there is an indication of the virtue of cooperation in religion, for it is among the ethics of the messengers, may the blessings and peace of God Most High be upon them all. The ministry commonly known among people is praiseworthy if the minister sows in its soil what he will not regret at harvest time before the King of kings. In it there is also an indication of the virtue of intermediating good for the deserving, especially if they are from among one's relatives.

Whoever withholds from the deserving has wronged. And in Moses, peace be upon him, being mentioned before Aaron, peace be upon him, though he was younger while Aaron was the elder, is evidence that excellence does not follow age; God Most High singles out with His grace whom He wills. ﴿Indeed You were ever observant of us﴾: in concluding supplications with this, there is good courtesy toward God Most High that is not hidden, and it is among the best means to God, Mighty and Majestic. Among its effects is the answering of supplication. ﴿And We had certainly conferred favor upon you another time﴾: a reminder to him, peace be upon him, of what increases his certainty; and in it is an indication that He, Most High, does not reject after acceptance and does not deprive after bestowal. From here it was said: when faith enters the heart, it is safe from being stripped away, and no one turns back except from the path. ﴿And I have chosen you for Myself﴾: I have singled you out for Myself through detachment, so nothing will distract you from Me. ﴿Then you remained for years among the people of Madyan﴾: by this is indicated his service to Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, and that was a training from Him, Most High, for him through companionship with the messengers, so that he would be characterized by their ethics, adorned with their courtesy, and fit for the divine presence. For the companionship of the good there is great benefit according to the Sufis, and the opposite is the companionship of the wicked. ﴿Then you came at an appointed time, O Moses﴾: that was the time of the full readiness, and the time of the mission of the prophets, peace be upon them, which is the time of their reaching forty years. Whoever reaches forty without his good prevailing over his evil should prepare his own mourning and get ready for the Fire. ﴿Go, both of you, to Pharaoh; indeed, he has transgressed﴾: he exceeded the limit in disobedience until he claimed lordship, and that was following the intoxication of domination, which is the attribute of the commanding soul (nafs ammara). Opposite to it is the intoxication of gentleness, which is the attribute of the spirit, and from it arises ecstatic utterance (shath) and the claim of selfhood. They said: its possessor is excused, otherwise there would be no difference between al-Hallaj, for example, and Pharaoh. The people of jealousy for God, Most High, say: there is no difference.

﴿So speak to him gently; perhaps he will be reminded or fear﴾: in this is an indication of teaching the manner of guidance. Al-Nahrajuri said: the command to that is because he (Pharaoh) had shown kindness to Moses, peace be upon him, at the beginning of the matter, and he did not reward him for it. ﴿From it We created you, and into it We will return you, and from it We will bring you forth once more﴾: an indication to the bodily frames and cages of the birds of the spirits; otherwise the spirits themselves are from the world of the dominion (malakut), and these forms have been illumined by it: ﴿And the earth shone with the light of its Lord.﴾ And God Most High knows best.

Some interpreters have interpreted this story and these verses with reference to what is within the selves, and that is a path we have left aside except briefly. And God Most High is the Guide to the right way.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 56:

﴿And indeed We showed him﴾ is another summary narration of what took place between Musa, peace be upon him, and Fir'awn, may the curse of Allah be upon him.

Its introduction with the oath serves to demonstrate the utmost care for its content. The verb ara'a (to show) derives from the visual sight (ru'yah basariyyah), which is transitive to one object, and it may be made transitive to a second object by the hamza (of causation); or it derives from the mental sight (ru'yah qalbiyyah) in the sense of knowing (ma'rifah), which is likewise transitive to one object by itself and to another by the hamza. It cannot be from the sense of ru'yah meaning 'ilm (knowledge), which is transitive to two objects by itself and to a third by the hamza, because that would require omitting the third object of i'lam (informing), and this is not permissible.

The attribution of the showing to the pronoun of Majesty (Allah) is in consideration of the reality, not to Musa, peace be upon him, in consideration of the outward appearance, in order to magnify the matter of the signs, exalt their status, and show the complete abominability of the accursed one and his persistence in tyranny. This attribution strengthens that what preceded it, the words of His Exalted saying (alladhi) etc., is from His speech, Mighty and Majestic; that is, by Allah, We indeed saw Fir'awn or knew him ﴿Our signs﴾ when he said to Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿If you have come with a sign, then produce it, if you are of the truthful﴾ ﴿So he threw his staff, and behold, it was a clearly visible serpent﴾ ﴿And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white for the observers﴾.

The plural form, although they are two, is either because the application of the plural to two is common, as has been said, or in consideration of what is within their details of wondrous matters, each of which is a clear sign for a people who reason. Other matters also appeared before Fir'awn, each of which was a grievous calamity. It is narrated that when he, peace be upon him, threw it, it turned into a serpent, a huge one, its mouth gaping between its jaws eighty cubits; its lower jaw was placed on the ground and its upper jaw on the wall of the palace. It turned toward Fir'awn, who fled and defecated, and the people fled in crowds, and twenty-five thousand of his people died. Fir'awn cried out: "O Musa, I implore you by the One who sent you, take it!" So he took it, and it returned to a staff. This has been previously mentioned from Wahb ibn Munabbih. It is also narrated that it turned into a snake that rose into the sky the distance of a mile, then descended advancing toward Fir'awn, and it began to say: "O Musa, command me with whatever you wish," and Fir'awn says: "I implore you," etc. And when he drew out his hand from his collar, behold, it was white for the observers, a luminous whiteness beyond the bounds of customary things, its ray overpowering the ray of the sun, and the spectators gathered around it in wonder at its matter. Thus within each of the two signs there are many signs, but since they were not mentioned explicitly, they were emphasized by His saying (all of them), as if it were said: We showed him Our signs with all their consequences and details, intending to make clear that no excuse whatsoever remained for him in that. The idafah (annexation) is, as established, for definiteness (al-'ahd). Some included within it the untying of the knot, as they included it in His saying ﴿Go, you and your brother, with My signs﴾. It has also been said: the intended meaning is the nine signs of Musa, peace be upon him, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas previously, and the idafah is also for definiteness. But in this is the objection that most of them appeared at his hand, peace be upon him, after he had overcome the magicians, gradually over about twenty years. There is no doubt that the matter of the magicians was still awaited. Some counted among them what was made for their destruction, not for their guidance to faith, such as the splitting of the sea, and the outward signs that appeared after his destruction for the Children of Israel, such as the lifting of the mountain and the stone from which the springs gushed forth. Others counted among them the outward signs upon the hands of the prophets, peace be upon them, and took the idafah to mean comprehensiveness of the individuals. Both groups based this on the premise that he, peace be upon him, related all that was mentioned to Fir'awn, and that narration is in the status of showing and display, since lying is impossible for him, peace be upon him. It is not hidden that his narrating those signs is something for which no mention occurred here, while what will come, Allah willing, of his interpreting what he displayed, peace be upon him, as magic and challenging with its like, is very distant. And even more remote than all of that is including what he, peace be upon him, detailed of the acts of Allah, Glorified be He, indicating His exclusive lordship and its rulings within the signs. It has been said: the idafah is for comprehensiveness of kinds, and (kull, all) is an emphasis of it, meaning: We showed him all kinds of Our signs. The intended meaning of the signs is the miracles and their kinds, which, as al-Sakhawi said, return to bringing into existence what did not exist, or annihilating what exists, or altering it while it remains. The accursed one was shown all of that in the staff and the hand. But there is room for scrutiny regarding the restriction, and even setting that aside, this is not free from distance. The Kashfiyyah claimed that the intended meaning of the signs is 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, whom Allah Exalted showed to Fir'awn riding a horse, and they mentioned descriptions of it. The plural is as in His saying ﴿Clear signs, the station of Ibrahim﴾, and the clear falsity of this makes refuting it unnecessary.

The fa' in His saying (fa-kadhdhaba) is for sequence, and the object is omitted, meaning: so he denied the signs or Musa, peace be upon him, without hesitation or delay. (Wa-aba) means: he refused to accept the signs, or the truth, or faith and obedience; that is, he refused in the utmost degree. According to most, his denial and refusal were out of obstinate denial and arrogance, and this is most fitting for censure. As for one who interpreted arana (We showed) as 'arafna (We made known) and supposed a genitive noun, meaning the validity of Our signs, and said that definiteness necessarily produces knowledge, he spoke thus without any doubt.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 57:

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿He said: "Have you come to us to drive us out of our land with your sorcery, O Moses?"﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) explaining the manner of his denial and refusal. The interrogative hamza (al-hamza) is for denying the occurrence of the matter and deeming it abhorrent. It was claimed that it is an impossible matter. The word "come" (al-maji') is either on its literal sense, or in the sense of turning toward a matter and undertaking it, meaning: "Have you come to us from your place where you were after you had been absent from us, or have you turned toward us to drive us out of Egypt by what you have displayed of sorcery?" This is something that does not proceed from a rational person, because it belongs to the category of attempting the impossible. He said this only to move his people to the utmost hatred of Moses, peace be upon him, by showing that his aim is not merely to rescue the Children of Israel from their hands, but to expel the Copts from their homeland and to seize their wealth and properties entirely, so that no one would turn to follow him and they would exert themselves in opposition and contention. For expulsion from the homeland is the brother of killing, as His saying, may He be exalted, indicates: ﴿And if We had decreed for them, "Kill yourselves or leave your homes," ...﴾ [al-Nisa': 66]. The miraculous sign that Allah, may He be exalted, manifested, the dazzling miracle, was called "sorcery" in order to embolden them to confront it. Then he claimed that he would counter it with its like, and so he said:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 58:

﴿So We will surely bring you magic like it.﴾ The fa' (fa') here indicates the sequence of what follows upon what precedes it, and the lam (lam) falls in the answer to an implied oath, as if it were said: "If it is so, then by God, we will surely bring you magic like your magic." ﴿So set up between us and you an appointment﴾, that is, a promise (wa'd), taking mawʿid (mawʿid) as a mimi (mimi) verbal noun and not as a noun of time or place, because the apparent meaning is that His saying, the Exalted, ﴿which we will not fail, neither we nor you﴾ is a description of it, and the pronoun in the accusative refers back to it. If it were a noun of time or place, the failing (ikhlaf) would have to be connected to the time or place, whereas it is only connected to the promise: one says "he failed his promise," not "his time of promise" or "his place of promise," meaning: we will not fail that promise. ﴿Neither we nor you﴾. The accursed one only delegated the matter of the appointment to Musa, peace be upon him, to avoid being attributed with weakness of heart, distress of circumstance, and to display steadfastness, and to show that he is able to prepare the means of opposition and arrange the instruments of overcoming, whether the time is long or short. Likewise, placing his pronoun before the pronoun of Musa, peace be upon him, and inserting the particle of negation between them, is to signal his hastening to not failing, and that his not failing does not necessarily entail the non-failure of Musa, peace be upon him. Therefore the negation is emphasized by repeating its particle.

Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read (lā nukhlifhu) with a jazm (jazm), on the basis that it is the answer to the command, meaning: if you make that, we will not fail it. ﴿A place equitable (suwan)﴾, that is, fair between us and you, as was narrated from Mujahid and Qatadah, that is, a place situated at the midpoint of the distance between us, equal in equality. This is the meaning of Abu 'Ali's saying: "Its nearness to you is like its nearness to us," and on this is the poet's verse:

"And if our father had settled among his people, equal between Qays, Qays of ʿAylan, and al-Fizr."

Or it means a place of half, that is, of justice, as was narrated from al-Suddi, because when a place does not favor being nearer to one side over the other, it is balanced between the two sides. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd that he said: that is, a place level in the ground, with no roughness in it, no mountain, no hillock, nor a depression in which some of those present would hide from others; and his meaning is a place where those standing there can be seen clearly, with nothing in it that would conceal any of them, so that he may see everything that proceeds from you and from the sorcerers. In it there is a display of steadfastness and strong confidence in victory, to the extent that it has. This meaning, in my view, is very good, and a group of scholars went to it. It was also said: the meaning is a place where our state is equal, and the ranks in it are one, where no leadership is considered and no governing is exercised, but the leader and the led, the ruler and the ruled, unite there. This is not without merit, and it may return to the meaning of "fair," that is, a place of half and justice.

It was also said: (suwan) has the meaning of "other than," and the intended meaning is a place other than this place. This is not correct, because suwa in this sense is never used except construed with what follows it in form, and is not separated from the construction. The accusative of (makānan) is as an object of a verb implied by (mawʿidan), that is: "Designate a place," not "appointment," because, as Ibn al-Hajib said, it is a verbal noun that has already been described, and what is governed by the verbal noun is part of its completion, and a thing is not described until after its completion, so it would be like describing the relative pronoun before the completion of its clause, which is not permissible.

It is reported from some grammarians that it is permissible to describe the verbal noun before it acts, absolutely, and this is weak. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is permissible to describe it before it acts when the object is an adverb of place, because of their latitude with it in what they do not allow with other things. From this, some permitted that (makānan) be accusative as an adverb of place governed by (mawʿidan). This was refuted on the basis that the condition for the accusative as an adverb of place is absent in it. Al-Radi said: the accusative of (makānan) as an adverb of place requires that its governing verb carry the sense of settling in the place, as in "you stood," "you sat," "you moved from your place," so it is not permissible to say "you wrote the writing in your place," or "you killed him in your place," or "you cursed him in your place." It was objected that what al-Radi mentioned is not accepted, for there is no barrier to saying to one who wants to approach you in order to speak to you: "Speak from your place," though this good usage is not applicable in every place. It is also permissible that it be an adverb governing the Exalted's saying, ﴿which we will not fail﴾, on the basis that it is implicitly containing the sense of coming or arriving. It was also permitted that it be an adverb of a verb that is omitted and occurs as a circumstantial clause from the subject of (nukhlifhu), and a specific sense is estimated because the indication is clear, that is: coming or arriving to a place.

Abu Ja'far, Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read (suwan) with a kasrah on the sin and tanwin when connected. The rest of the seven read with a dammah and tanwin likewise. Abu Bakr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i stopped with imalah, and Warsh and Abu 'Amr with a sound between sound.

Al-Hasan in one narration read like the rest of the seven, except that he did not pronounce tanwin in pause or in connection. ʿIsa read like the first ones, except that he also did not pronounce tanwin in pause or in connection. The reason for omitting tanwin in connection is treating it in the manner of pause, in omitting the tanwin and the dammah and kasrah, as Muhyi al-Sunnah said, and the other (reading) is two dialects for suwan, like ʿudan and ʿidan.

Some lexicographers mentioned that the pattern fiʿal with a kasrah on the first letter is specific to rigid nouns, like ʿinab, and that in adjectives there came from it only ʿidan, the plural of ʿaduww. Al-Zamakhshari added suwan, and others transmitted it with the meaning of marwi. Al-Akhfash said: suwan is maqsur if you kasra or damma its sin, and mamdud if you fatha it, so there are three dialects, and all of them have the meaning of "other than" and the meaning of "equitable and middle between the two parties." The best of the dialects, as al-Nahhas said, is suwan with a kasrah.

[Page 219]

﴿He said﴾: that is, Musa (peace be upon him) said. In al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's *al-Bahr al-Muhit*) it says: "The most remote opinion is that the speaker was Fir'awn. By my life, it should not be given any attention. It seems that the one who was driven to this view was the earlier report from Wahb ibn Munabbih, so let him consider this."

﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾: it is a day of festival that they had every year, when they adorned themselves and decorated their markets, as narrated from Mujahid and Qatadah. It was also said that it is the day of Nayruz (the Persian New Year), which was the beginning of their year.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that it was the day of 'Ashura', and this is how the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) were interpreted: ("Whoever fasts on the Day of Adornment will receive the reward for what he missed of the fasts of that year, and whoever gives charity on that day will receive the reward for what he missed of the charity of that year"). It was also said that it was the day the canal was broken open; al-Bahr says that it continues to this day. It was also said that it was the day of their market. It was also said that it was Saturday, a day of rest and tranquillity among them, just as it is among the Jews today. The apparent practice of Abu Hayyan is to prefer that it was a festival day that coincided with 'Ashura', and that it was a Saturday.

The apparent meaning is that *al-mawʻid* (the appointment) here is a noun of time (*ism zaman*), and it is described by "the Day of Adornment", meaning: the time of your appointment is the well-known day among you. The reason he (peace be upon him) did not state the appointment itself but specified its time, although the accursed one's first request from him (peace be upon him) was for it, is to indicate that he (peace be upon him) was more eager for it, because of what follows from it in terms of removing doubt and establishing proof, so that it is as if it had occurred from him (peace be upon him) before the request for it, and so it is not fitting for him to request it. It also signals his complete confidence in his matter. For this reason he (peace be upon him) singled out, from among the times, the Day of Adornment, which is a witnessed day and a day when people are gathered.

He (peace be upon him) did not mention the place which the accursed one had mentioned, because according to the first and third meanings, the accursed one mentioned it only to give the impression of superiority over him (peace be upon him), wishing thereby to show boldness. So he (peace be upon him) turned away from mentioning it, being content with mentioning the specific time, to indicate that he was independent of that, and that all places are equal in relation to him once the gathering takes place. As for the second meaning, it is possible that he (peace be upon him) was content with what the Day of Adornment itself implies, for it is the custom of people at festivals, at all times and in every land, to go out to level places and gather on flat ground where nothing blocks seeing one another. In sum, the Prophet (peace be upon him) answered him in the manner of wisdom, and may Allah the Exalted grant excellence to the Speaker (Kalim, i.e., Musa) and to His arrangement.

It was also said: *al-mawʻid* here is also a verbal noun (*masdar*), and a genitive construction is to be understood for the sentence to be correct, meaning: "Your promise is the promise of the Day of Adornment", and the place is omitted, being indicated by the Day of Adornment. It was also said: *al-mawʻid* in the question is a noun of place, and making it an object of *mukhallafan* is by way of extension, as in the line: "And a day we witnessed," or the pronoun in ﴿we shall not fail it﴾ refers to the promise contained in the noun of place, in the manner of ﴿Be just; that is nearer to piety﴾, or to *al-mawʻid* in the sense of *al-waʻd* by way of *istikhdam* (a figure where one word carries two meanings). In both of these possibilities the sentence is parenthetical (*iʻtiraD*).

It is not permissible for it to be a qualifying clause (*sifa*), because a qualifying clause must contain a pronoun referring back to the described noun itself, and the claim that it is omitted is worthless.

[Page 219, continued]

And *makanan* (a place), according to Abu Ali (al-Farisi), is the second object of *ajʻal* (make). It was also said: it is an apposition (*badal*) or a clarifying apposition (*ʻatf bayan*). The *mawʻid* in the answer is a noun of time, and the correspondence of the answer is in meaning: the Day of Adornment indicates a well-known place where people gather on that day, or it is also a noun of place, and its meaning is the place where the promised thing occurs, not the place of the word "promise", as it has been wrongly supposed. A genitive construction is to be understood for the sentence to be correct, meaning: the place of the Day of Adornment, and the correspondence is clear.

It was also said: *al-mawʻid* in the first case is a verbal noun, except that the genitive "place" has been omitted from it and the noun put in its position, and *makanan* is treated as a dependent of the understood word, or as a second object. In the second case, it is either a noun of time, meaning the time when the promised thing occurs and not the word "promise", as his saying indicates: "They said: separation. I said: its appointment is tomorrow." The correspondence is in meaning. Or it is a noun of place, and a genitive construction is understood in the predicate, and the correspondence is clear as you have heard. Or it is also a verbal noun, and two genitive constructions are understood, one in the subject and the other in the predicate, meaning: the place of your promise is the place of the Day of Adornment, and the matter of correspondence is not hidden. It was also said: in the first case two genitive constructions are understood, meaning: the place of fulfilling your promise; or one genitive construction only, but the attachment becomes to the slightest connection. The more apparent is to interpret the verbal noun as a passive participle (*maf'ul*), and to understand a genitive construction in the second, meaning: your appointment is the place of the Day of Adornment, and this is based on a false assumption that we have pointed out. It was also said: in both the first and second, it is a noun of time, and *lā nukhlifuhu* is from the class of omission and transitivity, and the original is *lā nakhlufu fīhi*; and *makanan* is an adverb of place for *ijʻal* (make). To this the author of *al-Kashf* (al-Zamakhshari) pointed when he said: "Perhaps the nearer in derivation is that *al-makan* be made an object of *mukhallafan* by extension, with correspondence in meaning, or the meaning is: make between us and between you, in a place of equal ground that is fair, a time of promise which we shall not fail, so the correspondence is achieved in both wording and meaning, and *makanan* is an adverb that is a complement (*zarf laghw*)." End of quotation.

It has been objected to, with things whose refutation is not hidden to one who knows well the details of what we have said. You know that the possibilities in this verse are very many, and the best of them is what is most suited to the eloquence of the revelation, together with few omissions, and free from pulling the shoe off before reaching the water. So reflect.

Al-Hasan, al-A'mash, 'Asim in one transmission, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi 'Abla, Qatadah al-Jahdari, Hubayra and al-Za'farani read ( يَوْمَ الزِّينَةِ ) with *yawma* in the accusative. This is clear that by *al-mawʻid* is meant the verbal noun, because a place and a time do not occur in a time, unlike an event. As for the first, there is no benefit in it, since it is present in all times; and as for the second, a time cannot be a time-container in the true sense of containment, because that would require a thing being contained in itself. As for something like "the forenoon of the day" within "the day", that is a containment of the whole in its parts, which is a figurative containment; and what we are dealing with is not of this kind. Thus it has been said, but there is an obvious objection to it.

It was also said: by the apparent form of this reading one derives that *al-mawʻid* in the first place is also a verbal noun, because the second is the same as the first, since an indefinite noun is repeated as definite. In the *Kashf* it is said: perhaps the nearer in derivation for this reading is that the first be taken as a noun of time and the second as a verbal noun, meaning: your promise occurs on the Day of Adornment.

The answer is in correspondence of meaning without artificiality, since there is no difference between: "The time of the promise is a day such-and-such" in the nominative, and: "The promise is on a day such-and-such" in the accusative, in what is achieved. Rather, it is of the wise manner, since it includes an addition. And His Exalted saying ﴿and that the people be gathered in the forenoon﴾ is coordinated with "the Adornment", and it was said: coordinated with "day". The first is more apparent, since it does not need interpretation. *Duha* (forenoon) is in the accusative as an adverb of time, and it is the rising of the day; it may be feminine or masculine. *Dahaʼ* with a fatha on the *dad* is a masculine noun with a long vowel, and it is the highest point of the rising of the day.

It was permitted, on the reading with *yawma* in the accusative, that *mawʻiduku* be the subject (*mubtada'*), with an understood temporal genitive as its complement, on the principle of "I came to you at the setting of the Pleiades" (*ataytuka khufuqa al-najm*). The adverbial phrase depends on it, and *wa-duha* is its predicate, with the intention of definiteness in it, because it is the forenoon of that very day. If it were not known, it would not correspond to their request, since they asked him (peace be upon him) for a specific appointment whose promise would not be broken. It was also said: it is permitted that the appointment be a time, with *wa-duha* as its predicate and "the Day of Adornment" as a fronted circumstantial (*hal muqaddam*), and then the definiteness of *duha* would be unnecessary; but this is not valid. Then this definiteness in the sense of specification is a meaning, not in the sense of making *duha* one of the conventional definite nouns, as may be wrongly supposed.

[Page 220]

Al-Tibi said: Ibn Jinni said: it is permitted that *an yuhsharu* (that it be gathered) be coordinated with *al-mawʻid*, as if it were said: "the fulfilment of your promise, and the gathering of people in the forenoon on the Day of Adornment." It seems he made *al-mawʻid* an expression of what renews on that day of reward and punishment and other things apart from the gathering; then the coordination of the gathering with it is the coordination of the particular with the general. End of quotation. And it is, as you see, far-fetched.

Ibn Mas'ud, al-Jahdari, Abu 'Imran al-Jawni, Abu Nuhayk and Amr ibn Qa'id read ( تَحْشُرَ النّاسَ ) with the second person (*ta'* of address) and *al-nas* in the accusative. The one addressed is Fir'awn. It is narrated from them that they read with the third person (*ya'* of absence) and *al-nas* in the accusative. The pronoun in *yuhsharu* in this reading is either for Fir'awn, and he was referred to in the third person in accordance with the customary manner of speech with kings; or it is for the day, and the attribution is figurative, as in "he fasted his day" (*sama nahāruhu*). The author of *al-Lawami'* said: the subject is omitted because it is known, meaning: "and that the gatherer gather the people."

You know that omitting the subject in such a case is not permitted according to the Basrans. Indeed, it was said regarding such an example: the subject is a pronoun that refers back to the active participle understood from the verb.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 60:

﴿Then Pharaoh turned away﴾, i.e., he departed from the assembly. It has been said that he took charge of the matter himself, but this is not the correct view.

It has also been said that he turned away from accepting the truth, but this is nothing (of substance). ﴿Then he gathered his scheme﴾, i.e., what is used for plotting against (Moses) from the magicians and their instruments, or the people of his scheme. ﴿Then he came﴾, i.e., to the appointed meeting, and with him was what he had gathered. In the word "thumma" (then, indicating delay) there is an indication that he did not hasten to it, but came to it after hesitation and dithering.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 61:

He, glorified is He, did not mention Musa's (peace be upon him) coming, but said, exalted is He, ﴿Musa said to them﴾, to indicate that it is a certain matter that needs no explicit statement. The sentence is a resumptive sentence of the explanatory type (istiʾnaf bayani), as if it was said: "What did Musa (peace be upon him) do when Fir'awn came with those whom he had gathered of the magicians?" So it was said:

He said to them, by way of counsel, ﴿Woe to you! Do not fabricate against Allah a lie﴾ by abandoning His signs, which will manifest at my hands, as magic, just as Fir'awn did, ﴿lest He destroy you﴾, that is, He uproot you because of that, ﴿with a punishment﴾ terrible, whose extent cannot be measured. A group of the Seven Readers and Ibn ʿAbbas read (fa-yusḥitakum) with a fatḥa on the yaʾ and the ḥaʾ, from the triliteral form, according to the dialect of the people of the Ḥijaz. Al-isḥat is the dialect of Najd and Tamim. The original meaning of this is thoroughly shaving the hair from the head, and then it was used for destruction and uprooting in general. ﴿And indeed, he fails who fabricates﴾, that is: against Allah, the Exalted, whoever he may be and in whatever manner, so the forbidden fabrication enters into it primarily; or it means: Fir'awn, the fabricator, has indeed failed, so do not be like him in failure and in the non-attainment of what you seek. The sentence is a parenthetical clause confirming the content of what precedes it.

Then they disputed among themselves over their affair, [the affair] for which they had been summoned to contend with him, peace be upon him. That is: the magicians, when they heard his words (peace be upon him), as if that had enraged them, "disputed about their affair," that is, they consulted and debated among themselves, and they "tugged at the fringes of speech" concerning that. "And they secretly conferred" — they went to great lengths to conceal their speech from Musa and his brother (peace be upon them both), lest they should stand over it and counter it. Their secret conferring, as stated by a group including al-Jubba'i (al-Jubba'i) and Abu Muslim, was what they uttered.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 63 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿They said﴾, i.e., by way of secret consultation and whispering, ﴿Indeed, these two are certainly sorcerers﴾ and so on, for this is an explanation of that, and the outcome of the dispute and the conclusion upon which their opinions settled after the debate and consultation.

It has been said: their secret talk was that they said, when they heard the speech of Musa (peace be upon him), "This is not the speech of a sorcerer." This was narrated from Muhammad ibn Ishaq. It has also been said: it was that they said, "If Musa overcomes us, we will follow him," and this is reported from al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. It has also been said: it was that they said, "If this is a sorcerer, we will overcome him, and if it is from the heaven, then it has a matter (of its own)," and this was narrated from Qatada. According to these statements, the meaning of "their matter" (amrahum) is the matter of Musa (peace be upon him), and its attribution to them is due to the slightest connection, since it occurred among them and they were concerned with it. Their secret talk would be from Pharaoh and his chiefs. Their saying, "Indeed, these two are certainly sorcerers" and so on, may be understood as meaning that they differed among themselves over the various opinions mentioned, then their views settled upon that, and they refused anything but opposition to the challenge. This is an independent statement, an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), as if it were said: "What did they say to the people after the dispute was over?" and it was answered: ﴿They said, "Indeed, these two are..."﴾ and so on.

The pronoun in "they said" is taken to refer to Pharaoh and his chiefs, on the basis that they said this to the sorcerers, to turn them away from disagreement and to command unity and resolve. Displaying firmness, however, detracts from the splendid eloquence of the noble composition, as sound taste bears witness. Yes, if the pronoun of "they disputed" and the pronouns following it were taken to refer to the sorcerers, as most exegetes also held, that defect would not arise. "Inna" here is the light (mukhaffafah) form of "inna," whose operation has been nullified, and the lam is the lam of distinction (lam al-fariqah).

Ibn Kathir read the nun of "hadhani" with a shadda, which is contrary to analogy, made to distinguish between declinable nouns and others.

The Kufans said: "in" is negative, and the lam means "illa" (except), i.e., "these two are not but sorcerers." This is supported by the fact that it was read in this way. In a narration from Ubayy, it was read: "in hadhani illa sahirani." And it was read: "in dhani" without the particle of admonition (ha' al-tanbih), "illa sahirani." Ibn Khalawayh attributed this to Abd Allah, and some attributed it to Ubayy, and it too supports this. It was also read: "in dhani lasahirani" with only the ha' al-tanbih dropped.

Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan, Shayba, al-A'mash, Talha, Humayd, Ayyub, Khalaf in his choice, Abu Ubayd, Abu Hatim, Ibn Isa al-Isbahani, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Jubayr al-Antaki, and the two brothers and the two companions among the Seven read "inna" with a shadda on the nun, and "hadhani" with an alif and a light nun. This reading has caused difficulty, to the extent that it was said to be a solecism and an error, based on what Abu Ubayd related in Fada'il al-Qur'an from Hisham ibn Urwa, from his father, who said: "I asked Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, about the solecism of the Qur'an, concerning the words of Allah, ﴿Indeed, these two are certainly sorcerers﴾, and concerning the words of Allah, ﴿And those who establish prayer and those who give zakat﴾, and concerning the words of Allah, ﴿And those who are Jews, and the Sabians﴾. She said: 'O nephew, this is the work of the scribes; they erred in the writing.'" Its chain is sound according to the conditions of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), as al-Jalal al-Suyuti said. This is extremely problematic, for first, how can it be supposed of the Companions that they would commit solecism in speech, let alone in the Qur'an, when they were the most eloquent and skilled in speech? Second, how can it be supposed of them that they erred in the Qur'an, which they received from the Prophet (ﷺ) as it was revealed, and spared no effort in memorizing, preserving and perfecting it? Third, how can it be supposed that they all agreed upon the error and wrote it down? Fourth, how can it be supposed that they did not notice it and did not retract it? Fifth, how can it be supposed that they continued in the error, when it is transmitted by mass transmission (tawatur), generation after generation? If such a thing were permissible, trust in the Qur'an would collapse.

This reading has been explained in several ways. The first: that "in" means "na'am" (yes). This view was held by a group including al-Mubarrad and al-Akhfash al-Saghir, and they cited the verse:

"The blamers rose early in the morning, blaming me and I blaming them,
And they said, 'Gray hair has overtaken you, and you have grown old.' I said, 'Indeed (inna-h).'"

The better argument is the statement of Ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with them both, to someone who said to him: "May Allah curse the she-camel that carried me to you, and her rider!" He said: "In (wa-)" ... Since it has been said regarding the verse: "We do not concede that 'in' in it means 'na'am' and the ha' is for pausing; rather it is the operative 'inna' and the ha' is a pronoun in the accusative governed by it, and the predicate is omitted, meaning 'indeed it is so.' It is not valid to say that the predicate is 'like that' and both parts were omitted, because omitting both parts together is not permissible."

This explanation was weakened on the ground that its use as "na'am" has not been established, or is rare. Even if it is established without rarity, there is nothing before it requiring an answer so that "na'am" would occur as its response. The claim that it is understood from the beginning of the speech that some of them said, "They are two sorcerers," and he spoke truly, and it was said: "na'am," is far-fetched. Similar is the claim that it is confirmation of what is understood from Pharaoh's words: "Have you come to us to drive us out of our land with your sorcery, O Musa?" Also, the lam of beginning (lam al-ibtida') does not enter the predicate of the subject.

This was answered: the lam is extra (za'idah) and is not the lam of beginning, as in the verse: "Umm al-Hulays is indeed an old woman, sharhaba, who is content with a bone of the neck from the meat." Or: it enters upon an omitted subject, i.e., "for them two are sorcerers," as al-Zajjaj chose, saying: "I presented it to our scholar, our shaykh and our teacher Muhammad ibn Yazid, i.e., al-Mubarrad, and to the judge Isma'il ibn Ishaq ibn Hammad, and they both accepted it, and they mentioned that it is the best we have heard on this." Or: it entered after this "in" because of its resemblance to the verbally emphatic "inna," as "ma" (the verbal) is added after "ma al-masdariyyah" because of its resemblance to the negative, in the verse: "And hope for the youth for good, whatever you see of him, upon age, good that does not cease to increase."

The first was rejected: its addition to the predicate is specific to poetry, and what is here is the point of dispute, so it is not valid to argue with it, as al-Naysaburi wrongly supposed. Abu Ali in al-Idah rejected the second, with a point whose essence is that emphasis is used where confusion is feared, and when the omission has reached fame, emphasis is dispensed with. Had what was mentioned been a valid reading, a phrase like "la-'ajuz sharhaba" would not be attributed to necessity, and it cannot be analogized to "inna" where the predicate is omitted with it, as in "inna mahallan" and "inna murtahalan" and "in ijtama'a fi at-ta'kid", because it is assimilated to "la" and the opposite is commonly treated as the opposite. Ibn Jinni said: the omission is from the category of brevity, and the emphasis from the category of elaboration, and combining them is impossible due to contradiction.

It was answered: that the omission is for the presence of a clear indication is not accepted, and the emphasis is for the content of the sentence, not for the omitted element, and the analogy in the verse is also possible, and their restriction of it to necessity is an oversight, and how much the earlier has left for the later. The combination of brevity and elaboration, with different aspects, is not impossible. The clearest evidence of the entry of the lam into such a construction is what al-Tirmidhi, Ahmad and Ibn Majah related: "The most beloved of My friends to Me is a believer, light of burden." Yes, there is no dispute that this omission is anomalous in usage and in analogy.
