The second: that "in" is among the operative particles, and its noun is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamir al-sha'n), and what follows is a subject and predicate, and the whole clause is its predicate. This was the view of the early grammarians. It was weakened on the ground that the pronoun of the matter is placed to strengthen the speech, and what is of this kind is not suited to omission, and what is heard of its omission is as in the verse: "Indeed whoever blames the sons of Bint Hassan, let him be blamed and disobeyed in calamities," and the verse: "Indeed whoever enters the church one day, he will meet in it gazelles and deer," being necessity or anomalous, except in the case of "an" with fath when lightened, which they found easy because it occurs in speech built upon lightening, so it was omitted following the omission of the nun, and because if it were mentioned it would require the shadda, since pronouns return things to their origins. Then the question of the lam's entry into the predicate arises, and even if it is maintained that there is a subject into which it enters, you have heard what is in it of criticism and approval.

The third: that it is the operative "in," and the ha' of the pronoun of the story is its noun, and the clause "dhani lasahirani" is its predicate. This was weakened on the ground that it requires joining ha' to "in" with the alif in writing and separating ha' from "dhani" in the script, and what is in the Mushaf is not like that. Furthermore, the question of the lam's entry arises.

The fourth: that "in" is nullified (mulghah), even though it is shadda, by analogy with the light form, as you have made the light form operative by analogy with it in the verse: "And indeed, all of them, He will surely pay them in full." Or it demotes its rank from the verb, since its operation is not essential but by resemblance to the verb, and what follows is a subject and predicate. This was the view of Ali ibn Isa. In it is that this nullification has not been seen outside this place, which is the point of dispute, and the question of the lam there remains as it was.

The fifth, which is the best and most probable of the aspects, was chosen by Abu Hayyan, Ibn Malik, al-Akhfash, Abu Ali al-Farisi and a group: that it is the operative "inna," the demonstrative noun is its noun, the lam is the lam of beginning, and "sahiran" is its predicate. The demonstrative coming with alif despite being accusative is according to the dialect of some Arabs who make the dual always with alif. The poet of them said:

"Alas for Rayya, then alas, alas! Would that her eyes and mouth were ours,
And the place of the anklet on her feet, for a price with which we might satisfy her father."

Another said:

"He lowered his gaze like the brave man, and if he saw an opening for us, the brave man's... would have been silent."

They also said: "I struck him between his ears (udhunahu)," and "whoever buys the two shoes (khuffan)." This is a dialect of Kinana, related by Abu al-Khattab, and of the Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b, Khath'am, Zubayd and the people of that region, related by al-Kisa'i, and of the Banu al-Anbar, Banu al-Hayjam, Murad and Udhra. Abu Zayd said: I heard from the Arabs one who converts every ya' preceded by an open vowel into alif. Ibn al-Hajib says that "hadhani" is indeclinable because it indicates the meaning of pointing, and that the saying of most people, "hadhayn" in the genitive and accusative, is not an inflection either.

Ibn Hisham said: On this basis, the reading "hadhani" is more analogical, since the original in the indeclinable is that its form does not vary, and in addition there is a correspondence with the alif of "sahirani." End quote.

As for the report earlier from Aisha, Ibn Ushta answered it, and Ibn Jubara followed him in his commentary on the Ra'iyya, that her saying "they erred" means they erred in choosing the preferable of the seven modes for gathering people upon it, not that what they wrote of that was an error that is not permissible; for whatever is impermissible in anything is rejected by consensus, however long its occurrence lasts. In a similar way answers are given to other reports narrated from her as well.

And regarding Ibn Abbas in this chapter, his apparent statements are problematic. Then he related from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i that he said: "Indeed these two are sorcerers" and "Indeed these two (hadhayn) are sorcerers" are the same; perhaps they wrote the alif in place of the ya', meaning it is the substitution of one letter for another in writing, as occurred in salat, zakat and hayat. Against this it is objected that it would only be suitable if the reading were with ya' in that. Then you know that the stated answer does not close the matter of the problem, since 'Urwa's designation of that in the question as a solecism remains; unless it is said: he meant by solecism the language, as Ibn Ushta said regarding Ibn Jubayr's report through several chains on "wal-muqimina as-salah," that it is a solecism of the scribe; or it is said: he meant by it solecism according to first impression. Ibn al-Anbari inclined to weaken the reports in

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 63 (part 2 of 2):

This chapter and its conflict with other reports from Ibn ʿAbbas and others indicate the establishment of the variant readings (aḥruf) that have been discussed in the recitations. Perhaps the earlier report, which was said to be sound in its chain according to the criteria of al-Shaykhayn (al-Bukhari and Muslim), falls within this category. But al-Jalal al-Suyuti said: the first answer that Ibn Ushtah mentioned is more preferable and more firmly grounded.

Al-ʿAlaʾ said, regarding what Ibn al-Anbari and others transmitted from ʿIkrimah, who said: "When the copies of the Qur'an (al-maṣāḥif) were written, they were presented to ʿUthman, and he found in them letters of error (laḥn). He said: 'Do not change them, for the Arabs will change them,' or he said: 'they will recite them with their tongues. If the scribe were from Thaqif and the dictator from Hudhayl, these letters would not have been found in it.'" That is not authentically transmitted from ʿUthman, for its chain is weak (ḍaʿīf), disturbed (muḍṭarib), and interrupted (munqaṭiʿ).

What I incline toward, and the one who protects is Allah the Exalted, is the weakening of all reports that contain a flaw and that conflict with what is mutawatir (transmitted by a number of narrators such that their agreement on falsehood is impossible), and that do not accept an interpretation which the heart finds acceptable and which sound taste accepts, even if whoever authenticated them did so. Impugning the narrators is far less serious than impugning the imams who received the Great Qur'an, which reached us through tawatur (mass transmission) from the Prophet (ﷺ), and who spared no effort in perfecting and preserving it.

The scholars of the terminology (ahl al-muṣṭalaḥ) have mentioned that among the things by which the fabrication (waḍʿ) of a report is recognized is what is derived from the state of the narrated content itself, such as it contradicting the text of the Qur'an, or the mutawatir Sunnah, or the definitive consensus (ijmaʿ, the agreement of the scholars), or clear reason, where none of these accept interpretation, or where it does not admit the removal of some part of it by which the problem would be eliminated. So if someone were to say that some of those reports are fabricated, it would not be far-fetched. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

Abu ʿAmr recited ﴿إنَّ هَذَيْنِ﴾ (inna hadhayni) with the nun of inna (إنَّ) doubled (tashdid) and with a yāʾ in hadhayni. This was transmitted from ʿAʾishah, al-Hasan, al-Aʿmash, al-Nakhaʿi, al-Jahdari, Ibn Jubayr, and Ibn ʿUbayd. The grammatical analysis (iʿrāb) of this reading is clear, since it follows the well-known pattern for such constructions. However, in al-Durr al-Maṣūn it is said: this reading has raised a difficulty, in that it contradicts the orthography of the Imam (the ʿUthmanic codex), for the demonstrative in it is without an alif and a yāʾ, so adding the yāʾ is an addition to it. For this reason al-Zajjaj said: "I do not permit it," but this is not a valid objection, because it applies equally to everyone, and even if it were sound, there are many readings whose orthography contradicts analogy (qiyās), and moreover the omission of the alif is also not according to analogy.

﴿يُرِيدانِ أنْ يُخْرِجاكم مِن أرْضِكُمْ﴾ "They both want to drive you out of your land": that is, the land of Egypt, by seizing control of it, ﴿بِسِحْرِهِما﴾ "by their magic," which they had displayed earlier. Attributing this to Aaron is because they saw him with Moses, peace be upon them both, following his method. This clause is either a qualifier (ṣifah) or a predicate after a predicate (khabar baʿda khabar).

﴿ويَذْهَبا بِطَرِيقَتِكُمُ المُثْلى﴾ "and take away your most excellent way of life": that is, your religion, which is the best and most excellent of religions, by making their religion manifest and elevating it. By this they meant what the people of Pharaoh were upon, not the way of magic, for they did not regard it as a religion. It was said: they meant the people of your way, so the speech contains an omitted modifier (muḍāf) in the sense of "the people of." By them is meant the Children of Israel, according to Moses' words, peace be upon him: ﴿أرْسِلْ مَعَنا بَنِي إسْرائِيلَ﴾ "Send with us the Children of Israel" (Q. 20:47), and they were people of knowledge among themselves.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted this from Ibn ʿAbbas, and it was criticized on the ground that expelling them from their land happens only through seizing control of it, with real possession and authority, so how could the transfer of the Children of Israel to Syria be conceived at that point? Interpreting the expulsion as the expulsion of the Children of Israel from it, while the people of Pharaoh remained in their situation, is something the revelation must be declared free of. Moreover, this statement from them was an incitement to exert maximum effort in the contest and to concern themselves with confrontation, so the warning and caution must have been with the most hateful and most grievous things for them. There is no doubt that expelling the Children of Israel from among them and taking them to Syria while they were secure in their homes contains little of what they would fear, and it is a statement which the signs of acceptance do not indicate. Perhaps, therefore, the report from the scholar (al-Ḥibr) is not sound.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from Mujahid that al-Ṭarīqah is a name for the notables and nobles of a people. It is reported: "So-and-so represented the way of his people," meaning their leader. Presumably the application of this term to the notables is figurative, because they are followed just as a path (ṭarīq) is followed. They also transmitted from ʿAli, may Allah honor his face, that applying this term to them is in Syriac (al-Suryaniyyah). It seems they meant by "these notables" the notables among the people of Pharaoh, the holders of offices and those with authority and rank. Then they would have been warning them of expulsion from their homelands and the removal of those in positions of office from their posts, and in that is the utmost humiliation and the extreme of the calamities of time. As for what was said, that specifying the taking away to be of them has no distinctive merit, this is not valid. It was said that they meant the Children of Israel also, because they were more numerous than them and more noble in lineage, but this has been addressed above. It was also objected that this contradicts their enslavement, their subjugation, the killing of their sons, and their imposing torment on them. It was answered: this is not accepted, for how many a leader is subdued, and how many a noble is captive in the hands of the base. And that, as you see, is [a weak answer].

[p. 226]

﴿So gather your scheme﴾: an explicit statement of the goal, after the preliminaries have been laid down. The *fa'* here is *fa' faṣīḥa* (the *fa'* that signals an implied condition). The meaning is: if the matter is as has been mentioned, that these two are sorcerers who intend against you what they intend, then resolve upon your scheme, make it unified so that none of you holds back from it, and advance together as one line.

Al-Zuhri, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub in one narration, and Abu Hatim read ﴿*fa-jma'ū*﴾ with a connecting alif and a fatha on the *mīm* from *jam'* (gathering). This is supported by the words ﴿then he gathered his scheme﴾. Scholars have discussed the difference between *jama'a* and *ajma'a*. Ibn Hisham said: *ajma'a* is used only with abstract meanings, whereas *jama'a* is used both with abstract meanings and with concrete things. The *'Umdat al-Huffaz* reports the view that *ajma'a* is used mostly of meanings and *jama'a* of physical things, so one says "*ajma'tu amrī*" (I resolved my affair) and "*jama'tu qawmī*" (I gathered my people), though the reverse is also said. The *Muhkam* states that one says *jama'a al-shay'* (he gathered the thing) from scattering, with the aorist *yajma'uhu jam'an*, and *ajma'ahu*, without distinguishing between them. Al-Farra' said: when you want to gather what is scattered, you say *jama'tu al-qawm* (I gathered the people), so they are *majmū'ūn* (gathered); when you want to gather wealth, you say *jamma'tu* with doubling, though it may be lightened. *Al-ijmā'* means resolving upon a thing and determination to it; it is transitive by itself and also with *'alā*: one says *ajma'tu al-khurūj* and *ajma'tu 'alā al-khurūj* (I resolved to go out). Al-Asma'i said: one says *jama'tu al-shay'* when you bring it from here and there, and *ajma'tuhu* when you make it a whole. Abu al-Haytham said: *ajma'a amrahu* means he made it a whole and resolved upon it after it had been scattered. Its scattering is when one says at one time "I will do this" and at another "I will do that," and its gathering is when one joins one thing to another. Al-Farra' also said: in this verse, on the first reading, it means: do not leave any part of your scheme without bringing it, ﴿then come in a row﴾, that is, lined up. They were ordered to do this because it is more awe-inspiring in the hearts of onlookers and more effective in drawing dread from spectators. It is said that they were seventy thousand, each with a rope and a staff, and they came toward him, peace be upon him, all at once. It is also said that they were seventy-two sorcerers: two of the Copts and the rest of the Children of Israel. It is said they were nine hundred: three hundred from Persia, three hundred from Rome, and three hundred from Alexandria. It is said they were fifteen thousand, and it is said they were some thirty thousand. The state of reports on this is not hidden, and the heart does not incline to exaggeration; and God knows best. Perhaps the appointed place was a wide area where Moses, peace be upon him, addressed them with what has been mentioned in one of its regions, and they disputed their affair in another of its regions, and then they were ordered to come to its middle in the state described. Abu 'Ubayda interpreted *al-ṣaff* as the place where they gathered for their festival and their prayers, but this is far-fetched; it seems he knew of a specific place from the site of the Day of Adornment. On this interpretation, *ṣaffan* is the direct object.

Shibl ibn 'Abbad and Ibn Kathir, in Shibl's narration from him, read ﴿*thumma ā-tū*﴾ with a kasra on the *mīm* and the hamza changed to a *yā'*. Abu 'Ali said: this is an error, and there is no basis for a kasra on the *mīm* of *thumma*. The author of *al-Lawāmiḥ* said: this is due to the meeting of two unvocalized letters, just as the fatha is in the common reading.

﴿And indeed he will have succeeded today who prevails﴾: this is a concluding parenthetical statement from them, confirming what preceded it of the two matters. That is: indeed whoever overcomes has attained the goal. *Istaf'ala* here has the meaning of *fa'ala*, as in the *Ṣiḥāḥ*; or it means seeking height and victory, and he strove in his striving, according to *al-Baḥr*. So *istaf'ala* is in its proper form. This may be more forceful in exhortation, since they made success belong to one who seeks victory, let alone one who actually prevailed. By "the goal" they meant what Pharaoh had promised them of reward and nearness, as expressed by His saying ﴿and indeed you will be among those brought near﴾. By "whoever prevails" they meant all of them together, following their statement about Pharaoh's might ﴿Indeed, it is we who will be the victors﴾; or [it means] whoever among them prevails, as an incitement to exert full effort in the contest.

Al-Raghib said: *al-istiʿlā'* may be for seeking blameworthy height and may be for something else, and here it allows both. Therefore it is permissible that this statement be quoted from those sayers, to urge their unity and concern; and that it be from the speech of God, Mighty and Majestic, in which case the one who prevails is Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them both, and there is no exhortation in it.

You know that the apparent meaning is the first.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 65:

﴿Qālū﴾ is a resumptive clarificatory sentence (isti'nāf bayānī), as if it had been asked: "What did they do after saying that?" So it was said: (They said) ﴿O Moses﴾. He did not mention their gathering together and their coming in rows (iṣṭiffān) except to indicate that the matter of the two of them was evident and that they needed no explanation. ﴿Either you throw﴾, i.e., what you throw first, with the object omitted because it is evident; or you do the throwing first, with the verb treated as if it were intransitive (munazzal manzilat al-lāzim). ﴿Or we will be the first to throw﴾, i.e., what he throws, or the first to perform the throwing. They gave him the choice (kh-y-r) and put him ahead of themselves, to show confidence in their affair; and it is said that this was out of consideration for courtesy toward him, peace be upon him. The clause introduced by an (that) with what follows it is in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb, i.e., "either you choose your throwing, or you choose that we be the first to throw." Or it is in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "the matter is either your throwing or our being the first to throw." Abū Ḥayyān preferred that it be a subject with an omitted predicate, i.e., "your throwing first," on the evidence of ﴿or we will be the first to throw﴾, and with this the antithesis is complete, but it is only a semantic antithesis.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 66:**

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive clause (istinaf), as explained earlier. It is as if it were asked: "What did he (peace be upon him) say then?" So it is answered: he said, ﴿Nay, you throw first﴾. He told them to throw first to show his indifference to their magic, and to meet what they had suggested, namely an inclination to begin with their side. They changed the wording to a more emphatic form, since the expected phrasing would have been "either we throw first, or you (Musa) throw first". They wanted to bring out whatever they had, exhaust their effort, and use up their utmost strength. Then God, exalted is His majesty, would display His authority, hurl the truth against falsehood, and it would crush it.

It has been said that this also contains a matching of courtesy with courtesy (muqabalat adab bi-adab). Some scholars found this command problematic, thinking that it implies permission for magic. To avoid this, they took it as a threat concerning magic, as one says to a disobedient servant, "Do what you want." Abu Hayyan said that it is connected to an implied condition, meaning: "Throw, if you are right (muhiqqin)." But in this there is a difficulty, because he (peace be upon him) knew that they were not right, so the supposition is of no use without considering something else.

You know that there is no need for this and no difficulty, for this is like the command to mention a doubt so that it may be exposed. The claim that presenting the doubt before the proof is impermissible, because one may not be free afterwards to grasp the proof and so the doubt would remain something one pays no heed to, is not accepted.

﴿Then suddenly their ropes and their staffs appeared to him, by their magic, to be moving﴾. The fa' here is an eloquent fa' (fa' fasiha), indicating their haste in throwing, as in God's words: ﴿Strike with your staff the sea, and it split﴾. That is, "they threw, and then suddenly their ropes..." etc. In reality it is a conjunction joining the sentence of suddenness (jumlat al-mufajaah) to the omitted sentence. Idha (إذا) here is a particle of suddenness (idha fujaiyyah). According to the Kufans it is a particle (harf), which is a weak view according to Abu Hayyan. According to al-Riyashi it is an adverb of time, and this is also his view. According to al-Mubarrad it is an adverb of place, and this is the apparent meaning of the words of Sibawayh, and it is what Abu Hayyan preferred. The governing element (al-'amil) in it here, according to Abu al-Baqa', is (ألقوا, throw). It has been objected that the fa' prevents governing. In al-Bahr, it is governed by the predicate of the subject, which is ﴿their ropes and their staffs﴾, if we do not make it itself in the position of the predicate, but make the predicate the clause (yukhayyilu, "appeared"). If we make it in the position of the predicate, and make the clause in the position of a circumstantial state (hal), then the matter is clear. This is like the example: "I went out, and suddenly the lion was lying down" (fa-idha al-asadu rabidun wa-rabidan). For its correct use as a predicate, it suffices with it and with the nominative noun after it as a complete sentence, so one says: "I went out, and suddenly the lion." Al-Akhfash stated in al-Awsat that it may be followed by a verbal clause accompanied by qad, so one says: "I went out, and suddenly qad Zayd had struck Amr." In al-Kashshaf, the verification of this is that idha, when it means "the time" and requires a verb governing it, is followed by a clause added to it. In some cases its governing element is a specific verb, namely the verb of suddenness, and the clause is an independent nominal clause only. So the interpretation of the verse is: "Musa was suddenly confronted at the time of the imagining of the motion of their ropes and staffs." This is an illustration (tamthil). The meaning is: the sudden appearance of their ropes and staffs, imagining to him that they were moving. There is in this what conflicts with what we have mentioned before, but the matter of coordination (al-'atf) on it is more fitting, as is not hidden. By his saying "this is an illustration," he means that it is a depiction of the grammatical analysis (i'rab), and that idha is a temporal idha on which he placed the verb of suddenness, in an extended usage, because it has taken the place of the verb and the object, and because the suddenness of a time includes the suddenness of what is within it, in a more eloquent way. As for what has been said, that he intended the figurative metaphor (isti'arah tamthiliyyah), it requires effort to establish it.

The pronoun in (إليه, to him) apparently refers to Musa (peace be upon him); indeed it seems almost certain. It has been said that it refers to Pharaoh, but this is nothing. The clause introduced by (أن, that) and what follows it is the deputy subject (na'ib fa'il) of (يخيل, appeared/was imagined), meaning: it was imagined to him, because of their magic, that their ropes were moving. This is apparently of the category of siymiya' (a kind of science of imagery), which is a science by which one is empowered to produce a mental image, but it is generally required that it have some material basis in external reality to some extent. This is as Shaykh Muhammad 'Umar al-Baghdadi mentioned in his gloss on the treatise of Shaykh 'Abd al-Ghani al-Nabulsi on the Unity of Being (wahdat al-wujud), through the medium of names and other things.

Al-'Allamah al-Baydawi mentioned in some of his treatises that the essence of the science of siymiya' is the creation of imaginary likenesses that have no existence in the senses, and that it is also applied to producing those likenesses with their forms in the senses, and that they become forms in the substance of the air, which are quickly dissipated because of the rapid change of that substance. The word siymiya' is an arabicized form of "shim yeh", and its meaning is "the name of God, exalted". This is what he mentioned. What he said about rapid dissipation is not accepted as an absolute rule, and in my view it is a part of the science of magic. Al-Baydawi defined it as a science from which the acquisition of a psychological faculty is derived, by which one is empowered to perform strange acts through hidden causes. Then he said: "Magic includes a real kind and a non-real kind, and the non-real kind is called 'seizing the eyes' (al-akhdh bi-al-'uyun). The magicians of Pharaoh brought together both matters." This is what he said. The well-known view is that these magicians placed mercury (zi'baq) in the ropes and staffs, and when the heat of the sun reached them, they moved and shook, so it was imagined to him (peace be upon him) that they were moving and walking, like something possessing life. It is also narrated that he saw them as if they were snakes, having made a movement after movement. It has also been said that they dug the ground and put fire in it, and placed those ropes and staffs above it, and when the heat of the fire reached them, they moved and walked. There is some doubt about the correctness of both views.

The apparent meaning is that the imagining from Musa (peace be upon him) truly occurred through their magic, and this is narrated from Wahb.

It has been said that it did not occur, and that what is meant by the verse is that he (peace be upon him) witnessed something which, if not for his knowledge that it had no reality, he would have thought that they were moving, so it is an illustration. But this is extremely contrary to the apparent meaning.

Al-Hasan and 'Isa read (عُصْيُهم, their staffs) with a damma on the 'ayn, a sukun on the ṣad, and a light ya' with a nominative case. This is a plural form, as in the well-known reading. Al-Zuhri, al-Hasan, 'Isa, Abu Haywa, Qatadah, al-Jahdari, Ruh, Ibn Dhakwan and others read (تُخَيَّلُ, is imagined) with a taʾ at the beginning, in the passive voice, and in it is the pronoun referring to the ropes and staffs. And ﴿that they were moving﴾ is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from that pronoun. The substitution from it does not harm its function as a linking pronoun, since it is not completely omitted in all aspects.

Abu al-Sammal read (تَخَيَّلُ) with a fatha on the taʾ, meaning (تَتَخَيَّلُ, is imagined), and in it there is also the pronoun of what was mentioned, and (أنها تسعى, that they were moving) is also a substitute from it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is an object of cause (maf'ul min ajlihi). Abu al-Qasim ibn Habarah al-Hudhali al-Andalusi said in his book al-Kamil: from Abu al-Sammal that it was read (تُخَيِّلُ) with a taʾ on top, a damma, and a kasra on the ya', and the pronoun in it is the subject, and (أنها تسعى) is put in the accusative as the direct object. Ibn 'Atiyyah attributed this reading to al-Hasan, 'Isa al-Thaqafi, and whoever read (تُخَيَّلُ) in the passive. So the one who causes them to appear as such is God, exalted, as a trial and testing.

Al-Hasan ibn Yaman narrated from Abu Haywa (نُخَيِّلُ) with a nun and a kasra on the ya', so the subject is His pronoun, exalted, and (أنها تسعى) is the direct object.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 67:**

﴿So Musa felt a fear within himself﴾. *Al-ijas* (a faint, hidden sensation) means concealment, and *al-kheefa* means fear. Its original form was *khiwfa*, in which the waw was changed to ya' because of the kasra before it. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is possible that it was *khawfa* with a fatha on the kha', the waw was changed to ya', and then the kha' was given a kasra for harmony (*tanasub*). The first form is preferable."

The tanwin (nunation) on *khifatan* indicates diminution (*lil-tahqir*), meaning: he concealed within himself some slight fear, arising from being suddenly confronted with that matter, in accordance with the natural human disposition upon seeing a terrifying sight. This is the view of al-Hasan. Muqatil said: he (peace be upon him) feared that doubt and misgiving about the miracle of the staff might enter the minds of the people, because of what they saw of their own staffs. He concealed his fear of this so that their souls would not be strengthened if it became apparent to them, which would lead to their not following him.

It was also said that the tanwin indicates magnitude (*lil-ta'zim*), meaning: he concealed within himself a great fear. Some have said that the form *fi'la* (*khifa*), because it denotes a lasting state and condition, points to this meaning, and that is why it was chosen over *al-khawf* in the Almighty's words: ﴿And the thunder glorifies Him with His praise, and the angels too, out of awe of Him﴾. The *ijas* does not contradict this. It was also said that it does contradict it. The first view is most fitting to the state of Musa (peace be upon him) if his fear was of what al-Hasan described, and the second is most fitting to his state (peace be upon him) if his fear was of what Muqatil described.

It was also said that this is equally fitting to the description of the magic as great, in the Almighty's words: ﴿And they brought great magic﴾. Some scholars supported the view that the tanwin indicates this by the fact that Musa is mentioned explicitly and not as a pronoun, so reflect on this.

It was also said that when they said *immā an tulqiya* ("either you throw...") etc., he (peace be upon him) heard them say: "Throw, O friends of Allah," and he feared for that reason, since he knew that the friends of Allah are not overcome. This is hardly sound, and the noble text rejects it.

The placement of the agent (*fa'il*) later is for the sake of observing the rhyme (*al-fawasil*).

﴿We said, "Do not fear."﴾ That is, do not persist in your fear of what you imagined, and push away from yourself what has overtaken you. So the prohibition is to be taken in its literal sense. It was also said that the prohibition departs from its literal sense, serving to encourage him and strengthen his heart. ﴿Indeed, you are the superior.﴾ This is the reason for what the prohibition requires, namely refraining from fear, and an affirmation of his dominance in the most eloquent and emphatic manner. This is indicated by the explanatory resumption (al-istiʾnaf al-bayani), the particle of confirmation (harf al-tahqiq), the repetition of the pronoun, the definiteness of the predicate, the word "superiority," which indicates manifest dominance, and the comparative form (ṣīghat al-tafḍīl), as more than one scholar has said. What I incline to is that the aforementioned comparative form is for mere excess. If its meaning were participation along with excess, it would require that the magicians also have superiority and manifest dominance, though this is not the case. Affirming that for them relative to the common people, as has been said, is worthless, since there is no contest between them and the common people.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 69:

﴿And throw down what is in your right hand﴾, that is, your staff, as occurred in Surah al-A'raf. It seems that referring to it in this way is to remind him of what happened and what he witnessed from it, on the day when He, glory be to Him, said to him, ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾. Some of the scholars who verify matters said: The indefinite reference was chosen to magnify its affair, to exalt its status, and to signal that it is not of the kind of ordinary staffs, which are followed by customary effects, but is beyond the limits of all other members of its kind. It is indefinite, yet it is followed by strange effects. Failing to observe this subtle point when the matter is reported in other places does not require that it be disregarded when the reported event itself occurred. End. The sum of this is that the indefiniteness serves to magnify, as if the staff, because of its great status, cannot be encompassed by the range of knowledge, like ﴿So there covered them of the sea that which covered them﴾. The report of the matter in other places is given in meaning, and the actual event contained this subtle point, even if not in Arabic wording. The reverse was not considered because what includes it is better suited to the context of forbidding fear and encouraging him, peace be upon him, against it.

Abu Hayyan said: He expressed it with that rather than "your staff" because of what the right hand implies of blessing and prosperity. It is also held that the address was not in an Arabic wording. It was said: The indefiniteness is for belittling, meaning: do not care about the abundance of their ropes and staffs, and throw the small stick that is in your hand, for by the power of God, Exalted, it will swallow them, despite its singleness and their multitude, its smallness and their greatness. This has been objected to: the manifest state of the staff in what passed twice prevents this, and moreover that meaning only suits a case in which the staff did what it did while in its original form, whereas some of its effects had already occurred. What is possible is that it is described (as an adjective) and that it is possible that it is relative (a relative clause); on each of the two readings, it was said, the more fitting for the first is the first, and for the second the second. His saying, exalted be He, ﴿will swallow what they have made﴾, with the jussive, is the answer to the imperative from laqifa, meaning he obtained it by taking hold, either with the hand or with the mouth; the meaning here is the second. The feminine form is due to ma referring to the staff, that is, it swallows what they made of ropes and staffs, which had been imagined to you as moving. The expression "what they have made" is for belittling and to signal deception and forgery.

Most readers read ﴿talaqqafa﴾ with a fathah on the lam, a shaddah on the qaf, and the dropping of one of the two taa's from the original form ﴿tatalaqqafu﴾.

Ibn Amir read the same way, except that he raised the verb, on the basis that the clause is a resumed statement, an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), or a presumed circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah) from the subject of "throw" on the basis of its causing it, or from its object, meaning "swallowing" or "swallowing" (feminine). The clause of the command is conjoined to the prohibition, completing it with what is within its scope, to give the reason for its requirement by explaining the manner of its superiority and dominance, peace be upon him. For the swallowing of his staff, peace be upon him, of their falsehoods, among which he sensed fear in his soul, uproots the source of fear entirely. Some claimed that this is explicit that his fear, peace be upon him, did not arise from the doubt of people concerning the miracle of the staff, for otherwise a reason would have been given to remove it, such as a promise of what would bring about their faith. There is consideration in this.

His saying, exalted be He, ﴿What they have made is only the plot of a sorcerer﴾, etc., is an explanation of His saying, ﴿will swallow what they have made﴾. Ma here is either a relative pronoun, or a descriptive ma, or a verbal-source ma: that is, that which they made, or that a thing they made, or that their making. ﴿Only the plot of a sorcerer﴾ is read with a damma as the predicate of inna, meaning the plot of the kind of sorcerer. Its indefiniteness is for the purpose of reaching, through it, what the context requires of making the annexed noun indefinite; had it been definite, the annexed-to noun would have been definite, and that is not intended. It was objected that its annexed definiteness could in that case be for the kind, which is equivalent in meaning to an indefinite noun, and the difference between them is only their presence in the mind. It was answered: there is no need to specify its kind, for it is known from His saying (it is imagined to them), etc. What is intended after specifying it is to state that it is a deceptive matter with no reality, and this is known by taste. It was also said: it was made indefinite so that it might be used to belittle the annexed noun. It was objected that, even granting that this yields the belittling of the annexed noun, it does not suit the context, and because it implies that sorcery is divided into the petty and the great, which is not intended. Moreover, His saying in another verse contradicts this: ﴿and they came with great sorcery﴾. Unless it is said that its greatness in one respect does not contradict its pettiness in itself, and this is what is meant by belittling it. It was also said: it was made indefinite lest the mind go to the idea that the intended sorcerer is a well-known one. So reflect.

Mujahid, Humayd, and Zayd ibn Ali, may mercy be upon them, read ﴿kayda﴾ with a fatha, as the object of "they made," and ma is a restrictive particle (kafffah).

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bahriyyah, al-A'mash, Talhah, Ibn Abi Layla, Khalaf in his choice, Ibn Isa al-Isfahani, Ibn Jubayr al-Antaki, and Ibn Jarir read ﴿sihrin﴾ with a kasra on the sin and a sukun on the ha, in the sense of "possessor of sorcery," or by naming the sorcerer "sorcery" as an intensive, as if, because of his deep immersion in sorcery, he became the very essence of sorcery. It was also said: the annexation is to show that the plot is of the kind of sorcery. This annexation is of the general to the specific. It is in the sense of "li" (belonging) according to the commentator of al-Hadi, and in the sense of "min" (of) according to what is understood from the apparent words of al-Sharif at the beginning of the commentary on al-Miftah. It is called the explicative annexation (idafah bayaniyyah). What is found is taken to be what is annexed to the annexed. It is not required that there be general and specific in a partial relation between the two terms, though some have stipulated that.

His exalted saying, ﴿and the sorcerer does not prosper﴾, that is, this kind, ﴿wherever he comes﴾, wherever he is and wherever he turns. So "wherever" is a locative adverb used for generality, and it is part of the completion of the reason. He did not address the status of the staff and its being a divine miracle, despite what this would add to strengthening the reason, to signal the manifestness of its matter.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Jundab ibn Abdullah al-Bajali, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'If you seize the sorcerer, kill him.' Then he recited: ﴿and the sorcerer does not prosper wherever he comes﴾, and said: 'He does not believe wherever he is found.'"

A group read ﴿ayna ataa﴾.

صفحة 229

صفحة 230

The fa' in His words ﴿Then the magicians were thrown down prostrate﴾ (fa' al-fasihah, the "eloquent" fa' (a particle that signals an omitted clause)) indicates clauses that are understood without being stated. The meaning is: his fear went away, he threw what was in his right hand, it became a serpent, it swallowed their ropes and staffs, and they knew that this was a miracle. Then the magicians were thrown on their faces prostrate before God, the Exalted and Majestic, repenting and believing in Him and in the mission of Moses, peace be upon him.

It is related that their leader said: "We used to overcome people, and the instruments were sparing us. If this were magic, where are the things we threw?" From the change in the states of bodies, the Creator, the Powerful, the All-Knowing, is inferred, and from the manifestation of this at the hand of Moses, peace be upon him, the soundness of his mission is established. It is as if those ropes and staffs became scattered dust, and their complete annihilation is possible in our view. In the expression "was thrown" (ulqiya) rather than "prostrated" (fa-sajada) there is an indication that they witnessed what alarmed them, so they could not contain themselves until they fell on their faces prostrate. This also alerts the listener to God's subtle kindness in transferring whom He wills of His servants from the extreme of disbelief and obstinacy to the height of faith and rectitude, together with the resemblance and fitting correspondence this involves. The intended meaning is that they hastened to prostrate. It is said that they did not lift their heads from prostration until they saw Paradise and Hellfire, and the reward and punishment.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ikrimah that when they fell prostrate, God showed them their places in Paradise during their prostration. al-Qadi rejected this, saying that it is like compulsion to faith and that it contradicts moral responsibility (taklif). It was answered that since faith preceded this unveiling, there is neither contradiction nor compulsion. In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim it is said that the statement of theirs ﴿We have believed in our Lord, that He may forgive us our sins﴾ and so on does not contradict this, because those places being their places is by virtue of this statement proceeding from them.

﴿They said﴾ is a resumptive clause, as has been mentioned more than once. ﴿We have believed in the Lord of Harun and Musa﴾: Moses, peace be upon him, is mentioned after Harun here, whereas in the account of their words in Surat al-A'raf, Moses is mentioned first, because Moses is nobler than Harun, and the call and the mission belong to him primarily and essentially, and the manifestation of the miracle was at his hand, peace be upon him, for the sake of the rhyme of the verse endings (fawasil). It is also permissible that their speech was in this order, and they mentioned Harun first because he was older in age. The statement of al-Sayyid in his commentary on Miftah al-'Ulum that Moses was older than Harun, peace be upon them both, is a mistake. Or the reason is to be extremely cautious against the false suspicion on the part of Pharaoh and his people, since Pharaoh had raised Moses, peace be upon him. So if they had mentioned Moses first, the accursed one and his people might have suspected from the outset that their meaning was Pharaoh. Its being placed first in Surat al-A'raf is a precedence in the narration for that very reason.

Abu Hayyan permitted that what is here was the statement of one group among them, and what is there was the statement of another, and that each observed every subtle point in what was done. However, since the statement is the same in meaning, it is correct to attribute each of them to all of them. The choice of this wording here is because it better suits the verses of this surah.

[Page 231]

﴿He [Pharaoh] said﴾, that is, Pharaoh said to the magicians: ﴿Have you believed in him?﴾, that is, in Musa (Moses), as is the apparent meaning. Originally, *iman* (belief) is transitive by itself, but its use with *bi* (in) became widespread because it includes the sense of *tasdiq* (affirmation), until it became the standard usage. It is construed here with *li* (to) because it is taken to include the meaning of *inqiyad* (submission), which takes *li*: one says *inqada lahu* (he submitted to him). It is not *al-ittiba'* (following), as some have said, because *ittiba'* is transitive by itself: one says *ittaba'ahu* and does not say *ittaba'a lahu*. In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit), it is said that *amana* is connected with *bi* when its object is God, may His name be exalted, and with *li* when its object is other than God, exalted is He, in most cases, as in the verse ﴿He believes in God and believes for the believers﴾. So ﴿they did not believe in Musa, etc.﴾.

﴿You do not believe us﴾, ﴿and you will not be believed by us﴾, ﴿so Lot believed him﴾. It is also permitted that the *lam* be causal (*ta'lili*), and the implied sense is: "You believed in God, exalted is He, because of Musa and what you saw from him." Some have chosen this reading, and there is no separation (*tafkik*) in it, as is imagined. It has also been said that the pronoun in ﴿lahu﴾ may refer to the Lord, mighty and majestic, and in that case there is a clear separation (*tafkik*) in the verse.

Most readers recite ﴿a'amantum﴾ with the interrogative for rebuke (*istifham tawbikhi*). Even according to the first reading, rebuke is what is meant by the sentence, not the informational value of the statement or its necessary implication: ﴿before I gave you permission﴾, that is, without my permission for you to believe, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Even if the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord are exhausted﴾. This does not mean that his permission for them in this matter comes later or is expected. Al-Tabarsi distinguished between *al-idhn* (permission) and *al-amr* (command), in that a command indicates the commander's will for the act commanded, whereas permission does not imply that.

﴿Indeed, he﴾, meaning Musa, peace be upon him, ﴿is surely your chief﴾, that is, your greatest in your craft, the most knowledgeable of you in it, and your teacher, ﴿who taught you magic﴾. It is as if the accursed one first rebuked them for believing in him, peace be upon him, without his permission, so that his people would see that their belief was not to be regarded, since it occurred without his permission. Then he anticipated that they might say: "What need is there for permission after we did what we did and what came from him, peace be upon him, came to pass?" He answered this with his saying: ﴿Indeed, he﴾, etc., meaning that this too is not to be regarded, because he is your teacher in magic, so you conspired with him in what happened, or he taught you one thing and not another, and therefore he overcame you. The sentence is thus a justification for something omitted. It has also been said that it is a justification for what was mentioned before. In sum, he said this because of the fear that had seized him that people would follow the magicians in believing in Musa, peace be upon him. Then he turned to them with an emphatic threat, saying: ﴿Then I will surely cut off﴾, that is, if the matter is as it is, then I swear that I will surely cut off ﴿your hands and your feet on opposite sides﴾, that is, the right hand and the left foot. The majority of exegetes hold this, and it is a specification from outside the text, since otherwise it is possible that something other than this is meant. (*Min*) here is *ibtida'iyyah* (indicating the starting point).

Al-Tabarsi said: it means *'an* (from) or *'ala* (upon), but this is not correct. What is meant by *khilaf* (opposition) is the opposing side or the opposing direction.

The prepositional phrase, as is apparent, is connected to ﴿la-uqatti'anna﴾. It has also been said that it is connected to an omitted element that serves as an adjective for an omitted verbal noun, meaning: a cutting that begins from an opposing side or an opposing direction. It is clear that the beginning of the cutting is from that. It is also permissible for *khilaf* to retain its literal meaning, namely opposition, and to make it the starting point by way of metaphor, since it accompanies what is actually the starting point. Some have construed the prepositional phrase as being in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*), and the meaning is: "I will surely cut them off in varied ways." Then consider. The specification of this manner has been said to serve to declare the matter definite and to ensure that it will certainly happen, by specifying its manner as is customary in matters of punishment. Perhaps its choice in this form rather than by simple cutting is a matter of agreement, because cutting involves destruction and the loss of benefit. Some have claimed that this form is more severe.

﴿And I will surely crucify you on the trunks of palm trees﴾, that is, upon them. The choice of the word *fi* (in) indicates their remaining upon them for a long time, comparing their continuance upon them to the settling of a container within what it contains. On this basis is his saying:

*They crucified al-'Abdi on the trunk of a palm,
So Shaiban never sneezed except with a split nose.*

In this there is a *isti'arah tab'iyyah* (a verbal metaphor based on a dependent element). The discussion of this is well known. It has also been said that there is no metaphor at all, because Pharaoh had bored into the trunks of the palm trees and crucified them inside them so that they would die of hunger and thirst. But this hardly holds, and there is debate about the very nature of crucifixion. Some have said that he carried out his threat against them and crucified them, and that he was the first to crucify. Nor does this contradict the saying of God, exalted is He: ﴿You two and whoever follows you will be the victors﴾, because what is meant is victory by argument.

Al-Imam (al-Razi) said: this has not been established in reports. You know that the apparent position is safety. The form *taf'il* in both verbs indicates intensification. It is also recited with the lighter form in both.

﴿And you will surely know which of us is more severe in punishment and more lasting﴾. By *nа* ("us") he means himself and Musa, peace be upon him, on the evidence of the earlier mention of him in His saying: ﴿You believed in him﴾, based on the apparent sense of that. Al-Tabari and a group chose this reading. Either this is meant to belittle Musa, peace be upon him, and to mock him, since he, peace be upon him, had no part in the punishment, or it is because their belief, according to his claim, was not based on witnessing the miracle and seeing the proof, but was out of fear of him, peace be upon him, when they saw his staff swallow their ropes and staffs, so they feared for themselves as well. Abu Hayyan chose that the other whom the pronoun indicates is the Lord of Musa, mighty and majestic, in whom they believed by their saying: ﴿We have believed in the Lord of Harun and Musa﴾.

﴿And you will surely know﴾ here is suspended (*mu'allaq*), and ﴿which of us is more severe﴾ is an interrogative clause consisting of a subject and predicate, in the position of an accusative that takes the place of its two objects if *'ilm* (knowing) is in its proper sense, or in the position of a single object if it means *ma'rifah* (recognition). It is also permissible in this case for ﴿ayyuna﴾ to be the object, and it is indeclinable according to the opinion of Sibawayh. ﴿More severe﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: he is more severe. The clause is the relative clause of *ayy* (which), and the returning pronoun is the front position (*al-sadr*). ﴿In punishment﴾ is a specification (*tamyiz*). Its mention together with ﴿more severe﴾ has made it unnecessary to mention it again with ﴿more lasting﴾, though it is also intended. The derivation of ﴿more lasting﴾ is from *al-baqa'* in the sense of continuance.

It has been said: it is not far-fetched, and God, exalted is He, knows best, that it is from *al-baqa'* in the sense of giving, since the accursed one used to give gifts to whomever he was pleased with. Thus the verse would have some resemblance to Nimrod's saying: "I give life and I cause death." That, however, is at the furthest extreme of distance for one who has sound taste. Then it is not hidden that the accursed one was in extreme audacity and the utmost boldness, since he threatened, menaced, flashed lightning and thundered, despite the recentness of what he had witnessed of the staff turning into a serpent and its tremendous effects, to the point that it sought to swallow his dome, so he cried out for help to Musa, peace be upon him. Nor is such a thing far-fetched from a wicked, tyrannical sinner like him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 72:

﴿They said﴾, paying no heed to his threat: ﴿We will not prefer you﴾, that is, we will not choose you over Allah in faith and submission, ﴿over the clear proofs that have come to us﴾ from Allah, the Exalted, through Musa, peace be upon him, ﴿from the clear signs﴾, that is, the manifest miracles which the staff included.

They made the coming (ja'a) to them and inna ('amma) because they are the ones who benefit from it, and who know it in the most perfect manner, without taqlid (blind imitation). ﻣﺎ (ma) is a relative pronoun and what follows it is its relative clause, and the returning pronoun is the hidden pronoun in jaa'. It has been said that the returning pronoun is omitted, and the pronoun in ﴿jaa'ana﴾ refers to Musa, peace be upon him, meaning: over those whom Musa, peace be upon him, brought to us. This is distant. Although some have chosen this view, there is discussion over the validity of omitting a prepositional phrase of this kind.

﴿And He who originated us﴾, that is, who brought us into being, created us, and all the higher and lower created things. It is conjoined to ﴿what has come to us﴾, and it is placed later because what it contains is a rational, theoretical sign, whereas what they witnessed is a manifest, sensible sign. Mentioning Him, exalted is He, under the title of Originator for them serves to indicate the cause of the ruling: His originating them, and Pharaoh being among His creatures, is what necessitates that they not prefer him over Him, glorified and exalted is He. In this there is a refutation of the one called Pharaoh in his claim to lordship. It has been said: the waw is for an oath, and its answer is omitted, being indicated by what was mentioned, meaning: "By the right of Him who originated us, we will not prefer you," etc.

There is no room for taking what was mentioned as the answer according to those who permit placing the answer before it as well, since the oath is for affirmation, as Abu Hayyan said: "with lan" only in rare poetry. And their saying: "this is an answer to the accursed one's reproach with his words: 'Did you believe...'" etc. And His, exalted is He, saying ﴿So decide what you are going to decide﴾ is an answer to his threat with his words: "I will surely cut off..." etc., meaning: do what you are about to do, or judge by what you are about to judge. The qada' is either in the sense of creative origination, as in His saying ﴿and He completed them as seven heavens﴾, or in its well-known meaning. In both cases the imperative is not meant literally, and ma is a relative pronoun with the returning pronoun omitted.

Abu al-Baqa' permitted it to be a verbal-noun (masdariyya) particle, which is based on the view of some grammarians that a masdariyya may be joined to a nominal clause, though some prohibited that. His, exalted is He, saying ﴿Indeed, you decide only regarding this worldly life﴾ together with what follows it is a reason for the indifference derived from the preceding command to decide. Ma is a restrictive particle (kafffa), and ﴿this worldly life﴾ is in the accusative position as a time adverb for ﴿you decide﴾; the qada' is as explained above, and its object is omitted, meaning: you only do what you desire, or judge by what you see, in this worldly life alone, and we have no desire for its sweetness nor fear of its punishment. It has also been permitted that ma be a verbal-noun particle, so it and what is in its scope are in the sense of the verbal noun of inna and its predicate, ﴿this life﴾, meaning: your deciding is occurring in this worldly life. It has also been permitted that the verb be treated as intransitive, so there is no omission. Abu Haywa and Ibn Abi 'Abla read ( إنَّما تُقْضى ) in the passive voice, with ( هَذِهِ الحَياةُ ) in the nominative, on the basis that the adverbial was treated with extension and made an object, then the verb was made passive with it, like "fasting was observed on Thursday" (ṣīma yawmu al-khamīs).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 73:

﴿Indeed, we have believed in our Lord, that He may forgive us our sins﴾ which we committed of disbelief and disobedience, and not hold us accountable for them in the Hereafter, not in order that He may grant us enjoyment of that transient worldly life so that we would be affected by what You have promised us.

And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and the magic to which You compelled us﴾ is a conjunction upon (our sins), meaning: and He may forgive us the magic which we were taught to oppose Musa, peace be upon him, by Your compulsion and by Your gathering us from the distant cities. They singled it out for mention, although it is included among their sins, to show the extent of their aversion to it and their eagerness for its forgiveness. The mention of compulsion serves to indicate that it is among the things that ought to be singled out for seeking forgiveness, even though it proceeded from them under compulsion, and there is in it a kind of apology in order to attract forgiveness. It is said that their leaders were seventy-two, two of whom were from the Copts and the rest from the Children of Israel, and Pharaoh had compelled them to learn magic.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, who said: Pharaoh took forty boys from the Children of Israel and commanded that they learn magic, and said: "Teach them a teaching by which no one among the people of the earth will overcome them." And they were among those who believed in Musa, peace be upon him, and they are the ones who said: ﴿Indeed, we have believed in our Lord, that He may forgive us our sins and the magic to which You compelled us﴾. Al-Hasan said: He would take the children of the people and force them to learn magic. It is also said that he compelled them to the opposition, for it is narrated that they said to him: "Show us Musa asleep," so he did, and they found his staff guarding him. They said: "This is not magic, for when a magician sleeps, his magic is nullified." Yet he refused except that they oppose him. This does not contradict their saying: ﴿By the might of Pharaoh, indeed we will be the victors﴾, since it is possible that this was before that, or it was a show of boldness, just as their saying: ﴿Indeed, there will be for us a reward if we are the victors﴾ was before it, as has been said. Abu Ubayd claimed that the mere command of the ruler to a person is compulsion, even if he does not threaten him, and our masters the Hanafis went to this, as is found in most of their books, because opposing his command entails the expectation of harm, especially if the ruler is a tyrant and oppressor. ﴿And Allah is better﴾ in Himself, exalted is He, ﴿and more enduring﴾, meaning: and more lasting in recompense, whether reward or punishment, or better in reward and more enduring in punishment.
Page 234

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 74:

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed﴾, up to the end of the two conditional clauses, it is an explanation on their part of His, exalted is His majesty, being "better and more enduring," a confirmation of it and a refutation of what the accursed one (al-La'in, Satan) claimed. The opening of both clauses with the pronoun of the matter (ḍamir al-sha'n, the "pronoun of the affair") serves to draw attention to the grandeur of their content and to add to its firm establishment, meaning: indeed the matter is momentous, namely this, that is, His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal﴾, by dying in disbelief and sins.

﴿For him there is Hell; he will neither die therein﴾, so that his punishment would come to an end, and this is a confirmation that His punishment, Exalted is He, is more enduring, ﴿nor live﴾ a life by which he benefits.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 75:**

﴿And whoever comes to Him as a believer﴾ in Him, the Mighty and Majestic, and in what He brought from Himself of the miracles, among which is what we have witnessed, ﴿has done righteous deeds﴾ of actions, ﴿then those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to (man) (whoever), and the plural is used in regard to its meaning, just as the singular was used in what preceded in regard to its wording. The sense of distance in it is to indicate the loftiness of their rank and the remoteness of their station. That is: ﴿then those﴾ are the believers who do righteous deeds. ﴿For them﴾, because of their faith and that deed, ﴿are the high ranks﴾, that is, the exalted stations.

**Page 235**

**﴿Gardens of Eden﴾** is either a substitute (*badal*) for "the high ranks," or an explanatory apposition (*bayan*). The word *'adn* has already been discussed. **﴿Beneath which rivers flow﴾** is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) describing "the gardens." His, may He be exalted, saying **﴿therein they abide forever﴾** confirms that His reward is more lasting. It is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in "for them." Its governing element (*'amil*) is the sense of settledness (*al-istiqrar*) in the adverbial phrase, or the sense of "I point to" (*ushir*) contained in "those." The circumstance is anticipated (*muqaddarah*). It is not permissible for "gardens" (*jannat*) to be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "they are gardens," because the sentence would then lack a governing element for the circumstance, according to what Abu al-Baqa' mentioned.

**﴿That﴾** refers to what has been granted to them of success through what was mentioned. The sense of distance in relation to what is pointed to, though it is near, serves to magnify it. **﴿Is the recompense of whoever purifies himself﴾**, meaning cleanses himself (*tatahhara*) from the filth of disbelief and sins through what was mentioned of faith and righteous deeds.

This is an explicit statement of what the conditional sentence (*shartiyyah*) conveys. The mention of the state of the criminal (*al-mujrim*) is placed first in order to hasten to clarify the severity and permanence of His punishment, may He be mighty and majestic. This is a refutation of what Pharaoh claimed in his saying **﴿Whose punishment is more severe and more lasting?﴾** Some have said that the two conditional sentences up to this point are a fresh statement from Him, may He be exalted, to alert to the ugliness of what Pharaoh did and the goodness of what the sorcerers did. The first view is preferable, contrary to what al-Naysaburi supposed.

The Mu'tazilah cited the first conditional sentence as evidence for the certainty of punishment for the perpetrator of a major sin (*kabirah*). They said: the perpetrator of a major sin is a criminal (*mujrim*), because the original meaning of *jurm* is cutting a fruit from its tree, and then it was used figuratively for acquiring something disliked. Every criminal, for him is Hell, according to the verse. The word "whoever" (*man*) in the conditional is general, as proven by the validity of exception. So it follows that the perpetrator of a major sin has Hell, and this indicates the certainty of the threat.

The People of the Sunnah replied that we do not accept the minor premise, since "the criminal" may be intended to mean the disbeliever. This meaning frequently occurs in the Qur'an, such as His saying **﴿they will question one another﴾** **﴿about the criminals﴾** **﴿What led you into Saqar?﴾** up to His saying, glorified is He, **﴿and we used to deny the Day of Judgment﴾**, and His saying, may He be exalted, **﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed﴾** to the end of the surah. Even if this premise is granted, we do not accept the major premise in its absolute form. Rather it is a universal only on condition of the absence of pardon. Moreover, we do not accept that the conditional "whoever" is definitive in generality, as the Imam (al-Razi) said. In that case, certainty of the threat is not achieved in an unqualified way.

Even if both premises are granted, it may be said that the general promise in His, may He be exalted, saying **﴿And whoever comes to Him as a believer…﴾** (etc.) opposes that argument, and makes the discourse concern one who believed, did righteous deeds, and committed a major sin. He is included in the generality of **﴿whoever comes to Him as a believer, having done righteous deeds﴾**, and his committing a major sin does not remove him from the generality. Whenever Paradise is for him, it is for one who believed and committed a major sin, even if he did not do righteous deeds, since there is no one who makes a distinction. If they say that the perpetrator of a major sin is not called a believer, just as he is not called a disbeliever, because they affirm the "intermediate position" (*al-manzilah bayn al-manzilatayn*), then he is not included in the generality. We have refuted that, and we have demonstrated, with what is mentioned in its proper place, the restriction of the accountable person (*mukallaf*) to believer and disbeliever and the negation of an intermediate position between faith and disbelief.

Even if we grant that **﴿whoever comes to Him as a believer﴾** (etc.) does not encompass the perpetrator of a major sin, it may be said: His, may He be exalted, saying **﴿Those will have the highest ranks﴾** indicates that pardon is attained by the people of major sins. This is because He, may He be exalted, made the highest ranks and the Gardens of Eden for those who came with faith and righteous deeds. Therefore the remaining ranks that are not highest, and the gardens, must be for others, and those others are none but the disobedient among the people of faith.

Abu Dawud and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Sa'id, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: **"Indeed, the people of the high ranks are seen by those beneath them as you see the bright star on the horizon of the sky, and indeed Abu Bakr and 'Umar are among them, and they bless."**

It was argued that **﴿whoever comes to Him as a believer﴾** includes the one who commits a major sin, by His saying **﴿And that is the recompense of whoever purifies himself﴾**, based on what has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the intended meaning of "whoever purifies himself" is whoever says "There is no god but Allah." It is as if he intended whoever purifies himself from the filth of disbelief. And Allah knows best.

Then, when the disobedient one enters Hell, his state is not like the state of the disbelieving criminal when he enters it. Rather, it was said that he dies, citing what Muslim, Ahmad, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) delivered a sermon and came to this verse, **"Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal…"** (etc.), and said, peace and blessings be upon him: **"As for its people, those who are its people, they neither die therein nor live. As for those who are not its people, the Fire will cause them to die a death. Then the intercessors will stand and intercede, and they will be brought forth in bundles and placed on a river called 'al-Hayah' or 'al-Hayawan,' and they will sprout as cucumbers sprout by the carried silt of the flood."**

The one who said this took **"will cause them to die"** in its literal sense, and took the verbal noun (*masdar*) as an emphasis to repel the suspicion of metaphor, as was said regarding His saying **﴿And Allah spoke to Moses, speaking﴾**. He mentioned that the purpose of their remaining in the Fire after their death, until where Allah wills, is to deprive them of Paradise during that period, and that this is added to their punishment by the burning of the Fire upon them.

Some said: "Will cause them to die" is metaphorical, and the intended meaning is that the Fire makes their state close to the state of the dead, so that they have no complete awareness of the punishment. It is not accepted that mention of the verbal noun contradicts metaphor, so it is permissible to say: "I killed Zayd with a stick, a killing," meaning "I struck him a severe blow." It is not valid to say that the verbal noun here expresses the kind, meaning "He causes them a kind of death," because death has no kinds. Rather it is a single kind, namely the expulsion of the soul. For this reason it was said:

*"Whoever does not die by the sword dies by other means; the causes are many, but death is one."*

The Mujassimah (anthropomorphists) cited His, glorified is He, saying **"Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord…"** as evidence for affirming a place for Him, exalted is His majesty.

It is answered that the intended meaning of "coming to Him" is coming to the place of His promise, may He be mighty and majestic, or something similar to that.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 77:**

﴿And We had certainly revealed to Musa﴾ is a general narration of what the matter of Pharaoh and his people had come to. Between this and that, the mention of what befell them after the magicians were overcome is omitted. Those were the detailed, manifest signs (al-ayat al-mufassalah) shown at the hand of Musa, peace be upon him, over about twenty years, as detailed in Surat al-A'raf. Whenever a sign of warning came, Pharaoh would promise to release the Children of Israel once the punishment was lifted, but as soon as it was lifted he broke his word. So when the signs were complete, God Most High revealed to Musa, peace be upon him, ﴿that travel by night with My servants﴾. The sentence is introduced with an oath to show the utmost care for its content.

"An" is either explanatory (mufassirah) of the sense of speech contained in the revelation, or it is a verbal particle (masdariyyah) from which the preposition has been dropped. The description of the Children of Israel with the title of servitude to God Most High serves to show mercy and concern for their affair, and to draw attention to the extreme ugliness of Pharaoh's conduct towards them, since he enslaved them although they were His servants, and inflicted upon them every kind of oppression, not heeding their true Master, may His majesty be exalted. The apparent view is that the revelation of what has been mentioned, and what follows it, took place in Egypt. That is, and with God Most High: We certainly revealed to him, peace be upon him, that he should travel by night with My servants, whom I sent you to rescue from the dominion of Pharaoh, out of Egypt. ﴿So strike for them﴾ with your staff ﴿a dry path in the sea﴾. "A dry path" is the direct object of "strike," used in a broad sense, and it is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli). The original sense is: strike the sea so that it becomes a path for them. ﴿Dry﴾, that is, parched, and Abu Haywah recited it this way, as a verbal noun (masdar) made into a descriptive adjective for "path" for emphasis, and it applies to the singular masculine and to other than it.

al-Hasan recited "yabsan" with a sukun on the ba'. This is either a lightened form of it by dropping the vowel, so it is also a verbal noun, or a sifah mushabbahah (a descriptive adjective of quality, like "sa'b," hard), or a plural of "yabis" (dry), like "sahb" and "sahib." Describing the singular with it is for emphasis, because the path, owing to its extreme dryness, was treated as though it were many dry things, as is said concerning the verse of al-Qutami:

"As if the saddle-straps of my riding-saddle, when the water-skins were tied, were hungry bellies and empty stomachs."

He treated the stomach, because of its extreme hunger, as a group of hungry men. Or he estimated each part of the path to be a dry path, as is said concerning ﴿a drop of mingled fluid﴾ and "a worn-out garment." Or the path is intended as a genus, and it was multiple according to the number of the tribes, not a single path, according to the sound view, so its description came in the plural. It is also said that it may be a collective noun (ism jam'). The apparent view is that there is no difference here in meaning between "yabas" with a vowel and "yubs" with a sukun, since the basic principle is the agreement of the two readings, even if one of them is irregular (shadhdhah). In the Qamus: "yubs" with a sukun is what originally was moist and then dried, and what is originally a state of dryness, which was not known to be moist, is "yabas" with a vowel. As for the path of Musa, peace be upon him, in the sea, it was not known as a path, neither moist nor dry; rather God Most High manifested it for them at that time, created in that state. (End of quotation.)

This contradicts what al-Raghib mentioned, that "yabas" with a vowel is what had moisture in it which then went away, and a place which had water and then the water went away. It is narrated that when Musa, peace be upon him, struck the sea and it split until paths appeared in it, God Most High sent the east wind, which dried those paths until they became dry. Some have also held that "strike" here means "make," as in the expression "he struck a share for him in his property" and "he imposed on them the tax (kharaj)," or means "take," so it takes two objects, the first of which is "a path," and the second "for them."

Abu Hayyan chose to keep it on its well-known meaning, and this agrees better with the words of God Most High: ﴿Strike the sea with your staff﴾. Abu al-Baqa' claimed that "a path," in this case, is an adverbial object of place (maf'ul fihi), and said: the estimate is "strike for them" in the place of a path. ﴿Do not fear being overtaken﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "strike," or is another description of "a path," with an omitted returning pronoun, that is, "in it," or it is a resumptive new sentence (isti'naf), as Abu al-Baqa' said, and he preferred it over the other possibilities. al-A'mash, Hamzah, and Ibn Abi Layla recited "la takhaf" with a jussive, as a response to the imperative "travel" (asri). It is possible that it is a new prohibition, as al-Zajjaj mentioned. Abu Haywah, Talhah, and al-A'mash recited "darkan" with a sukun on the ra'. It is a noun from "idrak," meaning overtaking, like "darak" with a vowel. al-Raghib said: "darak" with a vowel in the verse is what overtakes a person of consequence, that is, do not fear any consequence. The majority hold the first sense, that is, do not fear that Pharaoh and his armies will overtake you from behind ﴿and do not dread﴾ that the sea will drown you from in front of you. This is coordinated with ﴿do not fear﴾. This is clear under the three possibilities in the reading with the damma. As for the reading with the jussive, it is said that it is a new sentence, meaning "while you do not dread," and it is said that it is coordinated with the jussive verb, and the alif was brought for the sake of pause, observing the endings of the verses, as in His words: ﴿and they led us astray from the way﴾ and ﴿and you think about God with thoughts﴾. Or it is jussive by dropping the presumed vowel, as in the verse: "When the old woman becomes angry, divorce her, and do not appease her or flatter her." This is a rare dialect among some people and a poetic necessity among others, so it is not permitted to interpret the Revelation of exalted status by it, nor is it fitting when the two previous possibilities, or the first of them, are available. Dread (khashyah) is the greatest fear, and it seems that it was chosen here because drowning is greater than being overtaken by Pharaoh and his armies, since the former is a place of expected safety. This does not contradict the fact that they first mentioned what indicates their fear of being overtaken, when they said: ﴿Indeed, we are to be overtaken﴾, and for this reason haste was made to remove it by putting its negation first, as becomes clear upon reflection.

[Page 236]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 78:

﴿So Pharaoh followed them with his soldiers﴾. That is, he followed them, and his soldiers were with him, on the basis that atba' (to follow) means taba' (to follow), and it is transitive to one object, and the ba' is for accompaniment (musahabah), and the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). What supports this is that al-Hasan and Abu 'Amr, in one narration, recited: fa-ittaba'ahum (with a doubled ta'), and it was also read: (fa-atba'ahum Fir'awnu wa-junudahu) (Pharaoh followed them and his soldiers). It was also said: atba' is transitive to two objects here, as in His saying, exalted is He: (atba'nahum dhurriyyatahum) (We made their offspring follow them), and the second object is implied, that is, the chiefs of his state (ru'asa' dawlatihi) followed them, or his punishment ('iqabuhu). It was also said: it is himself, and the prepositional phrase is also in the position of a circumstantial clause. And it is reported from al-Azhari that the second object is junudahu and the ba' is for emphasis (sayf khatib), meaning: Pharaoh followed them with his soldiers, driving them behind them, so he was with them, urging them on to catch up with them. It is also permissible that the second object is junudahu and the ba' is for transitivity (ta'diyah), so the verb is transitive to one object by itself and to the other by the particle. In any case, the fa' is explanatory (fasihah), indicating an implied element that has been omitted, relying on its evident clarity and as a signal of Musa's (peace be upon him) complete haste in complying with the command, that is: so he did what he was commanded, of traveling by night with My servants and striking a dry path for them, and Pharaoh followed him with his soldiers.

Some have claimed that the revelation about striking the path came after Pharaoh followed them and the two hosts saw each other. The apparent meaning is the first. It is related that Musa (peace be upon him) set out with them at the beginning of the night, intending the Qulzum, and they had borrowed jewelry and animals from the people of Pharaoh for a festival they were going out to. They numbered six hundred thousand and three thousand and more, with none of them under sixty or over twenty. In another narration, they left numbering six hundred thousand and seventy thousand. They also took out with them the body of Yusuf (peace be upon him), because he had bound them to do so, and an old woman guided them to his place. Musa (peace be upon him) said to her: "Name your request." She said: "I would be with you in Paradise." The news reached Pharaoh, so he gathered his soldiers and went out with them. In his cavalry were seventy thousand dark-bay horses, and his vanguard, as is related, was seven hundred thousand horsemen; it was also said one million five hundred thousand. He tracked their trail until the two hosts saw each other. The fear of the Children of Israel grew great, so (peace be upon him) struck the sea with his staff, and it split into twelve parts, each part like a great mountain. They entered, and Pharaoh and his soldiers reached the entrance and saw the sea split apart, and they were astonished at the matter. Pharaoh said to them: "It only split from my awe." He entered on a noble mare, with Jibril (peace be upon him) before him on a dun mare, and the angels (peace be upon them) cried out, and they were thirty-three angels: "Enter!"
