They entered, until when they had completed their entry, Musa (peace be upon him) came out with those with him from the tribes, safe, and none came out from Pharaoh and his soldiers. ﴿Then the sea covered them with what covered them﴾. That is, it rose over them from it and overwhelmed them with what overwhelmed them, a terrifying matter whose measure cannot be estimated and whose reality cannot be reached.

It was said: what covered them is what you have heard of its story, but this is not the case, for the focus of the awe and magnification is its going beyond the bounds of understanding and description, not the hearing of the story. The apparent meaning is that the two plural pronouns refer to Pharaoh and his soldiers. It was said: only to his soldiers, due to proximity, and because he was cast onto the shore and was not submerged in the sea, as is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So today We will save you in your body﴾. But in this there is that the rescue after what had covered his soldiers covered him, and the Children of Israel doubted his destruction, and proximity is not a strong reason. It was also said: the first pronoun refers to Pharaoh and his soldiers, and the second to Musa (peace be upon him) and his people, and there is an omission in the speech, meaning: Musa (peace be upon him) and his people were saved, and Pharaoh and his soldiers drowned. End of quote. But this is nothing, as is not hidden.

The Qur'an reciter al-A'mash and a group among them read: (fa-gasshahum min al-yammi ma gasshahum), meaning: covered them what covered them. The agent here is also ma, and omitting the object adds to the vagueness. It was also said: the object is ﴿min al-yammi﴾, meaning: some of the sea. It is permissible that the agent is a pronoun for God, exalted is His majesty, and ma is the object. It was also said: it is a pronoun for Pharaoh, and the attribution is metaphorical, because he is the one who led them into destruction. This is made unlikely by the explicit mention in His saying, exalted is He,

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 79:**

﴿And Pharaoh led his people astray﴾, that is, he took them on a path that brought them to ruin in both religion and worldly life together, since they were drowned and then placed into the Fire. ﴿And he did not guide [them]﴾, that is, he did not guide them to a path leading to any of the goals, religious or worldly. The intended meaning of this is mockery (tahakkum) of him, as more than one commentator has mentioned. It has been objected that mockery means that something is said whose opposite is intended, as in a metaphor or the like, such as ﴿Indeed, you are the forbearing, the discerning﴾, when the intended description is the opposite of these two qualities; and that his not having been guided is a statement about what is in fact the case.

It is answered that the matter is indeed as stated, but the custom in an example such as "Zayd did not guide ʿAmr" is to establish that Zayd knows the way of guidance and is himself guided, but he did not guide ʿAmr. Pharaoh was the most misguided of the misguided in himself, so how could it be imagined that he guides others? What confirms this is that the first clause is sufficient to inform of his not guiding them, indeed with the added [fact] of his misguiding them, for one who does not guide may not even mislead. And when it is established that the first [clause] suffices to convey the information in the most complete manner, it is determined that the second has a meaning other than that, namely mockery. The scholar al-Tibi said: the clarification of the meaning of mockery is that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and he did not guide﴾ is of the category of allusion (talmih), and it points to the claim of the accursed one to guiding the people in his saying ﴿And I only show you the way of right conduct﴾. So it is like one who makes a claim and exaggerates in it; when its time comes and he does not bring it, it is said to him: you did not bring what you claimed, [said] in mockery and derision, end of quote.

From what has been mentioned, the difference between the two clauses is known, and that there is no repetition. It has also been said: the intended meaning is that he did not guide them at any time, and the difference is achieved thereby, because the first clause carries no indication of this generality. The first view is preferable. It has also been said: "guided" (hada) here means "was guided" (ihtada), i.e., he misled them and was not himself guided; but this is far-fetched. Some have taken misguidance and guidance in the sense specific to religion; but the context of his driving his soldiers to the path of worldly destruction rejects this, and to take them as referring to misguidance in the sea and deliverance from it is something the sound nature does not accept.

The judge (al-Qadi) argued from the verse that He, exalted is He, is not the creator of disbelief, because He, exalted is His majesty, has censured Pharaoh in it for misleading [others], and whoever censures someone for something is himself censured if he does it. It is answered by denying that this holds universally.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 80:**

﴿O Children of Israel﴾ is a narration of what Allah the Exalted addressed to them after drowning their enemy and delivering them from him, though not immediately after that, but after He had bestowed upon them the various kinds of blessings, religious and worldly, that He bestowed.

It has been said that this is a new address to those among them who were in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), on the meaning that Allah the Exalted has bestowed favour upon them by what He did to their fathers originally and to them by extension. It has been objected that this view is refuted by His words ﴿And what hastened you away from your people?﴾ and so on, since it is impossible to take it as a new address, and so is the context. Therefore the correct view is that it is a narration, with the implied verb "We said" (qulna), conjoined to ﴿We revealed﴾, meaning: "And We said: O Children of Israel, ﴿We have delivered you from your enemy﴾, Pharaoh and his people, when they were inflicting on you the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and sparing your women."

(Page 239)

Ḥumayd recited (najjaynākum) with a doubled jīm, without a hamza before it, and with the nūn of majesty. Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī, al-A'mash and Ṭalḥah recited (anjaytukum) with the tā' of the pronoun. ﴿And We appointed for you the right side of the mount﴾ is read with the accusative (al-yamana), on the basis that it is an adjective of the noun it modifies. It was also read in the genitive (al-yamini), and al-Zamakhsharī explained this by the attraction (al-jiwār), as in the phrase "this is the hole of a ruined lizard" (hādhā juḥru ḍabbin kharib). Abū Ḥayyān objected to this that the genitive in question is among the rare and anomalous usages, such that the recitation should not be based on it, and he said: "The correct view is that it is a qualifier of the mount (al-ṭūr) because of the blessing (al-yumn) in it, or because it lies on the right of one who faces the mountain."

The truth is that the rarity of a usage does not reach the point of forbidding the justification of a recitation, especially when it is anomalous, and the agreement of the two recitations requires it. His statement "or because it lies on the right of..." is not correct on the assumption that the ṭūr is the mountain. Had he said "or because it lies on the right of one who set out from Egypt toward Syria," it would have been correct. The accusative of (jāniba) is taken as adverbial of place, following what al-Khafājī related from al-Rāghib and what Ibn Mālik stated in his commentary on al-Tashīl, that the accusative of janb and what has its meaning, when governing a genitive, has been heard used adverbially. Some have prohibited this because the noun is determinate, and have made it an accusative object of wā'adnā in the figurative extension (al-ittisā') of language, or by supposing an elided genitive noun, that is, "the coming to the side of the mountain." This is the view of Abū al-Baqā'. When it is an adverb of place, the object is elided, meaning: "And We appointed you, through your Prophet, at that side, the coming of Mūsā (peace be upon him) for private conversation and the sending down of the Torah upon him." The attribution of the appointment to them, although it belonged to Mūsā (peace be upon him), is in view of its connection to them and the spread of its benefit to them, so that they are all as though they were appointed. Thus the figurative usage is in the attribution. In this there is what is contained of giving the context of favour its due.

Ḥamzah and those mentioned with him just now recited (wāʿadtukum) with the tā' of the pronoun too. It was also read (wa-ʿadnākum), from the verb "to promise."

﴿And We sent down upon you the manna and the quails﴾: the manna is the honey-dew (al-turanjabīn) and the quail (al-sumānī). The manna used to descend upon them while they were in the wilderness, like snow, from dawn until sunrise, a sa' for each person (the sa' being a dry measure), and the south wind would bring quails to them, so that each one of them took what sufficed him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 81:

﴿Eat of the good things We have provided for you﴾, i.e., of their delicacies or their lawful things, on the basis that by "good" (al-tayyib) is meant what the natural disposition (al-tab') or the Sacred Law (al-shar') finds good.

It is also permissible that by "the good things" is meant what combines the two qualities of enjoyment and lawfulness (al-hill). The sentence is then a resumption (mustaʾnafah), brought to explain the permissibility of what was mentioned to them and to complete the blessing upon them. The one mentioned above read ﴿razaqtukum﴾ ("I provided for you" in the first person). God, glorified is He, mentioned first the blessing of deliverance from the enemy, because it belongs to the category of averting harms, and averting harms is more important than attracting benefits. Whoever has tasted the bitterness of the schemes of enemies, when God has humiliated them and then delivered him and turned their scheming back upon them, knows the worth of this blessing. We ask God the Exalted to complete His blessings upon us and not to give any enemy a way over us. He, exalted is He, mentioned the religious blessing second, because it is the nose on the face of benefits (i.e., its most prominent part, its essence). He, mighty and majestic is He, put the worldly blessing last, because it is lower than that. So woe to him who sells his religion for the world.

﴿And do not transgress therein﴾, i.e., in what We have provided for you, by failing to thank Him for it and by exceeding the limits of God the Exalted concerning it, through extravagance and insolence, by using it to disobey God the Exalted, and by withholding the obligatory rights due from it. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: that is, do not wrong one another, so that one takes from the other's property without right. It has also been said: that is, do not hoard.

Zayd ibn ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with them, read ﴿wa-la tatghaw﴾ (with a ḍammah on the ghayn, i.e., "do not transgress" in a different vocalization). ﴿Fa-yahilla ʿalaykum ghaḍabī﴾ is the answer to the prohibition, meaning: then My wrath will fall upon you and become due to you. The verb from "ḥalla al-dayn yaḥillu" (the debt became due) with a kasrah on the ḥāʾ means that its payment has become obligatory. Its root is from ḥulūl (alighting, settling), which originally applies to bodies, then it was borrowed for other things and became so common that it became literal in that usage. ﴿And whoever has My wrath descend upon him, then he has indeed fallen﴾, i.e., perished. Its original meaning is falling from a height, like a mountain, and then it was used for destruction because it is a necessary consequence of it. It has also been said: that is, he fell into the Pit (al-Hawiyah), and this is the view of al-Zajjaj.

In some reports it is said that in Hell there is a palace from whose top the disbeliever is thrown, and he falls into Hell for forty autumns before he reaches the bottom (al-salsal). That is the meaning of His saying ﴿fa-qad hawā﴾. It therefore retains its original meaning when it is taken to refer to a specific individual, not in its general sense.

Al-Kisa'i read ﴿fa-yaḥull﴾ with a ḍammah on the ḥāʾ, and ﴿wa-man yaḥlul﴾ with a ḍammah on the first lām. This is the reading of Qatadah, Abu Haywah, al-Aʿmash and Talhah. Ibn ʿUtbah agreed in ﴿yaḥlul﴾ and so read it with a ḍammah. In al-Iqna' of Abu ʿAli al-Ahwazi, it is recorded that Ibn Ghazwan, on the authority of Talhah, read ﴿la yaḥillanna ʿalaykum﴾ with a doubled nūn, a fatḥah on the lām and a kasrah on the ḥāʾ, which belongs to the pattern of "la arayannaka hunā" (I will certainly see you here). In Kitab al-Lawami' it is recorded that Qatadah, ʿAbdullah ibn Muslim ibn Yasar, Ibn Wathhab and al-Aʿmash read ﴿fa-yuḥilla﴾ with a ḍammah on the yāʾ and a kasrah on the ḥāʾ, from al-iḥlāl (causing to descend). Then its subject is the pronoun referring to transgression, and "My wrath" is its object. It is also permissible that the subject is the wrath itself, with the object omitted, meaning "the punishment" or something similar. The meaning of yaḥull with a ḍammah on the ḥāʾ is "descends", from ḥalla bi-l-balad (he alighted in the land) when he settled, as in al-Kashshaf.

In al-Misbah al-Munir: ḥalla al-ʿadhāb yaḥillu and yaḥullu, these two forms alone with kasrah and ḍammah, while the rest have only kasrah. Anger in humans is the boiling of the blood of the heart when there is a desire for retaliation. In a hadith: "Beware of anger, for it is an ember kindled in the heart of the son of Adam. Have you not seen the swelling of his veins and the redness of his eyes?"

When anger is attributed to God the Exalted, this meaning is definitely not intended, and a meaning befitting His majesty, may His majesty be exalted, is intended. It may be meant as retribution and punishment, or the intention of them, we seek refuge in God the Exalted from that. Describing that as "descending" is literal according to some possibilities and figurative according to others. In al-Intisaf it is said that attributing "descending" to Him is not possible if what is meant is the intention to punish. That would be like the saying of the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him: "Our Lord descends to the lowest heaven," according to the well-known interpretation. Alternatively, the descending of the effect of the will is expressed by the descending of the will itself, expressing the effect by its cause, as when someone looking at a marvelous creation of God the Exalted says: "Look at the power of God the Exalted," meaning the effect of the power, not the power itself.

﴿And indeed I am Most Forgiving﴾, abundant in forgiveness, ﴿to those who repent﴾ from polytheism, according to what is narrated from Ibn Abbas. It was also said: from that and from the sins among which is transgression in what has been provided. ﴿And believe﴾ in what it is obligatory to believe in. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, in what is narrated from him, limited himself to mentioning belief in Allah, the Exalted. Perhaps this is from the category of limiting oneself to the most noble, otherwise the more appropriate reading is to intend generality together with mention of repentance from polytheism. ﴿And do righteous deeds﴾, meaning a deed that is upright according to the Sharia. Apparently it includes both the obligatory (fard) and the recommended (sunnah). From Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, it is also reported that this is explained as performing the obligatory duties. ﴿Then remains upon guidance﴾, meaning he adheres to guidance and stays firm upon it until he meets Allah. This is also reported from the Habr (the scholar, i.e., Ibn Abbas).

Guidance may be understood to mean faith, and He, glorified is He, has explicitly praised those who remain steadfast in this, in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast, the angels descend upon them, [saying], "Do not fear and do not grieve."﴾

Al-Zamakhshari said: Guidance is steadfastness and firmness upon the guidance mentioned, which is repentance, faith and righteous deeds. In any case, the word "then" (thumma) is either for sequence in terms of attainment, since its distance from the first stage of attainment, or to indicate the distance between the two ranks, for persistence is higher and greater than beginning, as it has been said:

For everyone there is a striving toward the heights of glory,
but steadfastness is [what matters], though it is rare among men.

It was also said: The intended meaning is "then he acted according to the Sunnah." Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated from the Habr that the meaning of "whoever is guided" is that he knows his deed has a reward that will be given for it, and other than this has also been reported from him. It was also said: The intended meaning is that he purified his heart from blameworthy traits, such as self-admiration, envy, arrogance and others. Ibn Atiyyah said: What appears strongest regarding the meaning of ﴿then remains upon guidance﴾ is that "then" means he preserved his beliefs from contradicting the truth in anything at all, for guidance in this sense is other than faith and other than action, end of quote. It is not hidden from you that this returns to our statement: "then he remained steadfast upon faith in what it is obligatory to believe in, in the correct manner."

The Imamiyyah (Twelver Shi'a) transmitted through several chains from Abu Ja'far al-Baqir, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Then remains upon guidance" means guidance to our wilayah (allegiance), the People of the House. By Allah, if a man worshipped Allah, the Exalted, his whole life between the Corner (of the Ka'bah) and the Station (of Abraham), then died without bringing our wilayah, Allah, the Exalted, would throw him into the Fire on his face.

You know that their wilayah and their love, may Allah be pleased with them, is something about which there is no dispute among us regarding its obligation. However, interpreting guidance in the verse as that, while the verse is a narration of what Allah, the Exalted, addressed to the Children of Israel in the time of Moses, peace be upon him, requires the claim that He, glorified and exalted, knew the People of the House among the Children of Israel and made their wilayah obligatory upon them at that time, and this is not established in authentic reports.

Yes, the Imamiyyah narrated from the report of Jarud ibn al-Mundhir al-Abdi that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "O Jarud, on the night I was taken up to the heaven, Allah, the Exalted, revealed to me: Ask those messengers whom We sent before you: On what were they sent? I said: On what were they sent? He said: On your prophethood and the wilayah of Ali ibn Abi Talib and the Imams from you two. Then Allah, the Exalted, made me know them by their names." Then he (ﷺ) mentioned their names one after another until al-Mahdi. This is a lengthy report in which falsehood gushes forth. They have reports on this subject, all of this kind, so there is no benefit in mentioning them except prolonging the discussion.

The verse indicates the certainty of forgiveness for whoever is characterized by the totality of the attributes mentioned. The most that can be understood from it, according to those who hold the doctrine of mafhum (implicature by inference), is the non-certainty of forgiveness for one who is not characterized by the totality, and non-certainty is more general than certainty of non-existence. Therefore the verse is far from being evidence for the Mu'tazili (who holds) the certainty of non-forgiveness for one who commits a major sin and dies without repentance. So understand.

Those who said that repentance from disbelief is obligatory first, then bringing faith second, have argued with it, because He put repentance before faith in it. Also those who said that righteous deeds do not enter into faith have argued with it, because of the conjunction (wa) which requires difference.

[Page 241]

﴿Wa-ma ajalaka 'an qawmika ya Musa﴾ [And what hastened you away from your people, O Musa?]. This is a report of what passed between God, exalted is He, and Musa, peace be upon him, at the beginning of his arrival at the appointed time (mīqat), in accordance with the appointment mentioned earlier. That is, it was said to him: "What hastened you away from your people, so that you went ahead of them?"

According to many, including al-Zamakhshari, the people here are the seventy chosen men (al-nuqaba' al-sab'un). By "hastening" is meant going ahead of them, not arriving before the set term of the appointment, contrary to what some have said. The interrogative is for denial (inkar), and it implies, as in al-Kashf (by al-Zamakhshari), the denial of the cause that would motivate it, namely the presence of an obstacle in between, which is the appearance of neglecting the people and not regarding them, even though he, peace be upon him, had been commanded to bring them along and have them present with him. It also denies the act itself, because hastening is in itself a deficiency, so how could it be from the ulu al-'azm (the steadfast messengers), to whom the utmost resolve is fitting?

**Page 242**

The Most High's words, ﴿He said, "They are right behind me, and I hastened to You, my Lord, that You might be pleased"﴾, contain an explanation of his excuse, peace be upon him. Its gist is a presentation of his error in ijtihad (independent legal reasoning). It is as if he, peace be upon him, said: "They have not fallen far behind me; my advance ahead of them was only a small step. I thought that such a thing is not objectionable, and what moved me to it was the continuance of Your pleasure, or the gaining of more of it. I thought that such a motive is fit to prompt an action of the kind mentioned, and it did not occur to me that there was any obstacle that would make it objectionable to me." This is similar to hastening, which removes khushu' (humble devotion), to catch up with the imam in the ruku' (bowing), seeking to perform this pillar of prayer together with the congregation in which the Lord's pleasure lies. They (the jurists) said that such a thing is not permissible. He, peace be upon him, put his excuse for denying the act itself first, because it is more important.

Some said: the interrogative is a question about the cause of the haste, and it implies its denial, because haste in itself is a deficiency, to which neglect and the appearance of disrespect were added. So he, peace be upon him, answered regarding the cause that it was the continuance of pleasure or the gaining of more of it, and regarding the denial with what sums up to this: they have not fallen far behind me, and I thought that a slight advance, being customary among people, is not denied and is not counted a deficiency. The placing of this answer first was explained by what has passed.

It was objected that the apparent course of his speech indicates that the question about the cause is on its literal meaning. You know that the literal meaning of a question is impossible for God the Most High. So there is no basis for building the speech upon it. It was answered that a question from the Knower of the unseen is impossible if it is to seek knowledge; but if it is to inform others, or to rebuke, or to alert, then it is not impossible. It was rebutted that it is not appropriate here for the question to be for any of the mentioned purposes, and what comes to mind is that it is for denial.

In al-Intisaf, it is said that what is meant by Musa's question about the cause of the haste, and He, glorified be He, knows best, is to teach him the etiquette of travel: that the leader of a people should lag behind them so that his gaze may be upon them and he may watch over them. This meaning is not achieved when one is ahead. Do you not see how God the Most High taught this etiquette to Lut, when He said, glorified be He, ﴿and follow behind them﴾, and so He commanded him, Mighty and Majestic, to be the last of them? Musa, peace be upon him, only neglected this matter in haste toward the pleasure of God the Most High and in eagerness toward the appointment. That is the state of one promised what has gladdened him; he would wish to ride the wings of birds. Nothing is more joyful than God the Most High's promise to him, peace and blessings be upon him. [End of quotation]

And you know that the question about the cause, unless what is meant by it is the denial of the one causing it, does not allow for this teaching. Some said: what appears to the mind is that the meaning is, "What hastened you to be alone away from your people?" The denial is directed at being alone away from them, so it is focused on the qualifier, as is known in similar cases. The denial of haste is only because it is a means to that. So Musa, peace be upon him, excused himself regarding it, saying: "I erred in ijtihad, and I reckoned that the small amount of advance does not undermine being together, is not counted as being alone, and does not impair keeping company. What moved me to it was seeking the continuance of Your approval by hastening to comply with Your command." So the answer is His words ﴿They are right behind me﴾, and His words ﴿and I hastened to You, my Lord, that You might be pleased﴾ serve as a completion of it. [End of quotation]. In my view, this is not without merit. It was also said: the question about the cause and the answer is only His words ﴿and I hastened﴾ and so on, and what precedes it is a preface to it. There is room for scrutiny in this. On this view, what precedes it was not Musa's answer to two matters, so that the question of sequence arises, to be answered by what has passed or by what al-Zamakhshari mentioned: that he, peace be upon him, was perplexed because of the awe that came upon him at God's rebuke, Mighty and Majestic, and this distracted him from the fitting answer that is ordered according to the bounds of speech. But Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: in this answer there is a breach of etiquette toward the prophets, peace be upon them. This is al-Zamakhshari's habit toward them, may God's blessings and peace be upon them. The meaning of (إلَيْكَ, "to You") is "to the place of Your promise," so it does not serve as evidence for the Mujassima (anthropomorphists) in establishing a place for Him, Mighty and Majestic.

His calling upon the Most High by the title of Lordship (Rububiyya) is for greater humility and supplication, out of desire that the excuse be accepted. (أُولاءِ, "these") is a demonstrative noun, as is well known, in the nominative case as the predicate (هُمْ, "they" being the subject). ﴿عَلى أثَرِي﴾ ("behind me") is a predicate after a predicate, or a circumstantial clause, as Abu Hayyan said. Al-Tabarsi permitted that (أُولاءِ) be an apposition to (هُمْ), and ﴿عَلى أثَرِي﴾ is the predicate. Abu al-Baqa said: (أُولاءِ) is a relative pronoun, and ﴿عَلى أثَرِي﴾ is its relative clause, and this is a Kufan view.

Al-Hasan and Ibn Mu'adh, from his father, read (أُولايِ) with a kasra on the ya'. Ibn Wathhab and Isa in one narration read (أُولى) with the alif maqsura. A group read (أُولايَ) with a fatha on the ya'. Isa, Ya'qub, and Abd al-Warith, from Abu 'Amr, and Zayd ibn Ali, may God be pleased with them both, read (عَلى إثْرِي) with a kasra on the hamza and sukun on the tha'. Al-Kisa'i reported (أُثْرِي) with a damma on the hamza and sukun on the tha', and it is narrated from Isa. In al-Kashshaf it is said that (al-athar) with two fathas is more eloquent than (al-ithr) with a kasra then sukun. As for (al-uthr), it is attested for the watered pattern of a sword's blade, recorded in the lexicons; it is said: uthr al-sayf and athruhu, and it has the same meaning as al-athar, but it is rare.

**Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah Ta-Ha, verse 85:**

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that answers an implied question), arising from the report of his (peace be upon him) excuse. This is the reason it comes in the third-person form. It is not a shift (*iltifat*) from the first person to the third, because the implied speech in what came before was in the first person. It is as if the listeners asked: "What did his Lord, exalted is He, say to him at that time?" So it is said: He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We have tried your people﴾, meaning We tested them by what the Samiri did, or We put them into *fitnah*, that is, inclination toward desires and falling into discord, ﴿after you﴾, after your departure from them and your leaving them, ﴿and the Samiri has led them astray﴾, when he brought out for them a calf, a body with a lowing sound, and invited them to worship it.

It is also said that he (the Samiri) said to them, after Musa (peace be upon him) had been absent from them for twenty nights: "Indeed the forty has been completed," so he made the twenty, with their days, forty nights. "There is no sign or trace of Musa, and his failure to keep his appointment with you is only because of the ornaments of the people that are with you, and they are unlawful for you." So they gathered them, and what happened with the calf happened.

The word "your people" here refers to those whom he left behind with Harun (peace be upon him). They were, it is said, six hundred thousand, and of them only twelve thousand were spared from worshipping the calf. Therefore the meaning here is other than the meaning of "your people" mentioned earlier. For this reason, a pronoun was not used for them. It is also said that the word "people" in both places refers to those left behind, because their being meant here is definite, and the repeated definite noun is the same as the first.

The meaning of ﴿they are those following my trail﴾ is: they are near me, awaiting me.

Al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) criticized this, saying that it does not fit the word *athar* (trace), nor does it match the preparation of the excuse for haste. And from where does the proponent of this interpretation get the transmission that they were near Mount Sinai? The discussion of the repeated definite noun applies only when there is no evidence of difference, and here there is evidence of difference. Moreover, we may say: it is the same as the first, because "people" in both places refers to the genus, but what is intended first is the chieftains (*nuqaba'*), and second, those who stayed behind. Similar usage is frequent in the Qur'an. End of quotation.

As for what he mentioned about denying a transmission that indicates nearness, there is room for objection. Later, if God Most High wills, among the reports there will be something which, on its apparent sense, indicates nearness, though we have not found it authenticated or weakened.

The interpretation of ﴿they are those following my trail﴾ as referring to those left behind, in the first place as well, was also transmitted by al-Tabarsi from al-Hasan. It is also transmitted from him that it means: they are upon my religion and my path. The matter is easier with this.

The *fa'* (the particle "then/so") is to give the reason for what the preceding speech implies, as if it were said: Your haste away from your people, your going ahead of them, and your neglect of their affairs for any reason is not proper, for they, because of the newness of their adherence to you and their extreme foolishness and stupidity, are in a position where the plotting of Satan can take effect and he can gain power to lead them astray. For the people whom you left behind with your brother have been tested, and the Samiri has led them astray by your departure from among them. So how can you be secure concerning these whom you have neglected and whose affair you have left unattended?

In *Irshad al-Aql al-Salim* (Abu al-Su'ud): it is for the sequence of the reports, namely the trial mentioned after the report about Musa's haste. But this is not because the report about the haste is a cause that necessitates the report about the trial. Rather, it is because of the relation between them, which justifies the transition from one to the other, in that the basis of the mentioned trial is the haste of the people. "But this is not so."

As for al-Khafaji's statement that it is for sequence without a further cause, I say to you: after what has been mentioned, "Indeed, We have been tested," and so on, there is a clear error. This meaning would only be possible if the *fa'* were attached to the saying, but it is attached to what follows it. The apparent sense of the verse indicates that the trials and the Samiri's leading them astray had already been realized and occurred before they were reported, since the past-tense form is clear in this. Also, the apparent sense, as we have established, is that the report took place at the time of his (peace be upon him) coming to the mountain, with nothing preceding it except reproach and excuse.

[p. 244]

The traditions indicate that the occurrence of what was mentioned was after twenty nights from his (peace be upon him) departure toward the side of the mountain. It is also said: after thirty-six days. In that case, the expression of this in the past tense is due to considering its realization in God's knowledge and will, or because it was near to occurrence and awaited, or because the Samiri had resolved to bring about the trial at the time of Musa's departure and had undertaken to arrange its beginnings and prepare its foundations. So he placed the direct undertaking of the causes in the position of the occurrence itself.

The Samiri, according to most scholars, as al-Zajjaj said, was one of the great men of the Children of Israel, from a tribe known as the Samirah, and they are known until this day in Syria as the Samiriyyin. It is also said that he was the son of Musa's maternal aunt, and it is said: his paternal cousin. It is said: he was a foreign man from Kirman. It is said: he was from the people of Bajirma, a village near Egypt, or a village among the villages of Mosul. It is said: he was a Copt who went out with Musa (peace be upon him) displaying faith, and he was his neighbor.

It is said: he was a worshipper of cows who came to Egypt and entered among the Children of Israel outwardly, while in his heart was the worship of cows. His name is said to be Musa ibn Zafar, and it is said: Munaja. The first is more famous. Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Abbas that his mother, when she feared he would be slaughtered, left him in a cave and closed it over him. Jibril (peace be upon him) would come to him and nourish him with his fingers: in one, milk; in another, honey; and in another, butter. He continued to nourish him until he grew up. To this refers the saying of one who said:

When a man is not created fortunate, the minds of those who raised him are bewildered, and the hopeful one is disappointed.

So Musa, whom Jibril raised, is a disbeliever, and Musa, whom Pharaoh raised, is a messenger.

In summary, according to the majority he was a hypocrite who showed faith and concealed disbelief. Mu'adh read *adallahum* (more misguided) as an elative form (*af'al tafdil*), meaning: the most misguided of them, because he was astray and also one who misguides others.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 86:

﴿So Moses returned to his people﴾ at his expected return, that is, after he had completed the forty nights: the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah and ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah, and had received the Torah. It was not immediately after the report mentioned. The causal sense of what precedes the fa' (the particle of consequence) for what follows is therefore only in relation to the qualifier of the return, which is derived from His words, ﴿angry and grieving﴾, and not in relation to the return itself. Although the return is in fact connected to it, the fact that the return came after the completion of forty days is an established and well-known matter, and the mind does not suppose that it happened at the time of the report mentioned. This is like when you say: "I accompanied the pilgrims and prayed for their safety, and so they returned safe." No one doubts that what is meant is their customary return, not a return caused by the prayer. The causal link of the prayer is through the attribute of safety, not through the return itself. So it is stated in Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, and it is a matter on which two rams do not butt heads.

Al-asaf (the grieving) is the sorrowful, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. His (peace be upon him) grief arose from the fact that what his people had fallen into would entail punishment, and he had no power to prevent it. Others said: it is one of intense anger. Al-Jubba'i said: longing for what had escaped him, perplexed about the affairs of his people, fearing that he could not make up for it. This meaning of asaf is not well known.

(He said) is a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani), as if it were asked: "What did he do to them when he returned to them?" So it was said: He said: ﴿O my people, did your Lord not promise you﴾. The hamza (interrogative particle) is for denying the absence of the promise and affirming its existence in the most emphatic and forceful manner. That is, He promised you ﴿a good promise﴾ which you have no way to deny. What is meant by this is the giving of the Torah, in which there is guidance and light. It was also said: it is what He, glorified be He, promised them of reaching the side of the right side of Mount Sinai, and what would follow of conquests in the land, forgiveness for those who repent and believe, and other things that God Most High promised the people of His obedience.

And from al-Hasan: the good promise is Paradise, which He promised to whoever holds fast to His religion. It was also said: it is that He, exalted be He, would let them hear His speech, mighty is His majesty. The first is perhaps preferable. The accusative of (promise) may be either as a second object (maf'ul thani), in which case it means "the thing promised," or as a verbal noun (masdar), in which case the second object is omitted.

The fa' in His words ﴿Then did the time seem long to you?﴾ is for coordinating with an implied prior clause, and the hamza is for denying and negating the coordinated clause only. It is permitted that the hamza be placed before the conjunction, moved from its delayed position because of its precedence, and that the coordination be upon (did not promise you), since it has the meaning of (has promised you). Many have preferred the first. The alif-lam in (the covenant) is for the known covenant, and what is meant is the time of fulfilment. It was also said: the time of separation, that is, did He promise you that, and then the time of fulfilment, or the time of separation for the arrival, grew long? ﴿Or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you﴾, that is, should be due, ﴿a great wrath﴾ whose measure cannot be estimated, arising ﴿from your Lord﴾, that is, from the Master of your affairs absolutely. What is meant by wishing that is doing what would necessitate it.

The fa' in His words ﴿So you broke your promise to me﴾ is for ordering what follows upon each of the two alternatives. The noun (mawid, promise) is a verbal noun (masdar) added to its object, in order to intensify the censure of their condition, for their breaking of the promise made between them and him (peace be upon him) is more shameful when it is ascribed to him (peace be upon him) than when it is ascribed to them. The meaning is: Did the time grow long for you, so that you forgot because of that, and broke your promise to me to remain steadfast in my religion until I returned from the appointed time, through forgetfulness? Or did you deliberately do what would be the cause of your Lord's wrath descending upon you, so that you broke your promise to me by that deliberately? Its sum is: you forgot, so you broke it, or you deliberately did it, so you broke it. From this the contrast between the two alternatives is known.

Al-Mufaddal permitted that (mawid) be a verbal noun added to the agent, and its (breaking) meaning finding a breach in it. It is said: he found the promise of Zayd broken, meaning he found a breach in it. Its parallel is: I praised Zayd, meaning I found him praiseworthy. So the meaning is: you found a breach in my promise to you after the forty. But this is not supported by the context or the preceding context at all. It was also said: the verbal noun is added to its object, except that what is meant by it is that he (peace be upon him) promised them to join him and to come to the mountain following his trail. In this there is what there is.

The Mu'tazilah used this verse as evidence that God, mighty and majestic is He, is not the creator of disbelief, for otherwise He would not have said, glorified be He, ﴿and al-Samiri led them astray﴾, and there would have been no reason for Moses' (peace be upon him) anger and grief. The problem with this is not hidden.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 87:**

﴿They said: "We did not break our promise to you﴾. That is: we promised you steadfastness in your religion and preference for it over [anything else]. "Our promise" is the verbal noun (masdar) annexed to its agent (idafat al-masdar ila fa'ilihi), as was mentioned just before.

﴿by our own authority (bi-mulkina)﴾, meaning: by our having control over our affair. They mean: had we been left to ourselves, and had al-Samiri not embellished for us what he embellished, and had certain circumstances not assisted him, we would not have broken it. Some of the Seven Readers [of the Qur'an] read *bi-milkina* with a kasra on the *mim*. Al-Akhawan (Hamzah and al-Kisa'i), al-Hasan, al-A'mash, Talhah, Ibn Abi Layla and Qa'nab read it with a damma on the *mim*. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, read *bi-malakina* with a fatha on both the *mim* and the *lam*. Abu Hayyan said in *al-Bahr* (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*): that is, "by our authority." He suggested that *al-mulk* with a damma, a fatha, or a kasra all have the same meaning.

Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) differentiated between them, saying: the meaning of the form with a damma is that we had no power by which we could break your promise; rather, we broke it through an opinion that led us to what al-Samiri did. The statement is in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿They do not ask people importunately﴾ [2:273], and the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

*No fall is complained of from it, though the deserts have made it dance until its back is bent.*

The form with a fatha on the *mim* is the verbal noun of *malaka*, and the meaning is: we did not do that by having mastered the right course and been granted success in it; rather, our own selves overcame us. The form with a kasra on the *mim* is commonly used for what a hand possesses, but it is also used for matters that a person settles and determines. Its meaning is like the meaning of the form with a fatha on the *mim*. In both of these readings the verbal noun is annexed to its agent or its object, with the object implied; that is, "by our control of the right course."

﴿But we were loaded with burdens of the ornaments of the people﴾. This is a corrective addition (*istidrak*) to what came before, and an excuse for what they did, by stating the source of the error. "The people" means the Copts. *Awzar* means loads, and it is also used for sins. By this they meant the jewelry they had borrowed from the Copts for the festive display of adornment on a day of their festival shortly before they left Egypt, as we have previously mentioned.

It has been said that they borrowed it under the pretext of a wedding. It has also been said that it was what the sea cast upon the shore from what had been on those who drowned. Perhaps they used the word *awzar* (burdens) to mean sins, because jewelry is generally a cause of sin, since it is usually worn for pride, vanity, and looking down on the poor. It has also been said that they sinned because of it, and worshipped the calf that was cast from it. It has also been said that after the death of its owners that jewelry came to have the status of spoils of war, and such spoils were not lawful for them; rather, the apparent meaning of the authentic hadiths is that spoils, whether movable property or not, were not lawful for anyone before our Prophet (ﷺ). The narration mentioned earlier about how the misguidance occurred agrees with this explanation, except that it raises a difficulty: it is narrated that Musa (peace be upon him) himself commanded them to borrow. It has even been said that the subject of *hummilna* ("we were loaded") is Musa (peace be upon him), since he obligated them to it by commanding them to borrow. He left the jewelry in their hands after the death of its owners and approved their use of it. If it was not lawful, how would he approve it? The same objection applies to the view that the meaning is what the sea cast upon the shore. As for the possibility that Musa (peace be upon him) had forbidden this and they assumed they were complying, without him realising they had not complied because the situation was concealed from him (peace be upon him), this is hardly worth considering at all, especially according to the narration that they were also commanded to borrow animals from the people, which they did, and they set out with them.

It may be said that all the property of the Copts, after their destruction, was lawful for the Israelites, as the apparent meaning of His saying, Exalted is He, suggests: ﴿How many gardens and springs they left behind﴾, ﴿and crops and a noble station﴾, ﴿Thus, and We gave them as an inheritance to the Children of Israel﴾ [26:57–59]. He, glory be to Him, also attributed the jewelry to them in His saying: ﴿And the people of Musa, after him, made from their ornaments a calf, a body that lowed﴾ [7:148]. Its apparent meaning indicates that the jewelry was their property. And the exemption from lawfulness is claimed for what cannot be returned because its owner has perished and whoever stands in his place is absent. This does not contradict his (ﷺ) saying: "Spoils have been made lawful for me, and they were not made lawful for anyone before me," because it is possible that the meaning is: spoils have been made lawful for me in whatever form they come, and they were not made lawful in that way for anyone before me. Their calling it *awzar* may then be due either to the two previously mentioned aspects, or to their belief that it was forbidden, out of their own ignorance, or because al-Samiri cast doubt upon them.

It has also been said that Allah, Exalted is He, commanded Musa (peace be upon him) to order them to borrow, so he ordered them, and what they had borrowed remained in their hands after the death of its owners, by the ruling of that command, awaiting whatever Allah, Exalted is He, would command afterwards. Some reports indicate that Allah, glory be to Him, made His ruling clear through Harun (peace be upon him) after Musa (peace be upon him) left for the appointed meeting, as we will mention shortly, if Allah, Exalted is He, wills. So reflect on this, and may Allah, Exalted is He, guide you.

The prepositional phrase *min zinat al-qawm* ("of the ornaments of the people") may be connected to *hummilna* ("we were loaded"), or it may be connected to an omitted element that functions as an adjective of *awzaran* ("burdens"). This is not necessarily fixed, based on the statement of the grammarians that clauses and adverbial phrases after indefinite nouns are adjectives, and after definite nouns are circumstantial clauses, because this is not an absolute rule.

Al-Akhawan (Hamzah and al-Kisa'i), Abu 'Amr, and Ibn Muhaysin read *hamalna* with a fatha on the *ha'* and the *mim*. Abu Raja' read *hummilna* with a damma on the *ha'* and a kasra on the *mim*, without a shaddah.

﴿So We threw it﴾ (*faqadhafnaha*), that is, we cast it into the fire, as the reports indicate. It has also been said that the meaning is: we threw it upon ourselves and our children, but this is not at all correct.

﴿Thus﴾ (*fa-kadhalika*), that is, in the same way, ﴿al-Samiri cast﴾, that is, what he had with him of [the jewelry]. It has been said that it seems he showed them that he too would cast what he had with him of the jewelry, and so they said what they said, according to their own assumption. What he actually cast was the dust that he had taken from the footprint of the Messenger (the angel Jibril), as will come, if Allah, Exalted is He, wills. It has also been said that he cast what he had of the jewelry and also cast with it what he had taken from the footprint of the Messenger, as though they only intended that he cast what he had of the jewelry. It has been said that they meant that he cast the dust. One of the scholars supported this by the change in expression, since he did not use the word *qadhf* (casting), which ordinarily implies that what was thrown was a mass of solid matter. There is room for debate on this. It may also be said that the meaning is: in the same way as what We have described to you, al-Samiri cast [the matter] to us and made it binding upon us. This is far-fetched. Although it is mentioned that he told them: "Musa's delay from you is only because of the jewelry of the people that you have with you, and it is forbidden for you. So the opinion is that we dig a pit, kindle a fire in it, and cast into it what we have of it." So they did this, and he had made a mould of a calf in the pit.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that when Musa (peace be upon him) departed to his Lord, glory be to Him, Harun (peace be upon him) said to them: "You have been loaded with burdens of the ornaments of the people, on the way to Pharaoh, and goods and jewelry. So purify yourselves from them, for they are an abomination." He kindled a fire for them and said: "Cast whatever you have of that into it." So they began to bring what they had and cast it into it. Then al-Samiri came, with dust from the hoof-print of Jibril's horse, and approached the fire. He said to Harun (peace be upon him): "O Prophet of Allah, shall I cast what is in my hand?" He said: "Yes." Harun (peace be upon him) did not suspect anything except that it was like some of the other jewelry and goods that others had brought. So he cast it into it, and [al-Samiri] said: "Be a calf, a body with a lowing sound." So it became a trial and a test.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him that the Children of Israel borrowed jewelry from the Copts and went out with it. Harun said to them, after Musa (peace be upon him) had gone: "Gather this jewelry until Musa comes, and he will decide about it as he decides." So it was gathered, then it was melted, and al-Samiri threw a handful upon it.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 88:**

﴿Then he brought out for them﴾, that is, al-Samiri brought out for the speakers mentioned, ﴿a calf﴾, from those ornaments that they had thrown. Its placement after the prepositional phrase, although it is an explicit object, is for the reason already mentioned more than once: giving attention to what comes first and creating anticipation for what comes later, together with the fact that it is a lengthy element whose fronting would disrupt the harmony of the noble arrangement of the text. For his saying ﴿a body﴾, meaning a corporeal form with flesh and blood, or a body of gold without a spirit, is a substitute (badal) for it. It has also been said that it is an attribute (na't) of it, meaning that it was reddish like a body. Likewise, his exalted saying ﴿having a lowing﴾ is an attribute of it, and al-khuwar is the sound of the calf.

This sound is either because he breathed the spirit into it, based on what Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ka'b ibn Malik, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When God, exalted is He, promised Musa (peace be upon him) that He would speak to him, he set out at the appointed time. While he was conversing with his Lord, he heard a sound behind him and said: 'My God, I hear a sound behind me.' He said: 'Perhaps your people have gone astray.' He said: 'My God, who has led them astray?' He said: 'al-Samiri has led them astray.' He said: 'How did he lead them astray?' He said: 'He fashioned for them a calf, a body having a lowing.' He said: 'My God, this al-Samiri fashioned for them the calf; so who breathed the spirit into it until it had a lowing?' He said: 'I did, O Musa.' He said: 'By Your might, no one has led my people astray except You.' He said: 'You have spoken truly, O Wisest of the wise. It is not fitting for a wise one to be wiser than You.'"

And in another narration, from Rashid ibn Sa'd, it came that He, glorified is He, said to him: "O Musa, your people have been tested after you." He said: "My Lord, how could they be tested when You delivered them from Pharaoh, delivered them from the sea, bestowed favours upon them, and did such things for them?" He said: "O Musa, they have taken after you a calf that has a lowing." He said: "My Lord, then who put the spirit into it?" He said: "I did." He said: "Then, my Lord, You led them astray." He said: "O Musa, O head of the prophets and father of the wise, I saw that in their hearts, so I facilitated it for them."

Or it is because the wind enters it and it makes a sound, based on what Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "It seems that the Children of Israel felt guilty about the jewellery of the family of Pharaoh that was with them, so they brought it out so that fire would descend and consume it. When they gathered it, al-Samiri threw the handful and said: 'Become a calf, a body having a lowing.' So it became as such, and the wind would enter from its rear and exit from its mouth, so a sound was heard from it."

﴿So they said﴾, that is, al-Samiri and those who were tempted by him at first sight of it. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to al-Samiri alone, and the plural pronoun was used to magnify his crime, but this is far-fetched.

﴿This is your god and the god of Musa, but he forgot﴾, that is, Musa forgot Him, and went to seek Him at Mount Sinai. So the pronoun in nasiya (he forgot) refers to Musa (peace be upon him), as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah. The fa' here is fasihah (the fa' that signals an implied conditional clause), meaning: "So worship it and keep to its worship, for Musa (peace be upon him) has forgotten." It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Makhul, that the pronoun refers to al-Samiri, and forgetting is a metaphor for abandoning. The fa' here is also fasihah, meaning: "So al-Samiri displayed hypocrisy and abandoned what he had been concealing of the secrets of disbelief." On this reading the report of this is from Him, exalted is He, and it is not within the scope of the speech of the speakers, unlike the first interpretation.

The approach of some of the verifying scholars indicates a preference for the first view. Nor is it hidden what is in the use of the demonstrative (hadha, "this"), with the referent being in plain sight of them, and its repetition; in the singling out of Musa (peace be upon him) for mention; and in the use of the fa' (indicating immediacy and consequence), which is a matter of exaggeration in the error. The report of the bringing out and what follows it is a narration of the outcome of al-Samiri's trial, in deed and in word, from Him, glorified is He, intentionally aiming to increase its establishment and then to reject it, not from the side of the speakers; otherwise it would have been said "He brought out for us." The interpretation that their shift to the third-person pronoun is to clarify that the bringing out and the stated speech belong to all of them, and not to the worshippers alone, is contrary to the apparent meaning, and moreover it undermines their excuse. For the dissent of some of them from al-Samiri, and their not being tempted by his deception, while the bringing out and the address were directed at them, makes their opposition to him easier to excuse. Thus their being tempted afterward is a greater offence and more shameful.

As for what has been said, that the excusers are those who did not worship the calf, and that the attribution of the misguidance to themselves while they are innocent of it is of the same kind as their saying "the sons of so-and-so killed so-and-so," even though the killer was one of them, [and that] they said: "We did not find any fault among ourselves in a matter we controlled; rather, doubt took hold in the hearts of the worshippers when al-Samiri did to them what he did, brought out for them what he brought out, and said what he said, so we were unable to turn them away from that, and we did not separate from them for fear of increasing the trial"; then Shaykh al-Islam said: "The context and the sequence of the noble text require its invalidity." Abu Muslim held that the speech of the excusers ends at their saying ﴿so we threw it﴾, and what follows it, from His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Thus did al-Samiri cast﴾ to its end, is a report from Him, glorified is He, that al-Samiri did as they did, ﴿so he brought out for them﴾, and so on; and this is contrary to the apparent meaning.

Furthermore, al-A'mash read ﴿fanasy﴾ with the letter ya' vowelless (sukun).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 89:

The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿Do they not see﴾ and so on to the end, are a rebuke and a censure from Him, exalted is He, directed at both the misguided and those who misguide them, together, and a mockery of them for what they undertook of the evil whose falsehood and impossibility are not unclear to anyone, namely taking that calf as a god. By my life, had they not been as dull as cattle, they would not have worshipped it. The fa' (ف) here is for conjunction (ʿatf) upon an implied clause that the context requires, meaning: "Do they not reflect, and so not know?" ﴿Does it not return to them a word﴾, meaning that it does not return to them speech, nor does it answer them with a reply, but rather it lows like the other calves. So how can one who is in this state be imagined to be a god?

Imam al-Shafi'i, Abu Haywa, Aban, Ibn Subayh and al-Za'farani read (يَرْجِعَ) with a fatha (accusative), taking an (أنْ) to be the governing particle (al-nasiba), not the lightened form of the heavy (al-mukhaffafa min al-thaqila). In that case the seeing (ru'ya) means sight (ibsar), not knowledge ('ilm), based on what al-Radi and a group [of grammarians] mentioned, that the governing (nasiba) particle does not occur after verbs of the heart that indicate certainty or strong supposition, because since it denotes the future, it enters upon what is not established and fixed, so its occurrence after something that indicates certainty or the like is not appropriate. The conjunction also, as previously stated, means: "Do they not look and so not perceive the non-return of it to them with any speech?" The linking of seeing to what has been mentioned, though it is a negative matter, is to draw attention to its complete manifestness, which calls for greater condemnation of them and disparaging of their intellects. It has also been said that the governing particle does not occur after the sight-verb (ra'y al-basriyya) either, because it conveys knowledge through the mediation of the sense of sight, as in Idah al-Mufassal. Al-Farra' and Ibn al-Anbari permitted its occurrence after verbs of knowledge, let alone verbs of sight.

The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿and it does not control for them any harm or benefit﴾, are a conjunction upon (لا يَرْجِعُ) (does not return), included together with it within the scope of seeing, meaning: "So do they not see that it has no power to repel harm from them or to bring them benefit, or that it has no power to harm them if they do not worship it or to benefit them if they worship it?"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 90:

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And Harun had already said to them before﴾, together with what follows, is a oath-clause (jumlah qasamiyyah) emphasizing what preceded of rebuke and censure, by showing their obstinacy and their defiance toward the Messenger, following the demonstration of their stubborn denial of the matter that reason dictates. That is: "By Allah, Harun had indeed advised them and alerted them to the reality of the matter before Musa, peace be upon him, returned to them and addressed them with what has been mentioned of statements." To the view that the genitive complement (al-mudaf ilayh) is taken as preceding what was mentioned, al-Wahidi went. And it has been said: "before the saying of the Samiri, 'This is your god and the god of Musa'." It is as if he, peace be upon him, when he first saw them as he emerged from the pit (al-hufayrah), perceived in them the affliction (al-iftitan), so he hastened to warn them. Sahib al-Kashf chose this, following his shaykh, and said: it is more eloquent and more indicative of their reproach by their turning away from the evidence of reason and revelation in "Do they not see?" And "indeed had said" — some of them chose the first view and claimed that the answer supports it, and the discussion of that will come, God willing, exalted is He.

Al-Allamah al-Tibi allowed two possibilities in this clause: that it is coordinated with His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Do they not see﴾, and he said: the choice of the present tense in it indicates the evoking of that dreadful situation in the mind of the listener and the summoning of denunciation against them; and that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of (yarawna), establishing the aspect of the denunciation — that is: "Do they not see, while Harun had alerted them before that to the reality of the matter, and said to them: ﴿O my people, you are only being tested by it﴾," that is, you have caused them to fall into temptation by the calf, or you have led them astray — according to directing the restriction derived from the word ﴿innama﴾ (only), in most of its usages, to the act itself in relation to its opposite which they claim, not to its stated condition in relation to another condition, meaning: "He only did to you the temptation, not guidance to the truth," not meaning "you were only tested by the calf and not by anything else." And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And indeed your Lord is the Most Merciful﴾, with the hamzah of (inna) kasra'd, coordinated with (innama), etc., is guidance for them to the truth after rebuking them against falsehood, and the mention of the title of lordship and mercy is for the sake of attracting them to the truth. In this is a reminder of their deliverance from Pharaoh at a time when the calf did not exist. Likewise, according to what has been said, it is an alert that they should repent before them. The definiteness of the two terms serves to express restriction, that is: "And indeed your Lord, the one deserving worship, is the Most Merciful, and no other."

Al-Hasan, Isa, and Abu Amr in one narration read ﴿wa-anna rabbakum﴾ with a fatha on the hamzah, and it was explained as: the verbal noun formed from it is the predicate of an omitted subject, that is, "and the matter is that your Lord is the Most Merciful," and the clause is coordinated with what has passed. Abu Hatim said: the estimate is "and because your Lord, etc.," and he made the prepositional phrase dependent on "follow me." A group read ﴿annama﴾ and ﴿wa-anna rabbakum﴾ with fatha on both hamzahs, and it was explained according to the dialect of Sulaym, where they pronounce the hamzah of inna with fatha after a saying in all cases.

The fa' in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So follow me and obey my command﴾, is for the consequence of what follows upon what precedes, from the content of the two clauses; that is: "If the matter is so, then follow me and obey my command in steadfastness upon the religion."

Ibn Atiyyah said: that is, "follow me to the Mount to which Allah has promised you." In this is that he, peace be upon him, was not about to go to the Mount, nor was he commanded to it, and Allah the Glorified did not promise those deluded ones that they would go to it by themselves. And it has been said — not without some goodness — that it means: "follow me in steadfastness upon the truth, and obey my command in this, and turn away from engaging in worship of what you have known its affair, or restrain yourselves from believing in its divinity and worshipping it."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 91:

﴿They said﴾ in reply to Harun, peace be upon him: ﴿We will not cease to be devoted to it﴾, meaning, we will continue to worship the calf (ʿākifīn) remaining [in that state] ﴿until Musa returns to us﴾. The apparent sense of their situation is that they did not take into account his return, peace be upon him, or what he would say about it. It is said that the words of the Samiri, ﴿This is your god and the god of Musa, but he has forgotten﴾, had taken hold in their minds, so they qualified their devotion with his return, by way of pretext and procrastination, and they harboured the intention that, if he returned, peace be upon him, he would agree with them in their worship, and far be it from him. This is based on the view that the exchange between them and Harun, peace be upon him, took place after the aforementioned words of the Samiri, so that (min qabl, "from before") means "before the return of Musa." It is also mentioned that this reply is supported by this meaning, because their saying ﴿We will not cease﴾ etc. indicates their devotion at the time he, peace be upon him, was speaking, while they had not devoted themselves to his worship before the Samiri's words; they devoted themselves only after them.

Al-Tibi said: their reply here belongs to the foolish style, the opposite of the wise style, because they said it out of little regard for the manifest proofs, as Nimrod said in reply to the Friend (Khalil, Abraham), peace be upon him: ﴿I give life and cause death﴾. So reflect. Abu Hayyan used this qualification (ghayya) as evidence that "lan" does not indicate perpetuity (ta'bid), because the qualification occurs only where the matter is open to possibility, so the possibility is removed by it.

You know that whoever holds that it indicates this does not claim that it indicates it in all contexts, and this is evident. In some reports it is said that when they said that, Harun, peace be upon him, withdrew from them with twelve thousand, who were those who had not worshipped the calf. When Musa, peace be upon him, returned and heard the clamour, and they used to prostrate whenever the calf lowed, not raising their heads until it lowed again (and in another report, they used to dance at its lowing), he said to the seventy who were with him: "This is the sound of trial (fitna)." When he arrived, he said to his people what he said, and he heard from them what they said.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verses 92–93:

And His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive clause (istinaf) arising from the report of their earlier answer, namely His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿We did not break our promise to you﴾, and so on. It is as if it were said: What did Musa say to Harun, peace be upon them both, when he heard their answer? And did he accept their silence after what he had witnessed from them?

It is said: He said to him, while he was angry, having seized him by his beard and head: ﴿O Harun, what prevented you, when you saw them going astray,﴾ by worshipping the calf, and they did not heed the proof of its falsehood, ﴿from following me?﴾ That is, from following me, on the condition that you do not draw the sword and do not hold forth in argument. This is like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ (7:12, 38:75). The phrase ﴿from following me﴾ is the second object of "prevented" (mana'a), and "when" (idh) is connected to "prevented." It is also said that it is connected to "following me." This is rejected on the ground that what follows "an" (anna) does not govern what precedes it. It is answered that adverbs of time may be given a wider scope than other elements, and that the preceding verb, when taken as having a second object, would be a case of the object being placed before its verb, which is, as you see, unlikely. The meaning is: What prevented you, when you saw their error, from following me and going along with my course in anger for the sake of God, Exalted is He, and in fighting those who disbelieved in Him? This is narrated from Muqatil. It is also said that it refers to reform and guidance, but the apparent sense of the reproach does not support this. Abu Hayyan preferred that the meaning be: What prevented you from joining me at Mount Sinai together with those of the Children of Israel who believed? This is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

Musa, peace be upon him, saw that his separation from them, and his leaving them after those verbal admonitions, would be a stronger rebuke to them than limiting himself to admonition, because it indicates greater anger and is more forceful in denunciation. This is especially so since he, peace be upon him, was their leader and beloved to them, and Musa knew this. The departure of a beloved leader, out of displeasure at a matter that deeply burdens souls and calls for abandoning the disliked matter that required his departure, is evident and beyond dispute to whoever is fair.

As for the view that Harun's admonitions, since they did not restrain them from what they were doing, his separation from them would be even less likely to restrain them, that view does not refute what we have mentioned. There is also no need to offer the excuse that, when they knew he would join Musa and inform him, peace be upon them both, of the story, they would fear Musa's return and would desist from that, so that it might be said that he was far from being accepted. How could that be, when they had declared that they would remain devoted to the calf until Musa returned, peace be upon him?

Ali ibn Isa said: "la" (not) is not superfluous here, and the meaning is: What moved you not to follow me? For prevention from a thing necessarily entails being moved toward its opposite. ﴿Have you then disobeyed my order?﴾ by governing them as is appropriate. For his, peace be upon him, saying ﴿Take my place among my people﴾, without adding his words ﴿and act rightly, and do not follow the way of the corrupters﴾ (7:142), already implies a definite command to do so. Succession is not realized except by the successor doing what the one who is succeeded would have done had he been present. Musa, peace be upon him, had he been present, would have governed them in the most effective manner. The "fa" (then) here is for conjunction with an implied element required by the context, that is: Did you not follow me, or did you oppose me, and so disobey my order?

[Page 251]

[Page 251]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 94:

﴿He said: "O son of my mother!"﴾ He specified "mother" with the possessive to win his sympathy and soften his heart, not because of what has been said, that he was his brother from his mother, for the majority hold that the two were full brothers (shaqiqan).

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (ya ibna umm) with a kasra on the mim: ﴿Do not seize me by my beard nor by my head﴾, i.e., by the hair of my head, for seizing is more fitting for it. Some claimed that his saying "beard" (lihyati) also means by the hair of my beard, since the original meaning of "lihyah" is the part of the body on which hair grows, and seizing is not very fitting for it. You know that the well-known usage of "lihyah" is for the hair growing on that specific part of the body. The apparent meaning of the verses and reports is that he (peace be upon him) did seize them thus. It is related that he seized the hair of his head with his right hand and his beard with his left. He (peace be upon him) was firm, unyielding, and fierce for the sake of God the Exalted. He had witnessed what he had witnessed and it prevailed upon his assumption that Harun (peace be upon him) had been negligent, deserving discipline for it, though this did not take him outside the circle of infallibility established for the prophets (peace be upon them). So he disciplined him as he did and personally undertook it, and there is no prohibition in it at all, nor any opposition to the Law. Therefore, what the Imam imagined is not refuted, when he said: The anger either removes his intellect first, and the first is not held by any Muslim, or the second does not remove the question, due to the implication of the absence of infallibility. He answered with what has no substance.

Isa ibn Sulayman al-Hijazi read (bilihyati) with a fatha on the lam, and it is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. (InnI khashitu) etc. is a resumptive clause giving the reason for the implied prohibition, establishing that he was not disobeying his command nor falling short in the interest. That is: I feared that if I fought some of them against others, and they destroyed one another and dispersed, or I feared that if I followed you with those who believed, ﴿you would say, "You have caused a division among the Children of Israel"﴾ by your own opinion, even though they are sons of one man, as the mention of them by this designation rather than "the people" or the like indicates. That fighting entails division is evident, and likewise following Musa (peace be upon him) together with those who believed, which may lead to fighting. It has been said: by division, on the first interpretation, he (peace be upon him) meant what fighting entails of a division after which reunion is not hoped for.

(Lam tarqub) i.e., and you did not observe (qawli), and the clause is coordinated with (farraqta), meaning: I feared that you would say the whole of the two clauses,
Page 252
and attribute to me the division of the Children of Israel and the failure to observe your word to me and your charge to me. It is permissible that the clause be in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (farraqta), meaning: I feared that you would say, "You have caused division among them, not observing my word," i.e., I feared that you would say the whole of this statement. By the saying of Musa referred to with the pronoun of the first person is his (peace be upon him) saying: ﴿Take my place among my people and set things right﴾ etc. The summary of his (peace be upon him) excuse: I saw that setting things right lies in preserving the common folk, dealing gently with them, and restraining them in a manner by which the order of their cohesion and unity is not disturbed, and which does not become a cause for your blaming me, so that you return to them and become the one who takes charge of the matter as you see fit, especially since the people had made me weak and came close to killing me, as he (peace be upon him) made clear in another verse.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Jurayj what indicates that the intended saying in the attributed phrase is the saying of Harun (peace be upon him), and the clause (lam tarqub) is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (taqula), meaning: I feared that you would say that without awaiting my word. Clarify the reality of the situation, so reflect.

Abu Ja'far read (wa lam tarqub) with a damma on the ta and a kasra on the qaf, the imperfect of arqaba. (Qala) is a resumptive clause that came as an answer to what arose from relating the earlier excuses of the people, attributing the corruption to the Samiri, and the excuse of Harun (peace be upon him). It is as if it were said: What did Musa (peace be upon him) do after hearing what was related of the two excuses and the root of the trial being established upon the Samiri? So it was said: He said, rebuking him, "Since the matter is this..."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 95:

﴿What is your matter, O Samiri?﴾ That is: what is your affair, and what is this great matter that has issued from you, and it is a question about the cause that prompted that. The interpretation of khatb (matter, affair) as this is the well-known one, and in al-Sihah (al-Sihah fi al-lugha, the lexicon of al-Jawhari) it says: "al-khatb is the cause of a matter."

Some of the trustworthy scholars said: it is originally the verbal noun of khataba al-amr (he sought the matter), so when one says to someone who is doing something: "ma khatbuka?" its meaning is "what is your seeking of it?" It became common for "affair" and "great matter," because it is sought after and desired. In the verse, the interpretation according to the original meaning was chosen so that the speech would be more eloquent upon it, since (Musa, peace be upon him) did not ask him about what had issued from him, nor about its cause, but about the cause of his seeking it. Al-Raghib made the original of this common usage, khatb, to mean takhatub (mutual address), i.e., mutual discussion in speech, and it was applied to it because a great matter involves much mutual address. In al-Asas (Asas al-balagha of al-Zamakhshari), khatb in the sense of seeking (talab) was made a metaphor, and he said: "Among the metaphors: so-and-so yakhtubu (seeks) the doing of such-and-such, i.e., seeks it. And ma khatbuka means: what is the affair that you seek?" Ibn 'Atiyya distinguished between khatb and sha'n (affair) by saying that khatb implies rebuke (intihar) and is used for disagreeable things and not for sha'n. Then he said: "It is as if it were said: what is your misfortune, what is your ill omen, and what is this khatb that has come from you?" End.

But this is not consistent, for Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said to the angels, peace be upon them: ﴿What is your matter, O messengers?﴾ and what was mentioned cannot apply there.

Some who derived its root from khitab (address) claimed that the meaning is: what moved you to address the Children of Israel with what you addressed them and to do with them what you did. This is not correct. Moses' (peace be upon him) address to him with this was so that he would make clear to the people the falsity of his scheme by his own admission, and would do to him and to what he brought forth something that would serve as a deterrent to those who are led into temptation and to those who come after them of the nations.

[Page 253]

﴿He said﴾, that is, al-Samiri, replying to him (peace be upon him): ﴿I perceived what they did not perceive﴾, with a *ḍammah* on the *ṣād* in both verbs (*baṣurtu* and *yabṣurū*), meaning: I knew what the people did not know, and I grasped what they did not grasp. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said *baṣura bi-l-shay'* when one knows it, and *abṣara* when one looks at it. It has also been said that *baṣara* and *abṣara* have the same meaning. Al-Raghib said: *al-baṣar* is applied to the seeing organ and to the power within it, and it is also applied to the power of the heart that perceives, which is called *baṣīra* or *baṣar*.
