From the first meaning one says *abṣartu*, and from the second one says *abṣartuhu* and *baṣurtu bihi*. It is rarely said *baṣurtu* when speaking of the sense of sight unless the heart's perception accompanies it. End of quotation.

[Page 253 continued]

Al-A'mash and Abu al-Sammal read *baṣirtu* with a *kasrah* on the *ṣād*, and *bi-mā lam yabṣarū* with a *fatḥah* on the *ṣād*. Amr ibn Ubayd read *buṣirtu* with a *ḍammah* on the *bā'* and a *kasrah* on the *ṣād*, and *bi-mā lam tubṣarū* with a *ḍammah* on the *tā'* (the second-person prefix) and a *fatḥah* on the *ṣād*, in the passive form.

Al-Kisa'i, Hamza, Abu Bahriyya, al-A'mash, Talha, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Manadhir, Ibn Sa'dan and Qunbul read *bi-mā lam tabṣurū* with a *fatḥah* on the *tā'* (the second-person prefix) and a *ḍammah* on the *ṣād*. The address is to Musa (peace be upon him) and his people. It has also been said that the address is to him alone, and that the plural pronoun is used for honour, as has been said concerning the verse ﴿My Lord, return me﴾. This is reported from the early grammarians, and al-Tha'alibi stated it explicitly in *Sirr al-'Arabiyya*. What al-Radi mentioned, that honorific plurality occurs only in the first-person pronoun with others, as in *fa'alna* ("we did"), is not accepted, although many have followed him. Some claimed that the most suitable interpretation, given what follows, *if Allah wills*, in His saying ﴿And thus my self prompted me﴾, is to take *baṣura* to mean *baṣura bi-ra'y* (he saw through his own opinion), especially on the reading with the second person, because claiming to know what Musa (peace be upon him) did not know would be a great audacity unbefitting his status and rank. By contrast, claiming to have seen what Musa (peace be upon him) did not see is something that may happen by chance.

It was reported by Ibn Jarir, from Ibn Abbas, that Jibril (peace be upon him) appeared on the day the sea was split, mounted on a horse, and al-Samiri recognised him, because when he was a child his mother had been afraid for him and had placed him in a cave, and Jibril had been nourishing him. So he took a handful from beneath the hoof of the horse and cast it into his heart that he would not throw it upon anything saying "Be" and it would not be.

[Page 254]

From Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, it is reported that he saw Jibril (peace be upon him) riding a horse when he came to take Musa (peace be upon both of them) to the appointed meeting, and no one among the people of Musa (peace be upon him) saw him except al-Samiri. So he took a handful of dust from the place where the horse had trodden.

In some reports it is said that he saw that whenever the horse lifted its forelegs or its hind legs upon the dry ground, plants would sprout from it. So he knew that it had a significance, and he took a handful from the place where it had trodden. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿So I grasped a handful from the footprint of the Messenger﴾, that is, from the footprint of the Messenger's horse. Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) also read it so. Thus the phrase involves an omitted *muḍāf* (a noun omitted in an idāfa construction, the word "horse" here), as most exegetes hold. The footprint of the horse is the dust beneath its hoof. It has been said that there is no need to supply an omitted noun, because the footprint of his horse is the footprint of him (peace be upon him) himself.

Perhaps the mention of Jibril (peace be upon him) by the title of "Messenger" is because al-Samiri knew him only by this title, or to indicate that he (Jibril) was aware of the divine secrets which the people were not aware of, confirming what al-Samiri's statement began with, and drawing attention, as has been said, to the time at which he took what he took.

The handful (*qabḍa*), a single act of grasping (*qabḍ*), has been applied to the thing grasped once. With this, one answers those who claim that a verbal noun used in this way does not take the feminine suffix *tā'*. They say: *hādhihi ḥullatu nasīji l-Yaman* ("this is a garment of Yemeni weaving"), and they do not say *nasījatu l-Yaman*. The answer is that what is prohibited is the *tā'* that indicates a unit (singularisation), not the mere feminine marking as here. According to this, the most fitting view is that one should not regard it as indicating a single occurrence, as is not hidden.

Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud), Ubayy, Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Hasan and Humayd read *qabaṣtu qabṣatan* with *ṣād* in both words. They distinguished between *qabḍ* with the dotted *ḍād* and *qabṣ* with the *ṣād*: the first means taking with the whole palm, the second taking with the tips of the fingers. Similar to these is *khaḍm* with *khā'* for eating with the whole mouth, and *qaḍm* with *qāf* for eating with the tips of the teeth. It has been mentioned that this is among the words whose form was changed to suit their meaning: the dotted *ḍād* is heavy and its articulation is prolonged, so it was placed in words denoting the greater amount, while the *ṣād* is narrow in its place of articulation and faint, so it was placed in words denoting the lesser amount.

Al-Hasan, in a variant transmitted from him, Qatada and Nasr ibn Asim read *qubḍa* with a *ḍammah* on the *qāf* and the unpointed *ṣād* (*quṣa*? in the sense): it is a noun for the thing grasped, as *al-muḍgha* is a noun for what is chewed. ﴿So I cast it﴾, that is, I threw it into the melted ornaments. It has also been said that I threw it into the belly of the calf, "and so there came about what came about."

[Page 254 continued]

﴿And thus my self prompted me﴾: that is, it adorned it and made it seem good to me. The demonstrative refers to the verbal action mentioned after it, as in His saying ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾. The sum of his answer is that what he did proceeded from him purely by following the desire of the self that commands to evil, and not from anything else, such as rational or transmitted proof, or divine inspiration.

Furthermore, what has been mentioned as the interpretation of the verse is what is reported from the Companions and the Successors, may Allah be pleased with them, and most of the eminent exegetes followed them. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: there is no explicit statement in the Qur'an for what they mentioned. There is another opinion here, namely that by "the Messenger" is meant Musa (peace be upon him), and "his footprint" means his practice, his way, and the course that he commanded and followed. One may say: "So-and-so follows the footprint of so-and-so, and traces his footprint," when he adheres to his path. The interpretation of the verse on this basis is that when Musa (peace be upon him) turned to al-Samiri with reproach and questioning about the matter which had led him to lead the people astray by the calf, he said: ﴿I perceived what they did not perceive﴾, meaning I knew that what the people held was not the truth. ﴿And I had grasped a handful from your footprint﴾, that is, some of your religion, ﴿so I cast it﴾, that is, I threw it away and did not hold to it. His referring to Musa (peace be upon him) by the third-person form is like the way one who addresses a prince says: "What is the opinion of the prince concerning such-and-such?" The use of "the Messenger" for him (peace be upon him) would be a kind of mockery, since he was an unbeliever who denied him, in line with His saying, related about the unbelievers: ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, you are surely mad﴾. End of quotation. Some have defended this view, saying it is closer to verification.

The opinion of the exegetes that Jibril (peace be upon him) was not known by the name "Messenger," and that no mention of him had preceded, so that the definite article in "the Messenger" would refer to someone previously mentioned, is far-fetched. Also, what they say requires supplying an omitted noun, and such supplying departs from the basic form. Moreover, it is very remote that al-Samiri alone among the people should have seen Jibril (peace be upon him) and recognised him.

Furthermore, how did he know that the trace of his horse's hoof would produce this strange and wondrous effect, turning lifeless matter into flesh and blood? And even if it were so, the trace itself would have been more deserving of life. Moreover, whenever an unbeliever comes upon dust of this nature, one may say: perhaps Musa (peace be upon him) came upon something else resembling this, and for its sake he brought the miracles; so that would be among the supernatural acts that the messengers (peace be upon them) brought. Also, it is remote that he should commit unbelief and lead astray after he had recognised the prophethood of Musa (peace be upon him) by the coming of this noble messenger to him. End of quotation.

It is answered that the use of "Messenger" for Jibril (peace be upon him) is well attested in the Noble Qur'an, for He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Indeed it is the word of a noble messenger﴾. That no mention of him has preceded does not prevent him from being known. It may also be that the use of "Messenger" for him (peace be upon him) was common among the Children of Israel, especially if we accept the soundness of the report that he (peace be upon him) used to nourish those of their children whom he found in the cave at the time when Pharaoh was killing them. Further, supplying an omitted noun in speech is more than can be counted, and this is well attested in the Book of Allah, the Exalted, more than once. Also, his seeing Jibril (peace be upon him) when others did not was a trial from Him, the Exalted, so that Allah might accomplish a matter that was to be done. Also, his knowledge of the effect of that trace, as mentioned, came from what was cast into his heart, that it would not be thrown upon anything with the words "Be" and it would be, as in the report of Ibn Abbas, or from what he witnessed of the sprouting of plants by the treading, as in some reports. It is possible that he heard this from Musa (peace be upon him). As for the claim that the trace itself deserves life more, this is not granted: do you not see that the elixir turns whatever it is cast upon into gold, while it itself is not gold? Also, a miracle is accompanied by the claim of prophethood from Allah and by a challenge, and they have said: whenever someone claims prophethood and displays a supernatural act which is due to a hidden cause unknown to those to whom he is sent, Allah, the Exalted, will inevitably raise up someone who clarifies the reality of that matter by producing a similar act not accompanied by a claim, or something of the kind; or He will make the claimant such that he does not undertake that supernatural act through that cause, by removing its power of effect or something similar, so that people should have no argument against Allah after the messengers, and so that the decisive proof belongs to Him, the Mighty and Majestic. They have permitted the appearance of a supernatural act without any cause, or through a hidden cause, at the hand of one who claims divinity, because his lie is evident by reason and by transmission; and establishing the proof does not depend on refuting him by means like those mentioned above. Also, what is mentioned of al-Samiri's unbelief and misguidance after he had recognised the prophethood of Musa (peace be upon him) is at the extreme of baseness, for He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them﴾. The unbelief of al-Samiri is no more remote than the unbelief of Pharaoh, who saw what he saw.

What Abu Muslim mentioned is refuted, together with its opposition to what is transmitted from the best generations, which is something that cannot be said on the basis of opinion alone, so it has the status of what is traced to the Prophet (peace be upon him). Also, the expression about Musa (peace be upon him) using the third-person form is remote, and the sense "and I had grasped a handful" etc. from the noble wording is even more remote. And casting away what is known to be not the truth is not counted as one of the self's enticements, so it does not fit to conclude his answer with that. Thus his claim that what he mentioned is closer to verification is, according to those expert in exact scrutiny, false.

The Jews claimed that what al-Samiri threw was a piece of ornament upon which some talismanic inscriptions were engraved, and that Ya'qub (peace be upon him) had hung it on the neck of Yusuf (peace be upon him) when he was small, as people today hang amulets on the necks of their children. Such amulets are sometimes of gold or silver, with some verses, names, or talismanic characters engraved on them. He had obtained it from whatever source he obtained it, and cast it together with the ornaments of the Children of Israel, and so there came about what came about, owing to the special property of what was engraved on it. According to this, he meant by "the Messenger" the earlier messenger of the Children of Israel in Egypt, namely Yusuf (peace be upon him). But no sound report has come to us on this, nor a weak one, nor even a fabricated one concerning what they claim. Yes, it has come to us that Ya'qub had placed the inherited shirt into an amulet and hung it on the neck of Yusuf (peace be upon him). Some have explained by this His saying ﴿Take this shirt of mine﴾, and so on. But how heedless are those slanderers of the claim that the trace is that shirt, for it is already known from what has preceded in the finest of narratives, in His saying: ﴿Take this shirt of mine and cast it upon the face of my father, and he will regain his sight﴾. Thus there is a complete correspondence between the healing of the afflicted and the giving of life to lifeless matter. This lie, had they committed it, would perhaps have found more acceptance among those like al-Isfahani, who cast aside behind their backs what is reported from the Companions and which cannot be said on the basis of opinion. We seek refuge in Allah, the Exalted, from misguidance.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 97:**

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), as has been mentioned more than once. That is, Musa (peace be upon him) said: "If the matter is as you have described," ﴿then go away﴾, meaning: from among the people. God Most High's words ﴿for you, in life, [there is that you say: No touching]﴾ up to the end are an explanation of what the command requires. The phrase ﴿in﴾ (fi) is connected to the stabilizing element (al-istiqrar) that governs ﴿for you (laka)﴾, meaning: it is established for you in life. Or it is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial state (hal) of the kaf (the pronoun "you"), and the governing element is the meaning of the aforementioned stabilizing, because it depends on what is in meaning a subject (mubtada'), namely God Most High's words ﴿that you say: No touching﴾. He did not permit it to be connected to ﴿you say﴾ because of the particle "an" (that). The excuse of those who connect the preceding adverbial phrase to what follows it has already been mentioned a little earlier. What satisfies the mind does not clearly appear in the view of the Allamah Abu al-Su'ud, who connected ﴿when﴾ (idh) in God Most High's words ﴿What prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me?﴾ to what comes after "an," and who did not permit connecting ﴿in life﴾ to what follows it. That is: for you, during the duration of your life, is that you separate from the people with a complete separation. However, it is not by choice in accordance with the obligation of religious duty, but by necessity compelling you to it. This is because God Most High struck him with an incurable disease (da' 'uqam), which does not allow anyone to touch him, or which, if anyone touched him, whoever he was, would immediately cause him to be struck with a severe fever. So the people kept away from him and avoided him, and he would cry out at the top of his voice: "No touching!" It became forbidden for them to meet him, speak with him, eat with him, trade with him, or do the other things that are customary between people in dealings. He became, among the people, more solitary than the murderer who seeks refuge in the Sacred Precinct (Haram), and than the wild beast fleeing in the desert. It is mentioned that he kept to the wilderness and abandoned the people. Al-Tabarsi reported from Ibn 'Abbas that what is meant is that for you and your offspring is that you say, etc. 'Amr restricted the fever to the case where the one touching is a stranger. It is mentioned that remnants of his offspring remain among them in that state until today. It was also said: he was afflicted with waswasa (whispering, compulsive doubt) when Musa (peace be upon him) said that to him. Upon this is based the verse of the poet:

*So that one became like the Samiri, when Musa said to him: "No touching."*

Al-Jubba'i denied what was previously related about the story of 'arr (scabies) and the fever upon touching, and said: he was frightened and fled, and began to wander in the wilderness, finding no one among the people who could touch him, until, because of his distance from the people, he became like one who says "No touching." But he confirmed the former view. The word *mis-as* (touching) is the verbal noun of *massa* (to touch), like *qital* is the verbal noun of *qatala* (to fight). It is negated by the particle "la" that negates the genus, and the negation is intended as a prohibition: that is, "Do not touch me, and I will not touch you."

Al-Hasan, Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi 'Ablah and Qa'nab read ﴿la misas﴾ with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the final sin, and it is of the form *fajar* (a pattern of the type used for a name). Similar to this is the saying about gazelles: "If you come to the water, then no 'ubab (a drink); and if you miss it, then no ubab." As al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah said, these are proper-noun-like forms (a'lam) for the touching, the 'abba and the abba, and the abba is a single instance of *abb*, meaning seeking. From this is the verse of the poet:

*Tamim is like the company of the Samiri; and his saying... Surely the Samiri does not desire mis-as.*

According to this reading, "la" is not the particle negating the genus, because that particle is restricted to indefinite nouns, and this word is definite, being one of the proper names of genus-type (a'lam al-ajnas). Nor is "la" in meaning governing it; rather the meaning is: "there is not, or let there not be, touching from you toward us." This is better than the meaning being "I do not say: touching."

The apparent sense of Ibn Jinni's statement is that it is an ism fi'l (a verb-noun, a word functioning as a verb), like *nizal* (a word meaning "dismount"). The intended meaning is the negation of the act: "I will not touch."

As for the reason he was punished for his crime with what has been mentioned, it is said that it was the opposite of what he intended by making that display, so that the people would unite around him and support him; but it became the cause of their distancing from him and their contempt for him, and he became in their sight more hateful than the *talya* (a particular kind of animal) and more contemptible than a *m'abia'a* (a kind of vessel).

It was also said: perhaps the secret in that is the relation of opposition between them. For when he initiated the trial by means of which his touching had been the cause of the life of the lifeless, he was punished with what is its opposite, since his touching was made the cause of the fever, which is among the causes of the death of the living. It was also said: he was punished with that so that the requital would be of the same kind as the deed, since he *nabadha* (cast away) and so he was *nabadha* (cast away), for that avoidance resembles most closely the casting away. This punishment was, according to what is in the Sea (al-Bahr al-Muhit), by the ijtihad (independent judgment) of Musa (peace be upon him). It has been related about him that he intended to kill him, but God Most High prevented him from that, because he was generous. This is related from al-Sadiq, may God be pleased with him. It is also reported from some of the shaykhs that something close to this has occurred in our Sharia, in the case of the three who were left behind. The Prophet (ﷺ) commanded that they not be spoken to and not be mixed with, and that they should withdraw from their wives until God Most High accepted their repentance. The position of Imam Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with him, regarding the murderer who seeks refuge in the Sacred Precinct is something similar to this, so that he is compelled to come out and be killed outside the Sacred Precinct.

﴿And indeed, for you there is an appointment﴾, that is, in the Hereafter, ﴿which you will not fail to meet﴾, that is: God Most High will not fail you in that promise, but will certainly fulfil it for you after He has punished you in this world.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-A'mash read ﴿tukhlafahu﴾ with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the lam, in the active voice, as being from *akhlaftu al-maw'id* when you find it to be unfulfilled (*khalaf*), like *ajbantuhu* when you find him to be a coward (*jaban*). Upon this is the verse of al-A'sha:

*He stayed, and shortened his night so that he might take provision; then he went, and failed the appointment with Qutaylah.*

It is also permissible that the sense is: "you will not cause the one who promised it to fail his promise," so the first object is omitted and the second is mentioned because it is the intended one. The meaning is: you will not be able to make the promiser one who fails his promise; rather he will certainly do it. Ibn Khalawayh related from Ibn Nahik that he read ﴿lan takhulufahu﴾ with a fatha on the second-person ta' from above and a damma on the lam. In the *Lawami'* it is read ﴿lan yakhulafahu﴾ with a fatha on the third-person ya' from below and a damma on the lam, and it is from *khalafahu yakhlifuhu*, when he came after him. It was said: the meaning according to the first reading is: "and indeed for you there is an appointment which you must certainly encounter." According to the second reading: "and indeed for you there is an appointment which does not repel the saying 'No touching,' so understand."

Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan, with a variant from him, read ﴿lan nakhlifahu﴾ with a fatha on the nun and a kasra on the lam, on the basis that this is a quotation of the words of God, Mighty and Majestic. Ibn Jinni said: that is, "we will not find it to be unfulfilled (khalaf)," and so it would be a statement of Musa (peace be upon him), not in the manner of a quotation. This is clear if the nun were damma-ed.

﴿And look at your god﴾, that is: your object of worship, ﴿which you have been devoted to﴾ (zaltu), meaning *zilta*, as Ubayy and al-A'mash read it, so the first lam was omitted for lightness. Abu Hayyan related from Sibawayh that this omission is among the anomalies of analogy (shudhudh al-qiyas), and that it occurs only when the final letter of the verb is made sukun. From some of his contemporaries it is related that this omission is regular in every verb whose middle and final radicals are doubled, in the dialect of Banu Sulaym, where the final letter of the verb is made sukun. Some said that it is regular in the doubled verb when its middle radical is kasra-ed or damma-ed.

Ibn Mas'ud, Qatadah, al-A'mash (with a variant from him), Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, and Ibn Ya'mur (also with a variant from him) read ﴿zilta﴾ with a kasra on the zad, on the basis that the vowel of the lam was transferred to it after its own vowel was dropped. From Ibn Ya'mur it is also related that he read the zad with a damma, and it seems to be based on the verb coming in some dialects in the pattern *fa'ula* with a damma on the middle letter; in that case the transfer applies just as in the kasra reading.

﴿Upon it﴾, that is: upon its worship, ﴿devoted﴾, that is: persisting. He addressed him (peace be upon him) rather than the rest of those devoted to its worship, who said: ﴿We will not cease to be devoted to it until Musa returns to us﴾, because he was the head of misguidance and the leader of those ignorant ones.

﴿We will surely burn it﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath, meaning: by God Most High, we will surely burn it with fire, as Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas. This is supported by the reading of al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Abu Ja'far in one narration, and Abu Raja' and al-Kalbi, who read ﴿lanuhriqannahu﴾ with the form of the quadriliteral verb *ahraqa* without doubling, since *al-ihraq* (burning) is common for what is done by fire. This clearly indicates that it had become something with flesh and blood. Likewise is what is in the codex of Ubayy and 'Abd Allah: ﴿we will surely slaughter it, then we will surely burn it﴾.

Abu 'Ali allowed that *nuharriqu* may be an intensive form of *haraqa al-hadid*, meaning *harqan* with a fatha on the ra' when he filed the iron with a file (*mibrad*). This is supported by the reading of 'Ali, may God honour his face, and Humayd, 'Amr ibn Fa'id, and Abu Ja'far in one narration, and likewise Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, who read ﴿linahrunannahu﴾ with a fatha on the nun, a sukun on the ha', and a damma on the ra', since *haraqa yahruqu* with a damma is specific to this meaning, as has been said. This clearly indicates that it had not become something with flesh and blood, but remained in the state of inanimate matter.

Some claimed that there is no difficulty, on the assumption that it was alive, in its being burned with a file, since it is permissible that life be created in gold while it remains gold, according to the people of the truth (ahl al-haqq). Some of those who hold that it became an animal with flesh and blood said: the burning with a file was for the bones. This, as you see, is not sound. Al-Nasafi said: its breaking apart with a file is the way of burning it with fire, for gold is not separated except by this means. It was permitted on this basis to say that Musa (peace be upon him) burned it with a file and then burned it with fire. This was criticized on the ground that fire melts it and gathers it together and does not burn it and make it ash. So perhaps that was by alchemical stratagems (al-hiyal al-iksiriyya) or the like.

﴿Then we will surely scatter it﴾, that is: we will surely winnow it (la-nudhriyannahu). One group, among them 'Isa, read it with a damma on the sin. Ibn Muqsim read ﴿lanunassifannahu﴾ with a damma on the first nun, a fatha on the second, and a shadda on the sin. ﴿Into the sea﴾ (al-yamm), that is: into the sea (al-bahr), as Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas.

It is related from 'Ali, may God honour his face, that he interpreted it as the river (al-nahr). The words of God Most High ﴿a scattering (nasfan)﴾ are an emphatic verbal noun, meaning: we will certainly do to it that, in such a way that no trace or effect of it remains, and nothing of it is found so as to be taken. Peace be upon him indeed did all that he swore to do, as the command to look at it indicates. The reason it was not explicitly stated is to draw attention to its complete clarity and to the impossibility of breaking his promise, which was emphasized with an oath. In this there is additional punishment for the Samiri and a demonstration of the foolishness of those who were led into trial. The Sea (al-Bahr) says, clarifying the secret of this act: it appears that when the Samiri had taken the handful from the trace of Gabriel's horse while he was inside the sea, it was fitting that he (Musa) should scatter that calf which he had fashioned from the ornaments that originally belonged to the Copts, and that he cast the handful into the sea, so that this would be a warning that what had been the means of the sustaining of life had come to nothingness, and he cast it into the place where life had subsisted; and that the wealth of the Copts, which God Most High cast into the sea, is of no benefit, just as He, glorified be He, cast their persons and their owners into it and drowned them. What is in this is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 98:

﴿Indeed, your god is only Allah﴾. This is a resumptive statement (istiʾnaf), brought to establish the truth after the refutation of falsehood, by shifting the address and directing it to all of them. That is: indeed, your object of worship, the one deserving worship, is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿He other than whom there is no god﴾, alone, without any of the things sharing with Him in any respect, among which are the attributes of divinity (ahkam al-uluhiyyah).

Talhah recited: "Allah, there is no god but Him, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate, Lord of the Throne," ﴿who has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾. That is: His knowledge encompasses everything that is capable of being known. Thus "thing" here includes both the existent and the non-existent. The word ﴿knowledge﴾ is in the accusative as a tamyiz (specification) transferred from the subject (al-tamyiz al-muhawwal ʿan al-fāʿil). The clause is a substitute (badal) for the relative clause, as if it were said: indeed, your god is He who has encompassed all things in knowledge, none other, whatever it may be, so that the calf, which is a proverb for stupidity, enters into it at the first level of inclusion.

Mujahid and Qatadah recited "wassaʿa" with a shadda on the sin and a fatha on it, so that "knowledge" is in the accusative as a second object (maful thani). Since in the first reading the word is in meaning the subject, it is validly transferred by way of transitivity to the object position, as you say, "Zayd feared ʿAmr" becomes "I made Zayd fear ʿAmr," meaning: I caused Zayd to fear ʿAmr. The meaning here according to this is: He made His knowledge encompass all things. But you know that the speech is not on its apparent sense, because His knowledge, glorified is He, is not something made, and one should not imagine that the essence's requirement of it, upon the assumption of addition, is an act of making. With this the discussion of Moses, peace be upon him, is complete.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 99:

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Thus We relate to you﴾, is a resumed statement (kalam mustanaf) addressed to the Prophet ﷺ by way of a good promise, that there will be sent down the like of what has passed of the reports of the earlier nations. The prepositional phrase (al-jarr wa al-majrur) is in the position of an adjective to an implied verbal noun (masdar muqaddar), or the kaf (ka-) is in the accusative position as an adjective to that verbal noun, meaning: We relate to you ﴿from the reports of what has already preceded﴾ of the past events that befell the bygone nations, relating them as a relating that is like the relating that has passed, or a relating like that. The fronting (al-taqdim) here serves restriction (al-qasr), which conveys added specificity, meaning: thus, not less than that. The min in ﴿from the reports﴾ is either related to an implied element that is an adjective to the object, meaning: We relate to you a report or some part, being from among the reports.

It is also permitted that it be in the accusative position, as the object of ﴿We relate﴾ considered in terms of its content, meaning: We relate some of the reports. Its delay after ﴿to you﴾ is due to what has been mentioned more than once, namely the concern with what is foregrounded and the arousing of desire for what is postponed. It is also permitted that ﴿Thus We relate﴾ be like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And thus We made you a median community﴾, with the demonstrative referring to the verbal noun of the verb mentioned after it; the verification of this has already passed.

Page 259

The benefit of this relating is to amplify His knowledge, peace be upon him, to multiply his miracles, to console him, and to remind those of insight among his ummah ﷺ. ﴿And We have certainly given you from Us a reminder﴾, a Book comprising these narratives and reports, worthy of being remembered, reflected upon, and taken as a lesson. The min is related to ﴿We have given you﴾. The indefiniteness of ﴿a reminder﴾ is for magnification, and its postponement after the prepositional phrase is because the point of the statement lies in the fact that the thing given from Him, Exalted is He, is a great reminder and a noble Qur'an comprising every perfection, not in the fact that this reminder is given from Him, Mighty and Majestic is He, together with what there is in it of a kind of length by what follows it of the attribute.

It is also permitted that the prepositional phrase be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from ﴿a reminder﴾, but that is not the case. The interpretation of the reminder as the Qur'an is what the majority (al-Jumhur) have adopted, and it is related from Ibn Zayd. Muqatil said: that is, an explanation, and its outcome is what has been mentioned. Abu Sahl said: that is, honour and a remembrance among people, and this does not suit it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 100:

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Whoever turns away from it﴾. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (ʿanhu, "from it") refers to the Reminder (al-dhikr), and the clause stands in the position of a qualifier (ṣifah) for it. It is not fitting to describe the honour or the Reminder among people by this. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to God, Exalted is He, by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), but this is very much contrary to the apparent meaning. (Man, "whoever") is either conditional (sharṭiyyah) or relative (mawṣūlah), meaning: whoever turns away from the Reminder, which is of great importance, which entails the happiness of both abodes, and does not believe in it. ﴿Then indeed he﴾, that is, the one who turns away from it, ﴿will bear on the Day of Resurrection a burden (wizr)﴾, that is, a heavy punishment for his turning away and for the rest of his sins.

Al-wizr (burden) in its original usage denotes two meanings: a heavy load and sin. Its application to punishment, considering the first meaning, is by way of explicit metaphor (al-istiʿarah al-muṣarriḥah), since punishment is likened to a heavy load. Considering the second meaning, it is by way of metonymic metaphor (al-majaz al-mursal), in that punishment is the consequence of sin, so it is either a necessary result of it or its cause. Then it was used for punishment by the indication of the mention of the Day of Resurrection. The first meaning is more fitting with His saying afterwards, ﴿and evil it is﴾, etc., because it is a continuation (tarshīḥ) of it, and it is supported by His saying in another verse, ﴿and they will surely bear their burdens﴾. Interpreting wizr as sin, and reading the speech as having an elided modifier, i.e., "the punishment of sin" or "the recompense of sin," is not appropriate.

A group among them, including Dawud ibn Rufayʿ, read (yuḥammalu) with a doubled mim in the passive voice, because he is charged with that, not that he bears it willingly, and in this reading (wizran) would be the second object.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 101:**

﴿Abiding therein﴾: that is, in the burden (*wizr*), whose intended meaning is the punishment.

It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to the verbal noun (*masdar*) of *yahmilu* (﴿will bear﴾), and that *khalidina* (﴿abiding﴾) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*) of the hidden pronoun (*mustakinn*) in *yahmilu*. The plural is used in view of the meaning of *man* (﴿whoever﴾), because abiding in the Fire is something that occurs when its people are gathered together, just as the singular forms in the three pronouns mentioned earlier are used in view of their wording.

﴿And evil it is for them on the Day of Resurrection as a burden﴾: this is a statement of blame, on the basis that *sa'a* (﴿evil it is﴾) is a verb of blame with the meaning of *bi'sa* (﴿evil is﴾), which is one of its two well-known meanings. On this view its subject here is a hidden pronoun that refers to *himlan* (﴿as a burden﴾), which is the specifier (*tamyiz*) of the one who is most high in burden (*a'laa wizran*). This is because the subject of *bi'sa* can only be an ambiguous pronoun, explained by the specifier that refers back to it, even though the specifier comes later, since this is one of the distinctive features of this construction. The one being blamed is omitted, and the estimated meaning is: evil is their burden as a burden, their load. The *lam* in *lahum* (﴿for them﴾) is the *lam* of clarification (*lam al-bayan*), as in *saqyan lahu* (﴿watering for him﴾) and *hayta laka* (﴿come, you﴾). It is connected to an omitted element, as if it were said: "To whom is this said?" And it is answered: "It is said to them, and concerning them." The repetition of *yawm al-qiyamah* (﴿the Day of Resurrection﴾) is for the sake of added emphasis and to magnify the matter.

It is also permissible that *sa'a* means *ahzana* (﴿grieved﴾), which is the other of its two meanings. The estimated meaning according to what has been said is: the burden grieved them while being a burden for them. Al-Kashshaf commented on this: what benefit is there in it? The burden is more indicative of heaviness, so why restrict it? Then the restriction with *lahum* (﴿for them﴾) is unnecessary, and its placement before the object is not appropriate to the context, and the omission of the object also (is problematic). After all this, it does not suit what the speech was intended for, nor does it add any intensity to the threat.

[Page 260]

Through this, after what preceded it, he then said: Likewise is what al-Allamah al-Tibi said, that the meaning is "the burden of the load grieved them," with *himlan* as a specifier and the *lam* in *lahum* as a *lam* of clarification, for the reason mentioned, namely that the grandeur of the meaning is lost. And that if the clarification is for the exclusivity of the load to them, then in it there is sufficiency; and if it is for the place of the griefs, then it is not so, the way of its clarification (is invalid); and if it is on the basis that this threat is for them, then its position is not before the Day of Resurrection, and the appropriate form then would be *wizran sa'a lahum himlan* (as a description), not like this, interposed and emphasized. End of quote.

There is no room for justifying the use of the *lam* by considering implicit meaning (*tadmin*), because no verb is realized that suits the mentioned verb and is appropriate for it. This is because the *lam* is apparent in exclusivity that is beneficial, while the verb here concerns a harmful event. The claim that the *lam* is extra, as in *radifa lakum* (﴿followed you﴾), or that the burden is understood in a sarcastic sense (*tahakkum*), is a forced interpretation to correct the wording without any need for it, and the question of the grandeur of the meaning would remain with it. The conclusion is that what has been mentioned is supported neither by the wording nor by the meaning.

It is also permissible that *sa'a* means *qabuha* (﴿was ugly﴾). He mentioned its use with this meaning, although whether it is a literal meaning is open to consideration. *Himlan* is a specifier, *lahum* is a circumstantial element (*hal*), and *yawm al-qiyamah* is connected to the adverbial element. The meaning is: that burden was ugly from the aspect of being a load for them on the Day of Resurrection. And in it is what is in it.

﴿On the Day the Trumpet is blown﴾ is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb of remembrance (idmar al-dhikr). It is also permitted that the adverbial element was omitted, to signal that the expression is too constrained to contain or explain it. Alternatively, it may be a substitute (badal) for ﴿the Day of Resurrection﴾, or an explanatory apposition (bayan) for it, or an adverbial complement of ﴿they will whisper﴾.

Abu 'Amr, Ibn Muhaysin and Humayd read ﴿nunfakh﴾ (نُنْفِخُ) with the first-person plural "we" of majesty (nun al-'azama), attributing the verb to the one who commands it, namely Allah, may He be exalted. This is to magnify the blowing, since what proceeds from the Magnificent is magnificent. Or it is attributed to the one who blows, by making his act equivalent to the act of the Exalted, and this form is used only for one who has special closeness and high rank. It has also been said that it is permitted for the "we" to refer to the Day in which the event occurs.

It was read as ﴿yanfukh﴾ (يَنْفُخُ) with an open ya', so that its pronoun refers to Allah, glorious and mighty, or to Israfil, peace be upon him, even though his name has not been mentioned before, due to his being well known.

al-Hasan and Ibn 'Iyad, together with a group, read ﴿fi al-suwar﴾ (فِي الصُّوَرِ) with a damma on the sad and a fatha on the waw, as the plural of ṣūrah (form), like ghurfah and ghuraf (room and rooms). What is meant by it is the body that is given form.

It was objected that the blowing is repeated, because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then it will be blown a second time﴾, and blowing into the trumpet is a giving of life, while life is not repeated after death; and what is in the graves is not intended by the first blast, by general agreement.

It is answered that we do not concede that every blowing is a giving of life. Some have also interpreted the trumpet, according to the well-known recitation (al-qira'ah al-mashhurah), in this way too. The correct view is to interpret it as the horn into which one blows. ﴿And We will gather the criminals on that Day﴾, that is, on the Day when the trumpet is blown. This is mentioned explicitly, although it is certain that gathering does not occur except on that Day, for the sake of terrifying the hearer.

al-Hasan read ﴿yuḥsharu﴾ (يُحْشَرُ) with a ya' and in the passive voice, and ﴿al-mujrimūn﴾ (المُجْرِمُونَ) with a damma, as a substitute for the agent (na'ib 'an al-fa'il). It was also read ﴿yaḥshuru﴾ (يَحْشُرُ) with a ya' and in the active voice, its subject being His pronoun, glorious and mighty; that is, Allah, may He be exalted, will gather the criminals.

﴿Zurqan﴾ (زُرْقًا) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥal), meaning that they will be blue of body. This is an extreme form of disfigurement. Bodies only turn blue from enduring hardships and the drying out of their moisture.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it means blue of the eyes. This is then a description of a thing by a quality of one of its parts, as one says "a boy with kohl-darkened eyes" (aknal) and "a boy who is cross-eyed" (ahwal), where kuhl and hawal are attributes of the eye. Perhaps this is a well-known metaphor (majaz mashhur). It is also permitted that it be literal, like "a blind man" (a'mā). They were made this way because blueness is the worst of eye colours and the most hateful to the Arabs, for the Romans, who were their fiercest enemies, were blue-eyed. For this reason they described the enemy as "black-livered, reddish-bearded, blue-eyed" (aswad al-kabid, asbah al-sibal, azraq al-'ayn). The poet said:

*"I never feared that his death would come at the hands of a blue-eyed, lowered-gazed, short-spear man from the Sabanat (tribe)."*

They used to mock with blueness, as in the saying:

*"Your eyes have turned blue, O son of Mukaʻbar, except for every Dabbi (man) of the Dabb tribe, who is blue from baseness."*

Ibn 'Abbas was asked about the combination of ﴿zurqan﴾ (blue), as is reported from him, with ﴿ʻumyan﴾ (blind) in another verse, and he said: "For the Day of Resurrection there are states: a state in which they will be blind, and a state in which they will be blue." al-Farra' said that what is meant by ﴿zurqan﴾ is blind, because when the light of the eye departs, its pupil turns blue, and the reason for the plural in this interpretation is clear. al-Azhari said that what is meant is thirsty, because intense thirst changes the blackness of the eye so that it becomes like a blue one. It has also been said that it makes it white, and azraq has come with the meaning of white, as in the phrase "a blue spear" (sinan azraq), and in the line: *"When we came to the water, its waves were blue."* Interpreting it as thirsty accords with His saying, exalted is He, as I have heard: ﴿And We will drive the criminals to Hell as a thirsty herd﴾.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 20, verse 103:

﴿They will whisper among themselves﴾, meaning they will lower and hide their voices because of the severity of the terror of the Rising. The clause is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*), explaining what they say and what they leave unsaid at that time, or it is another circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to ﴿the criminals﴾. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿If you tarried not but ten﴾, is, by the implied presence of a verb of saying, a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿they will whisper﴾, meaning: saying, "You tarried in the graves not but ﴿ten﴾," that is, ten nights or ten days. Perhaps this is more fitting to the words of al-Amthal.

When the masculine noun is omitted and its number is retained, the feminine marker (*ta'*) may not be attached. Al-Kisa'i reported: "We fasted five of the month," and from this is what came in the hadith: («Then he follows it with six of Shawwal»), where what is meant is six days. The omission is good here because it makes the word a verse-ending (*fasila*), which is the rhyme-closing word of the verse. Their intention from this saying is to belittle the duration and its swift passing, and to rebuke them for what they used to claim, since the matter has become the opposite of what they were upon, namely denying the Resurrection and considering it among impossibilities. As if they said: "You have been raised, and you tarried in the grave only a brief period, while you used to claim that you would never rise from it."

It is narrated from Qatadah that they meant their tarrying in the world, and said this to belittle the period of their stay there, because it has passed, and because they found the duration of the Hereafter long, or out of regret over it, when they witnessed the hardships and became certain that they deserved them for wasting days on satisfying desires and following appetites. This was objected to on the grounds that they were preoccupied with a distraction that prevented them from remembering that, so the earlier explanation is more fitting to their condition. It was also objected to on the grounds that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿You have indeed tarried in the Book of God until the Day of Resurrection﴾ is explicit that the tarrying was in the graves. There is discussion on this point.

In *Majma' al-Bayan*, it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah that they meant their tarrying between the two blasts, during which they will remain forty years with the punishment lifted from them.

ﷺ-free passage; translating faithfully.

"We know best what they say" — that is, we know what they are saying, which is the length of their stay. "When the best of them in conduct says" — that is, the most upright of them in opinion and the most sound of them in intellect. ("Idh" is an adverbial complement [ẓarf] of "yaqūlūn".) "You stayed only a day" — one day; and to it the number in paucity terminates.

It has been said: the intended meaning of "day" is any unspecified period of time, and its indefiniteness is for diminution and belittling, so the meaning is "only a short while." The apparent contrast with "ten" makes this unlikely. Attributing this statement to "the best of them" is Allah's, exalted be He, declaring it more correct, but not because it is closer to truth; rather because it is greater in rebuke, or because it is more indicative of the severity of the terror. This indicates that the one who said it was more knowing of the gravity of the matter and the severity of the punishment.

[p. 261]

﴿They ask you about the mountains﴾. The questioners were the deniers of resurrection from Quraysh, as reported by Ibn al-Mundhir from Ibn Jarir. They said, mockingly, "How will your Lord deal with the mountains on the Day of Resurrection?" It is also said that they were a group from Thaqif, and it is said that they were some of the believers. ﴿Say: My Lord will blow them away with a blast﴾. He, glory be to Him, will make them like sand, and then send winds over them that scatter them. The fa' (so) indicates haste in removing what was in the questioner's mind about the mountains remaining, based on the assumption that this is a consequence of there being no gathering. Do you not see that those who deny the gathering maintain that this observed order in the earth and the heavens will not change? Or it indicates haste in establishing the truth, as a safeguard against any notion that would lead to corrupt belief.

This is based on the premise that the questioner was a believer. The first view is that he was one of those who deny resurrection. For this reason the Imam said: The intent of the questioners was to challenge the gathering and the raising of the dead. Therefore the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to answer, with the particle of sequence attached, because delaying clarification on this fundamental (usuli) matter is not permissible. As for delaying it on subsidiary legal (furu'i) matters, that is permissible. That is why the fa' was not used in the command to answer in God's words: ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin﴾, and the rest of the verse; and His words ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: The surplus﴾; and His words ﴿They ask you about the spoils. Say: The spoils belong to God and the Messenger﴾; and His words, glory be to Him, ﴿They ask you about orphans. Say: Setting things right for them is best﴾; and so on.

In another place he said: The question mentioned is either about the eternity of the mountains or about the necessity of their remaining. This is one of the principal issues of the foundations of religion. Therefore the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to answer it with the fa' that indicates sequence, as if He, glory be to Him, had said: O Muhammad, answer this question immediately, without delay, because the claim that they are eternal or that their remaining is necessary is disbelief. The answer indicates the negation of that, because blowing them away is possible, since it is possible for every part of the mountain, and the senses confirm this. So it must be possible for the whole mountain. Therefore it is not eternal and not necessarily existent, because the eternal cannot undergo change, and blowing away is a change. End of quotation.

It has been objected that the impossibility of change and blowing away is accepted only regarding what is eternal in its essence. None of the two questioners held that the mountains were eternal in that sense. As for what is eternal in time, it is not impossible for it, in itself, to undergo that; and if it is impossible, it is impossible for another reason. Moreover, regarding the mountains being eternal in time, there is room for doubt according to the two questioners, and likewise according to others among the philosophers. Rather, it is apparent that the philosophers hold that they have a temporal origin, even if they do not know a specific beginning for their origin. So reflect.

Then he (may God have mercy on him) mentioned that the question and answer have been mentioned in several places in the Book of God. Some of them are subsidiary, and some are fundamental. The fundamental ones are in four places: this verse; His words ﴿They ask you about the crescent moons. Say: They are timings for people﴾; His words ﴿They ask you about the spirit. Say: The spirit is of my Lord's command﴾; and His words, mighty and majestic, ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when will it arrive?﴾. It is not hidden that counting all that was mentioned as fundamental is not evident, and even if it were evident for all of them, the question would arise about the secret of attaching the fa' to the command to answer in some cases but not in others.

And that which is attached to the fa' is the more important within the scope of prohibition. If the command to answer the question about the spirit concerns its eternity or the like, then it is important, like the command to answer in the present case. Indeed, it may be even more important, because there is an actual proponent of the temporal eternity of the spirit, based on the view that it is the rational soul, as held by Plato and his followers. It may be said: since the answer here is to dispel a question about the preceding statement, namely His words ﴿they whisper among themselves﴾, it is as if it were said: how can the whispering of the guilty be valid, given that it requires gathering, and the mountains stand in between as an obstacle? So if you say it is valid, then explain to us how God deals with them. The answer is that the mountains will be blown away at that time, so no obstacle remains to gathering and whispering. The command was joined with the fa' to hasten the defense of the preceding claim. The verses in which the command is not joined with the fa' were not brought in this manner, as is not hidden from people of spiritual perception.

Al-Nasafi and others said: the fa' is the answer to an implied condition, meaning: if they ask you about the mountains, then say. This is based on the view that the question about this did not occur as it occurred in the story of the spirit and others, which is why the fa' was not used there, but was used here. Thus ﴿they ask you﴾ is purely for the future. Abu Hayyan considered this unlikely. What Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj, that Quraysh said: "O Muhammad, how will your Lord deal with these mountains on the Day of Resurrection?" and then ﴿They ask you about the mountains﴾ was revealed, indicates otherwise.

Al-Khafaji said: The apparent reason it is joined with the fa' here and not there is to indicate that the answer was already known to him (ﷺ) beforehand, so he was commanded to hasten to it, unlike the other case. End of quotation.

You know that the claim that the answer about the spirit, about menstruation, and similar matters was not known to him (ﷺ) beforehand is something that not even ordinary people would venture, let alone the elite. So what he mentioned is not worth paying attention to.

[p. 262]

Among the things that make the bereaved laugh is that some of the contemporary scholars heard the question about the secret of the fa' being attached to the command here and not attached in the other verses. He said: How ignorant this questioner is of what is permissible and impermissible among questions! Has he not heard God's words ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾? Does he not know that its meaning is a prohibition on one who wishes to ask, from asking? And what shows the man's ignorance even more is that he is lower than what he said, and he did not care about what was said and what is said. My relating this is for the sake of exposing and reminding those who are safe from such a disease of the great and broad favour God has bestowed upon them.

The initial fa' in His words ﴿So He leaves it﴾ is quite clear. The pronoun may refer either to the mountains, considering their lower parts that remain after being blown away, which are their bases and their foundations; that is, "then We leave what has spread out of them and whose surface has become level with the surfaces of the rest of the earth, after the protrusions and elevations have been blown away." Or it may refer to the earth, which is implied by the context, since it is what remains after the mountains are blown away. On both interpretations, the Exalted leaves all of it as a ﴿level plain﴾ (qa', safsafan), because when the mountains are leveled and their surfaces are made equal to the surfaces of the parts of the earth, the whole becomes a single surface. As for qa' (a plain), it has been said to mean a flat tract (sahl), and al-Jawhari said it means level ground (al-mustawi min al-ardh). From this is the verse of Dirar ibn al-Khattab:

"Quraysh will surely be in the valleys like the scum (fuqa'at al-qa') of the plain in the hands of slave-women."

Ibn al-A'rabi said: it is the smooth land with no vegetation or buildings. Makki related that it is an uncovered open place. It has also been said to be the firm level land, and it has been said to be a pool of water, but this is not the intended meaning. Its plurals are aqwu', aqwa', and qi'an. As for safsaf (a level plain), it is smooth, level land, as if its parts were a single row on every side. It has also been said to be land with no vegetation. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid took qa' and safsaf to have one meaning, namely level ground with no vegetation in it. The accusative of qa' is in the circumstantial (hal) position from the pronoun in the accusative, which is the second object of yadhar, with the sense of "make" (tadmin ma'na al-taslir) implied. And safsafan is either a second circumstantial or an apposition to the second object.

And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿You will not see in it﴾, meaning in the places where the mountains were settled, or in the earth, as has been detailed, ﴿any crookedness or any elevation﴾. This is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*), explaining the state of the smooth level ground mentioned earlier. It may also be a circumstantial clause (*hal*), or a descriptive qualifier (*sifa*) of "ground". The seeing is visual (*basariyya*), and the address is to everyone who is capable of it.

The word *iwaj* is attached to the verb "see". The *iwaj* with a kasra on the ʿayn denotes what cannot be perceived by the eye but only by insight (*basira*), because what is meant by it is the crookedness that is hidden, to the extent that establishing it requires geometrical measurement (*misaha handasiyya*), which is grasped by the intellect. Thus it is joined to what is purely intellectual, and so it is applied to it for that reason. This is in contrast to *iwaj* with a fatha on the ʿayn, which denotes what can be perceived with the eye, such as the crookedness of a wall or a stick. On this basis, the lexicographers distinguished between the two in *al-Jamhara* and elsewhere.

Al-Marzuqi, in his commentary on *al-Fasih*, chose the view that there is no difference between them. Abu ʿAmr said: *iwaj* with a kasra is used for the lack of straightness, both abstract and perceptible. As for *awaj* with a fatha, it is the verbal noun of *awija*, and its waw has remained sound because it is a contracted form of *a'waj*. Since it is sound in the verb, it is also sound in the verbal noun. *Amt* means a protrusion, and the indefiniteness of the word in the verse is for diminution.

From Ibn ʿAbbas: *iwaj* means a slope (*mayl*), and *amt* means a trace like a sandal strap (*shirak*). In another report from him: *iwaj* means a valley (*wadi*), and *amt* means a hill (*rabiya*). From Qatada: *iwaj* means a fissure (*sadʿ*), and *amt* means a mound (*akama*). It was also said that *amt* means the cracks in the earth. Al-Zajjaj said: it is that one place becomes elevated and another place becomes depressed. It was also said that *amt* in the verse is crookedness in the sky facing the air, while crookedness in the earth is specific to breadth.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the direct object is for the reason already mentioned more than once.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 108:

Page 264

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Yawma'idhin﴾ (on that day), means: the day when the mountains are blown away. The idafa (annexation) of "day" to the time of the blowing is an annexation of the general to the specific. Therefore it is not necessary that time should have a time as its adverbial container, although there is no objection to this according to one who holds that a renewed thing may be measured by another renewed thing. It has been said: it is an annexation of the named to the name, as is said regarding "the month of Ramadan." It is an adverbial complement (zarf) of His saying, the Exalted, ﴿yattabi'ūna al-dā'iya﴾ (they follow the summoner). It has also been said: it is a substitute (badal) for "the Day of Resurrection."

The governing element for it is the same governing element (al-'amil fihi huwa al-'amil fihi), and in this there is a great separation and a loss of the connection of yattabi'ūna with what precedes it. Accordingly, His saying, the Exalted, ﴿wa-yas'alūnaka﴾ (and they ask you) etc. is a digressive parenthetical interjection, and what follows is a new resumption. The pronoun in (yattabi'ūna) refers to the people. By the summoner is meant the summoner of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to the place of assembly, and he is Israfil, peace be upon him, who places the Trumpet in his mouth and calls the people at the second blast, standing upon the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis, and says: "O decayed bones, torn skins and scattered flesh, come forward to the Presentation before the Most Merciful." They then come from every direction toward his voice.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, who said: Allah, the Exalted, will gather the people on the Day of Resurrection in darkness; the sky will be folded up, the stars will scatter, the sun and the moon will depart, and a caller will call out, and the people will follow the voice, heading towards it. This is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿On that day they will follow the summoner﴾ etc. Ali ibn Isa said: "al-dā'i" (the summoner) here means the Messenger who used to call them to Allah, Mighty and Majestic; but the first (interpretation) is more correct.

﴿lā 'iwaja lah﴾ (there is no crookedness in him/it): that is, for the summoner, meaning that no one summoned deviates from him or turns away from him. This is like one saying: "There is no disobedience to him," i.e., he is not disobeyed, and "no injustice to him," i.e., he is not wronged. The basis of this is that the restriction of a verb to its object is established just as it is to the agent. It has also been said: meaning there is no crookedness in his call, so he does not incline towards some people over others, but hears all of them. This is related from Abu Muslim.

It has also been said: it is reversed (qalb), meaning there is no crookedness for them away from him; rather, they come towards him, facing him, following his voice without deviation. This is related from al-Jubba'i, but it is nothing. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relative to the summoner, or it is a new independent clause, as Ibn 'Atiyya said: it may be that the meaning is "there is no doubt in it, and its existence does not contradict its report."

﴿wa-khasha'at al-aswat li-l-Rahman﴾ (and voices are humbled before the Most Merciful): that is, they become hushed out of awe of Him, the Exalted, and the severity of the terror of the appearing. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: they became still. Khushu' here is a metaphor for this. It has been said: there is no metaphor, and the speech is by the elision of a modifier, meaning "the owners of the voices," but this is not the case.

﴿fa-la tasma'u﴾ (so you will not hear): an address to everyone capable of hearing, ﴿illa hamsan﴾ (except a whisper): that is, a faint, subdued voice, as Abu 'Ubayda said. From Mujahid: it is inaudible speech. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy: (fa-la yanṭiqūna illa hamsan) (they will not speak except in a whisper). From Ibn 'Abbas: it is the moving of the lips without speech, but this is considered unlikely, since that is something seen, not heard. In another narration from him: it is the scuffling of feet. This was related from 'Ikrima, Ibn Jubayr and al-Hasan, and was chosen by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj.

From this is the saying of the poet:

"And they walk with us in whispers (hamisan)"

It is mentioned that the lion is called al-hamus because of the faintness of its tread. So the meaning is that their voices became still and their words ceased, so that nothing was heard from them except the shuffling of their feet, and their being conveyed to the place of assembly.

[p. 265 of the source edition appears here]

﴿That Day﴾, meaning: the day on which the aforementioned terrifying events occur. It is an adverbial complement (*zarf*) of His words, Exalted is He, ﴿intercession will not benefit﴾. It is also permitted that it be a substitute (*badal*, a grammatical apposition) for "the Day of Resurrection," or for ﴿That Day they will follow﴾. The meaning is that intercession will not benefit anyone from among the intercessors ﴿except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted﴾ to intercede.

﴿for whom the Most Merciful has given leave﴾. Here the exception is from the most general of the objects (*al-mafa'il*), and "man" (whoever) is the object of "tanfa'" (benefit). It refers to the one for whom intercession is made. The phrase "lahu" (for him) is connected to a implied element that is linked to "adhina" (gave leave). In *al-Bahr*, it is stated that the lam (*lam*) here indicates cause (*lil-ta'lil*), and likewise in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿and He is pleased with his speech﴾, meaning: He is pleased with the speech of the intercessor for his sake and concerning him. Or: He is pleased with the speech of the intercessor for his sake and concerning him. Thus, according to both readings, "speech" refers to the speech of the intercessor. It is also permitted that the lam not be causal, and the meaning would then be: He is pleased with a speech that belongs to him (the one interceded for). In that case, "speech" refers to the speech of the one interceded for, which, according to what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, is "There is no god but Allah." The sense of the verse on this reading is: intercession will not benefit anyone except one for whom the Most Merciful has given leave to intercede on his behalf, and who was a believer. On every reading, the meaning is that intercession will not benefit anyone except those mentioned; as for others, intercession hardly benefits them, even if it is assumed to be issued by intercessors who take it upon themselves to intercede for people, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿so the intercession of the intercessors will not benefit them﴾.

*Al-Bahr* and *al-Durr al-Masun* permit that no object be implied for "tanfa'" (benefit), treating it as if it were intransitive (*tanzilan lahu manzilata al-lazim*), and the exception is then from "shafa'a" (intercession). "Man" would then be in the nominative position as a substitute (*badal*) for it, with an implied qualifier (*mudaf*), or in the accusative position as an exception, with the same implied qualifier, meaning: "except the intercession of one whom He has permitted," and so on. "Man" here refers to the intercessor. The exception is then continuous (*muttasil*), but it may also be discontinuous (*munqati'*, an exception that is not of the same kind) if nothing is implied. In that case, the position of "man" is accusative according to the dialect of the Hijaz and nominative according to the dialect of Tamim.

It has been objected that making the exception from intercession, with an implied qualifier, is problematic, because the ruling on intercession regarding one who has not been given leave is that he does not possess it, and it is never issued by him at all. And the meaning of His words, ﴿nor will intercession be accepted from it﴾, is that it will not be given leave to be offered, not that it will not be accepted after it has been made. Thus, reporting about intercession merely as not benefiting the one interceded for may suggest that it could occur at a time when he has not been given leave, which also disrupts what is required by the grandeur of the Day's terrifying description.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 110:

﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾. The apparent meaning is that the plural pronoun refers to the created beings who are gathered (for judgment), namely those who follow the caller. It has also been said that it refers to people in general, without the restriction of gathering and following. It has also been said that it refers to the angels, peace be upon them, but this is wholly contrary to the apparent meaning. The two relative phrases, according to what has been said, refer to the states that preceded them and what comes after them that they will encounter; or the reverse; or the affairs of this world and the affairs of the Hereafter; or the reverse; or what they perceive and what they do not perceive. The discussion of this has already passed.

﴿But they cannot encompass Him in knowledge﴾. That is, their knowledge does not encompass His known things, may He be exalted. So ʿilman (knowledge) is a tamyiz (accusative of specification) transferred from the subject, and the pronoun in (bihi, "Him") refers to God, may He be exalted. The sentence is constructed with an elided noun (mudaf, an omitted genitive term) understood. It has also been said that the meaning is that their knowledge does not encompass His essence, may He be glorified, that is, in terms of His being described by the attributes of perfection, among which is all-encompassing knowledge. This implies the validity of saying, "I know God, may He be exalted," since what is negated is knowledge in the manner of encompassing.

Al-Jubbaʾi said: the pronoun refers to both relative phrases together, for they do not know all that has been mentioned, nor the detail of what they know of it. It has been permitted that it refers to one of the two relative phrases, though not specified.

﴿And faces will be humbled before the Ever-Living, the Sustainer [of all]﴾. That is, they will be abased and submit with the submission of the ʿunāh, meaning captives. By "faces" is meant either the persons themselves or the well-known organs. They are singled out for mention because they are the noblest of the visible organs, and the traces of humiliation appear first upon them. The *alif-lam* in *al-wujūh* is either for a previously known referent (*al-ʿahd*), or it replaces the omitted genitive, meaning "the faces of the criminals." In that case the verse is similar to His saying: ﴿The faces of those who disbelieved will be disgraced﴾. Al-Zamakhsharī chose this reading and treated His saying ﴿And he has failed who carries injustice﴾ as a parenthetical clause (*iʿtirāḍ*), and placed the relative pronoun in the position of their pronoun for greater emphasis. It has also been said: "faces" means the nobles, that is, the great among the disbelievers, because the context is one of awe, and humiliation is more fitting for them. "Injustice" here means polytheism. The clause ﴿And he has failed﴾ and so on is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), and the linking element is the *wāw*, not a parenthetical clause, because it stands in contrast with ﴿and he is a believer﴾ that follows. End of quotation. The author of al-Kashf said: "The apparent reading agrees with al-Zamakhsharī, and the semantic contrast suffices, for a parenthetical clause does not fall short of the status of a circumstantial clause." End of quotation.

You know that explaining "injustice" as polytheism does not depend on explaining "faces" as the nobles or on making the clause a circumstantial clause. Rather, it also holds on the first reading, on the basis that "the criminals" means the disbelievers. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, that concerning His saying ﴿And he has failed﴾ and so on, he said: "He loses who associates partners with Allah and does not repent." Many others have said: the apparent meaning is that *al-* is for totality, that is, all faces submit and surrender. His saying ﴿And he has failed﴾ and so on may be a new sentence or a circumstantial clause. The relative pronoun may refer either to the polytheists, or to them and others among the sinners. The failure of each one who carries injustice is in proportion to the injustice he carried. So the failure of the polytheist is permanent, while the failure of the believing sinner is limited to the time of punishment, if he is punished. The meaning of *al-Ḥayy al-Qayyūm* (the Ever-Living, the Sustainer) has already been explained for you in the verse of the Throne. It is apparent that His saying ﴿...﴾

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 112:

﴿And whoever does righteous deeds﴾ is a counterpart (qasim) to His, glorified is He, saying ﴿and faces will be humbled﴾ through to the end of what preceded it, and to the saying of the Mighty and Majestic ﴿and he has failed who carries an injustice﴾. On this (reading), as Ibn 'Atiyyah and others have stated explicitly, the meaning is: and whoever does some of the righteous deeds, or some portion of the righteous deeds, ﴿while he is a believer﴾, that is, in what belief in it is obligatory. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), and the restriction by this is because faith is a condition for the soundness of acts of obedience and the acceptance of good deeds. ﴿So he will not fear injustice﴾, that is, the withholding of a reward that is due by the binding of the promise, ﴿nor diminution﴾, nor the withholding of part of it. The Arabs say: "you diminished (hadamta) my right", meaning you reduced it; and from it comes "hadim al-kashhayn", meaning slender of the two flanks, and "hadm al-ta'am", meaning the food dissolving in the stomach. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah that the meaning is: he will not fear that he will be wronged so that his evil deeds are increased, nor that he will be diminished so that his good deeds are reduced. The first (interpretation) is narrated from Ibn Zayd. It has also been said that the speech contains an elision of a genitive (mudaf), meaning: he will not fear the recompense of injustice and diminution, since no injustice has proceeded from him, nor has he diminished anyone's right, so that he should fear that; or that by injustice and diminution is meant their recompense, metaphorically. Perhaps the intended meaning, as has been said, is the negation of fear from him in respect of that, on account of his faith and his doing some of the righteous deeds; and this includes the negation that the righteous deed, together with faith, could be an injustice or a diminution.

It has also been said: the intended meaning is that whoever does that while he is a believer, this is his state, owing to God the Exalted's preserving him from injustice or diminution, and because the righteous deed is not counted as valid together with it. Therefore there is no objection to what has been said, that it does not follow from faith and some deeds that he does not wrong others or diminish their right. It is not hidden from you that the claim of an elision of a genitive and a metaphor in this verse is extremely remote, and the objection that has been raised is strong, and what has been answered to it is as you see. Furthermore, the apparent sense of al-Jawhari's words is that there is no difference between injustice (zulm) and diminution (hadm), while the apparent sense of the verse requires a distinction; likewise the saying of al-Mutawakkil al-Laythi:

"Indeed the abased and the base are a people whose master is the diminished, the wronged."

Among those who explicitly stated it is al-Mawardi, who said: the difference between them is that injustice is the withholding of the whole of a right, and diminution is the withholding of part of it. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin and Humayd read ﴿fa-la yakhaf﴾ (so let him not fear) as a prohibition. Al-Tibi said: the recitation of the majority agrees with His saying ﴿and he has failed﴾ etc. in terms of being a report, and is more eloquent than the other recitation in terms of continuity; and the other is more eloquent in that it does not admit hesitation in the report.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 113:**

﴿وكَذَلِكَ﴾ (*wa-kadhālika*, "And likewise") is a *ʿaṭf* (coordination) on ﴿كَذَلِكَ نَقُصُّ﴾ ("Thus do We relate"). The demonstrative refers to the sending down of the earlier verses that contain the warning and foretell what will happen of the states and terrors of the Resurrection. That is, "like that sending down" ﴿أنْزَلْناهُ﴾ (*anzalnāhu*, "We sent it down"), where the pronoun refers to the whole Qur'an. This is a comparison of the sending down of the whole with the sending down of a part, and what is meant is that it is of one single pattern. Its pronoun is used without a prior mention, to signal the prominence of its status, and that it is fixed in minds and present in understandings. ﴿قُرْآنًا عَرَبِيًّا﴾ ("a Qur'an in Arabic") so that the Arabs may understand it and recognize in it the inimitable composition that shows it lies beyond the capacity of human beings and was sent down from the Lord of the worlds. ﴿وصَرَّفْنا فِيهِ مِنَ الوَعِيدِ﴾ ("And We have varied in it some of the warning") means: We repeated in it some of the warning, or some portion of the warning. This clause is coordinated with the clause ﴿أنْزَلْناهُ﴾, and making it a *ḥāl* (circumstantial clause) qualifying the sending down is very much contrary to the apparent sense.

﴿لَعَلَّهم يَتَّقُونَ﴾ ("so that they may fear God") — the object is omitted. The discussion of *la'alla* ("perhaps", expressing hope or purpose) has already been presented. What is meant is: "so that they may guard themselves against disbelief and sins in practice." ﴿أوْ يُحْدِثُ لَهم ذِكْرًا﴾ ("or it may create for them a remembrance") means: admonition and lesson, which in the Hereafter leads to taqwa (God-consciousness). It seems that, since *taqwa* is what is sought from them in itself, its verb was ascribed to them; and since *dhikr* is not like that, the construction was changed to what you have heard. So it has been said. It has also been said: what is meant by *taqwa* is its *malakah* (settled disposition), and it was ascribed to them because it is an inner disposition, which suits ascription to the one in whom it resides. By *dhikr* is meant the admonition resulting from listening to the Qur'an, which restrains from sins. Since it is a matter that renews itself through its hearing, it suited ascribing it to the Qur'an, and describing it with *ḥudūth* (coming into being), which suits the renewal of the words heard. It is not hidden that, after explaining *taqwa* as a disposition, there remains in the heart something of the matter of causal justification.

In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit), he ascribed the hoped-for *taqwa* to them because *taqwa* is an expression for the absence of the performance of ugliness, and that is a continuation in the original non-existence. And he ascribed the hoped-for coming into being of *dhikr* to the Qur'an because that is a matter that came into being after it had not existed. This is taken from the words of the Imam. But his statement, "because *taqwa* ..." to the end, in its absolute form, is a clear objection. Some have explained *taqwa* as abstaining from sins and *dhikr* as performing acts of obedience, since it is applied to it figuratively, because of the causal relation between them. So the particle ﴿أوْ﴾ (*aw*, "or"), as it has been said, is for distribution (*tanwīʿ*). In the statement there is an indication that the matter revolves around *takhliyah* (emptying of the vices) and *taḥliyah* (adorning with virtues).

The Imam mentioned two possibilities in the verse.
