The first: the meaning is that We sent down the Qur'an so that they may become cautious against doing what is not fitting, or that it may create for them a remembrance that calls them to doing what is fitting. The statement thus also indicates emptying and adorning, except that it does not involve the figurative usage. The second: the meaning is that We sent down the Qur'an so that they may fear God; if that does not come about, then at least it may create for them remembrance, honour, and a good reputation. It is not hidden that this is nothing. Al-Tibi said: the meaning is "And thus We sent it down as a Qur'an in Arabic," that is, eloquent, speaking the truth, its proofs shining clearly, "so that there may arise in them reflection and contemplation upon its verses and its clear, sufficient, and healing proofs, so that they submit and obey, and We have varied in it some of the warning, so that they may fear the punishment." So in the verse there is *laff* without order (*lafṭ bi-lā tartīb*), and it is on the pattern of His Exalted saying: ﴿لَعَلَّهُ يَتَذَكَّرُ أوْ يَخْشى﴾ ("perhaps he will be reminded or will fear"). In my view, the verse including both *takhliyah* and *taḥliyah* is not without beauty, so consider it.

Al-Hasan recited ﴿أوْ يُحْدِثْ﴾ with a sukun on the *thāʾ*. ʿAbd Allah, Mujahid, Abu Haywa, al-Hasan in one narration, al-Jahdari, and Sallam recited ﴿أوْ نُحْدِثُ﴾ with a *nūn* and a sukun on the *thāʾ*. That is either *ḥaml waṣl ʿalā waqf* (treating a connected reading as if it were a pause), or the sukun of the case-ending letter (*ḥarf al-iʿrāb*) because its vowel is heavy, as Ibn Jinni said, like the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*Today I drink, not bearing a sin against God, nor being one who seeks what is forbidden of drink.*

And the verse of Jarir:

*Travel, sons of the paternal uncle; al-Ahwaz is your dwelling, and the river Tiri; and may the Arabs not recognize you.*

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 114:

﴿So exalted is Allah﴾, an exaltation of Him, the Exalted, and of what has been variously expressed in the Qur'an of promise and threat, commands and prohibitions, and other matters; and a declaration of the transcendence of His exalted Essence, that the sending down of His noble Qur'an should not fall short of the utmost perfection, in that it causes those to whom it was sent to abandon sins and to perform acts of obedience. In it there is also an expression of wonder and an invitation to turn towards it and to glorify it. And in describing Him, exalted is He, with His saying, glorified is He, ﴿the King﴾, meaning: the One who disposes of command and prohibition, the one truly deserving that His promise be hoped for and His threat be feared. This indicates that the thunderous admonitions of the Qur'an are divine policies that contain the welfare of both abodes, and that none turns away from them except one forsaken and destroyed. And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿the Truth﴾, is an attribute following another attribute of Allah, meaning: the One who is established in His Essence and His attributes, mighty and majestic. Al-Raghib interpreted it as the One who brings things into existence in accordance with what wisdom requires.

Many have permitted that it be an attribute of "the King," and its meaning is the opposite of falsehood, meaning: the Truth in His kingship, which is due to Him, glorified is He, by His very Essence. In this there is a hint that the Qur'an and what it contains of promise and threat are wholly true, and that falsehood does not approach its sanctuary in any way; and that the one who is guided is he who turns towards it, seeking its good tidings and its warnings, while the one who is misguided is he who turns away from pondering its admonitions. In this there is also a preparation for linking the prohibition of hastening with it, in His saying, glorified is He, ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation is completed to you﴾, i.e., before its completion, ﴿its revelation﴾, i.e., Gabriel's conveying of it to you, peace be upon him, for turning towards it entails this, and likewise entails glorifying it.

Al-Tibi mentioned that this sentence is conjoined to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So exalted is Allah, the King, the Truth﴾, because it contains the expression of wonder. It is as if it were said: since you have drawn attention to the greatness of the majesty of the One who sent it down and have guided to the magnificence of what was sent down, then magnify His presence, the King, the Truth, who disposes of the kingdom and the dominion, and turn with all of yourself to the preservation of His Book and the verification of its meanings, and do not hasten with it. The Prophet ﷺ, whenever Gabriel, peace be upon him, recited the Qur'an to him, would follow it at the pronunciation of every letter and every word, fearing that it might escape him and he would not have memorized it. So the Prophet ﷺ was forbidden from that, since pronouncing one word may distract from hearing what follows it. And there was also revealed to him, ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it﴾, the verse. And the Prophet, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, was commanded to seek the abundance of knowledge and to ask Allah, glorified is He, for more of it, so it is said: ﴿And say﴾, i.e., within yourself, ﴿My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾, i.e., ask Allah, mighty and majestic, instead of hastening, for an increase of knowledge in general or of the Qur'an, for beneath every word, indeed beneath every letter of it, there are secrets, symbols and abundant sciences; and that is the most beneficial for you. It has also been said that the sentence ﴿And do not hasten﴾ is a new sentence mentioned after the sending down by way of digression. It has also been said that this is a prohibition from conveying what was ambiguous before its explanation came; but this is not so, for conveying and reciting the ambiguous before its clarification is something whose soundness and legitimacy are beyond doubt.

Similar to this is what has been said: that it is a prohibition from commanding its writing down before its meanings are explained to him and established for him, peace be upon him; rather, that is far less than this. It has also been said that he was forbidden from judging by what might be the subject of a Qur'anic revelation, based on what a group related from al-Hasan: "A woman complained to the Prophet ﷺ that her husband had slapped her, and he said to her: 'Between you is retaliation.' Then this verse was revealed, so the Prophet ﷺ paused until there was revealed, ﴿Men are the protectors of women﴾." Al-Mawardi said: he was forbidden from hastening to seek its revelation. That is because the people of Makkah and the bishop of Najran said: "O Muhammad, inform us about such-and-such, and we have set you a term of three days." Revelation was delayed to him, the rumour spread among the Jews, and they claimed that the Prophet, peace be upon him, had been defeated. This grieved him, ﷺ, and he hastened the revelation, so there was revealed, ﴿And do not hasten﴾, etc. In both of these views there is what is not hidden.

ʿAbd Allah, al-Jahdari, al-Hasan, Abu Haywa, Salam, Yaʿqub, al-Zaʿfarani and Ibn Miqsam read (naqḍiya) with the first-person plural of majesty and the letter yāʾ vowelled with a fatḥah, and (waḥyahu) in the accusative. Al-Aʿmash read likewise, except that he made the yāʾ of (naqḍī) sukūn. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: this is according to the dialect of those who do not allow the yāʾ to take a fatḥah in any case when the letter before it is kasrah and it falls at the end. The verse has been cited as evidence for the excellence of knowledge, since the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to seek its increase; and some have mentioned that the Prophet, peace be upon him, was not commanded to seek increase in anything except knowledge.

al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say: "O Allah, benefit me by what You have taught me, teach me what will benefit me, increase me in knowledge, and all praise is due to Allah in every state." Sa'id ibn Mansur and ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn Masʿud that he used to supplicate: "O Allah, increase me in faith, understanding, certainty and knowledge." And this is only for the increase of the excellence of knowledge, and its excellence is too evident to be mentioned. We ask Allah, exalted is He, to grant us an increase in it and to enable us to act in accordance with what it requires.

﴿And We had certainly taken a covenant from Adam﴾. It is as if, when Allah, glorified is He, praised the Qur'an and urged the use of deliberation and gentleness in receiving it, and enjoined resolve in acting upon His command and avoiding forgetfulness concerning it, He cited the account of Adam as an example of forgetfulness and of abandoning resolve.

Ibn ʿAtiyya (Ibn ʿAtiyya) mentioned that this contains an additional warning to the Prophet (ﷺ) against haste and lack of deliberation, lest he fall into what is not fitting, as Adam (peace be upon him) fell. Thus the discourse is connected to His words, ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an﴾, and so on. Al-Zamakhshari (al-Zamakhshari) said: it is an ʿatf (coordinating conjunction linkage) of the story upon the story, ʿatf al-qissa ʿala al-qissa, to [the verb] "ṣarrafna" (We have varied). The difference in it, between the performative (inshaʾ) and the declarative (khabariyya) forms, does no harm, together with the fact that the purpose of the conjunction is the response to the oath. The meaning on this reading is: We have varied the warning and repeated it, perhaps they will be mindful, or it will produce a remembrance for them; but they did not heed it and forgot it, just as their father did not heed the warning and forgot the covenant made with him. The benefit in this is to indicate that their opposition is a trait of the Akhzamī kind (a proverbial saying, shanshana akhzamiyya, meaning inherited disposition), and that the root of their affair and their stock is firmly established in it. Something similar to this is related from al-Ṭabarī (al-Ṭabarī).

Ibn ʿAtiyya criticised this, saying that it is weak because of the disparagement it involves toward the station of Adam (peace be upon him), since his story is made an example for those who deny the signs of Allah, Exalted is He, whereas what befell him (peace be upon him) occurred only through interpretation (taʾwil). End of quotation. Fairness requires that it be judged sound, so do not heed what has been said, that there is in it a point of consideration. Abū Muslim said: it is connected to His words, ﴿Thus do We relate to you of the tidings of what has passed before﴾, but this is not so. Yes, together with what preceded it, there is in it the fulfilment of the promise in that verse. Ibn ʿAtiyya inclined to one of two possibilities: that it is connected to "lā taʿjal" (do not hasten), or that it is the beginning of a new discourse with no connection to what precedes it. This latter, though he put it forward in his speech, arises from narrowness of outlook, as is not hidden.

The ʿahd (covenant) is the charge, wasiyya (instruction). It is said: ʿahida ilayhi al-malik, wa waghara ilayhi, wa ʿazama ʿalayhi, wa taqaddama ilayhi, meaning when the king commanded him and enjoined him. The object of the covenant is omitted, indicated by what follows it. The lam (la-) is in the response of an omitted oath, meaning: and by Allah, We had certainly commanded him and enjoined him. ﴿min qablu﴾ means: before this time. It is said: before the existence of these opponents.

From al-Ḥasan (al-Ḥasan): that is, before the sending down of the Qur'an. It is said: that is, before he ate from the tree. ﴿But he forgot﴾ the covenant and did not give it attention, and did not occupy himself with preserving it, until he became heedless of it. The reproach came because of his lack of concern, and one like him (peace be upon him) is reproached for such a thing.

From Ibn ʿAbbas (Ibn ʿAbbas) and al-Ḥasan, the meaning is that he abandoned what he had been enjoined regarding guarding against the tree and eating its fruit. Thus "forgetting" is a metaphor for "abandoning", and the fāʾ (fa-) is for sequence, which is a customary usage. It is also said that the fāʾ is faṣīḥa (explanatory), meaning: he did not give it attention, so he forgot, and the object is omitted, which is what we indicated. It is said: what was forgotten was the warning of expulsion from the Garden if he ate. It is also said: His words, ﴿Indeed this is an enemy to you and to your wife﴾. It is also said: the deduction that the prohibition concerns the genus and not the individual. The apparent meaning is what we have indicated.

Al-Yamānī (al-Yamānī) and al-Aʿmash (al-Aʿmash) read "fa-nasiya" with a ḍamma on the nūn and tashdīd on the sīn, meaning: the Devil caused him to forget. ﴿And We did not find in him resolve﴾: determination of purpose and firmness of foot in affairs. This accords with both interpretations of forgetting. It is said, however, that it is more suitable to the second and better fits the context of the verse according to what we mentioned at the outset.

A group related from Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatāda that the meaning is: We did not find in him patience (ṣabr) in refraining from eating from the tree. From Ibn Zayd and a group: the meaning is: We did not find in him resolve to commit the sin, for he (peace be upon him) erred and did not intend it. This is the view of those who said that forgetting is in its literal sense, and something indicating it has come from Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkār (al-Zubayr ibn Bakkār) in al-Muwaffaqiyyāt transmitted from him that he said: ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) said to me: "Indeed your companion here, that is ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may Allah honour his face), indeed I am of the view that he is ascetic, but I fear the pride of his soul will carry him away." I said: "O Commander of the Faithful, our companion, whom you know, by Allah, we do not say that he changed, nor altered, nor angered the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) during the period of his companionship," and he said: "nor regarding the daughter of Abū Jahl," while he (ʿUmar) wanted to propose to her over Fāṭima. I said: "Allah, Exalted is He, said concerning the disobedience of Adam (peace be upon him): ﴿And We did not find in him resolve﴾. So our companion did not resolve to displease the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but there are thoughts that no one can ward off from himself, and perhaps they come from the jurist in the religion of Allah, Exalted is He, the one who knows the command of Allah, glorified is He. So when he is alerted to them, he returns and repents." Then he (ʿUmar) said: "O son of ʿAbbās, whoever thinks he can come to your seas and dive into them with you until he reaches their depth, has thought himself incapable." But it is not hidden from you that this interpretation is neither the immediate meaning nor closely suited to the context, and what results from reading "lam najid" in its sense on this view is that he forgot, so it repeats what precedes it.

Then, if "lam najid" is from the existential finding of knowledge (al-wujūd al-ʿilmī), then "lahu ʿazman" has two objects, the second having been placed before the first because it is a complement of place (ẓarf). If it is from the finding that is the opposite of non-existence, as some of them preferred, then "lahu" is connected to it and was placed before its object for the reason mentioned more than once, or it is connected to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from its indefinite object. The meaning on this reading is: and We did not encounter in him resolve.

﴿And [mention] when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam"﴾ This begins the explanation of the matter already known (al-ma'hud) and of how his forgetfulness became evident and his resolve failed. "Idh" (when) is in the accusative as an object (maf'ul bihi) of an implied verb addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, meaning: "Remember the time when We said to the angels, etc." It has been said that it is conjoined (ma'tuf) to an implied element, meaning: "Remember this, and remember when We said," or that one who conjoins the narrative to another narrative [has done so].

Whichever is the case, the intended meaning is: remember what occurred at that time from Us and from him, so that his forgetfulness and the failure of his resolve become clear to you. ﴿So they prostrated, except Iblis﴾. The discussion of this has already passed many times. ﴿He refused﴾ is a new (resumptive, mustaʾnafah) sentence that comes as an answer to a question arising from the report that he did not prostrate, as if it were said: "What is the matter with him that he did not prostrate?" So it is said: ﴿He refused﴾. "Ibā' (refusal) is abstention, or its intensity. Its object (maf'ul) is either omitted, meaning "he refused to prostrate," as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He refused to be among those who prostrate﴾; or it is not intended at all, being treated as an intransitive verb (lazim), meaning: he performed the act of refusal and made it manifest.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 117:

﴿So We said﴾ immediately after that, showing concern for the counsel given to Adam, peace be upon him, ﴿"O Adam, indeed﴾ this one whom you have seen what you have seen ﴿is an enemy to you and to your wife﴾. The lam (la) is repeated because, according to the majority, a pronoun in the genitive case cannot be conjoined (ya'ṭifu) without repeating the preposition (al-jar). It has been said: it is repeated to indicate that the enmity of the accursed one toward the wife is original, not secondary. This is evident according to the view that repeating the preposition in such a case is not obligatory, as Ibn Malik held. As for the view that it is obligatory, it has been said in its justification that the thing being obligatory according to the grammatical rule does not preclude intending to convey what the context requires.

Al-Sayyid al-Sanad, in his commentary on al-Miftah (Sharh al-Miftah), explicitly stated, in a justification that made Sahib al-Miftah's indefinite form of the specification (tamyiz) in His words, exalted is He, ﴿and the head has blazed with white hair﴾ serve to convey intensification, by what points to that. And the mention of "your wife" rather than Eve carries, as is not hidden, an added sense of repulsion and warning against him. The cause of the enmity has been disputed. It has been said that it is merely envy, and he, may God the Exalted curse him and curse his followers, was the first to envy. It has been said: it is his being an ignorant old man and Adam, peace be upon him, being a young scholar, and an ignorant old man is always an enemy to a young scholar; indeed, the ignorant in general are enemies to the learned in this way, as it has been said: "And the ignorant are enemies of the people of knowledge." It has been said: it is the contrariness of the two origins, for the accursed one was created from fire, Adam, peace be upon him, was created from clay, and Eve was created from him. Al-Imam al-Razi mentioned all of that.

﴿So let him not expel you both﴾, that is, let him not become a cause of your expulsion ﴿from the Garden﴾. This is a metaphor (kinayah) for forbidding them from being in a state where Satan could cause their expulsion from it, like His words, exalted is He, ﴿so let there be no constriction in your breast﴾. The fa' (fa) is for arranging the cause of the prohibition upon his enmity toward them, or upon the informing of it. ﴿Then you will be distressed (fa-tashqa)﴾, that is, you will be exhausted by the hardships of the world, which cannot be counted, and none is spared from them. The attribution of this specifically to him, peace be upon him, after the expulsion, which causes it, is linked to both of them together, is because he is the principal in affairs, and his fatigue entails hers, along with what this contains of observing the rhyme (fawasil) in the most complete manner. It has been said: the intended meaning of distress is toil in obtaining the means of livelihood, and this is among the duties of men. This has been supported by what 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn 'Asakir, and a group have narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: (When Adam, peace be upon him, was sent down from the Garden, a dappled bull met him, and it was said to him: "Work on it." So he began wiping the sweat from his forehead and saying: "This is what my Lord promised me." ﴿So let him not expel you both from the Garden, then you will be distressed﴾.) Then he called out to Eve: "Eve, you did this to me. There is not a son of Adam who works on a bull except that he says: 'Hu' (a call to the bull), because of you." And it has been said that the hardship is a general one. It is supported by the verse after this, though there is room for reflection on that. And perhaps the view of generality is preferable. (Tashqa) may be in the accusative, with an implied "an" after the fa' in answer to the prohibition, and it may be in the nominative as a new clause, with the estimate "fa-anta tashqa" ("then you are distressed"). This latter has been deemed unlikely, because the intent is not to inform about him being distressed; rather, the intent is that if the expulsion occurs, that [distress] results.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verses 118–119:**

﴿Indeed, for you there is that you will not hunger therein, nor will you go naked﴾ ﴿and that you will not thirst therein, nor will you be struck by the sun﴾. That is, the sun will not strike you. It is said: *ḍaḥā* like *saʿā*, and *ḍaḥiya* like *raḍiya*, *ḍaḥwan* and *ḍaḥyan*, when the sun strikes him. It is also said: *ḍuḥan*, *ḍaḥwan*, *ḍuḥūwan* and *ḍuḥiyyan* when he comes out into it. They recited the verse of ʿAmr ibn Abi Rabiʿa:

*She saw a man: as for when the sun confronts him, he is struck by it (yaḍḥā), and as for in the evening, he is sheltered (yakhḍuru).*

Some interpreters explained what is in the verse by this meaning. The first explanation (the one given above) is related from ʿIkrima. Whichever it is, the intended meaning is the negation of the opposite of these conditions. The clause is a reason for what the prohibition requires, for the gathering of the causes of comfort therein necessitates exaggerated care in securing the sources of remaining there, and diligence in refraining from whatever leads to leaving it. There is also a deviation from explicitly stating that he, peace be upon him, enjoys therein the various kinds of blessings in foods and drinks, and the pleasures of beautiful garments and pleasing dwellings. Yet there is in this, beyond what is plain, an encouragement to remain therein. Furthermore, it negates their opposites, which are hunger, thirst, nakedness and exposure to the sun, in order to remind of these disagreeable matters and to alert to the kinds of misery in them, from which He, glory be to Him, warned him, so that he would strongly avoid the cause that leads to them.

The meaning of ﴿that you will not hunger﴾ and what follows is that none of the four matters will afflict him at all. For satiety, quenching of thirst, clothing and shelter may be attained after their opposites have arisen, but this is not the case there. Rather, whenever a desire or inclination toward any of the matters mentioned arises therein, one enjoys it without reaching the point of necessity. Moreover, the encouragement has already been achieved by what was permitted to him of enjoying everything therein except the tree, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿O Adam, dwell you and your wife in the Garden, and eat from it freely wherever you wish﴾. Its mention is omitted here, being sufficient by that, and it is restricted to what has been mentioned of encouragement, which includes a warning.

Some said: the restriction to what has been mentioned is due to what occurred in Adam's question, peace be upon him. It is related that when He, glory be to Him, commanded him to dwell in the Garden, he said: "My Lord, is there for me therein what I may eat? Is there for me therein what I may wear? Is there for me therein what I may drink? Is there for me therein what I may shelter under?" So he was answered with what has been mentioned. But there is some doubt about the soundness of this report.

The reason for singling out what has been mentioned for him, peace be upon him, is what has passed just now. It was also said: his being the questioner. The apparent expectation was that there would be no separation between hunger, thirst, nakedness and exposure to the sun, for the sake of homogeneity and closeness. However, he deviated from the evident correspondence to a more complete correspondence: hunger is the emptiness of the inner self, and nakedness is the emptiness of the outer self. So it is as if it were said: "Neither your inner self nor your outer self is empty of what concerns them both." He combined thirst, which produces heat within, with exposure to the sun, which is exposure to the sun and produces heat without. So it is as if it were said: "The heat of neither the inner nor the outer self will harm you." This hidden connection is a wondrous secret of the secrets of eloquence.

In *al-Kashf* (Zamakhshari): he deviated to this arrangement only to alert that satiety and clothing are the two principal matters, and that the latter two complete them in order. Thus the favour bestowed in this way is more manifest. For this reason the two clauses were distinguished, so that first it said (*inna laka*) and second (*annaka*). This point was also noted by al-Tibi, who then said: "In the orderly arrangement of the four mentioned matters in this way, the more important is placed first, then the more important; and in making them an elaboration of the content of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So let him not expel you both from the Garden, for then you would be miserable﴾, and in repeating the word *fīhā* (therein) and placing them in the form of negation with a repeated particle, there is an allusion to the circumstances of this world and that one must endure them (*fīhā*), because it was created for that, whereas the Garden was created only for enjoyment, and nothing else can be conceived therein."

In *al-Intiṣaf* (Ibn al-Munayyir): in the verse there is a wondrous secret of eloquence called *qaṭʿ al-naẓīr ʿan al-naẓīr* (severing one counterpart from its counterpart). Its purpose is to establish the enumeration of these blessings, for if each were joined with its pair, the two joined would be taken as one blessing. The people of eloquence aimed at the summit of this meaning, both in earlier and later times. The first al-Kindi said:

*As if I had never ridden a steed for pleasure, nor embraced a maiden with anklet-bells,*

*and had never poured out the sealed wineskin, nor said to my horses: "Turn back, a return after a rout."*

He severed riding the steed from his saying to his horses, "Turn back, a return," and severed embracing the maiden from draining the cup, with the correspondence maintained. His purpose was to enumerate his delights and glories and to multiply them. The other al-Kindi followed him and said:

*I stood, and there is no doubt in death for one who stands, as if you were in the sheath of destruction, and it is sleeping.*

*The heroes pass by you, wounded in defeat, while your face is laughing and your mouth smiling.*

Sayf al-Dawla objected to him, since he severed a thing from its counterpart, and said to him: "If you erred in that, then Imru' al-Qays erred with his saying," and he recited the two verses preceding. In the verse there is also a secret for that, beyond what has been mentioned: the intention of suiting the closing rhymes (*fawāṣil*). End of quotation.

It may be said regarding my first verse: he combined riding horses for pleasure and recreation with embracing the maiden for the pleasure obtained in both, and he combined pouring out the wineskin with saying to his horses "Turn back," because of the courage in both. Then, what has been mentioned about the intention of suiting the closing rhymes in the verse is evident in that if he had deviated from this order, that would not have been achieved. This is not accepted without question.

Shayba, Nafiʿ, Ḥafṣ and Ibn Saʿdan read *innaka* with a kasra on the hamza. The majority read it with a fatḥa, on the basis that the conjunction is upon *an lā tajūʿa*, which is in the sense of a verbal noun standing for *an*. The occurrence of a clause introduced by the fatḥa *an* as the subject of the kasra *inna*, which shares with it the function of emphasis, is valid, while its occurrence as the predicate of *inna* is impossible, because the prohibited matter, namely the gathering of two emphatics in one same clause, does not exist here, owing to the difference of the locus of emphasis in what is within its scope. This is unlike when it occurs as a predicate, for then the unity of the locus is beyond doubt. Its explanation, according to *Irshad al-ʿAql al-Salim* (Abu al-Suʿud): each of the two particles is set for emphasising the content of the declarative sentence composed of its subject and predicate. It is not hidden that the basis of its being declarative is what it contains of wisdoms, and that its locus is the predicate, not the subject. Thus the signification of each of them is the affirmation of the predicate's ascription to its subject, not the affirmation of the subject in itself. What necessarily follows from the occurrence of the sentence introduced by the fatḥa as the subject of the kasra is the affirmation of the ascription of its predicate to that sentence understood as a verbal noun. As for the affirmation of its subsistence in itself, that is the signification of the fatḥa. Therefore, there is absolutely no necessity of gathering two emphatics in one same material. It was not permitted to say "*inna anna Zaydan qāʾimun ḥaqqin*" with the difference of locus; rather they stipulated a separation by a predicate, as in our saying "*inna ʿindī anna Zaydan qāʾimun ḥaqqin*", to avoid the appearance of gathering. The conjunctive *wāw*, though it stands in place of the kasra *inna* here, which may not enter upon the fatḥa *anna* without a separation, and though it takes its place in conveying its meaning and in making its complement subject to its rules, yet, since it is not a particle set for emphasis, there is no necessity from its entry of the gathering of two emphatics in emphasis at all. So the meaning is: "*Inna laka* (indeed for you) the absence of hunger, the absence of nakedness and the absence of thirst," except that it did not restrict itself to stating that what is established for him is the absence of thirst and of exposure to the sun absolutely, as was done with its like in the conjoined clause; rather, the intention was to state that what is established for him is the affirmed absence of these two, and so the verbal particle *anna*, which conveys this, was placed in the position of the pure verbal particle, as if it were said: "*Inna laka fīhā ʿadama ẓamaʾika ʿalā al-taḥqīq*" (indeed for you therein is the absence of your thirst, in affirmed certainty). End of quotation.

It requires of him an explanation of the point in not restricting the statement to the fact that what is established for him is the absence of thirst absolutely, as was done with its like in the conjoined clause. So reflect, and do not be heedless.

It was said: the conjunctive *wāw*, though it stands here in place of *inna*, nevertheless the word *laka* that follows it, which came after the *anna* it replaces, is taken into account, so there is a separation there, and entry with it is not impossible. But this is as you see. It is not hidden from you that the conjunction upon the kasra reading is upon the first clause together with its two complements, not upon its subject. There is no dispute about that.
