Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 120:

﴿Then Satan whispered to him.﴾ Al-Waswasa (whispering) here means "conveying the whispering to him." Its meaning, as al-Raghib said, is: an evil passing thought, and its root derives from al-waswas, which is the sound of jewelry or a faint, hidden murmur. Al-Layth said: al-waswasa is the soul's inner speech (hadith al-nafs), and the verb is waswasa in the active form. It is said: "rajulun muwaswis" (a man who is whispered to), with kasra and fatha both used, but this is a solecism (lahn).

Many have mentioned that waswasa is an intransitive verb, derived from al-waswasa, which is an imitation of a sound like the wailing of a bereaved woman, the howling of a wolf, or the clucking of a hen. When it is followed by "ila" (to), it carries the sense of conveying (al-infa'), and when it is followed by "li" (for) as in waswasa lahu, the "li" is for specification (li-l-bayan), as in ﴿Hayta laka﴾ (Come, for you). Al-Zamakhshari said: it is for cause (li-l-ajl), meaning he whispered on account of him. The same applies when it follows verbs similar to this one, as in the saying of the poet:

"Ajris laha ya ibna Abi Kibash, fa ma laha al-laylata min infash"
(Make her bark, O son of Abu Kibash, for tonight she has no rest from her panting.)

In al-Asas it is mentioned that waswasa ilayhi is under the literal usage section, and its apparent meaning is that the implication of conveying (al-tadmin) is not considered, and that the many-usage view would be based on considering it.

(Qala) is either a substitute for (waswasa), or a resumptive clause that answers an implied question, as if it were said: "What did he say to him in his whispering?" So it was said: He said, ﴿O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity?﴾ He addressed him by name so that he would be more attentive to him and more able to listen. Then he presented to him what he presented, in the form of a question that conveys sincere advice. The meaning of "shajarat al-khuld" (the tree of eternity) is a tree whoever eats from it will live forever and never die at all, whether he remains in his state or becomes a king, based on the words of the Exalted: ﴿Except that you become angels or become of the immortals.﴾

In al-Bahr it is said that what is related here precedes what is related in al-A'raf from His words, Exalted: ﴿What your Lord has forbidden you from this tree...﴾ etc., as if the accursed one, when he saw from him, peace be upon him, a kind of attentiveness to what was presented to him, moved on to informing and restricting. End quote. But the truth is that there is no certainty about what was mentioned.

﴿And a kingdom that does not decay﴾, i.e., does not perish, or does not become worn out. It is said: this is one of the necessary consequences of eternity, so it was mentioned for emphasis and to increase the encouragement.

﴿So they both ate﴾, meaning he and his wife, ﴿from it﴾, meaning from the tree which the accursed one called the tree of eternity, ﴿and their private parts became apparent to them﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: they were stripped of the light with which Allah had clothed them, so their private parts became visible. In another report from him, their garment was the nail, and when they committed the sin it was removed from them, and these remnants were left at the tips of the fingers. And Allah knows best the soundness of that. Then what has been mentioned may be a punishment for eating, and it may be that it was ordained as a consequence of it for another benefit. ﴿And they began to fasten upon themselves some leaves of the garden﴾. Its tafsir has already passed.

﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord﴾ by what has been mentioned, namely eating from the tree, ﴿and so he went astray﴾: he strayed from his aim, which was eternity, or from the thing that was required of him, which was abstaining from eating from the tree, or from right guidance, in that he was deceived by the words of the enemy. It was said: *ghawa* means his livelihood was spoiled. From this comes the saying *al-ghiwa'* for bad nursing. It has been read as *fa-ghawiya* (فَغَوِيَ) with a fatha on the ghayn, a kasra on the waw and a fatha on the ya', meaning he became bloated from excessive eating, from *ghawiya al-fasil* when the young camel became distended from milk, and the other reading has been explained by this. Al-Zamakhshari criticised this, saying: this may be valid according to the dialect of those who turn a ya' preceded by a kasra into an alif, so that they say in *faniya* and *baqiya*, *fana* and *baqa* with an alif, and they are the Banu Tayy, but it is a wicked explanation. The apparent sense of the verse indicates that what occurred was a grave sin, and this is what is understood from the words of the Imam. If its occurrence was after the mission (prophethood), deliberately and not out of forgetfulness or interpretation, it becomes problematic in light of what the verifiers and the precise scholars agreed upon, namely the necessity of the infallibility of the prophets, peace be upon them, after the mission from the occurrence of the like of that from them in that manner. Hardly anyone holds this except the Azariqa of the Khawarij, for upon them is what they deserve; they permitted disbelief for them, and Allah forbid, so what is less than it is more fitting to permit. If its occurrence was before the mission, as a group has said, and the Imam said: it is our school, then if it was deliberate it becomes problematic in light of the view of most of the Mu'tazila and the Shi'a, who hold their infallibility, peace be upon them, from the occurrence of the like of that deliberately before the mission as well.

Yes, there is no problem in it according to what Qadi Abu Bakr said, that it is not impossible, either rationally or by revelation, that a disobedience of any kind should proceed from the Prophet, peace be upon him, before his prophethood. Rather, it is not rationally impossible for one who converted after his disbelief to be sent. Al-Amidi, in *Abkar al-Afkar*, said that most of the companions agreed with him, as did many of the Mu'tazila. If it was by forgetfulness, as the words of the Exalted indicate: ﴿but he forgot, and We found in him no resolve﴾, according to one of the two opinions concerning it, it becomes problematic in light of what has been transmitted from the Shi'a, namely the prohibition of a grave sin proceeding by forgetfulness before the mission as well. There is no problem in it according to what you have heard from Qadi Abu Bakr. If it was after the mission by forgetfulness, it also becomes problematic according to some and not others. ʿAdud al-Millah said in *al-Mawaqif* that most of them permitted the occurrence of a grave sin, meaning other than disbelief and lying in what the miracle has shown to be true for them, peace be upon them, by forgetfulness and by way of error from them. Al-ʿAllamah al-Sharif said that the opposite is chosen. Many have held that what occurred was a minor sin, and the matter in that is light, for minor sins that do not imply baseness are permitted, as the second ʿAllamah mentioned in his commentary on *al-ʿAqaʾid*, to proceed from them, peace be upon them, deliberately after the mission according to the majority, unlike al-Jubba'i and his followers. Their proceeding by forgetfulness is permitted by consensus. However, the verifiers stipulated that they be alerted to it, so that they desist from it.

Yes, it has been mentioned in *Sharh al-Maqasid* that they are protected from the occurrence of that deliberately. The safer course, considering the station of Adam, peace be upon them, is to say: the occurrence of what has been mentioned from him was before prophethood, and was by forgetfulness or through interpretation, except that the matter weighed heavily upon him and was grave in his sight,
[p. 275]
in view of the exaltedness of his rank and the abundance of Allah's grace and kindness towards him. It is well known that: *the good deeds of the righteous are the bad deeds of those brought near*. Among what indicates the magnitude of that from him, given his lofty rank, peace be upon him, is what al-Bayhaqi reported in *Shuʿab al-Iman* from Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Maghribi, who said: Ibrahim reflected upon the case of Adam, peace be upon them both, and said: "O Lord, You created him with Your hand, breathed into him of Your spirit, made Your angels prostrate to him, and then, for one sin, You filled the mouths of people with mention of his disobedience." Allah the Exalted revealed to him: "O Ibrahim, do you not know that opposing the Beloved, in relation to the Beloved, is severe?"

Some have mentioned that in the magnification of that from him, may the blame be upon him, there is a powerful deterrent to his children from its like. In any case, it is not fitting for anyone today to be attributed disobedience, or to report that, unless he is reciting what contains that, or relating it from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. As for beginning it from his own part, that is not permitted. Qadi Abu Bakr Ibn al-ʿArabi explicitly stated that it is not permissible to attribute disobedience to the near ancestors who are like us, so how can it be permissible to attribute it to the prophets, the forefathers, and the most excellent, most honoured Prophet? Al-Qurtubi approved of that, and claimed that beginning reports with some of the ambiguous attributes of Allah, such as the hand, the finger and descent, is more deserving of prohibition and impermissibility. Then, what occurred was in reality by the sheer decree and destiny of Allah the Exalted. Otherwise, it has been narrated from Abu Umama al-Bahili and al-Hasan that his intellect, peace be upon him, was like the intellect of all his offspring, and the enmity of Iblis, may the curse be upon him, towards him, peace be upon him, is most evident. In that is evidence that no intellect benefits and nothing avails against the decree and judgment of Allah the Exalted.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 122:**

﴿Then his Lord chose him (ijtaba-hu)﴾. That is, He, glorified is He, selected him and brought him near to Himself by guiding him to repentance and enabling him to do it. It is said that "ijtiba" (choosing, gathering to oneself) comes from "ijtaba al-shay'" (he gathered the thing for himself), i.e., he collected it, as in your saying "ijtama'tuhu" (I gathered it). Or it comes from "jaba ila kadha" (he gathered toward such-and-such), so "ijtabaytu" (I gathered), like "jalaytu 'ala al-'arus fa-ijtalaytuha" (I displayed the bride and then unveiled her). The original meaning of the word is gathering, so the one chosen (al-mujtaba) is, as it were, originally one in whom the good qualities have been gathered until another chooses him and brings him near. In the use of the title of Lordship (al-Rububiyyah) together with its attribution to his pronoun, peace be upon him, there is added honour for him, peace be upon him.

﴿And He turned to him (fa-taba 'alayhi)﴾. That is, He returned to him with mercy and accepted his repentance when he repented, which was when he and his wife said: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers﴾.

﴿And guided him (wa-hada)﴾. That is, to steadfastness in repentance and holding fast to what pleases the Master, glorified and exalted is He. It is said that it means to the manner of repentance by teaching him the words. The "wa" (and) denotes mere joining, so it does no harm that this occurred before his repentance. It is also said: to prophethood and the carrying out of what it requires. Abu Hayyan gave this precedence over the other possibilities he mentioned. Al-Nisaburi explained "ijtiba" as choosing for the message, and took the verse as evidence that what occurred was before the mission (ba'tha).

He, glorified is He, did not explicitly attribute disobedience and misguidance to Hawwa' by ascribing them to the dual pronoun which refers to her and to Adam, peace be upon him, just as He attributed the eating and what followed to that (dual pronoun). This is to turn away from further censure of the Sanctuary, and because, in view of the course of the narrative, what is more important is to state explicitly what was attributed to Adam, peace be upon him. This also includes observing the rhyme of the verse endings (fawasil). Since the Majestic and Exalted did not explicitly mention her disobedience, He did not address her being guided to repentance or its acceptance from her.

Some have said: the Most High mentioned only the matter of Adam, peace be upon him, because Hawwa' follows him in the ruling, and for this reason the mention of women is omitted in most places of the Book and the Sunnah.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 123:**

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that answers an implied question), arising from the report that God dealt with him in the manner He did. It is as if it were said: "What did He command him after that?"

So it is said: He said to him and to his wife, ﴿Go down from it, all of you﴾, meaning: descend from the Garden to the earth, together. It is also said that the address is to him, peace be upon him, and to Iblis, may the curse be upon him, since he entered the Garden after it was said to him, "Get out of it, for you are accursed" (for the whispering). The address to the two of them, according to the first view, is by God's words ﴿some of you are enemies to others﴾, because they are the origin of the offspring and the source of the children. Thus the enmity, in reality, is between their children. This is the reverse of the address to the Jews and the attribution to them of what their fathers did. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: enemies to one another in the matter of livelihood and the desires of the souls.

According to the second view, it is clear, because of the manifest enmity between Adam, peace be upon him, and Iblis, may the curse be upon him, and likewise between the descendants of Adam, peace be upon him, and the descendants of the accursed one. From here it was said: the pronoun refers to Adam and his descendants and Iblis and his descendants.

Some claimed that it refers to Adam, Iblis and the serpent, but the preferred view is the first. This is supported by God's words ﴿But if there comes to you guidance from Me﴾ etc., meaning: a prophet He sends to you and a book He sends down to you. ﴿Whoever follows My guidance﴾: here the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun (*mudmar*, the pronoun), together with its attribution to His pronoun, the Exalted, to honour it and to emphasise the obligation of following it.

Al-Tabarani and others related from Abu al-Tufayl that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited ﴿whoever follows My guidance, he will not go astray﴾ in the world ﴿nor will he be distressed﴾ in the Hereafter. Some of them interpreted the guidance (*huda*) as the Qur'an, because Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim related it, and al-Hakim graded it sound (*sahih*). Also al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman*, through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: Allah the Exalted protects the follower of the Qur'an from going astray in the world or being distressed in the Hereafter, then he recited the verse. A group related from him, traced to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), with the wording: "Whoever follows the Book of Allah, Allah will guide him out of error in the world and protect him from the evil of the reckoning on the Day of Resurrection."

The generality of the term is outweighed by the contextual indicator (qarina) for it, which is His saying, ﴿And whoever turns away from My remembrance﴾, on the basis of interpreting the remembrance (dhikr) as the Qur'an. Likewise is His saying after it, ﴿Thus did Our signs come to you, but you forgot them﴾. The preferred view is the generality: the remembrance applies to the Qur'an and to all the divine books, and likewise the signs (ayat) mean evidences in general. The remembrance has also been interpreted here as guidance, because it is the cause of remembering Him, the Exalted, and worshipping Him, the Glorified. So the effect (musabbab) is mentioned and its cause (sabab) is intended, because they occur in opposition to each other. What is in the report (khabar) is a case of explicitly stating the ruling on the most noble of the individual instances that the generality indicates, out of concern for its importance.

Then, restricting ﴿he will not go astray﴾ to our saying "in this world" and ﴿nor will he be unhappy﴾ to our saying "in the Hereafter" is what the report requires.

Some scholars allowed the reverse: that is, ﴿he will not go astray﴾ means he will not lose the way to Paradise in the Hereafter, and ﴿nor will he toil over the matter of livelihood in this world.' They made the first correspond to ﴿and We will raise him on the Day of Resurrection blind﴾, and the second to ﴿for him is a constricted life﴾. Then he said: The mention of the state of the Hereafter before the state of this world, in the case of the guided, is because the aim of their outlook is the matter of their Hereafter, unlike the opposite case, where their outlook is confined to their worldly life. It is not hidden that what the traditions (athar) have affirmed is the first view, and some have said it is the most apparent. Indeed, what was mentioned is not free from good sense, even if it is said that it involves artificiality. The Imam allowed that both matters could be in the Hereafter, or both in this world. It has been mentioned that, on the latter, the intended meaning is: he will not go astray in the religion and will not be unhappy because of the religion, not absolutely. So if the one who follows the guidance encounters misery in this world, it is due to another cause, and that does no harm. End of quotation. What is relied upon is what you have heard.

The intended meaning of turning away from the remembrance is not following it. So it is as if it were said: and whoever does not follow, ﴿for him is a constricted life﴾, that is, narrow and severe. It is a verbal noun (masdar) of ḍanaka, and likewise ḍanākah. For this reason it is applied to the masculine and feminine, singular and dual and plural. Here it is applied to the feminine on the basis of the original form.

Al-Hasan read ﴿ḍankā﴾ with the feminine alif, like ﴿sakrā﴾, and with imala. This feminization is in view of its interpretation as a description. It is reported from Ibn Abbas that its tafsir is "severe in every respect," and he recited the poet's verse:

"The horses have overtaken us in a narrow pass,
Its sides are narrow, its front severe."

The more apparent view is that this livelihood is for him in this world. This was reported from ʿAṭāʾ and Ibn Jubayr. The reason for the narrowness of the livelihood of the disbeliever who turns away in this world is that he is greedy for this world, intensely eager to increase it, fearful of its decrease, and dominated by stinginess with it, since he has no aim other than it. This is unlike the believer who seeks the Hereafter. It has been said that ḍank is a metaphor for what has no good in it. Describing the disbeliever's livelihood in this way is because it is a burden upon him and an increase in his punishment on the Day of Resurrection, as the verses indicate. This is derived from what Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, that he said regarding the verse: "He says: every wealth I have given to a servant of Mine, whether little or much, if he does not fear Me regarding it, there is no good in it, and that is the ḍank in the livelihood."

It has been said: the meaning of its being ḍank is that it is a cause of ḍank on the Day of Resurrection, so describing it as ḍank is for emphasis, as if it were the very essence of ḍank. This is like what is said of a ruler: "death is between his lips," meaning by death what is a cause of death, such as an order to kill and the like. This is also indicated by what was reported from ʿIkrimah and Mālik ibn Dīnār.

Some said: that livelihood is for him in the grave, by being punished therein. A group reported this from Ibn Masʿud, Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, Abu Salih, al-Rabiʿ, al-Suddi and Mujahid. In al-Bahr, from Ibn Abbas, the verse was revealed concerning al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-Asad al-Makhzumi. The intended meaning is the squeezing of the grave, until his ribs interlock. This has also been reported as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in "Dhikr al-Mawt" transmitted it, as did al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Abu Yaʿla, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban and Ibn Mardawayh, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The believer in his grave is in a green garden, and his grave is made spacious for him seventy cubits, and it is illuminated until it is like the moon on the night of the full moon. Do you know what this verse was revealed about: ﴿for him is a constricted life﴾?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "It is the punishment of the disbeliever in his grave. There are imposed upon him ninety-nine tinnin. Do you know what the tinnin are? Ninety-nine serpents, each serpent having seven heads. They scratch him, they sting him, and they blow into his body until the Day they are raised."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Saʿid ibn Mansur, Musaddad in his Musnad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, al-Bayhaqi in "Kitab ʿAdhab al-Qabr," and a group, transmitted from Abu Saʿid, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said regarding His saying, ﴿a constricted livelihood﴾: it is the punishment of the grave." The wording of ʿAbd al-Razzaq is: "his grave is constricted for him until his ribs interlock." The wording of Ibn Abi Hatim is: "the squeezing of the grave," and other wordings.

As for the one who said: "this world is what is before the Greater Resurrection," he said: what occurs after death is an occurrence in this world, like what occurs before death.

Some said: it will be on the Day of Resurrection in Hell. Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted this from al-Hasan. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Zayd, who said: "The constricted livelihood is in the Fire: thorns, zaqqum, ghislin and dari'. There is no livelihood in the grave, nor in this world, and there is no livelihood or life except in the Hereafter." Perhaps the previous reports did not reach this speaker, or were not authentic according to him. You know that if they are authentic, there is no room to depart from what they indicate. And if they are not authentic, the better view is that it is in this world and not in the Hereafter, because of the apparent sense of His saying, ﴿and We will raise him﴾ etc., after the information that ﴿for him is a constricted livelihood﴾.

A group of reciters, among them Aban ibn Taghlib, read ﴿wa-naḥshuruhu﴾ with the letter ra' sukun (wa-naḥshurhu). This was explained as a lightening (takhfif), or as a jussive by coordination with the position (mahall) of ﴿fa-inna lahu﴾ etc., since it is the answer of the condition, as if it were said: "whoever turns away from My remembrance, there will be for him a constricted livelihood, and We will raise him" etc.

Ibn Khalawayh transmitted from Aban that he read ﴿wa-naḥshuruh﴾ with the ha' sukun, treating the connection as if it were a pause. In al-Bahr: the better explanation of this is according to the dialect of the Banu Kilab and ʿUqayl, for they make such a ha' quiescent. It has been read ﴿li-rabbihi la-kanūd﴾ with the ha' sukun.

A group read ﴿wa-yaḥshuruhu﴾ with the ya'. ﴿On the Day of Resurrection blind﴾. The apparent meaning is that it means one who has lost his sight, as in His saying, ﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, mute and deaf﴾.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 125:**

﴿He says﴾: this is a resumptive sentence (*istiʾnaf*), as has passed. ﴿My Lord, why have You raised me up blind, when I was seeing?﴾ That is, in the world, as is the apparent meaning. Perhaps this is with regard to most individuals of those who turned away, because among them are some who were born blind in the world. The apparent meaning is that this is a question about the cause that made him deserve being raised up blind, because he was ignorant, or thought that he had no sin that would make him deserve that.

Al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on Surah 20, verse 126:

Allah the Exalted says in His reply, ﴿Thus did Our signs come to you﴾. The kaf (ك) here is redundant (muqhamah), as in the saying "Someone like you does not withhold," and the demonstrative "that" (dhalika) refers to the verbal noun (masdar) of "came to you," meaning: like that wondrous coming, there came to you the clear and radiant signs. According to al-Zamakhshari, there is no redundancy; "that" refers to his being raised blind, meaning: like that act, you did it yourself. The words of the Exalted, ﴿came to you﴾ and so on, are an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "My Lord, what did I do?" It was said: "Our signs came to you ﴿but you forgot them﴾," meaning you abandoned them as one abandons what is forgotten and never mentioned at all. The intended meaning is "you became blind to them," but the cause was put in place of the effect, because whoever is blind to something has forgotten and abandoned it.

The demonstrative in the words of the Exalted, ﴿And thus﴾, refers to the forgetting implied by "you forgot them," and the kaf retains its literal sense: like that forgetting which you practised in the world, ﴿today you are forgotten﴾, meaning you are left in blindness as a fitting recompense. It was also said that the kaf here carries the sense of the causal lam (al-lam al-ajaliyyah), as has been said of the words of the Exalted, ﴿and remember Him as He has guided you﴾, meaning: and because of that forgetting proceeding from you, you are forgotten. This abandonment will last for as long as Allah wills, after which the blindness is removed from him, so he sees the terrors of the Resurrection and beholds the Fire, as the Exalted says, ﴿And the criminals will see the Fire and will think that they are going to fall into it﴾, the verse. This will be a punishment for him above punishment. Likewise, dumbness and deafness: Allah removes them from them, as the words of the Exalted indicate, ﴿How clearly will they hear and see on the Day they come to Us﴾.

In a report from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, the disbeliever is first raised seeing, then he becomes blind. The statement that he had been seeing is then a report about what he was like at the start of his resurrection. It is apparent that this blindness is also removed. From 'Ikrimah it is reported that he will see nothing but the Fire, and perhaps this too is for some portion of that day, for otherwise how would he read his book?

It is also reported from Mujahid, Muqatil, al-Dahhak and Abu Salih, and it is a report from Ibn 'Abbas too, that the meaning is: We will raise him on the Day of Resurrection blind to the proof, that is, he has no proof by which he can be guided. This is the meaning intended by those who say "blind of heart and insight." Ibrahim ibn 'Arafah chose this and said: whenever Allah the Exalted mentions blindness in His Book and censures it, what is meant is blindness of the heart. He the Exalted said: ﴿For indeed, it is not the eyes that are blinded, but the hearts that are within the breasts are blinded﴾. On this basis, the intended meaning of His words ﴿and I was seeing﴾ is: I was knowing of My proof, seeing it, pleading on my own behalf in the world. From this it becomes clear that the objection of Ibn 'Atiyyah is refuted, to those who take the blindness to mean blindness of insight, that if it were so the disbeliever would not feel it, since he was blind of insight in the world and died in that state. The answer to this is: I raised you blind of heart, unable to find the proof that would save you, because you abandoned My signs and My proofs in the world, and just as you abandoned them, you will remain in this blindness forever. It was also said: the intended meaning of "blind" is bewildered, not knowing what stratagems to employ to repel the punishment, like a blind man who is bewildered in warding off what he cannot see.

There is no evidence in the verse, as is imagined, for counting the forgetting of the Qur'an, or of a single verse of it, a major sin, as Imam al-Rafi'i held. The words of Imam al-Nawawi in al-Rawdah suggest that he chose this view, because the intended meaning of forgetting the signs, once they are taken to include the verses of the Qur'an, is abandoning them and not believing in them. As for one who counts forgetting any part of the Qur'an as a major sin, he means by "forgetting" its literal meaning. Yet Abu Shamah, the teacher of al-Nawawi, took a figurative sense and read "forgetting" in the hadiths that censure forgetting any part of the Qur'an as abandoning acting upon it. The verification of this matter is that forgetting in the first sense being a major sin, according to those who hold it, is conditional, as al-Jalal al-Bulqini, al-Zarkashi and others said, on its being due to laziness and negligence, such that it is sought from its place. Likewise, the verification of the state of the hadiths reported on this matter.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read ﴿a'mi﴾ with imalah in both places, because it is from the ones with a ya' (dhawat al-ya'). Abu 'Amr applied imalah only to the first occurrence, because it is suited to alteration by being the end of the verse and the place of pause.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 127:

﴿And thus﴾ i.e., and like that recompense, which corresponds to the transgression, ﴿We recompense him who transgresses﴾ by being immersed in the desires, ﴿and does not believe in the signs of his Lord﴾ — rather he denies them and turns away from them. What is intended is the comparison of the general recompense to the specific recompense. ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter﴾ — absolutely, or the punishment of the Fire — ﴿is more severe﴾ than the punishment of the former life, ﴿and more lasting﴾; i.e., it lasts longer than it, or it is more severe and more lasting than that and than the punishment of the grave, or than both of them, and than the gathering on blindness.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 128:

﴿Has it not guided them?﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), brought to confirm what precedes it, namely His words ﴿And thus do We recompense﴾ and what follows. The interrogative hamza (alif) is for reproachful denial (inkar tawbikhi), and the fa' is for coordination with an implied element that the context requires. The use of al-hidaya (guidance) with the preposition lam may be either because it has been placed in the position of an intransitive verb, so no object is needed, or because it means "to make clear" (al-tabyin), in which case the second object is omitted. In either case, the subject is the pronoun for God, and the pronoun in (lahum) refers to the polytheists who were contemporaries of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The meaning is: they were heedless, so God did not provide them with guidance, or He, mighty and majestic, did not make the lessons clear to them.

His words, ﴿How many generations did We destroy before them?﴾, are either an explanation of that guidance by way of iltifat (a shift in grammatical person or address), or serve as an elaboration of the omitted object. It has been said that the subject of (yahdi) is a pronoun for the Prophet (ﷺ). It has also been said that it is a pronoun for the destruction understood from His words ﴿How many did We destroy﴾, and the clause explains it. It has further been said that the subject is omitted, meaning reflection and consideration, and this is attributed to al-Mubarrad. But this involves omitting the subject, which the Basrans (Basriyyun) do not permit. al-Zamakhshari said that the subject is the clause ﴿How many did We destroy﴾ and so on. Making a clause the subject is the view of the Kufans (Kufiyyun), while the majority (al-Jumhur) disagree, but this view is preferred here because what follows gives the reason and requires it. It is also preferred that the subject is the pronoun for God, exalted is His state, because a group of reciters, including Ibn 'Abbas and al-Sulami, read (afa-lam nahdi) with the letter nun. Some scholars chose, over this reading, that the verb is placed in the position of an intransitive verb, and that the clause ﴿How many did We destroy﴾ explains that guidance. Others held that it is transitive, and its object is the content of the clause, meaning: has God not made clear to them the content of this statement? It has also been said that the clause fills the place of the object and the verb is suspended from it (mu'allaq). This was objected to on the ground that (kam) here is khabariyya (declarative), and declarative kam does not suspend the verb from its operation. Rather, it is the interrogative kam that does so, as Abu Hayyan stated explicitly in al-Bahr. But you know that when the basis of suspension is the initial position (al-sadara), as is apparent, Ibn Hisham has stated that both interrogative kam and declarative kam have this property. In al-Mughni there is the statement of Ibn 'Usfur that (kam) in the verse is the subject of (yahdi) because it holds the initial position. He then said: his claim that this came in a poor dialect, which al-Akhfash reported from some people, who say "malaktu kam 'abid" (I owned how many slaves), and that this removes it from the initial position, is a great error, since he has made the speech of God exalted be His state conform to this dialect, end quote. This clearly shows that he holds that (kam) here is declarative and has the initial position. Yes, al-Hufi reported from some scholars that they rejected the view that it is the subject, on the ground that it is interrogative and what precedes it does not operate on it. But the apparent view is that it is declarative, and it is the object placed before (ahlakna), and ﴿from the generations﴾ is attached to an implied element that functions as an adjective for its specifier, meaning: how many generations that existed among the generations.

﴿walking in their dwellings﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) either from (the generations) or from the object of (ahlakna), meaning: We destroyed them while they were in a state of security and moving freely in their homes. Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr preferred that it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (lahum), emphasising the denial, with (yahdi) as the governing element, meaning: has it not guided the polytheists while they were walking in the dwellings of those whom We destroyed from the earlier generations, from the people of al-Hijr, Thamud and the people of Lut, observing the traces of their destruction when they travelled to al-Sham and elsewhere? Some have supposed that the clause is in the position of an adjective for (the generations), but this is not so. Ibn al-Sumayfa read (yumashshun) with the doubled letter and the passive form, meaning they are enabled to walk.

﴿Indeed in that﴾ is a causal explanation of the denial and an affirmation of the guidance, despite their failure to be guided. (That) refers to the content of His words ﴿How many did We destroy﴾ and so on, and the sense of distance in it indicates the high rank of that matter and the exalted status of its kind.

﴿are signs﴾, many, great, and clearly indicative of the truth. It is permissible that the word (fi) is tajridiyya (abstractive, expressing the intensity of the quality in the thing itself), as has been said regarding His words ﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of God you have a good example﴾ (Q 33:21).

﴿for people of intellect (ulu al-nuha)﴾, that is, for those of sound reason who restrain themselves from ugly acts. Among the worst of these is what these deniers engage in: disbelief in the signs of God, feigned blindness to them, and other kinds of disobedience.

﴿Had it not been for a word that had already gone forth from your Lord﴾: this is a resumed statement, brought to explain the wisdom behind the non-occurrence of what His words ﴿Has it not become clear to them﴾ and what follows suggest, namely that they would be struck with the like of what befell the destroyed generations before them. The "word that had already gone forth" is the promise to delay the wholesale annihilating punishment (ʿadhāb al-istiʾṣāl) from this nation. This is either out of honour for the Prophet (ﷺ), as is suggested by the mention of the title of Lordship (al-Rubūbiyyah) together with its attachment to his pronoun (ﷺ), in His words ﴿Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾; or because among their descendants there will be one who believes; or for another wisdom which Allah, exalted is He, knows best. That is: had it not been for the word that had already gone forth and the promise to delay the punishment, ﴿the punishment would have been⦅ that is, the retribution for their crimes⦆ ⦅lizām⦆⦅ meaning binding⦆⦅ upon these disbelievers, such that it would not be delayed from their crimes even for an hour, from the time the like of what descended upon their counterparts of the earlier generations became binding.⦆ The word lizām (binding) is either a masdar (verbal noun) of the form of khiṣām (mutual dispute), used as a description for the sake of emphasis, or an ism al-āla (noun of instrument) like ḥizām (belt) and rikāb (stirrup), and its use as a description is also for emphasis, like laziz khaṣm (an adversary who presses his opponent). Abū al-Baqāʾ permitted that it be the plural of lāzim (binding), like qiyām as the plural of qāʾim (standing), though this is contrary to the apparent meaning.

﴿And a term appointed⦆ is conjoined to ﴿a word⦆, as Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Qatādah and al-Suddī. That is: had it not been for the promise to delay their punishment and the appointed term for their lives, their punishment would not have been delayed at all. Its separation from what it is conjoined to is for the sake of hastening to explain the answer of lawlā (had it not been), and to indicate that each of the two is independently sufficient in negating the necessity of the punishment, as well as observing the rhyme endings of the noble verses. It has also been said: that is, had it not been for an appointed term for their punishment, which is the Day of Resurrection.

This was objected to on the grounds that the term would then coincide with the previously mentioned word, so it is not correct to include the independence of each of them through negation among the subtleties of the separation.

It was answered that it does not follow from the delay of the punishment beyond this world that it must have a time which it cannot be delayed beyond or fail to meet; so there is no obstacle to independence.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Mujāhid that the appointed term is the word that had gone forth. It has also been said: the appointed term for the punishment is the Day of Badr. This was objected to on the grounds that it contradicts the word being the promise to delay the punishment of this nation. It was answered that what is meant by that punishment is the annihilating punishment, and it did not occur on the Day of Badr.

Al-Zamakhsharī permitted that the conjunction be to the pronoun concealed in kāna (was), which refers to the immediate seizure (al-akhdh al-ʿājil) understood from the context, treating the separation by the predicate as equivalent to emphasis. That is: the immediate seizure and the appointed term would have been binding upon them, as was the custom of ʿĀd, Thamūd and their counterparts. The appointed term did not stand alone apart from the immediate seizure. But you know that this is not feasible if lizām is an ism al-āla (noun of instrument), because the dual would then be required for binding in that case.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 20, verse 130:**

﴿So be patient over what they say.﴾ That is: if the matter is as has been mentioned, namely that the delay of their punishment is not neglect but respite, and that it is certainly bound to befall them, then ﴿be patient over what they say﴾ of the words of disbelief. His knowledge ﷺ that they will certainly be punished consoles him and moves him to patience. What is meant by it is not being agitated, not abandoning fighting, so that the verse would be abrogated (mansukhah, i.e., its ruling superseded by a later one).

﴿And glorify﴾, being engaged ﴿in praise of your Lord﴾. That is: pray while you are praising your Lord, Mighty and Majestic, who brings you to perfections through His guidance and His enabling, glorified is He. ﴿Before the rising of the sun﴾, that is, the dawn prayer, ﴿and before its setting﴾, that is, the sunset prayer. The apparent view is that the adverbial phrase is connected to ﴿sabbih﴾.

It has been transmitted that the explanation of glorifying at these two times is what al-Tabarani, Ibn 'Asakir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Jarir, traced back to the Prophet ﷺ.

al-Hakim reported that the Prophet, peace be upon him, said to Fadalah ibn Wahb al-Laythi: "Guard the two 'asr prayers." He asked: "And what are the two 'asrs?" He said: "A prayer before the rising of the sun and a prayer before its setting."

It has also been said that what is meant by glorifying before its setting is the noon and afternoon prayers, because the time of each of them is before sunset and after its decline, and that they are gathered together for the sake of the correspondence with His words, Exalted is He, ﴿before the rising of the sun﴾. But you know that "before the setting," although in its lexical meaning it is true of the time of noon and the time of afternoon, the common usage of it is the time of the afternoon.

As for His words, Exalted is He, ﴿and during the hours of the night﴾, that is, from its hours. It is the plural of *inyun* and *inwun* with a *ya* or *waw* and a kasra on the hamza, and *inna* with a kasra and short vowel, and *ānā'* (آناء) with a fatha and a long vowel. The last is not as well known as the first three. It was mentioned by trustworthy exegetes. Al-Raghib said in his *Mufradat*:

God Exalted said: ﴿not waiting for its time (inah)﴾, meaning its time. *Al-inah*, when its first letter is kasrah, is shortened, and when it is fathah it is lengthened, as in the words of al-Hutay'ah:

*"I delayed the 'isha prayer until Suhayl or al-Shi'ra, so the delay (al-ina') lengthened for me."*

Then he said: It is said *ana'tu al-shay'* (I delayed the thing), meaning I put it after its time, and *yana'tu* (I was late). In *al-Misbah*: *ananahu* with fatha and lengthening means I delayed it, and the noun is *anā'* on the pattern of *salām*.

It has been said that it is in the accusative as an adverb of time governed by an implied verb. His words, glorified is He, ﴿fa-sabbih﴾ are conjoined to it, meaning: stand during some hours of the night and then glorify. This, as you see, is [weak]. It has also been said that it is in the accusative governed by *sabbih*, on the pattern of ﴿and fear Me﴾, and the *fa'* is conjunctive according to the first view and explanatory according to the second. It has also been said that it is an object of (*fa-sabbih*), and the *fa'* is superfluous, its benefit being to indicate the necessity of what follows for what precedes.

Al-Khafaji mentioned that it is an object of what was mentioned, without any need for claiming the *fa'* is superfluous, because it does not prevent the governing of what follows over what precedes, as the grammarians have stated explicitly. What is meant by glorifying during some hours of the night is the sunset prayer and the night prayer. Because of the importance of these two, the command was not restricted to their performance by the preceding verb, by conjoining (*min ana'i al-layl*) to one of the two preceding adverbs without mentioning *fa-sabbih*. And because of the importance of the hours of the night and their distinction over all other times by special and general qualities, their mention was put before the command and they were not treated in the same manner as what came before.

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿and the extremities of the day﴾ are conjoined to the position of His words, glorified is He, (*min ana'i al-layl*). It has also been said that they are conjoined to His words, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿before the rising﴾. What is meant by glorifying the extremities of the day, according to what Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and others reported from Qatadah, is the noon prayer, and al-Jubba'i chose this. The reason for applying "extremity" (*taraf*) to its time is that it is the end of the first half of the day and the beginning of the last half of it. The plural is used in view of the two halves, or because the definite article on "day" is for the genus, which includes every day, so the plural is in view of the multiplicity of days, and each has an extremity, so it has been said.

It was objected to this that the beginning and the end in it are not on one and the same footing, because its being an end is in view of the fact that the first half ends at it, and it is outside of it; and its being a beginning is in view of the fact that the second half begins from it, and it is inside it. There is no doubt about the remoteness of the plural being in accordance with this consideration. Moreover, it must be said that the least of the plural is two. Also, applying "extremity" to the extremity of one of its halves is a strain, for it is not an extremity of it but of its half.

It has also been said that this is a repetition of the dawn and sunset prayers, to indicate that these two are specially distinguished by additional excellence. What is meant by the day is what lies between sunrise and sunset, and by the extremity is what adjoins the beginning and the end of a thing. The use of the plural form, although what is meant is two, is not confusing, since the day has only two extremities. A parallel is the words of al-'Ajjaj:

*"And two wastelands, two rough tracts, twice, whose backs are like the backs of two shields."*

The preferred view is the harmony with *ana'i al-layl*. This was chosen by those who included noon among what comes before sunset. And it is objected that the extremity is literally what a thing ends with, and it is part of it, and it is also applied to its beginning and end. Applying it to the adjacent [part] mentioned is not literal. The answer is that it is permissible and common, even if not literal. It was also allowed that it is a repetition of the dawn and afternoon prayers, with the day meaning what lies between the break of dawn and sunset, and the first extremity and the second according to custom. If the day is taken to mean what lies between sunrise and sunset, this supposition becomes remote, since the two extremities are then not on one and the same footing.

It has also been said that this is a command to supererogatory prayer in the last hours of the day. But in this there is a diversion of the command from its apparent meaning, and furthermore, that the last hours of the day are a time for supererogatory prayer involves a discussion that is not hidden from the jurist.

Abu Hayyan said: The apparent meaning of His words, Exalted is He, ﴿and glorify with the praise of your Lord﴾ is a command to glorify joined with praise. In that case, either the wording is intended, i.e., say "Glory be to God and praise be to God," or the meaning is intended, i.e., declare Him, glorified is He, free from imperfection and praise Him with what is beautiful.

In a report mentioned by Ibn 'Atiyyah: "Whoever glorifies seventy times at the setting of the sun, his sins set with it."

Abu Muslim said: It is not remote to take that as declaring Him free of imperfection and exalting Him, and the meaning is: he occupied himself with declaring God Exalted free of imperfection at these times. Al-'Izz ibn 'Abd al-Salam also took it this way, and made the *ba'* in His words, glorified is He, ﴿with the praise of your Lord﴾ instrumental. He said: This is to specify the negation of attributes of deficiency, because whoever negates something has affirmed its opposite, and the opposites of attributes of deficiency are attributes of perfection. So whoever declares Him glorified free of imperfection has affirmed attributes of perfection.

It was also allowed, regarding the annexation of praise to the Lord, that it be an annexation of a verbal noun to its subject, or of a verbal noun to its object, or an annexation of specification in which "praise" means "praises." Then the first was considered better, because true and complete praise is that by which God Exalted praised Himself. The most evident reading is that the *ba'* indicates accompaniment and the annexation is of a verbal noun to its object.

Al-Imam [al-Razi] preferred taking glorification as declaring Him free from association, and said: It is closer to the apparent meaning and to what was mentioned before, because He, glorified is He, first commanded him to be patient over what they say of denial and the manifestation of disbelief and association. What suits that is to be commanded to declare Him, Exalted, free from what they say, so that he would be manifesting that and calling to it. It was objected that in that case there is no reason to single out these times for mention. The answer was that their mention is meant to indicate constancy, as in His words, Exalted is He, (*bil-ghadati wal-'ashiyy*, "in the mornings and the evenings"), together with the fact that some times have a distinction for a matter known only to God Exalted. It was rejected that the partitive *min* in His words, glorified is He, (*min ana'i al-layl*) rules this out, and that this indication is sufficiently conveyed by saying "before the rising of the sun and after it," since it includes the night and the day. So the addition indicates that the intended thing is the particularity of the time. It is not hidden that His words, glorified is He, (*min ana'i al-layl*) are connected to the second *sabbih*, so the first should be for generality and the second for specifying a part for its importance. Yes, it may be objected that declaring Him free of association has no sense in being specified, unless by it is meant the saying "Glory be to God" intended as declaring Him free of association.

It was said: It is permissible that what is meant by glorification is its apparent meaning, and what is meant by praise is the prayer, and the adverbial phrase is connected to it, so the wisdom of the specification becomes evident. So it is in the Shihabi glosses.

What al-Imam said has been opposed on the ground that the more suitable thing, given the command to patience, is the command to prayer, so that it would be a guidance to what His words, Exalted is He, ﴿and seek help through patience and prayer﴾ contain. Also, the command that follows fits better with taking the command to glorify as a command to prayer, and you know that the reports demand this.

Then it is permissible that by "extremity" is meant a portion of a thing, for this is one of its meanings, as in the *Sihah* and the *Qamus*. And if the definite article on "day" is for the genus according to this, the discussion about what was reported from Qatadah no longer remains as it was. So reflect.

﴿So that you may be pleased﴾. It has been said that it is connected to *sabbih*, that is, glorify during these times in the hope that you will obtain from Him, Exalted, what will please your soul of reward. It has been used as evidence against the obligation upon God Exalted. It was also allowed that it is connected to the command to patience and the command to prayer, and that what is meant by ﴿so that you may be pleased﴾ is in this world, by attaining victory and the spread of the matter of the call, and the like.

Abu Hayyah, Talhah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr, Aban, 'Isma, Abu 'Imarah from Hafs, Abu Zayd from al-Mufaddal, Abu 'Ubayd and Muhammad ibn 'Isa al-Isfahani read *turḍā* (تُرْضى) in the passive form from *arḍā*, meaning: your Lord will make you pleased.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 131:

﴿And do not strain your eyes﴾, i.e., do not prolong your gaze with a look of desire and inclination, ﴿toward that which We have given enjoyment to﴾ of the adornments of the world, such as children, wealth, dwellings, clothing and food, ﴿as pairs among them﴾, i.e., kinds of the disbelievers. The phrase ﴿as pairs among them﴾ is the object of "We have given enjoyment," and the prepositional phrase (bihi) has been placed before it for the sake of emphasis; "min" here is explanatory (bayaniyyah). It has been permitted that it be a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the pronoun in "bihi," and that "min" be partitive (tab'idiyyah), either the object of "We have given enjoyment," or related to an omitted element that functions as a qualifier of its omitted object; i.e., "do not strain your eyes toward that which We have given enjoyment to, and it is kinds and types, some of them or some of them being from among them."

According to what has been said, the intended meaning is: persist in leaving that. It has also been said that the address is to him (ﷺ) while the intended meaning is his community, because he (ﷺ) was the furthest of anything from prolonging his gaze at the adornment and ornaments of the world, and the most attached to what is with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, of anyone. And he (ﷺ) is the one who said: ("The world is cursed, and cursed is what is in it, except what is sought by it the face of Allah, the Exalted.")

He (ﷺ) was strict in forbidding being deceived by the world and gazing at its ornaments. The speech is either by omission of a modifier, or it is a figurative attribution in the relation. In the shift from "do not look at what We have given enjoyment to..." etc. to what is in the noble composition, there is an indication that a gaze that is not prolonged is forgiven. What is actually forbidden is admiration for that, desire for it, and inclination toward it. However, some of the God-fearing went to extremes in lowering the gaze from that, to the point that they did not look at the buildings of the oppressors or the number of the wicked in clothing, mounts and other things. That is for a distant purpose: they adopted these things for the eyes of onlookers and for pride in them, so looking at them would achieve their aim and be like an incitement to them to adopt them.

﴿the splendor of the life of this world﴾, i.e., its adornment and its brightness. It is in the accusative governed by an omitted element indicated by "We have given enjoyment," i.e., "We made for them a splendor," or by "We have given enjoyment" as a second object because it is implicitly containing the meaning of "We gave." Or it is a substitute (badal) from the place of "bihi." Ibn al-Hajib criticized this in his Amali, because substituting an accusative for the place of a prepositional phrase is weak, as in "I passed by Zayd, your brother," and because substitution from the resumptive pronoun is disputed. Similar to this is what has been said: that it is a substitute from "ma" (the relative pronoun), because of the separation by the substitute between the relative clause and its complement. Or it is a substitute from "azwajan," with an omitted modifier, i.e., "those possessing" or "the people of" splendor. It has also been said without any omission, with "azwajan" as a circumstantial accusative in the sense of "kinds of enjoyments," or by making them the very splendor for emphasis. This was criticized on the ground that such a thing applies to the qualifier, not to the substitute, since it resembles a substitution due to error in that case; or it is a specifier (tamyiz) for "ma" or for the pronoun in "bihi." It is related from al-Farra' that it is a qualifier of "azwajan," but this was refuted because the specifier is definite and the qualifier of an indefinite noun is definite. It has also been said: it is a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in "bihi" or from "ma," and the nunation was dropped because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters, and "al-hayah" is in the genitive as a substitute from "ma." This was chosen by Makki, and what is wrong with it is not hidden. It has also been said: it is accusative by way of dispraise, i.e., "I dispraise the splendor of..." This was objected to on the ground that the context rejects it, since the intended meaning is that souls are naturally inclined to look at it and desire it, and belittling it does not suit that. This was answered: in the attribution of "splendor" to "the life of this world" there is every dispraise, and what was mentioned of desire is from the appetite of the foolish souls that were deprived of the light of success.

Al-Hasan, Abu Haywah, Talhah, Humayd, Sallam, Ya'qub, Sahl, 'Isa and al-Zuhri read ﴿zahrata﴾ with a fatha on the ha', and it is a dialect like "al-jahrah" for "al-jahrah" (open). In al-Muhtasib by Ibn Jinni, the position of our companions regarding every guttural letter that is unvocalized after a fatha is that it is not vowelled except as a dialect, like "nahar" and "nahr," "sha'ar" and "sha'r." The position of the Kufans is that vowelling the second is regular because it is a guttural letter, even if not heard, unless some barrier prevents it, as in the word "nahw," because if it were vowelled the waw would change into an alif. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that "zahrah" with vowelling is a plural of "zahir," like "kafir" and "kafarah," and it is a qualifier of "azwajan," i.e., pairs from among the disbelievers who shine with the life of this world, because of the purity of their complexions from what they amuse themselves with and enjoy, and the brightening of their faces and the splendor of their dress, unlike what the believers and the righteous have of pallor of complexion and austerity in clothing. On this basis it was also permitted that it be a circumstantial accusative, because its genitive attachment is verbal.

You know that what is apparent from this description is the intention of permanence, not occurrence, so its attachment is not verbal. Moreover, the meaning under the circumstantial reading is not that good.

﴿so that We may test them therein﴾ is connected to "We have given enjoyment," i.e., so that We may treat them as one who tests and examines them by it, or so that We may punish them in the Hereafter because of it. In it there is a warning against that by explaining its bad outcome in its end, as opposed to its brightness in its present state. Al-Asma'i, from 'Asim, read ﴿linuftinahum﴾ with a damma on the nun, from "aftana," if he made the trial occur in it, as Abu Hayyan said.

﴿And the provision of your Lord﴾, i.e., what He has stored up for you in the Hereafter, or what He has provided you in this world of prophethood and guidance. The owner of al-Kashf claimed that it is more fitting to this context. Or what He has stored up for you in it of the conquest of lands and spoils. It has been said: contentment. ﴿is better﴾ than what these have been given enjoyment with, because it, along with being in itself among the most precious things that competitors compete for, is secure from harm, unlike what they have been given enjoyment with. ﴿and more lasting﴾, for it, itself or its effect, hardly ever ceases, unlike what they have been given enjoyment with.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 132:

﴿And enjoin your family to prayer (al-salah)﴾. He (ﷺ) was commanded to order his family to pray after he himself had been commanded to pray, so that they would help one another in seeking relief from their need, and would not be preoccupied with the matter of livelihood or look to the wealthy. By "his family" (ﷺ) is meant, it is said, his wives, his daughters, and his son-in-law ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with them. It is also said that it includes them and all the believers of the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib. It is also said that it means all who follow him (ﷺ) from among his community. It was inferred (istazhara) that what is meant is the people of his household (ﷺ), and this is supported by what Ibn Mardawayh, Ibn ʿAsakir and Ibn al-Najjar narrated from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, who said: "When the verse ﴿And enjoin your family﴾ and so on was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would come to the door of ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his countenance, at the time of the dawn prayer for eight months, saying: 'The prayer, may Allah have mercy upon you. ﴿Allah only intends to remove from you the impurity, O people of the household, and to purify you thoroughly﴾'." The Imamiyyah (Twelver Shiʿa) narrated something similar through many chains.

The apparent meaning is that by "the prayer" is meant the obligatory prayers, and a child is to be commanded to perform them even though they are not obligatory upon him, so that he becomes accustomed to them. Abu Dawud narrated with a sound chain (isnad hasan), traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Command your children to pray when they are seven years old, and strike them for it when they are ten years old, and separate them in their beds."

﴿And be steadfast in it﴾, that is, persist in it. Here "steadfastness" (al-sabr) is a metonymy (majaz mursal) for persistence (al-mudawamah), since the latter is a necessary implication of its meaning. This contains an indication that worship, in observing it with its full observance, is a hardship upon the self. The address is general, encompassing the family even though it takes the form of a specific address, and likewise what follows. There is no concealing the indication of elevated rank for him (ﷺ) in the expression by glorification (al-tasbih) first and by prayer (al-salah) second, together with directing the address of persistence to him (ﷺ). And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We do not ask you for provision; We provide for you﴾ is a removal of what may occur to someone's mind, namely that persistence in prayer might harm the matter of livelihood. It is as if it were said: persist in prayer without being preoccupied with the matter of livelihood to the neglect of it, since We do not burden you with the provision of your own selves, as We are the ones who provide for you. The placement of the predicate's subject first (al-musnad ilayhi) is for exclusivity (lil-ikhtisas) or to convey strengthening (li-ifadat al-taqwa).

Some claimed that the address is specific and so is the ruling, for if it were general, every Muslim would be granted leave to persist in prayer and abandon earning a living, and that is not the case. In reply: at most, what generality entails, whether the family is specific or general to all believers, is that the one who prays be given leave to abandon earning that prevents prayer. But what preventing is there from that? Rather, abandoning earning in order to perform the obligatory prayer is an obligation. What is meant by persistence in it is nothing other than performing it constantly at its appointed times, not spending the night and day entirely in it. The one making this claim thought that by "the prayer" is meant what includes the obligatory and other prayers, and by persistence in it is performing it constantly in a manner that prevents earning a living. That is not the case. From what we have mentioned it is known that there is no need, in refuting what that claimant said, to restrict the generality to the Prophet's address to his family only, excluding all people, as is not hidden. Yes, it may be inferred from the verse that prayer in general is a cause for the abundance of provision and the removal of distress, and the reports that have come concerning this are to be understood accordingly. Abu ʿUbayd, Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, Abu Nuʿaym in al-Hilyah, and al-Bayhaqi in Shuʿab al-Iman narrated with a sound chain from ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam, who said: ("The Prophet (ﷺ), whenever hardship or constraint befell his family, would command them to pray, and he recited: 'And enjoin your family to prayer'.")

Ahmad in al-Zuhd and others narrated from Thabit, who said: ("The Prophet (ﷺ), whenever his family suffered want, would call to his family: 'Pray! Pray!'")

Thabit said: "The prophets, peace be upon them, whenever a matter befell them, would turn to prayer."

Malik and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Aslam, who said: "ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab would pray during the night as much as Allah willed for him to pray. When it was the last part of the night, he would wake his family for prayer, saying to them: 'The prayer, the prayer!' and reciting this verse: ﴿And enjoin your family﴾ and so on." It is permissible, owing to the apparent meaning of the reports, that by "the prayer" is meant prayer in its general sense, so consider this carefully.

Ibn Wththab and a group read ("narzuquka") with the assimilation (idgham) of the qaf into the kaf, and this is also reported from Yaʿqub. ("And the final outcome") (al-ʿaqibah) is the praiseworthy end, which is more general than Paradise and other things, though al-Suddi interpreted it as Paradise. ﴿Is for righteousness﴾, that is, for its people, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ("And the final outcome is for the God-fearing"). Even if the implied noun were not supposed, the sense would still be sound. In what has been mentioned there is an alert that the essence of the matter is righteousness (taqwa).

[Page 285]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 20, verse 133:

﴿And they say: "Why does he not bring us a sign from his Lord?"﴾ This is a report of some of their false statements, concerning which the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to be patient. That is: "Why does he not bring us a sign that proves his truthfulness in his claim to prophethood, or one of the signs that they proposed, not specifically any one of them?" They reached such a degree of obstinacy and stubbornness that they did not count what they had witnessed of miracles, before which the solid mountains would crumble, as among the signs, until they dared to utter this monstrous and shameful statement.

And His Exalted saying, ﴿Has there not come to them the clear proof of what is in the former scriptures?﴾ is a rebuttal from Him, Exalted is He, of their abominable saying, and a denial of what they concealed beneath it, namely their denial that a sign has come, by the coming of the Noble Qur'an, which is the mother of signs, the foundation of miracles, and the highest and most beneficial of them. This is because the reality of a miracle is an extraordinary matter that breaks habit and appears at the hand of one who claims prophethood at the time of challenge, whatever it may be, and there is no doubt that knowledge is the most noble and most exalted of matters, since it is the root of deeds and the origin of actions, and through it the lofty ranks and everlasting happiness are attained. Indeed, it appeared, while he possessed all the sciences of the former and latter peoples, at the hand of one who had not practised any of the sciences and had not studied with anyone of their people at all. So what miracle is sought after his coming, and what sign is demanded after his arrival? Therefore, by "the clear proof" is meant the Noble Qur'an, and by "the former scriptures" is meant the Torah, the Gospel, and all the other heavenly books, and what they contain of sound beliefs and the fundamental rulings upon which all the Messengers, peace be upon them, agreed. The meaning of it being a clear proof of that is that it is a witness to their truth. In presenting it under this title there is evident honouring of its status and illumination of its proof, as it points to its distinction and its sufficiency, as a witness to the truth of what it contains, through its inimitability. The attribution of the coming to it, while they made it something brought, is to draw attention to its originality in this, along with what there is of suitability to "clear proof." The hamzah is for denying that it occurred, and the waw is for conjunction with an implied element required by the context, as if it were said: "Did not there come to them all the other signs, and did there not come to them specifically the clear proof of what is in the former scriptures," affirming its coming and announcing that it is so manifest that no denial could be made from them at all, even if they dared to deny all the other signs out of obstinacy and stubbornness. Interpreting the verse in the manner mentioned is what the eloquence of the revelation requires.

Al-Imam [al-Razi] and al-Tabarsi asserted that the meaning is: "Has there not come to them in the Qur'an an explanation of what is in the earlier books of the accounts of the nations whom We destroyed when they proposed signs and then disbelieved in them? So what assures them that their situation in asking for a sign with their saying, ﴿Why does He not bring us a sign?﴾ will not be like the situation of those destroyed ones?" End quote. And this is far from acceptable, as is not hidden from people of intellect. Most of the Seven Readers, and Abu Bahriyyah, Ibn Muhaysin, Talhah, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Manadhir, Khalaf, Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Sa'dan, Ibn 'Isa, and Ibn Jubayr al-Antaki, read ﴿يَأْتِهِمْ﴾ (ya'tihim) with the yā’ (third person masculine), because the word "sign" is feminine metaphorically and the verb is separated from it.

A group among them, Abu Zayd on the authority of Abu 'Amr, read ﴿بَيِّنَةُ﴾ (bayyinatu) with nunation, on the basis that "mā" is in apposition (badal). The author of al-Lawami' said: "It is possible that 'mā' in this reading is negative, meaning by 'the coming' what is in the Qur'an of the abrogating and the excellence not found in other books," and this is as you see. A group read ﴿بَيِّنَةً﴾ with a fatha and nunation, taking it as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), with "mā" as the subject. A group, including Ibn 'Abbas, read ﴿الصُّحْفِ﴾ (al-ṣuḥfi) with a sukun on the ḥā’ for lightness.
